The concept of integrated function of multiple body systems will be developed in each region. A strong focus on functional anatomy and on applying anatomy to a living body will prepare students for using this knowledge in a professional context.
learning_outcomes: Identify musculoskeletal structures through surface anatomy.
Describe normal structure and function of the central nervous system including neural pathways for sensation and motor control.

Describe normal structure and function of the musculoskeletal and nervous systems within the upper limb, lower limb, and trunk (vertebral column, and the thorax in relation to mechanisms of respiration).
Analyse movements and exercises in terms of muscle activation and function, and joint range of motion.

Apply observational and communication skills, using appropriate anatomical and lay terminology for use with clients or other health care professionals, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, the living body or medical imaging.

title: INSPECT AND MONITOR CULTURALLY SIGNIFICANT PLACES
syllabus_overview: Students will learn the skills and knowledge required to inspect and monitor the fabric and setting of heritage or culturally significant places in order to identify non-conformities with site records and conservation and management plans.
learning_outcomes: Prepare for inspection.
Monitor stakeholder views on significance.
Monitor cultural area and surrounds.
Carry out comprehensive inspection.
Submit report and recommendations.

title: ANATOMY FOR PHYSIOTHERAPY B
syllabus_overview: In this subject, the anatomical principles and terminology introduced in ANA1003 will be applied to the detailed anatomical study of the upper limb and back, as relevant to physiotherapy. Teaching will include both online learning and face-to-face teaching sessions including practical classes involving cadaver materials and clinical anatomy. You will be required to work together in small groups, to take responsibility for your own learning and understanding of anatomy so that you are able to identify anatomical structure and function on a living body as you would in a clinical physiotherapy context.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the vertebral column, including its role in support and posture.
Apply foundational biomechanical principles, including the concepts of force, motion and leverage, to analyse human movement within the upper limb and trunk.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the upper limb, including its role in support, posture and grasp.
Identify musculoskeletal structures of the upper limb and trunk through surface anatomy.

Apply observational and communication skills, individually or as part of a team, using appropriate anatomical and lay terminology for use with clients or other health care professionals, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, anatomical models, the living body or medical imaging.

title: ANATOMY OF THE TRUNK WALL & UPPER LIMB
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will gain knowledge in the anatomical principles of the regional anatomy of the trunk wall and upper limb. Topic material will be presented face-to-face and online through lectures, video clips and worksheets, but you will be responsible for your own learning through supported practical activities, including the examination of appropriate cadaver materials. Emphasis is placed on the application of anatomical principles to reinforce how structure relates to function.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of anatomical principles to describe the normal structure and function of the body systems.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to analyse normal development, structure, and function of body systems within the upper limb, including its role in manipulation and posture.

Apply observational and communication skills, including appropriate medical terminology, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, the living body or medical imaging in a laboratory environment.
Interpret pathology based on sound understanding of systemic, structural, functional and developmental anatomical principles.

title: ANATOMY FOR PHYSIOTHERAPY C
syllabus_overview: In this subject, the anatomical principles and terminology introduced in ANA1003 and expanded on in ANA1004 will be applied to the detailed anatomical study of the head and neck, thorax and abdominopelvic regions, and to the study of neurosciences, as relevant to physiotherapy. Teaching will include both online learning and face-to-face teaching sessions including practical classes involving cadaver materials and clinical anatomy. You will be required to work together in small groups, to take responsibility for your own learning and understanding of anatomy so that you are able to identify anatomical structure and function on a living body as you would in a clinical physiotherapy context.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the thorax and abdominopelvic regions, including their role in housing visceral structures and their function in breathing.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of the central nervous system, including neural pathways for sensation and movement.

Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the head and neck, thorax and abdomen, including their role in housing visceral structures, special sense organs and the central nervous system.

Apply observational and communication skills, both individually and as part of a team, using appropriate anatomical and lay terminology for use with clients or other health care professionals, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, anatomical models, the living body or medical imaging.

title: ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY 2
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to human anatomy and physiology – the structure and function of body systems. This will provide the foundation for the study of the major body systems important for protection (integumentary system); fluids and transport (cardiovascular and lymphatic systems); environmental exchange (respiratory and renal systems); and the continuity of life (reproductive systems).
learning_outcomes: Explain the function of major body systems (cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, renal, reproductive and integumentary) that sustain essential life processes.
Analyse and communicate the relationship between structure and function of the body systems (cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, renal, reproductive and integumentary).

Identify and describe the anatomical structure of major body systems (cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, renal, reproductive and integumentary) in everyday life using the appropriate anatomical terminology.

title: CULTURE AND GLOBALISATION: INTRODUCTION TO ANTHROPOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In our rapidly changing world a stunning diversity of rituals and spiritual beliefs coexist with mobile phones, driverless cars, transnational travel and rapid urbanisation. Anthropology explores the vast range of human possibilities and our complex relationships with transforming habitats and environments. In this subject fascinating case studies from around the world form a basis for understanding how and why people develop and express their cultural identities. In this subject, you will explore the relevance of anthropology in helping make sense of the many cultural contexts and problems that define humanity today. As well as developing an informed and critical outlook on your own social worlds, you will gain skills relevant to multicultural and global contexts. This subject is a level 1 subject and is suitable as an elective for all students.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate literature relevant to a topic in anthropology
Apply a critical anthropological perspective to global issues and problems
Apply knowledge of anthropological issues to solve problems
Summarise and research knowledge about global issues

title: ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY 1
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to human anatomy and physiology – the structure and function of body systems. This will provide the foundation for the study of the major body systems important for regulation, integration and control (nervous and endocrine systems); how the body absorbs and uses nutrients (digestive system including metabolism) plus support and movement (musculoskeletal system).
learning_outcomes: Explain the function of major body systems (nervous, endocrine, digestive and musculoskeletal) that sustain homeostasis
Identify and describe the anatomical structure of major body systems (nervous, endocrine, digestive and musculoskeletal) in everyday life using the appropriate anatomical terminology
Analyse and communicate the relationship between structure and function of the body systems (nervous, endocrine, digestive and musculoskeletal)

title: TRANSFORMING LIVES THROUGH CARE
syllabus_overview: Care is crucial to human existence. Babies cannot survive without care; through our lives we are called to care for others; and we often need to be cared for ourselves. So it is that nurses, social workers, psychologists, teachers and others care in a variety of professional contexts. We can also care in informal and personal ways, such as with our family, congregation, community, and other groups. Indeed, care is central to many contemporary social issues, including aging populations, healthcare systems, and social justice. But it ialso takes different forms in different cultures. So what is care? How and why do we care for others? How does caring transform them and us? Anthropologists have provided fascinating insight into these questions. In this subject, you will learn the basics of anthropology and how these can apply to caring in diverse places and circumstances. This Level 1 subject is suitable as an elective for all students.
learning_outcomes: Research and write thoughtfully about social and cultural change
Apply ethical and cultural awareness to issues of cultural and social change.
Develop an introductory knowledge of key concepts, topics and issues in anthropology and the social sciences.

title: ANTHROPOLOGY OF WITCH HUNTS
syllabus_overview: During Europe's Great Witch-Hunt, around 60,000 people were tried and killed under suspicion of attending Satanic sabbats. In 1690s Salem, frightening visions and fits led to dozens of hangings. But witch-hunts are not just things of the past. Today, persecution is part of life in many societies. Anthropologists offer unique and profound insights into witch-hunts by applying sophisticated analytical tools, and in more recent occurrences, by actually being there when such victimisation occurs. In this subject, we critically examine their research. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.You will be assessed on your ability to analyse persecution from an anthropological perspective.
learning_outcomes: Write a critical and coherent essay that demonstrates awareness of benefits and shortcomings of various anthropological theories.
Critically evaluate key texts related to witch-hunts.

title: CULTURE AND ENVIRONMENT: ANTHROPOLOGICAL APPROACHES TO ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES
syllabus_overview: Environmental issues such as climate change, population growth, consumption, globalisation and loss of biodiversity are increasingly impacting all human societies. Considering the diversity of human environmental knowledges, beliefs and behaviours, anthropology has an important contribution to make in understanding these issues in terms of theory, empirical research and proposed solutions. Drawing on a range of interdisciplinary ethnographic case studies from industrial, rural and small scale societies to illustrate the diversity of human responses to environmental change this subject will familiarise you with the main theoretical and methodological currents in environmental anthropology. You will gain knowledge of a range of social scientific frameworks for thinking about human - environment interactions as well as the various applied contexts where social scientists are involved in efforts to address environmental issues. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the need for interdisciplinary approaches in solving environmental problems
Research and develop coherent written arguments relating to the social and cultural dimensions of environmental issues
Develop an understanding of the social and cultural dimensions of environmental issues
Apply ethical and cultural awareness to Environmental Anthropology

title: CULTURE, HEALTH AND HEALING
syllabus_overview: In this subject we offer an anthropological perspective on health, illness and healing. You will explore the ways in which culture shapes how we experience and understand states of health and illness and the diversity of approaches to diagnosis and healing. Medical anthropology is one of the largest sub disciplines of applied anthropology and students will explore its historical underpinnings, its contributions to theory and research methodology both within anthropology and other health disciplines more broadly. You will also be offered opportunities to learn about medical anthropology in practice including how it contributes to interdisciplinary team work and community partnerships as applied to health and development, health promotion and public health, Aboriginal health and cultural diversity in communities and in the clinic.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of social and cultural factors and issues relating to health and medicine.
Apply ethical and cultural considerations to issues in medical Anthropology.
Research and develop a coherent written arguments relating to culture, health and healing.

title: HUMANS AND ANIMALS: ANTHROPOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVES
syllabus_overview: Human and animal relations are basic to society; across all walks of life and in all cultures humans and animals have formed diverse and enduring relationships, and animals have long been used to tell us about what it means to be human. This subject will explore historical, cross cultural and contemporary anthropological perspectives on human and animal relations in small scale societies, in agriculture, in industrialised societies and in leisure culture. In doing so, it will investigate themes such as totemism, animal utility, animal companionship, endangered animals, the human/animal divide and post-humanism. This is a level 2 subject.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical and cultural awareness to issues in Anthropology
Apply an anthropological perspective to human and animal relations
Produce a well researched response to a relevant topic in Anthropology

title: CULTURE AND POWER: CORE ISSUES IN ANTHROPOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject we explore the practical, theoretical and ethical advances of the vibrant discipline of anthropology, from its Victorian beginnings to present-day engagements with globally important topics such as poverty and inequality, cultural identity and nationalism, gender-based violence and human rights. In doing so, we learn how the study of culture, identity and human behaviour can be critically and meaningfully employed to positively transform the world we share. This subject provides students with tools for understanding the dynamics of change both within and through anthropological practice. Through critical inquiry, collaboration, and effective communication students will further develop their creative capacity to critique complex socio-cultural phenomena, as well as to apply theory, locate and synthesise knowledge resources, prioritise meaningful action, and manage associated risks. This is a second year level subject. Students would normally be expected to have completed at least 30 credit points before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse key ethical and cultural issues in anthropological theory and methodologies
Analyse the impact of historical and global change on the discipline of anthropology
Analyse the emergence of contemporary anthropological perspectives
Evaluate key anthropological concepts and theories

title: KINSHIP, GENDER AND MARRIAGE
syllabus_overview: Anthropologists have long been fascinated by kinship and marriage, which are central to human social organisation and to relationships of gender and power. In this subject you will look at how anthropological approaches to these forms of relationships have changed over time and critically assess recent work in this field. You will examine the role and significance of kinship and marriage in many different societies, looking at the diverse ways humans create families, and topics such as the concept of love and the darker side of kinship - family violence. The future of kinship and marriage will also be considered in the light of continuing social change and the development of new reproductive technologies. This is a level 3 subject.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine the local and global dimensions of social and cultural changes to kinship and marriage.
Apply kinship terminology and notation to a complex genealogical diagram.
Construct a complex kinship diagram using genealogical information.
Produce a sustained and complex written argument about a specific topic in kinship studies.
Evaluate different theoretical and methodological approaches to the study of kinship and marriage.

title: ANIMAL HEALTH
syllabus_overview: Disease poses a threat to animal populations in both natural and domestic settings, making them vulnerable. This subject presents the principles of common/exotic animal diseases and parasitology as they pertain to domestic animals and wildlife. Major components include understanding the diagnosis and control of infection and disease; common parasitic diseases of animals and animal biosecurity. You will perform laboratory testing on samples and undertake problem-based disease-solving exercises. This subject promotes students’ abilities to tackle problems creatively and generate innovative approaches to disease control that are applicable currently, and in the future.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret experimental results from practical exercises and research articles to expand and consolidate understanding of concepts behind diagnosis of infection, parasite life cycles and drug resistance in parasites.
Synthesise information from a range of sources on animal diseases, treatment and prevention to provide advice to farmers and/or pet owners.
Understand, describe and explain concepts in disease diagnosis, the importance of managing disease in animals, treatment therapies, parasitology, zoonotic diseases and animal biosecurity.

title: VETERINARY IMMUNOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a foundational understanding of veterinary immunology, tailored for students pursuing animal-related careers . It explores the immune system’s role in protecting animal health, with a comparative focus across species. Core topics include the structural and functional organisation of the immune system, the immune cells and chemical mediators, antigens, antibodies, and cellular processes related to innate and adaptive immune responses against infectious agents. This subject will describe immunological mechanisms: immunosuppression, hypersensitivity, neonatal immunity, immunological tolerance, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, vaccine and immunotherapy. Students will gain practical and theoretical skills in immunological techniques relevant to disease diagnosis in animals. Throughout the semester, you will also complete a module focusing on developing a professional social media presence and forming and maintaining professional connections.
learning_outcomes: Build and reflect on your experiences that develop your career readiness, and make judgements on your employability strengths

Demonstrate the basis of immune mechanisms underlying immunosuppression, hypersensitivity; neonatal immunity, immunological tolerance, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency hypersensitivity reactions, immunodeficiency diseases, vaccine and immunotherapy.

Ability to perform immunological techniques in disease diagnosis; Analyse and interpret experimental results to make evidence‐based conclusions and accurately present scientific findings to provide advice to control diseases.
Describe and explain concepts in the role the immune system plays in host defence against infectious agents to maintain healthy life in animals.

title: HONOURS IN NATURAL AND PHYSICAL SCIENCES A
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and have fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree with a major in a relevant discipline. The Bachelor of Science (Honours) program provides undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program imparts undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Under supervision of a La Trobe University academic, you will formulate a research question, conduct a research study, and write a research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words in which you demonstrate the capacity to make an original contribution to your discipline. APH401A is the first subject of a sequence of four subjects in which students undertake a research project in a natural and physical sciences discipline and write a thesis. You must obtain approval from an academic supervisor prior to enrolment and must complete APH401A first.
learning_outcomes: Communicate scientific ideas orally and in writing using basic disciplinary conventions, with guidance.
Design ethical approaches to investigate problems and test possible solutions relevant to a natural and physical sciences discipline, with guidance.
Interpret and compare scientific information from multiple sources within a natural and physical sciences discipline.
Demonstrate intellectual curiosity and apply guided judgement in scholarly activities under supervision.
Analyse discipline-specific literature to propose informed approaches to research questions, with guidance.

title: HONOURS IN NATURAL AND PHYSICAL SCIENCES D
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and have fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree with a major in a relevant discipline. The Bachelor of Science (Honours) program provides undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program imparts undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Under supervision of a La Trobe University academic, you will formulate a research question, conduct a research study, and write a research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words in which you demonstrate the capacity to make an original contribution to your discipline. APH401D is the final subject of a sequence of four subjects in which students undertake a research project in a natural and physical sciences discipline and write a thesis. You must complete APH401D last.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate, interpret and synthesise scientific information in a natural and physical sciences discipline to support reasoned arguments.
Justify approaches used to investigate problems by drawing on advanced knowledge and evidence in a natural and physical sciences discipline.
Demonstrate independent and reflective learning and scholarly practice with ethical and academic integrity.
Communicate complex scientific ideas orally and in writing to scientific audiences, demonstrating knowledge of scholarly conventions in a natural and physical sciences discipline.
Apply advanced knowledge and technical skills in a natural and physical sciences discipline to address research questions.

title: HONOURS IN NATURAL AND PHYSICAL SCIENCES C
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and have fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree with a major in a relevant discipline. The Bachelor of Science (Honours) program provides undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program imparts undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Under supervision of a La Trobe University academic, you will formulate a research question, conduct a research study, and write a research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words in which you demonstrate the capacity to make an original contribution to your discipline. APH401C is the third subject in a four-part sequence where students conduct a research project in a natural and physical sciences discipline and write a thesis. While APH401B and APH401C may be completed in either order, APH401A must be completed first, and APH401D must be completed last.
learning_outcomes: Communicate scientific ideas clearly and effectively to scientific audiences, demonstrating sound use of disciplinary conventions.
Demonstrate intellectual initiative and sound judgement in independently planning and executing scholarly activities with ethical and academic integrity.
Apply advanced knowledge and technical skills in a natural and physical sciences discipline to address research questions, with minimal guidance.
Evaluate and integrate scientific information from diverse sources to support reasoned arguments in a natural and physical sciences discipline.

title: ARCHAEOLOGY OF ANCIENT CIVILISATIONS
syllabus_overview: This subject reviews what archaeology has discovered about the world's great civilisations. We investigate how civilisations developed and the implications of this knowledge for our own survival. We embark on a survey of the variety of complex human societies that have arisen in the last 6,000 years: in Egypt and the Middle East, the Mediterranean and Western Europe, China, South and Southeast Asia, Mesoamerica and South America.
learning_outcomes: Develop appropriate questions for archaeological case studies
Answer research questions about archaeological case studies using relevant literature on ancient civilisations
Integrate key methodological and theoretical skills
Accurately interpret the relationship between variables in a given dataset and draw supported conclusions
Recognise and discuss the cultural diversity of world civilisations and varying attitudes to individual human rights

title: THE HUMAN JOURNEY: ARCHAEOLOGY AND EVOLUTION
syllabus_overview: ‘The Human Journey; archaeology and evolution' looks at the origins and evolutionary paths of humans, from our earliest potential ancestors 7 million years ago, to the first occurrence of own species around 300,000 years ago. To do this we examine the fossil, archaeological and behavioural records of our ancestors as well as looking at the climatic and environmental backdrop to our evolution. The subject is built around a historical understanding of how key discoveries have changed our understanding of our ancestry and case studies of pivotal archaeological and fossil sites, including the active research of the teaching staff - who have discovered key early human fossils in Africa. The subject takes a global outlook, from our earliest origins in Africa, the dispersal of the first human species out of Africa and into Asia and Europe, to the origin and relationship of our own species to our close cousins the Neanderthals and Denisovans. Taught by La Trobe researchers working at key palaeoanthopological and archaeological sites such as Drimolen and Amanzi Springs in South Africa, the subject presents upon their active fieldwork and research within a historical context to understand our evolution, and to explore how views of our human ancestry have changed through time - highlighting the shared ancestry of all humans alive today and the epic journey that our ancestors took to becoming us.
learning_outcomes: You will be able to interpret differing views on the origins of humans
You will examine how new discoveries have changed our understanding of human evolution through time by outlining the history of archaeological and fossil discoveries
You will define what it means to be human through an understanding the behavioural and cognitive evolution of our ancestors.
You will examine the sensitivities surrounding discussions of our human origins and the importance of understanding our shared ancestry in the modern world.
You will identify the primary scientific methods that influence our understanding of key events in human evolution with a focus upon archaeological and fossil case studies

title: DIGGING ARCHAEOLOGY: AN INTRODUCTION TO ARCHAEOLOGICAL EXCAVATION
syllabus_overview: This hands-on subject provides an introduction to practical archaeological methods and techniques in both the field and the laboratory. Working through a simulated archaeological excavation, students will be introduced to the methods and techniques of archaeological fieldwork. Working in small groups, students will excavate and record a simulated site and its material culture, sharing their findings with other teams in order to interpret how people lived at this site in the past. Through this subject, students will gain practical experience in the generation, collation, analysis and interpretation of archaeological data through field recording and the preparation of a professional excavation report.
learning_outcomes: Develop and express an argument clearly, developing and managing new ideas in teams convincingly, and with the use of appropriate methods and archaeological evidence

Understand a range of methods used by archaeologists when they undertake fieldwork and followup analysis. Students will directly apply these methods in their practical field and lab classes to produce professional quality data.
Engage and communicate with peers in effectively to answer archaeological questions and meet challenges encountered in practical research.

title: INTRODUCTION TO ARCHAEOLOGY: FROM AUSTRALOPITHECUS TO THE ANTHROPOCENE
syllabus_overview: From our earliest ancestors in Africa, humans have spread across the globe and transitioned from foragers and hunter-gatherers to complex agricultural societies - domesticating crops and animals and changing their environments as they did so, as well as harnessing complex technologies such as stone tool production, ceramics and metallurgy, and creating symbolism, art, religion, language and literature. Leading ultimately to our diverse and dense contemporary urban societies. Today, we understand this global past by studying the archaeological evidence left behind, and this subject introduces you to that study. Using examples from different periods and geographic locations you will be introduced to the world of archaeology and in turn the archaeology of the world. You will learn about the wide range of methods and theoretical approaches modern day archaeologists employ to understand ancient cultures and how and why these past societies changed, thrived or perished. Each week a case study will focus on a different period, location and methodological specialism to enable you to explore the ancient world and learn about how archaeologists take the physical remains of past societies and interpret them.
learning_outcomes: Appraise and interpret archaeological evidence to explore how we infer past events from material remains.
Identify, locate, analyse, and synthesise relevant peer-reviewed literature.
Demonstrate an understanding of archaeological theory, methods and concepts and their application of the archaeological record.
Recognise the professional and ethical standards that practising archaeology professionally in an Australian context.
Demonstrate an appreciation and understanding of the breadth and time depth of archaeology as a discipline.

title: PAST LANDSCAPES AND ENVIRONMENTS
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the concept of landscapes as aggregations of long-term human activity and natural processes. Throughout the subject we will examine archaeological and environmental data to provide insights into human-environment interaction at a range of temporal and spatial scales. Students will explore the ways in which human social-ecological systems have dramatically shaped our world over thousands of years, culminating in our present-day environment. We will also consider the ways that natural environmental changes have influenced past human societies, and the insights these offer to current environmental challenges. A range of theoretical perspectives and methodological principles will be introduced in seminars through the semester. Practical classes will allow students to understand and apply field and lab techniques used in recording, analysing and reconstructing past landscapes and environments.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles behind paleoenvironmental methods and their application in studying past landscapes.
Demonstrate awareness of paleoenvironmental field and laboratory methods, including the literature and current thinking associated with them.

Evaluate different methods for investigating landscape modification in a variety of settings, plus more focused application of paleoenvironmental analysis to landscape modification in a temporal and spatial setting (to be agreed upon with student).

title: PALAEOLITHIC ARCHAEOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Our ancestors first appeared on the African landscape between 7 and 6 million years ago, but it was not until 3 million years ago that they began to litter the landscape with durable material remains. These early tool-users unwittingly provided their descendants with a unique, if enigmatic, record of their activities. Although this record comprises little more than chipped stone tools and broken-up animal bones, it yields a wealth of information about the behavioural innovations that are integral to the story of human evolution. This subject explores how Palaeolithic archaeologists decode the behavioural and evolutionary significance of these remains and study the technological, economic, social and artistic innovations that are the hallmarks of our evolutionary story. You will study key innovations in human behavioural evolution, from the advent of the world's earliest technology to the key turning points in diet and foraging strategies, social organisation, and creative achievements. This subject has face-to-face workshops with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Understand the way in which archaeology contributes to accounts of human evolution
Evaluate the import of all humanity sharing a deep-time history
Understand how archaeologists use material traces to generate information about the behaviour of our ancestors
Evaluate alternative accounts of human evolution and assess the import of new discoveries as they are announced
Recognize cultural values, awareness and sensitivities surrounding discussions of human evolution
Identify the scientific methods and deep-seated beliefs that influence understanding of key events in human evolution

title: HONOURS IN NATURAL AND PHYSICAL SCIENCES B
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and have fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree with a major in a relevant discipline. The Bachelor of Science (Honours) program provides undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program imparts undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Under supervision of a La Trobe University academic, you will formulate a research question, conduct a research study, and write a research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words in which you demonstrate the capacity to make an original contribution to your discipline. APH401B is the second subject of a sequence of four subjects in which students undertake a research project in a natural and physical sciences discipline and write a thesis. You must complete APH401A before APH401B.
learning_outcomes: Design ethical approaches to investigate problems and test possible solutions relevant to a natural and physical sciences discipline, with guidance.
Analyse discipline-specific literature to refine approaches to research questions, with guidance.
Demonstrate developing intellectual initiative and apply informed judgement in conducting scholarly tasks with ethical and academic integrity, with moderate guidance.
Interpret and compare scientific information from multiple sources within a natural and physical sciences discipline to support research and analysis.
Communicate scientific ideas orally and in writing using appropriate disciplinary conventions, with some independence.

title: INTRODUCTION TO ARCHAEOLOGICAL SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn how scientific techniques can be used to answer archaeological questions. Through the exploration of a virtual simulated site, students are introduced to the theory behind a range of common archaeological science techniques, applying this to their own archaeological datasets. Students uncover, analyse and interpret archaeological data on past landscapes, dating, materials analysis, biochemical techniques and bioarchaeology. We will investigate how to interpret scientific data and how this is in turn used in archaeological interpretation, improving scientific literacy in both academic and professional contexts. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject credit point requirement before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Examine and analyse scientific data applied to archaeological problems, generating arguments based on appropriate graphical and numerical manipulations

Demonstrate an understanding of current trends and arguments in areas of archaeological science and how these areas have contributed to archaeological knowledge by composing a well justified argument using correct referencing
Locate and appropriately use relevant sources investigate and present justifiable arguments about the validity and usefulness of scientific techniques applied to archaeological questions.
Explain and discuss common archaeological science techniques used in the field. The principles behind the techniques and what they are used for and their limitations.

title: SUSTAINABILITY, RESILIENCE, AND COLLAPSE: FROM PAST SOCIETIES TO THE END OF CIVILISATION
syllabus_overview: Issues of sustainability and resilience are prominent today in light of accelerating climate change (or deterioration), rising and falling populations, and declining resources. However, these issues are not new, and many human societies have faced these crises in the past. In this subject you will learn about a range of past societies, from all around the world, that failed to adapt or respond to changing circumstances (including climate change), resulting in their collapse. However, you will also learn about societies in the past that were able to develop sustainable and resilient long-term economies, or who innovated and adapted successfully to climate change - resulting in societies that thrived for centuries (or even millennia) despite significant challenges. This subject takes an interdisciplinary approach to examining the success or failure of past societies within their respective social-environmental systems - including how those systems were impacted by climate change in the past, and how ongoing climate deterioration might impact our society, or even bring about its end. This is a level 2 subject, please consider the subject level and prerequisites before enrolling.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate alternative models and theories of societal collapse - recognising how such understandings are constantly re-framed by new theoretical perspectives, new evidence, and/or new analytical techniques.
Identify how new scientific techniques can challenge deep-seated narratives around key events in past societal-transformations.
Demonstrate an understanding of the difference between sustainability and resilience, using archaeological and/or historical examples of both.
Apply novel analytical perspectives to archaeological and historical data in order to generate new understandings of societal adaptation to changing environmental conditions.
Recognise and describe the limitations of archaeological and historical data in the study of changing societal interactions during times of crisis and change.

title: THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF AUSTRALIA'S FIRST PEOPLES
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will journey through 65,000 years of First Peoples settlement in Australia. Contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander voices and perspectives are embedded throughout this subject and you will learn through both Traditional and Western knowledge systems. You will investigate a series of major themes, including the first settlement of different parts of the continent; interactions with and adaptations to varied and changing environments; technological choices; and patterns of economy and land use. You will investigate a range of case studies to evaluate archaeological and ethnohistorical information and how they have been used to provide insights into past ways of life. You will also explore the history of Australian archaeological theory and practice, providing critical links with developing contemporary professional best practise approaches. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Interpret temporal and spatial changes in material culture and environmental settings from different Aboriginal archaeological site types.
Understand and evaluate best practise models from the scale of individuals through to Communities of Practice.
Explore and evaluate different theoretical models within Australian Archaeology.

Demonstrate knowledge of the cultural values, awareness and ethical sensitivities towards Indigenous Australians and their archaeological materials across the continent. Appreciate and be sensitive to cross-cultural protocols and language and be able to deal with unfamiliar situations.

title: FROM FORAGING TO FARMING
syllabus_overview: The shift from foraging to farming is one of the most dramatic developments in human history and has remained an area of intense interest in archaeology for over a century. Beginning some 15,000 years ago, this fundamental transition laid the foundations for modern urban living - but also had huge impacts upon the environmental footprint of such societies, which in turn significantly affected their societal and environmental sustainability and resilience. At a time of rapidly accelerating climate deterioration and resource shortfalls, these themes are more relevant than ever. In order to better understand this seismic transition, particular attention is paid to the problems archaeologists face in differentiating the material residues of early farmers from those of hunter gatherers. In this subject you will learn about the earliest agricultural developments in the Middle East and how they are placed in a global perspective by considering the advent of farming in Europe, north and sub-Saharan Africa, East Asia, Melanesia, Mesoamerica and South America. ARC3FFF is a face-to-face subject. where attendance in tutorials is vital to undertake assignment tasks effectively.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate creativity in developing solutions to a range of problems related to food production and environmental management
Apply theoretical frameworks and archaeological evidence of different kinds to construct global narratives of regional historical trajectories and social systems
Construct a sustained argument based on the application of adequate research to current academic issues
Identify lessons from the past that can be applied to sustainability and resilience challenges in the 21st century
Critically reflect upon the impact that the development and adoption of agriculture had upon environmental and societal sustainability in a range of temporal and geographical contexts

title: IN YOUR BONES: THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF DEATH
syllabus_overview: In this summer intensive subject you will be introduced to the archaeological analysis of human and animal remains - in order to answer key questions about the lives and deaths of people in the past. Through preparatory online material ahead of seven days of hands-on laboratory classes, the subject will introduce you to a range of scientific techniques that allow us as archaeologists to assess an individual's age at death; their sex; the activities, accidents, and diseases that formed their lives (and often deaths); and even their diets and movements, all of which can be recorded in their (or your) bones. Finally, we will examine the ethical issues stemming from the archaeological analysis of human remains, from modern best-practices to past scandals and abuses. This subject is suitable for humanities and science undergraduate students.
learning_outcomes: Examine and analyse scientific data applied to archaeological problems, generating arguments based on appropriate graphical and numerical manipulations

Explain and discuss scientific techniques applied to human osteoarchaeological remains in both the field and the laboratory. This includes the principles behind the techniques and what they are used for and their limitations.

Demonstrate the ability to locate and appropriately use relevant sources investigate and present justifiable arguments about the validity and usefulness of scientific techniques applied to osteoarchaeological remains.
Synthesise and communicate an understanding of current trends, arguments, and controversies in areas of archaeological and forensic science.

title: OBJECTS, THINGS, & ARTEFACTS (A): MANAGING AND RECORDING
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the field and laboratory management and analysis of archaeological artefacts in Australia through the detailed study of stone artefacts. The subject features practical hands-on classes focusing upon the identification of materials, the recording and analysis of artefacts, and the cataloguing and management of archaeological assemblages. You will learn industry standards of best practice for artefact handling, cataloguing, and data management, as well as engaging with the theoretical underpinnings of material culture and what that tells us about humanity.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in artefact analysis in order to interpret a body of data
Demonstrate knowledge of the elements of a research design
Work as a member of a team to acquire archaeological information
Contribute to class discussions evaluating different approaches to the interpretation and analysis of artefacts
Use descriptive statistics to analyse an artefact assemblage
Demonstrate knowledge of the theoretical and analytical approaches used to construct and interpret archaeological data
Identify and record the most common stone artefacts found in the Australian archaeological record

title: ARCHAEOLOGY OF AUSTRALIA SINCE 1788
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of the archaeological record of Australia from the 18th century to the present day. You will learn how material culture provides new perspectives on the recent past. Over the course of the semester you will learn about the continuity of the archaeological record of Aboriginal people and explore aspects of rural, urban, industrial, and maritime archaeology across Australia with an emphasis on the archaeology of Victoria. You will hear from some of the leading archaeologists in the field and learn about how non-Aboriginal archaeology is managed in Victoria. Through weekly self-paced units you will develop first-hand experience with researching and recording Australian historical-archaeological sites. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Locate and interpret archival evidence relevant to understanding Australian colonial sites.
Identify theoretical approaches and research questions appropriate to the archaeological evidence from a local site and apply this in designing and carrying out research to address those questions.
Understand role and responsibilities of professional heritage practitioners and community groups, and demonstrate familiarity with relevant local, national and international legislation.
Communicate and work effectively, ethically, and respectfully with colleagues during group discussions and activities.
Demonstrate knowledge of how material culture, including landscapes, archaeological sites and artefacts, provides evidence of the development of culture and society in Australia since 1788.

title: CULTURAL HERITAGE MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you are introduced to concepts, processes and outcomes of cultural heritage management. We take a holistic approach to identifying, assessing and managing the tangible heritage of built and archaeological places, landscapes, objects and the intangible heritage of stories, traditional knowledge, songs and language. Using Australian and international case studies we explore core issues in conservation management planning including significance assessment, the inclusion of multiple stakeholders and values, identifying impacts and managing change, interpretation and sustainability. You will also be introduced to the regulatory framework governing cultural heritage management in Australia and the roles and relationships of various professions involved in the industry. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the range of heritage values considered important by Australians
Display knowledge of ethical issues and understanding of the application of statutory frameworks in the protection of archaeological sites
Demonstrate effective teamwork skills through clear communication, organisation of tasks and responsibilities
Apply analytical research skills to the investigation of both heritage sites and relevant legislation.

title: OBJECTS, THINGS, & ARTEFACTS (B): ANALYSING AND UNDERSTANDING
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on skills introduced in ARC3MTA. Students apply the field and laboratory management and analysis methods learned in Semester 1 to the study of industrial artefacts (ceramics, glass, metal etc.), and osteological remains (animal and human bones). Students will be introduced to each category of artefacts and ecofacts in turn, with practical hands-on classes focusing upon the identification of materials, the recording and analysis of artefacts, and the cataloguing and management of archaeological assemblages. Students will learn the theoretical and analytical approaches that archaeologists use to manage and make sense of material culture, and use that knowledge to analyse and interpret an artefactual assemblage.
learning_outcomes: Contribute to class discussions evaluating different approaches to the interpretation and analysis of artefacts
Demonstrate knowledge of the elements of a research design
Apply skills in artefact analysis in order to interpret a body of data
Identify and record the most common faunal ecofacts and industrial artefacts found in the Australian archaeological record
Use descriptive statistics to analyse an artefact assemblage
Demonstrate knowledge of the theoretical and analytical approaches used to construct and interpret archaeological data
Work as a member of a team to acquire archaeological information

title: OBJECTS, THINGS, & ARTEFACTS (A): MANAGING AND RECORDING
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the field and laboratory management and analysis of archaeological artefacts in Australia through the detailed study of stone artefacts. The subject features practical hands-on classes focusing upon the identification of materials, the recording and analysis of artefacts, and the cataloguing and management of archaeological assemblages. Students will learn industry standards of best practice for artefact handling, cataloguing, and data management, as well as engaging with the theoretical underpinnings of material culture and what that tells us about humanity. This subject is face-to-face with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Conceptually map the elements of a research design
Critically analyse different approaches to the interpretation and analysis of artefacts.
Critically analyse the most common stone artefacts found in the Australian archaeological record
Apply descriptive statistics to the analysis of an artefact assemblage
Analyse an artefact assemblage and interpret a body of data
Apply teamwork skills in order to acquire archaeological information
Apply advanced knowledge of theoretical and analytical approaches to construct and interpret archaeological data

title: THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF AUSTRALIA'S FIRST PEOPLES
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will journey through 65,000 years of First Peoples settlement in Australia. Contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander voices and perspectives are embedded throughout this subject and you will learn through both Traditional and Western knowledge systems. You will investigate a series of major themes, including the first settlement of different parts of the continent; interactions with and adaptations to varied and changing environments; technological choices; and patterns of economy and land use. You will investigate a range of case studies to evaluate archaeological and ethnohistorical information and how they have been used to provide insights into past ways of life. You will also explore the history of Australian archaeological theory and practice, providing critical links with developing contemporary professional best practise approaches. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and evaluate different theoretical models within Australian archaeology.

Demonstrate knowledge of the cultural values, awareness and ethical sensitivities towards Indigenous Australians and their archaeological materials across the continent. Appreciate and be sensitive to cross-cultural protocols and language and be able to deal with unfamiliar situations.
Interpret temporal and spatial changes in material culture and environmental settings from different Aboriginal archaeological site types.
Understand and evaluate best practise models from the scale of individuals through to Communities of Practice.

title: RICE, RITUAL AND EMPIRE: ASIAN ARCHAEOLOGIES
syllabus_overview: Asia is the largest of the continents, home to over half the world's population, and historically the birthplace of some of the world's first civilisations, of global religions, and multiple independent centres of plant and animal domestication. Adopting a thematic approach, this subject presents a comparative overview of the archaeologies of several different regions of Asia, with specific focus upon China, the Indian subcontinent and southeast Asia. From the Bronze Age civilisations of China and South Asia, to the mediaeval empires of Cambodia and Sri Lanka, this subject will teach you about the full range of Asian archaeologies.
learning_outcomes: Locate and synthesise a range of relevant digital data sources in order to answer research questions relating to Asian archaeologies.
Appreciate the diverse nature of archaeological data and argumentation, often through the study of the culture history of specific regions or periods of Asia.
Critically appraise the application of archaeological methods and theories across Asia.
Recognise and characterise the development of diverse past human societies across Asia
Critique the modern social and political values of archaeological heritage.

learning_outcomes: Apply advanced knowledge in a specialised aspect of Australian archaeology

Apply advanced knowledge to a specialised aspect of Australian archaeology

title: PRACTICAL ARCHAEOLOGY
syllabus_overview: You will focus on the techniques of field archaeology and concentrate on acquiring skills used in survey, recording of artefacts and features. You will be introduced to a range of methods from the basics through to Total Stations Theodolites and DGPS. Emphasis is placed on the building of interpretive links between theory and fieldwork. The field school is face to face over 10 days (weekdays over 2 consecutive weeks, 10-4pm each day), and is run in off campus in Brimbank Park in collabroation with Wurundjeri and Parks Victoria. There are further unscheduled onlines materials throughout semester period. Attendance of the field school is a hurdle requirement for passing this subject.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop a research programs
Develop effective team work skills through clear communication, organisation of tasks and responsibilities
Report in an accomplished manner on the survey of archaeological material and its spatial distribution
Demonstrate a capacity to critique field work strategies.

title: ARCHAEOLOGY OF ABORIGINAL VICTORIA
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn about thousands of years of Aboriginal culture and management of Country in southeastern Australia, with particular reference to Victoria. Aboriginal voices and perspectives are foregrounded across a wide range of themes through both recorded and in-person conversations. You will learn about the many different sources of knowledge about culture and Country, including traditional knowledge, archaeological, environmental, and historical evidence. Throughout the subject, you will investigate conflicting explanations for social, technological and demographic change. You will also investigate the role of contemporary Aboriginal communities in shaping archaeological and heritage management practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify theoretical approaches and research questions appropriate to the evidence from different types of Aboriginal archaeological sites.
Interpret and apply the link between theory and data within Victorian archaeology.

Understand different sources of archaeological evidence of Aboriginal people in Victoria, different taphonomic and environmental issues relating to its interpretation, and its significance to contemporary Aboriginal peoples.
Understand culturally competent approaches to archaeological investigations of Aboriginal Victoria.

title: ISSUES IN CONTEMPORARY ARCHAEOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In the subject we will revisit some major and enduring theoretical issues in contemporary archaeology. The subject forms a bridge between the structured world of undergraduate learning and the more individualistic spheres of postgraduate research and employment in public archaeology. This subject requires you to develop the initiative required to cross from one realm to the other. Seminar-style classes place strong emphasis on student participation.
learning_outcomes: Develop appropriate questions for the interrogation of theoretical issues in archaeology
Demonstrate advanced academic and individual research skills
Oral presentations during seminars that reflect upon archaeological theory and disciplinary politics
Research and apply ethical frameworks and policies in the practice of archaeology and inclusion of stakeholders in cultural heritage issues

title: HUMAN AND ANIMAL BONES
syllabus_overview: Osteoarchaeology is the study of remains such as bones, teeth, shell, feathers, fur, scales, proteins, and DNA in the archaeological record. Studying these remains can help us better interpret interactions between humans, animals, and the environment from deep time to the present. They can also help identify past social, political, and economic systems. Morphological skeletal changes can occur due to disease, nutrition, workload, environmental stress, and domestication. This information is gleaned from studying a range of different archaeological contexts including burials and cemeteries, historical settlements, middens, caves, hearths or fireplaces, and other well-preserved sites. The focus of this intensive summer subject includes techniques of analysis for interpreting health, diet, ageing and sexing of skeletal remains, as well as quantitative techniques. This subject has a strong practical focus, and you will learn about the native and introduced animal species most commonly found in Australian archaeological assemblages. During this course you will be introduced to human osteology and learn about the main differences between human and animal bones. This subject is suitable for humanities and science postgraduate students.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise and communicate an understanding of current trends, arguments, and controversies in areas of archaeological and forensic science.
Understand and identify the basic structure of the vertebrate skeleton.
Identify the most common animal bones found in Australian archaeological assemblages.
Demonstrate knowledge of the theoretical and analytical approaches used to construct and interpret osteoarchaeological data
Examine and analyse scientific data applied to archaeological problems, generating arguments based on appropriate graphical and numerical manipulations

title: THEORETICAL ISSUES IN ARCHAEOLOGY
syllabus_overview: As Matthew Johnson once wrote about archaeologists, " we don't 'need' theory, we all use theory whether we like it or not ". But what is archaeological theory? Where did it come from? And how has it developed and changed over time, changing the way(s) in which we understand and engage with the archaeological record. In this subject you will explore and engage with some of the major and enduring theoretical perspectives and issues in archaeology. Scaffolded within a chronological and geographic framework, you will be introduced to the major paradigms and schools of archaeological theory before exploring how they have impacted the ways in which archaeologists past and present have carried out research and interpreted archaeological data. Through lectures, discussion, and readings you will study how broader political and social shifts have impacted archaeological theory over time and space, and will explore some of the challenges and issues faced by contemporary archaeologists today.
learning_outcomes: Research and apply ethical frameworks and policies in the practice of archaeology and inclusion of stakeholders in cultural heritage issues
Demonstrate advanced academic and individual research skills
Interpret and transmit knowledge of archaeological theory and contemporary practice to specialist and non-specialist audiences
Demonstrate specialist knowledge of theoretical issues in archaeology

title: METHODS IN GIS: FROM DIGGING TO DATA/DIGGING DATA - PREDICTIVE MODELS, MAPPING AND MORE
syllabus_overview: This subject looks at some of the pressing current issues in archaeology: Can we predict where sites are? Can we preserve sites digitally (e.g. in 3D)? We will be looking at these issues and more in this subject. As archaeologists we generate vast quantities of data from a diverse range of sources (e.g. spatial data from excavation; dates from dating samples; analytical measurement data from the analysis of stone tools, pottery etc.). This data comes in a range of scales, for example from continental scale data syntheses, landscape level network analyses, site level artefact distribution, right the way down to micro-scale wear on artefacts at the sub millimetre scale. It is impossible to integrate, plot or analyse this data by hand – GIS offers the only way to compile and analyse data from the multiple spatial and temporal scales that archaeological sites generate – and to present these in graphical format, most commonly manifest as maps. A key practical takeaway skill from this subject will be the ability to process raw archaeological data to create a map that complies with Victorian Heritage legislation (e.g. for submission to ACHRIS). You will also explore analysis and 3D presentation of archaeological data.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement appropriate analyses of spatial data
Prepare and present maps encapsulating spatial analysis to a professional standard
Interpret, explain and present the results of complex spatial analysis
Understand and apply the principles of data collection for spatial analysis
Use GIS software to address a range of analytical problems in archaeology

title: PROFESSIONAL ARCHAEOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with a practical introduction to the role played by archaeology in the heritage industry. You are introduced to the conceptual and procedural skills required to work effectively as a professional archaeologist. You will review the development of cultural heritage management, the main provisions of legislation and policy relating to archaeology in Australia, and the role and responsibilities of Indigenous communities, government departments and other stake-holders. You will develop skills in preparing Cultural Heritage Management Plans and will consider ethical and OHS issues of the archaeological workplace.
learning_outcomes: Understand the policies and practices applicable to archaeology in the management of heritage places in Victoria.
Identify the range of heritage values considered important by Australians and the legislative means of protecting them.
Identify common safety issues pertaining to the archaeological workplace and means of mitigating them.
Balance the values and viewpoints of a range of stakeholder groups including Aboriginal communities, descendant communities, and clients when recommending management outcomes.

syllabus_overview: You will develop expertise in designing and carrying out archaeological research through the excavation of a simulated archaeological site on the Bundoora campus. You will work independently and as part of a team to identify research questions and plan the excavation, with additional attention to Occupational Health and Safety requirements and obtaining the appropriate permits. You will use a variety of techniques to record archaeological evidence in the field. You will apply skills in interpreting the evidence to answer your research questions and in preparing final reports and publications.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the principles of archaeological excavation and reporting.
Demonstrate project management skills through allocation of time and funding

title: REPRESENTING BODIES: GENDER, SEXUALITY AND IDENTITIES
syllabus_overview: How does representation shape our understanding of bodies? How have ideas about gender, sexuality, race and disability been informed by visual culture? In this subject you will interrogate art, film and media from a range of time periods and cultural contexts to see how dominant concepts of the body and identity are communicated. From painting to protest, from film to fashion, you will look at examples of visual culture that have challenged convention and changed the way we understand our own and others’ bodies. Across the learning materials and in the weekly seminar you will engage critically with a range of visual and textual sources and formulate independent arguments across critical and creative tasks. This subject introduces you to key approaches in the study of visual cultures, and interdisciplinary knowledge relevant to range of other majors including History, Gender Sexuality and Diversity Studies, English, and Sociology. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Develop skills in research and academic writing through critical analysis tasks and essay writing.
Reflect on the role of visual culture in ideas of the body through creative and critical assignments.
Assess a range of different viewpoints of the body through visual and textual analysis.
Apply key theoretical frameworks around the body and identity to the analysis of visual culture.

title: VISIONS OF MODERNITY: ART, FILM AND VISUAL CULTURES
syllabus_overview: How has visual culture changed the way we see the world? What can we learn by looking more closely? In this subject you will be introduced to the study of visual cultures through the radical developments in art, film, design and media that reshaped the world from the 19th century to the 1960s. Focusing on key examples from revolutionary movements such as Surrealism, Dada and Pop, you will engage with a range of mediums and works to develop critical skills in visual analysis and cultural literacy. You will see how the political, social and technological changes of modernity were articulated through new visual forms and reflect on how this has shaped our contemporary image culture. In this subject you will learn how to place visual culture in theoretical, critical and historical contexts. You will apply knowledge in practice during your weekly two-hour seminar, and test your responses through a range of critical and creative tasks. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Identify and contextualise theoretical concepts in visual and textual materials, articulating these in creative and critical assignments.
Analyse key artworks and examples of visual culture within cultural and theoretical contexts.
Apply basic critical concepts and terminology in the analysis of visual culture.
Develop skills in research and academic writing to articulate independent arguments.

title: STUDIO PRACTICE B: SCULPTURE AND PHOTOGRAPHY
syllabus_overview: This practical subject introduces you to the dynamic hands-on learning environment of the studio through focused exploration in sculpture and photography workshops. In this subject you will develop technical and conceptual approaches to art making in relation to contemporary and historical art practices. By the end of the subject, you will have gained an understanding of what it means to develop your own studio practice, acquiring skills relating to processes and materials; critical and reflective thinking; and experimentation, risk taking and problem solving.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the creative, critical, and reflective thinking skills required in photography and sculpture.
Develop the capacity to respond creatively and flexibly to feedback and learn how to manage deadlines.
Develop artworks that effectively employ techniques and approaches in photography and sculpture.
Explore connections between your work, the work of others, and issues of personal or social concern.

title: STUDIO PRACTICE A: DRAWING AND PRINTMAKING
syllabus_overview: This practical subject introduces you to the dynamic hands-on learning environment of the studio through focused exploration in the drawing and printmaking workshops. In this subject you will develop technical and conceptual approaches to art making in relation to contemporary and historical art practices and concepts. By the end of the subject, you will have gained an understanding of what it means to develop your own studio practice, acquiring skills relating to processes and materials; critical and reflective thinking; and experimentation, risk taking and problem solving
