Explore connections between your work, the work of others, and issues of personal or social concern.
Develop artworks that effectively employ techniques and approaches in drawing and printmaking.
Demonstrate the creative, critical, and reflective thinking skills required in drawing and printmaking.

title: ICONS AND ANTI-ICONS: TEN WORKS OF ART
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will study ten key works from the 1960s to the early 2000s, to understand how the art and visual culture of the late 20th century paved the way for contemporary practices. Focusing on a selection of artists from around the world, from blockbuster stars to political provocateurs, these artworks will introduce you to the period’s new experimental processes, such as performance, installation, public interventions and video art. Through visual and textual analysis, you will critically engage with the role of art in the emergence of political and theoretical ideas such as feminism and queer theory, environmentalism, postmodernism and postcolonialism. In Icons and Anti-Icons you will gain insight into important theoretical movements, and develop detailed understanding of the practices of influential artists. You will participate in weekly seminars to develop your own perspective and point of view, in addition to engaging with a range of learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret textual and visual material in relation to a theoretical position.
Critically research a relevant topic using appropriate data sources.
Communicate verbally, visually and in writing ideas relating to relevant theoretical material and visual arts practice.
Investigate a broad range of theoretical positions that relate to late 20th century art and visual culture.

title: COLLECTING POWER: MUSEUMS, COLONIALISM, AND RESTITUTION
syllabus_overview: Museums are widely considered the custodians of what our cultures deem most valuable. Yet what is collected, and how, tells us a great deal about the ongoing violence of colonialism. In this subject, you explore the relationship between collecting, conflict and power, and how the role of art in conquest, nation-building and religious conflicts can lead to its destruction or censorship. You will consider several case studies drawn from a Western context, such as the Elgin marbles, Nazi looting and terrorist destruction of cultural heritage, and explore the wider ethical and legal context of collecting, destruction and theft. You will also explore broad cultural responses to redressing this legacy in ‘decolonising’ actions that include the restitution and repatriation of cultural objects and the transformation of institutional practices in response to First Nations advocacy. You will be introduced to the ethical, moral and legal issues involved in the circulation of art around the world to facilitate the development of your global and cross-cultural thinking. You will participate in weekly seminars to develop your own perspective and point of view, in addition to engaging with a range of learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Gain an understanding of the role that collecting art and visual culture plays in broad political and historical developments.
Expand skills in research, critical and reflective thinking, and writing by evaluating key ideas and concepts.
Develop and strengthen understanding and engagement with ethical debates that apply to collecting, ownership and censorship within historical and contemporary arts contexts.

title: STUDIO PRACTICE D: VIDEO AND PERFORMANCE
syllabus_overview: In this practical subject you will explore technical, experimental, and conceptual approaches to artmaking in relation to contemporary and historical art practices. Through focused engagement with video art and performance art techniques and processes you will further develop the ability to situate your practice within the field and in response to specific project briefs. Practical workshops and group discussions about performance and video support further development of your independent studio practice, providing skills relating to techniques and processes; critical and reflective thinking; experimentation, risk taking and problem solving.
learning_outcomes: Develop independent studio practice through the exploration of materials, techniques, and processes specific to the study of video and performance
Work collaboratively and independently on set and self-directed video and performance projects.
Respond creatively and flexibly to feedback and learn how to manage deadlines.
Engage critically with contemporary art and apply discipline specific knowledge to set and self-directed video and performance projects.

title: STUDIO PRACTICE C: PAINTING AND SPATIAL PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: In this practical subject you will explore technical, experimental, and conceptual approaches to art making in relation to contemporary and historical art practices. Through focused exploration in painting and spatial practice you will further develop your experience in the dynamic hands-on learning environment of the studio. Practical workshops and group discussions support your independent studio practice, providing skills relating to processes and materials; critical and reflective thinking; experimentation, risk taking and problem solving.
learning_outcomes: Engage critically with contemporary art and apply discipline specific knowledge to set and self-directed painting and spatial practice projects.
Work collaboratively and independently on set and self-directed painting and spatial practice projects.
Respond creatively and flexibly to feedback and learn how to manage deadlines.
Develop independent studio practice through the exploration of materials, techniques, and processes specific to the study of painting and spatial practice.

title: VISUALISING ''NATURE'': LANDSCAPE, LAND ART AND ENVIRONMENTAL ETHICS
syllabus_overview: Our understanding of what is ‘nature’ or ‘natural’ is embedded in systems of value that are thoroughly mediated by representations in art and visual culture. In Western philosophical traditions, ‘nature’ has been understood as separate from ‘culture’ and as such more easily cast as a resource to be exploited for the benefit of humans. First Nations peoples have a more relational integrated worldview where human beings are but one component of a complex and ever-changing web of relationships. In this subject, you explore how these ideas are shaped by and reflected in various visual approaches over time, and critically consider the role that visualisations of ‘nature’ play in processes of social change. You focus on: the Western landscape tradition and its transformation at the encounter with Indigenous representations of Country; the influence of land art in its many manifestations on how we conceive of human/nature relations; and the long history and contemporary examples of artistic projects and interventions driven by the desire for environmental justice. You will participate in weekly seminars to develop your own perspective and point of view, in addition to engaging with a range of learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and develop an understanding of changing interpretations of the landscape tradition and their relation to ecological issues.
Consolidate advanced research, critical and reflective thinking and writing skills by evaluating key ideas and concepts.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of how art is made and responds to its cultural, political and historical context.
Analyse and evaluate ethical debates and ideas that apply to current ecological and environmental issues within a contemporary art context.

title: PAINTING TO PIXELS: CONTEMPORARY VISUAL CULTURES
syllabus_overview: What does contemporary art tell us about the world and our place within it? How do artists, museums and curators contribute to debates around globalisation and capitalism? Do we shape our identities through the images we make and consume? How are our ideas of sex, gender and race formed through looking or being looked at? Painting to Pixels interrogates the relationship between images and power in our increasingly visual world. You will examine a number of political, economic and ethical positions through case studies drawn from contemporary art and visual cultures. By developing skills in research, visual and textual analysis, and critical and creative thinking, you will formulate your own responses to vital questions facing our world. Across the learning materials and the weekly seminar, you will be encouraged to develop your own perspective on key issues in visual culture today and into the future. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in research and analysis across visual, theoretical and contextual material.
Recognise and reflect on social, cultural, and ethical issues of contemporary visual cultures.
Formulate reasoned and substantiated arguments about contemporary visual cultures through written and curatorial assignments.
Critically discuss a range of ideas and theories related to contemporary visual cultures

title: STUDIO PRACTICE E: INDEPENDENT PROJECT 1
syllabus_overview: This practical subject will consolidate your experience in the studio through the development of an independently led semester-long creative project. You will be guided through the process of producing a sustained body of practical work, while also developing the relevant conceptual frameworks and research skills to contextualise your practice within the field of contemporary art. You will engage in a range of activities designed to assist in your professional development as an artist.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrated ability to engage critically and reflectively with advanced conceptual and technical practice-based approaches.
Consolidate independent studio practice through the exploration of materials, techniques, and complex processes.
Recognise and reflect on some of the significant cultural, historical, ecological, and ethical issues of our time and identify how they are articulated through practice.
Respond creatively and efficiently to progressive feedback; demonstrate an ability to work independently managing time effectively building towards a semester long studio project.

title: STUDIO PRACTICE F: INDEPENDENT PROJECT 2
syllabus_overview: This practical subject will further consolidate your experience in the studio through the development and resolution of an independently led semester-long creative project. Building on your experience in Studio Practice E, you will be supported through the process of creating a second advanced body of practical work, while also developing the relevant conceptual frameworks and research skills to contextualise your practice within the field of contemporary art. You will work as part of team contributing to the project management, promotion and delivery of the public facing end of year graduation exhibition.
learning_outcomes: Work as part of a team to demonstrate the relevant industry skills to present a professional public facing graduation exhibition.
Demonstrate an ability to work independently and collectively, managing time and progressive deadlines in the process of delivering a resolved body of creative work.
Further consolidate independent studio practice, evidencing the progression and resolution of advanced material and technical processes.
Evidence an advanced ability to engage critically and reflectively with complex conceptual, material, and technical approaches to contemporary artistic practice.
Identify, contextualise, and articulate how practice-based research responds to the significant cultural, historical, ecological, and ethical issues of our time

title: AUSTRALIA AND ASIA: ENDURING ANXIETIES
syllabus_overview: This first year subject investigates the dynamics of Australia’s longstanding and complex relationship with the Asian region. We adopt a thematic approach while drawing on timely and relevant examples from across the region, including Japan, China, Indonesia, India, and more. The subject begins with a brief survey of Australia’s historical ties with Asia, then moves on to Australia’s contemporary regional setting. We explore Australia’s dense web of connections to Asia through personal, trade, security and cultural ties. We also consider the sources of tension that complicate the relationship, such as the threat of terrorism, rise of China, democratic rollback, and political instability, while unravelling the differences in history, culture and values that spur, at times, mutual suspicions and ambivalence about Australia’s place in Asia. We also explore efforts to improve Asia literacy and the role of migration and diasporic communities in Australian multiculturalism. The subject is delivered in StudyFlex mode and can be completed fully online or face-to-face at the Bundoora campus.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the complexities of Australia’s historical and contemporary relationship with the Asian region.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the key drivers underlining the enduring anxieties about Australia’s past and future relationship with Asia through the subject’s assessments
Compare how Australia and Asia have responded to political, economic and social change since the 19th century, and how it has impacted relations
Employ research and communications skills to develop a clear, coherent and independent exposition of knowledge as it relates to Australia’s relationship with Asia

title: THE MAKING OF MODERN ASIA
syllabus_overview: The twenty-first century is already being called the Asian Century. What were the countries and peoples we call Asia like 100 years ago, at the start of the twentieth century? How did they change across the century? And how did this process influence their current prosperity and sense of national identity? The subject will survey the major social, political and cultural changes of the past 100 years of so, including European colonisation, the impact of the expansion of Japan and the Second World War, the rise of Asian nationalisms and the wars of independence, consolidation of national political regimes, economic development and modernisation, the rapid recent rise of China and India. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Investigate the problems of the Asian Century and develop Asia Literacy to develop future career skills
Construct a critical argument or narrative in oral and written forms about the making of modern Asian nations, such as China, Japan, South Korea, India, Pakistan and Indonesia etc.
Critically analyse how the making of modern Asia connects to the history and the present in Asian societies, as well as how to envisage new futures in Asia.
Analyse changing and contested nature of the internal and external cultural and political boundaries of contemporary Asia
Discuss the diversity of social experience and cultural traditions that have contributed to contemporary Asia.

title: CHINA AND JAPAN: ASIAN PERSPECTIVES
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will study the civilisations of Australia’s Asian neighbours, China and Japan, in an historical perspective. Our understanding of China and Japan via the media and the public discourse is often based on Anglophone Western perspectives. However, there are also ‘Asian’ understandings deriving from long-existing interactions, for example, how Japanese people see China as a nation and ordinary Chinese people, and vice versa. You will critically examine different aspects of the two societies from pre-modern to modern times, including religions, modernity governance, social relations, ‘culture’ and engagement with the outside world. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Contribute meaningfully to critical discussions and debates about China and Japanese history, politics and culture.
Apply knowledge of China and Japan and research skills to construct an essay with a coherent argument.
Compare how China and Japan have responded to political, economic and social change since the 19th century.
Understand the basic parameters of Chinese and Japanese history, politics and culture.

title: ADVANCED CHINESE AND JAPANESE LANGUAGE 7: HISTORY THROUGH FILM AND DOCUMENTARY
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students with an advanced level of proficiency in either Chinese (native or non-native Chinese speakers) or Japanese. You will deepen your reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills through engagement with historically themed audio-visual materials (films and documentaries), authentic archival sources, and scholarly works. The focus is on understanding historical narratives of China and Japan as represented on screen and in primary sources. You will critically analyse how filmmakers and historians construct representations of major historical events, figures, and cultural transformations—from imperial dynasties to modern nation-building—and how these representations shape cultural memory. Through comparative analysis, you will explore how films and documentaries can illuminate, distort, or challenge historical understanding. For the Chinese studies stream, you will additionally read and discuss authentic historical essays, memoirs, and literary works besides cinematic depictions, increasing your knowledge to approximately 2,000 Chinese characters (HSK Level 4–5 range). For the Japanese studies stream, you will extend your advanced level language learning in addition to viewing films and documentaries, expanding your kanji knowledge to approximately 800, aiming towards Level N2 of the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLTP).
learning_outcomes: Analyse the societies, civilizations and cultures of historical China and Japan, and of East Asia as a whole, through multiple perspectives.
Produce advanced written and spoken discourse in Chinese or Japanese that integrates research from archival documents, historical literature, and scholarly analysis.
Read, write listen and speak in either Chinese or Japanese to interpret and discuss complex idea and themes of cultural and historical significance.

title: ADVANCED CHINESE AND JAPANESE LANGUAGE 8: SOCIETY THROUGH FILM AND DOCUMENTARY
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students with an advanced level of proficiency in either Chinese (native or non-native Chinese speakers) or in Japanese. You will further develop reading, writing, aural and oral language skills through audio-visual materials (films and documentaries), textbooks, and selections from authentic texts. You will also advance your critical understanding of issues in contemporary China and Japan (e.g., gender, minorities, social inequality, aging, social norms and popular culture). For the Chinese Studies component, this subject is designed to enable high-level students to further extend their professional Chinese language abilities and orient themselves in China-related studies. This subject is somewhere between the Chinese Proficiency Test (Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi HSK) Level 4 and Level 5. You will increase your total number of Chinese characters to approximately 2500, making progress towards Level 5. You will also read authentic texts by renowned Chinese writers and scholars. For Japanese Studies component, the entry point is somewhere between Level N4 and Level N3 of the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT). You will increase your total number of kanji to approximately 800, working towards Level N2 of the JLPT.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills in either Chinese or Japanese to interpret and discuss (individually or as part of a group) culturally and historically socially significant materials.
Engage in open inquiry and critically evaluate complex audio-visual and textual sources to synthesise insights in advanced Chinese or Japanese, demonstrating linguistic and cultural proficiency.
Analyse the societies, civilizations and cultures of contemporary China and Japan, and of East Asia as a whole, through multiple perspectives.

title: CRITICAL ISSUES IN CONTEMPORARY ASIA
syllabus_overview: The subject aims to explore the diversity of Asia, problematize the neat categories and ideas that underpin popular perceptions about 'Asia', while showcasing the research expertise of those working within Asia within the School of Social Sciences and Humanities. The broader and critical issues examined include identity, education, culture, language and minorities, development, displacement, environmental concerns, politics, and conflicts, etc. We explore these topics by first framing them in terms of long-term questions raised in the humanities and social sciences. Second, we sketch out the relationships between these questions. While the disciplinary backgrounds we bring to these questions include sociology, anthropology, linguistics, education, cultural studies, religion, philosophical studies, and political science, it will become evident that answers to these questions require a multidisciplinary approach. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject prerequisites before enrolling.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate diverse positions and/or arguments regarding a relevant topic in Asian Studies.
Summarise research and arguments on a relevant topic in Asian Studies.
Analyse local social and cultural groups and institutions in Asia in relation to historical and contemporary global processes.
Engage in peer teaching/learning activities in pairs and in groups.
Identify and evaluate the ethical and moral implications of key stereotypes and ideas as they relate to Asian societies.

title: ASIAN POP CULTURE
syllabus_overview: This subject takes a broad interdisciplinary approach to engage with and critique various elements of popular culture across East Asia, South Asia and South East Asia. You will reflect on what makes something 'popular' across five categories: film, fashion, music, novels and media mixes, and anime/ manga. These categories are explored in terms of, for example, nationalism, religion, education, technology, media, and language. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject enrolment requirements before enrolling in this subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate issues in Asian Studies from a variety of disciplinary perspectives in the humanities and social sciences (e.g. History, Sociology, Anthropology, Cultural Studies etc)
Critically analyse the nature of social, economic and cultural change in Asia in a variety of contexts
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of Asian popular culture across Asian societies

title: UNDERSTANDING JAPANESE SOCIETY
syllabus_overview: Japan is well known in Australia for its delicious cuisine, powder snow, fantastic hospitality and amazing tourism. In this subject, we dive deeper to understand contemporary Japanese society by exploring some of the social and political issues that characterise today’s Japan. Topics include social inequality, education, gender issues, religion, politics and peace. This subject is conducted entirely in English and the reading material is in English. You will come away with a sophisticated understanding of contemporary Japan. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Produce an original well presented analysis or response to a relevant topic at an advanced standard
Present a persuasive argument in Japanese Studies an advanced standard
Contribute to and lead discussions on the daily readings on a daily basis
Comprehend, analyse and articulate diverse positions/arguments at an advanced standard

title: DIAGNOSTICS I: ADULT ASSESSMENT TECHNIQUES
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the fundamental clinical assessment procedures and the relevant acoustics and psychoacoustics used in the audiological evaluation of adult patients. You will gain a theoretical understanding of how to take case histories, perform otoscopy, pure tone audiometry, acoustic immittance, and speech discrimination tests. You will explore clinical decision-making skills as you learn to select appropriate tests, interpret and integrate your audiological findings, and write comprehensive reports incorporating referrals and appropriate management strategies.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, interpret, and apply the principles of acoustics to audiology practice.
Develop appropriate management plans and referral pathways based on professional knowledge and test results.
Integrate theoretical knowledge about diagnostic pure tone audiometric assessment techniques to generate sound clinical hypotheses.
Accurately determine the nature and level of hearing impairment diagnostic test results.
Clearly report complex audiological problems and proposed solutions based on test results.
Integrate theoretical knowledge about tympanometry, acoustic reflex testing and speech audiometry assessment techniques to generate sound clinical hypotheses.

title: AUDIO-VESTIBULAR ANATOMY, PATHOLOGY AND PHYSIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Audiologists need a good working knowledge of the anatomy and physiology of the structures involved in hearing, and understanding of the diseased or disordered auditory system. This subject introduces elements of acoustics and psychoacoustics to deepen your understanding of auditory function. Through lectures, this subject will provide you with knowledge about the structure and function of the peripheral/central auditory system and the vestibular system. It will further provide you with an understanding of common auditory pathologies resulting from disease or injury, and the impact of those pathologies on a patient's hearing. Your learning in the subject will be assessed through exams and a written assignment.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and apply theoretical knowledge about the anatomical and physiological processes of the auditory systems for the diagnosis and treatment of common pathologies.
Investigate and apply theoretical knowledge about the anatomical and physiological processes of the vestibular system for the diagnosis and treatment of common pathologies.
Investigate and apply theoretical knowledge about common pathologies of the auditory and vestibular systems.
Apply and integrate the principles of acoustics and psychoacoustics to the auditory system.

title: FOUNDATIONS OF COMMUNICATION AND AURAL REHABILITATION
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce you to hearing aid systems and the principles of person-centred care (PCC) and professional communication. Through lectures and tutorials, you will develop a comprehensive understanding of the styles and components of hearing aids, as well as the theory of acoustics. Additionally, the subject will cover reflective practice, interprofessional communication, and overall communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise knowledge of electroacoustic properties of hearing aids to optimise client outcomes.
Integrate and apply knowledge of psychoacoustics to solve problems in audiology.
Critically evaluate the importance of effective communication, cultural sensitivity and advocacy in establishing foundational person-centred care strategies in healthcare
Critically analyse client information and make evidence-based decisions on hearing aid candidacy to ensure optimal client outcomes.
Critically apply and reflect on interprofessional collaboration and conflict resolution strategies in audiology care.

title: DIAGNOSTICS II: OBJECTIVE ASSESSMENT TECHNIQUES
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will learn about concepts and procedures used in objective measurements of hearing, balance and site-of-lesion testing in audiology. You will learn about the origin of otoacoustic emissions and acoustically evoked potentials of the auditory pathway, including electrocochleography, auditory brainstem responses, middle and late latency potentials, auditory steady state responses. Building on this theoretical knowledge, you will be taught skills in assessing otoacoustic emissions, auditory evoked potentials, and integrating the results of these objective techniques with behavioural tests used in audiological evaluations. You will further gain knowledge and practical skills in the assessment of vestibular function and central auditory function. You will build on practical knowledge and be taught skills in the diagnosis of pathology and interpretation of advanced diagnostic assessments particularly in relation to vestibular pathology.
learning_outcomes: Design and critically review the protocols and procedures for oto- acoustic emission and auditory evoked response measurements to inform sound clinical decision-making.
Integrate and consolidate theoretical information on the anatomical and physiological principles as they apply to objective assessment techniques.
Critically evaluate and contrast clinical frameworks for decision- making and implementing diagnostic assessment strategies for vestibular pathologies.
Integrate theoretical knowledge and clinical and/or technical skills to assess vestibular function and rehabilitation.
Apply cognitive and technical skills to interpret clinical tests and generate differential diagnoses.

title: PAEDIATRIC ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: The audiological assessment of young children requires specialised clinical knowledge and skills. In this subject, you will develop a broad understanding of the principles underlying the assessment and clinical management of neonates, infants and children under 5 years of age. Through lectures, you will learn about normal child development, causes of hearing loss in children, auditory processing disorders and the impact of childhood hearing impairment. The subject will include newborn hearing screening programs aimed at identifying hearing loss as early in life as possible. Behavioural assessment techniques used in screening and diagnostic paediatric audiology are presented. Through a series of workshops, you will acquire skills in behavioural audiological assessments including Visual Reinforcement Audiometry (VRA), Play Audiometry and Auditory Processing Disorders.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the role of hearing screening in early identification of hearing impairment
Critically reflect on the epidemiology and aetiology of childhood hearing impairment and relate to normal developmental milestones.
Critically evaluate research findings to determine appropriate clinical choices in paediatric hearing assessments
Integrate information from subjective reports, research publications, ethical considerations and behavioural test results, to formulate sound clinical recommendations for paediatric clients

Implement and justify developmentally appropriate hearing assessments including behavioural response audiometry (BOA), visual reinforcement audiometry (VRA), play audiometry, and auditory processing disorder testing.

title: RESEARCH METHODS IN AUDIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will learn the skills needed to understand, evaluate, design and carry out research in audiology. You will learn a variety of research methods, including quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods as well as meta-analysis. At the completion of this subject you will be able to critically appraise research literature, design a research study, generate and write hypotheses, analyse and interpret data, and report on the results of your research. Students will further gain insight into the dissemination of their research findings.
learning_outcomes: Integrate and consolidate the conceptual interpretation of statistical outcomes (descriptive and/or inferential) to appraise conclusions, external validity and communicate results.
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of various research designs, data analytic procedure and choose suitable methods to address research questions.
Demonstrate an understanding of specific methodological challenges inherent in both quantitative and qualitative research approaches.
Integrate and consolidate theory and experimental methods to critically evaluate research literature for scientific validity and clinical applicability

title: ETHICAL BUSINESS PRACTICE IN AUDIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Audiology is a profession which engages with both healthcare and industry to provide innovative solutions for people with hearing loss. In this subject you will learn how to plan and prepare a business idea, manage business risks and opportunities, and prepare a business plan. You will be introduced to concepts of professional business conduct and responsible leadership in the context of professional standards, ethics and best practices in audiology.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate business ideas in the context of business framework in relation to audiological practice.
Design a business plan for an audiology practice in line with professional and ethical standards.
Evaluate the ethical implications of business decisions in the context of audiological practice.
Integrate knowledge about the core elements of business and its management in relation to audiological practice.

title: PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE - CLINICAL AUDIOLOGY A
syllabus_overview: This is the first of your clinical practicum subjects. You will be taught to develop competence in basic adult audiological assessment through a combination of observation in clinical environments, computer simulations, independent learning and practice hearing assessments, on real clients. You will apply your knowledge of fundamental clinical assessment procedures, including history taking, client preparation, otoscopy, pure tone audiometry, acoustic immittance assessment and speech discrimination testing. You will be introduced to critical and analytical thinking skills required to select appropriate tests and interpret and integrate findings across the test battery. In addition, you will be taught skills in client interaction and professional conduct in a clinical setting. Your learning in this subject will be assessed through skills test and assignment work. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Apply technical knowledge and skills to perform basic pure tone audiometry, immittance audiometry and speech audiometry on adult patients.
Demonstrate proficient reflective practice by critically evaluating learning experiences and identifying opportunities for personal and professional development in the clinical environment
Integrate and apply knowledge of safety and compliance to maintain clinical environments and equipment
Analyse and interpret information from the basic test battery to determine the nature and degree of hearing impairment.
Evaluate and select appropriate clinical tests required to conduct basic audiological evaluations.

title: SOLUTIONS IN HEARING CARE AND AURAL REHABILITATION 3
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will gain both knowledge and practical skills in advanced aspects of rehabilitative audiology. You will learn about pediatric rehabilitation, the management and rehabilitation of complex clients and explore strategies for hearing preservation. Additionally, you will develop expertise in effective communication with this a focus on the complex client.
learning_outcomes: Apply culturally sensitive communication techniques to meet the specific needs of clients from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds in audiological practice
Critically evaluate and refine advanced communication strategies to optimise person-centred interactions with complex clients.

Recognise strength-based approaches for culturally safe communication to foster trust and building of respectful relationship with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in their audiological care.
Synthesise advanced rehabilitation strategies to effectively manage diverse and complex audiological conditions across different age groups, emphasising inclusivity and cultural competence

Recognise and advocate for the integration of multidisciplinary approaches in client management, emphasising the value of collaboration with clients, colleagues, and external organisations to achieve optimal client outcomes.

title: PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE - CLINICAL AUDIOLOGY B
syllabus_overview: Building on the knowledge and practical skills gained in Clinical Audiology A, this subject provides you with an opportunity to consolidate your skills in audiological assessment of adults and children. Through a combination of off-campus clinical placements and focused workshops, you will be taught to develop independence, professionalism and communication skills. You will be provided with an expanded range of casework, including hearing aid assessments and objective techniques. The learnings in this subject will be assessed by examination, portfolio, a written report and assessment at clinical placement. Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure. Students attendance at professional placements will contribute to meeting this requirement for professional recognition as an audiologist. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and synthesise case histories and audiometric data, demonstrating the ability to accurately interpret results and ascertain the nature and degree of hearing impairment, within a patient-centred diagnostic framework.
Exhibit an advanced knowledge of and commitment to professional and statutory requirements, ensuring public safety and the integrity of audiological practice.
Articulate and advocate for the diverse hearing needs of all individuals with an emphasis on ensuring accessible care and services.

Demonstrate proficiency in performing and adapting audiometric evaluations, including pure-tone audiometry, immittance, and speech audiometry, to meet the specific needs of adult and paediatric clients

Apply the principles of the Health Records Act to ensure the ethical management and protection of client information, upholding confidentiality and privacy in all clinical documentation and communication.

title: SOLUTIONS IN HEARING CARE AND AURAL REHABILITATION 2
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will gain comprehensive knowledge of implantable devices, including their functions and applications, the assessment and management of tinnitus and enhance your understanding of Deaf awareness. Alongside these topics, you will continue to develop and refine your skills in reflective practice, ensuring you can critically evaluate and improve your professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and synthesize knowledge of the Deaf community's cultural and communication requirements to develop advanced advocacy strategies.
Develop and critically evaluate strategies to optimise the clinical environment and modes of communication, including the effective use of interpreters.

Critically apply evidence-based knowledge to assess and manage audiological conditions in adults and children, integrating person-centred care principles to tailor interventions and support individual client needs.

Apply evidence-based practices to identify and defend the selection of suitable candidates for implantable devices and develop comprehensive management plans and referral pathways based on professional knowledge and diagnostic outcomes.

title: SOLUTIONS IN HEARING CARE AND AURAL REHABILITATION 1
syllabus_overview: Building on the foundational knowledge and skills acquired in AUD4003 (Foundations of Communication and Aural Rehabilitation), this subject will enhance your understanding of hearing aid devices, focusing on their electroacoustic characteristics and methods for measuring client outcomes. Through a combination of workshops and self-directed learning modules, you will develop skills in patient-centred audiological rehabilitation and counselling techniques. Additionally, the subject will introduce you to First Nations hearing health and rehabilitation.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and refine communication styles, counselling techniques, and rehabilitation plans to effectively address the unique needs and goals of diverse client populations, while systematically assessing clinical outcomes.

Critically evaluate the social determinants of health that impact ear health and integrate this understanding with the specific rehabilitation needs and considerations for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, to develop informed and culturally appropriate care strategies.

Synthesise knowledge of electroacoustic properties and technical specifications of hearing aids to construct well-informed clinical hypotheses that address diverse auditory needs and optimise client outcomes.
Critically evaluate and review the measurement of hearing aid and device performance to ensure sound clinical decision making and trouble-shooting.

Critically assess the role of effective communication, cultural competence, and advocacy in developing and implementing inclusive, person-centered rehabilitation programs that address the diverse needs of clients.
Integrate and consolidate information on commonly used assistive listening devices to generate sound clinical hypotheses.

title: REHABILITATION III: ADVANCED HEARING DEVICES AND INSTRUMENTATION
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will gain knowledge and practical skills in advanced aspects of rehabilitative audiology. You will learn about pediatric rehabilitation, the management and rehabilitation of complex clients, the technical and medical aspects of implantable devices and candidacy, and tele-audiology.
learning_outcomes: Critically review and evaluate the evidence to make informed decisions on suitable candidates for implantable devices
Critically evaluate and review information from a wide variety of sources to develop clinically-sound rehabilitative strategies for special population groups.
Develop appropriate management plans and referral pathways based on professional knowledge and test results.
Integrate theoretical knowledge about diagnostic assessment techniques to generate sound clinical hypotheses.

title: CLINICAL AUDIOLOGY D
syllabus_overview: This subject provides you with an opportunity to further advance your skills in audiological assessment and rehabilitation. Through community clinical placements, you will gain experience in complex case management in both adult and paediatric populations. Though you will be working under the supervision of qualified audiologists, you will begin to assume responsibility for all aspects of audiological healthcare, thereby enhancing your independence and job readiness. Your learning in this subject will be assessed through clinical examinations, assessment of clinical performance during placements and different assignments. . Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure. Your attendance at professional placements will contribute to meeting this requirement for professional recognition as an audiologist. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Practice with autonomy and accountability in professional placement settings.
Apply advanced theoretical knowledge in professional practice.
Investigate, analyse and synthesise complex clinical data to generate clinical management appropriate to adults and children.

title: REHABILITATION I: HEARING DEVICES AND INSTRUMENTATION
syllabus_overview: Hearing aid systems are a major component of the audiological management of hearing impairment. In this subject, you will develop a comprehensive understanding of the styles, components and electroacoustic characteristics of hearing aids. You will develop the skills necessary to select an appropriate hearing aid and/or assistive listening device based on a client's hearing loss, lifestyle and communication needs. Through hands-on workshops, you will learn how to take ear impressions, modify a selected device and verify its fitting in a clinical setting. Your learning in this subject will be assessed through written exams and assignments.
learning_outcomes: Integrate information on the electroacoustic and technical features of hearing aids and apply this knowledge to generate sound clinical hypotheses.
Critically evaluate and review information to develop clinically-sound decisions about suitable candidates for hearing aid settings.
Critically design, evaluate and review the measurement of hearing aid and device performance to ensure sound clinical decision making and trouble-shooting.
Synthesise specialist knowledge to create and modify high quality earmould/shells, to improve clinical outcomes.
Integrate and consolidate information on commonly used assistive listening devices to generate sound clinical hypotheses.

title: REHABILITATION 2 - LIFESPAN REHABILITATION
syllabus_overview: Aural rehabilitation is an integral component of clinical audiology. Building on the foundation knowledge and skills gained in AUD5RHD (Rehabilitation I - Hearing Devices and Instrumentation), in this subject you will further develop your understanding of the impact of hearing impairment on individuals, their communication partners and the wider community. Through a combination of workshops and self-directed learning modules, you will develop skills in patient-centred audiological rehabilitation and counselling techniques.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate mastery of the theory of aural rehabilitation and the psychosocial impacts of hearing loss on the individual, family unit and community as a whole.
Critically design, evaluate and review individually-tailored client needs, rehabilitation goals, communication strategies, and clinical outcomes.
Critically review and adapt your communication style, counselling techniques and rehabilitation plans for different client population groups.
Critically reflect on clinical practice as an audiology practitioner.

title: METABOLIC BIOCHEMISTRY AND CELL BIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Biochemistry explores the molecules and interactions that drive life itself, from the tiniest molecules to complex biological systems. This field is a cornerstone of biology, essential for breakthroughs in biomedical research and biotechnology. In BCH2MBC, students are introduced to cell biology and cell metabolism, building on the concepts developed in Introduction to Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (BCH2IBM). Students study the mechanism by which enzymes promote sequences of chemical reactions; concepts of bioenergetics and thermodynamics; the different and interconnected metabolic pathways that oxidise macronutrients such as carbohydrates, lipids and proteins into ATP, the energy currency of cells; and how cells dynamically adapt their metabolic utilisation to generate biomolecules for their function. Learning is consolidated through problem-based learning workshops, where you'll apply threshold concepts to real-life scenarios enhancing your critical thinking and scientific reasoning. Practical laboratory classes will give you experience with key biochemistry techniques including enzyme kinetics, metabolism assays and analysis of complex data.
learning_outcomes: Summarise scientific literature relating to cellular metabolism in a visual format
Analyse and present data accurately and consistent with scientific conventions.
Demonstrate effective communication , interrogating, evaluating and presenting relevant scientific information.
Describe fundamental concepts in protein function and metabolic biochemistry which underlie cellular life.
Conduct biochemistry techniques in a safe and professional manner in a laboratory setting

title: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH IN AUDIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Research in audiology is a rapidly progressing field which translates into changes in clinical practice. Audiologists require a strong grasp of how to search for evidence in the literature to inform their own clinical practice. This subject will provide students with the knowledge of how clinical decisions can be based on valid and reliable evidence, with particular reference to a chosen area of interest within the field of audiology. Learning in this subject will be assessed through an individually written thesis and a research project.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and critique the literature in the field of Audiology
Generate and address answerable evidence-based hypotheses of relevance to the field of Audiology.
Communicate complex concepts regarding the validity of scientific evidence and clinical applicability/potential for change in clinical practice.
Design, implement and disseminate an independently directed research study of relevance to the field of audiology.

title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Biochemistry explores the molecules and interactions that drive life itself - from the tiniest cells to complex biological systems. This field is a cornerstone of biology, essential for breakthroughs in biomedical research and biotechnology. In BCH2IBM, students are introduced to the chemical and cellular basis for life, the blueprint for which is encoded in DNA. The subject will cover processes that govern DNA replication, transcription and translation, prior to examining the 3D structure and function of proteins. A broader overview of cellular operation will also be examined through discussion of lipids, membranes and signalling mechanisms. Learning is consolidated through problem-based learning workshops, where you'll apply threshold concepts to real-life scenarios, enhancing your critical thinking and scientific reasoning. Practical laboratory laboratory classes will give you experience with key biochemistry and molecular biology techniques, including PCR, manipulation of recombinant DNA, and protein analyses.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the importance of biochemical processes.
Describe the structure and function of biological macromolecules and biochemical processes underlying cellular life.
Demonstrate effective communication , interrogating, evaluating and presenting relevant scientific information.
Analyse and present data accurately and consistent with scientific conventions.
Conduct biochemistry techniques in a safe and professional manner in a laboratory setting.

title: ADVANCED ANALYTICAL BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject students extend previous knowledge and practical skills gained from second year Biochemistry. The laboratory component emphasizes the underlying theory, provides experience in experimental design and provides hands-on practical instruction in analytical biochemistry techniques including organelle isolation, enzyme assays, electrophoresis, nucleic acid isolation and gene expression. In addition to the practicals, students will complete workshops where additional theory will be presented, extending the techniques demonstrated in the laboratory. The workshops will also provide an opportunity to further develop skills in quantitative literacy, scientific communication and critical analysis of scientific methodology and data.
learning_outcomes: Be able to follow detailed protocols, follow best occupational health and safety practice and apply advanced techniques in analytical biochemistry to generate and analyse data.
Explain concepts in analytical biochemistry and molecular biology using appropriate vocabulary.
Collect, analyse and evaluate information from literature to prepare a thorough scientific report.
Discuss and present information in the field of Biochemistry orally to peers.

title: ADVANCED TOPICS IN BIOCHEMISTRY AND SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you extend their previous knowledge gained from second year Biochemistry in relation to proteins (structure and function), bioinformatics and genomics. There will be an emphasis on how integrating and applying proteomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic data can provide a predictive understanding of biological systems as well as how a molecular understanding of proteins and proteostasis and the regulation of genes can lead to biotechnological and medical applications. During the semester you will undertake a major bioinformatics project (supported by online modules) based on annotation of metagenomic data. You will also complete a group assignment to produce a multimedia, webinar-style presentation of an emerging technology related to one of the lecture topics. In addition, you will complete an in-class test on Bioinformatics and Systems Biology.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, interpret and present bioinformatic data using online tools.

Explain concepts in biochemistry and molecular biology using appropriate vocabulary, including protein structure, function and analysis, bioinformatics and systems biology, gene structure and function and DNA technology.
Evaluate and analyse proteomic and bioinformatic data.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of current and emerging technologies related to systems biology/biochemistry (including advances in genome editing, DNA sequencing and proteomic analysis).

Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Biochemistry and Cell Biology consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part-time) individual research project, supervised by a SABE scientist whose research is in the disciplines of biochemistry, cell biology and/or cancer medicine. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. The School Honours co-ordinator will provide more information on the application process including a comprehensive list of available research projects. BCH401A is the first subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in SABE. Students must take BCH401A first.

Apply concepts in biochemistry and molecular biology to solve theoretical problems and interpret experimental data.

title: PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE - CLINICAL AUDIOLOGY C
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore advanced clinical audiology skills, with an emphasis on rehabilitative audiology in adults. Through focused and intensive external clinical placements, you will enhance your clinical competence and reasoning skills, and will further develop your own professional identity. Through professional practice workshops, you will be taught to develop an understanding of ethical practice and legislation regulations in audiology. Your learning in this subject will be assessed by assignments, clinical and oral examinations and by assessment of clinical performance during placements. Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure. Your attendance at professional placements will contribute to meeting this requirement for professional recognition as an audiologist. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate professional and ethical issues in audiological practice.
Apply knowledge and skills in Audiology with autonomy and accountability
Plan and execute time management strategies applicable to a range of clinical settings
Apply advanced theoretical knowledge and practical competency to plan and implement audiology assessment and management of adults and children, using Patient Centred Care principals

title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Biochemistry and Molecular Biology is concerned with the function of biological systems at the molecular level. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology is central to most studies in biology and life sciences and is directly related to biomedical research and biotechnology. In this subject, students are introduced to gene structure and function, DNA replication, transcription and translation; molecular biology; protein structure and its relationship to protein function and enzyme kinetics. Students will investigate a typical biochemistry technique and conduct research on a specific protein.
learning_outcomes: Prepare scientific reports that present coherent, concise and evidence-based explanations to communicate to peers, using a variety of presentation modes.
Participate as an effective team member and collaborate on selected learning exercises.
Demonstrate independent learning and research skills by locating, interrogating and evaluating relevant and reliable scientific information.
Compute basic mathematical calculations and prepare graphical representations of information, to aid in the interpretation of biochemical data consistent with scientific standards.
Apply biochemical and molecular biology techniques, principles and methodologies in addressing research problems.

Use the basic vocabulary of biochemistry and molecular biology to describe the structures and functions of biological macromolecules, in order to demonstrate their knowledge and understanding of the concepts underlying structure-function relationships that affect cellular processes in health and disease.

title: ANIMAL AND PLANT LIFE
syllabus_overview: All organisms face challenges if they are to survive. In this subject we will explore how structures that have evolved within animals and within plants function to address key challenges that living organisms face. You will discover the differences between plants and animals in how they capture and distribute energy and nutrients around their bodies and then utilize them for growth and movement. Other interactions between an organism and its environment that you will learn are how an immobile plant defends itself from predators and how animals regulate their internal temperature. You will examine plant structures critical for growth and learn of the role of plant growth regulators. Animal development and animal adaptations for feeding and moving will be explored. This subject may involve working with live arthropods.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to record biological observations
Distinguish and describe plant and animal structures and their functions.
Conduct simple scientific experiments that address biological questions and communicate the interpretation of results scientifically.

learning_outcomes: Refine practical experience and advanced knowledge in the fields of biochemistry, cell biology and/or cancer medicine.

Compare and contrast published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Develop intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice
Develop advanced oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.

title: BIOLOGY OF CELL AND ORGANISM
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students are introduced to the vast and exciting field of biology. Our emphasis is on cells and the processes that allow cells to function and grow. In lectures we discuss topics including cell biology and diversity, genetics, molecular biology and how these influence our latest thinking about evolution. We also dip our toes into a little plant biology and cell growth and division to show how cells cooperate in an organism. Lecture material and relevant questions will be presented in advance on the LMS site for students to work through, and workshops will be used to explain the more difficult concepts and for interactive problem solving. The practical component focuses on biological observation, laboratory skills and data interpretation, and introduces a number of biological disciplines. BIO1CO is a cornerstone subject, so there is some emphasis on the graduate capabilities, especially creative/critical thinking and communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Complete scientific experiments that examine aspects of cell biology, and involve: interpreting data, recognizing methodological issues, identifying the theoretical basis for the experiment, and communicating observations and results.
Describe and discuss the morphological and functional features of different cell types.
Develop and apply creative/critical thinking skills in a collaborative setting to problem-solve complex biological challenges and communicate solutions as a team.
Explain the biological and physical processes occurring in different cell types.

title: ECOLOGY, EVOLUTION AND BIODIVERSITY
syllabus_overview: The evolution of life on earth is a product of the interaction between organisms and the environment. BIO1EEB will explore the amazing diversity of life from a global and Australian perspective. How population genetics allows evolutionary changes of adaptation over both short and long periods of time will be discussed. BIO1EEB will explore the ecological forces that determine the distribution of life forms, the flow of energy through ecosystems and the dynamics of natural populations as well as the impacts of humans on ecosystems . This subject addresses La Trobe's Sustainability Thinking Essential, which entails deep appreciation of how the choices we make affects the natural, economic, social, political and cultural systems; now and in the future.
learning_outcomes: Classify the main kingdoms and phyla of eukaryotes using diagnostic characteristics, phylogenetic criteria and/or taxonomic keys
Distinguish, describe and/or explain the processes that have led to the current distribution of organisms in populations, communities and biomes, with a focus on Australian plants and animals
Distinguish, describe and /or explain the evolution of organisms by natural selection and other processes
Distinguish, describe and/or explain the principles of population genetics and their relationship to natural selection
Distinguish, describe and/or explain ecosystem processes including species interactions and energy flow, and the economic, social and environmental impacts of humans on ecosystems.

title: PRACTICE OF SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: This is a second year level biology subject which explores both experimental design issues and the use of statistics to analyse data from experiments. Basic statistical concepts and aspects of experimental design will be introduced, followed by in-depth exploration of case studies of biological research. Using this knowledge, you will work in small groups to identify a gap in knowledge by locating and synthesising published research on a topic, create a novel research aim and hypothesis and, further develop the design of a theoretical experiment to test the hypothesis (including consideration of ethical issues associated with the proposed research). Group work will commence in week 1.
learning_outcomes: Identify the appropriate statistical test for analysing data for selected experimental designs and produce and interpret statistical software outputs
Be recognised by peers as an active group member in researching for the group oral presentation and for the experimental design task
Identify types of variables and apply this knowledge to experimental design and statistical analysis.
Identify and explain the applicability of experimental design concepts to biological research questions and hypotheses
Describe and interpret the results of analysis of biological experiments using statistical and biological terms

title: CLINICAL BIOCHEMISTRY AND HAEMATOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject addresses the commonly encountered pathology tests in the two major clinical pathology areas of haematology and biochemistry. Topics include blood cell morphology; full blood examination (FBE); leukaemia, haemoglobinophathies; haemostasis; drug-induced blood dyscrasias; introduction to blood group serology. The clinical biochemistry component encompasses serum components, enzymes, proteins, lipoproteins and other components of diagnostic interest such as bilirubin, sugars, minerals, hormones and blood gases. Numerous case studies will be examined with a view to developing the analytical skills of the student. Discipline knowledge and change management skills will be further applied in the development and proposal of novel ideas designed to bring about improvements in diagnosis, service, quality or efficiency in clinical pathology environments.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate complex case studies involving diverse pathology to the extent that a reasonable hypothesis can be constructed.
Demonstrate active pursuit of independent learning strategies and critical analysis of information sources and tools.

Investigate the dynamic changes taking place in Point of Care Testing (POCT and other technologies and reflect on how these have come about and why by considering the competing interests of stake holders such as general practitioners (GPs), pathology laboratories and pharmacists.
Collaborate effectively in teams to address problems and future challenges in haematology and biochemistry.
Accurately interpret essential laboratory tests used to diagnose common disorders of a haematological and biochemical nature and be able to apply this knowledge to the solving of simple case studies.

Present case studies and innovative ideas in a professional, engaging and persuasive manner including consideration of new technologies that will influence the future of pathology diagnosis and generate novel ideas about how these will benefit stakeholders such as patients, pathology laboratories and GPs.

title: MOLECULES, GENES AND CELLS
syllabus_overview: Living organisms, with their many intricate and intriguing processes, are composed of lifeless molecules. BIO1MGC takes a look at how those molecules are organised into the smallest unit of life, cells, across a range of organisms. BIO1MGC also covers how those cells capture light energy, break down molecules to release energy, synthesise new molecules, communicate with other cells, and how the instructions to perform those functions are stored and passed on to the next generation.
learning_outcomes: Name the classes of biological molecules, describe their function in cellular processes, and describe and explain typical separation technologies for those molecules.
Describe and distinguish the features of prokaryotic and eukaryotic (i.e. plant and animal cells, and explain the function of organelles.
Describe and explain Mendelian genetics and its role in inheritance.

Describe and explain basic cell biology processes, including energy metabolism (photosynthesis and cellular respiration), DNA replication, transcription and translation and their regulation, and cell signalling.
Apply critical laboratory skills such as microscopy and micro pipetting to complete scientific experiments that examine different aspects of cell biology.
Locate and critically evaluate scientific information and effectively communicate scientific ideas in written and oral formats.

title: ADVANCED SKILLS IN LIFE SCIENCES
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn about techniques in Life Sciences, covering approaches from genetics, ecotoxicology, behaviour, physiology and ecology. Application of these techniques will span questions from the species to the landscape and ecosystem level. Students will work with research scientists who are specialists in techniques relevant to industry, the research laboratory, and the field. The subject has a strong focus on providing students with the opportunity to understand, design, apply and analyse experiments based on current techniques. This subject delivers theoretical concepts in concert with experimental design, application and analysis from a range of techniques used in Life Science research. The breadth of such techniques is rapidly growing, so students will be exposed to techniques at the current forefront of experimental applications in a modern research group.
learning_outcomes: Convey an expert understanding of scientific methods and their application through verbal communication
Explain research techniques from a diverse range of fields
Recognise and apply established knowledge and concepts relating to a range of current techniques in the fields of environmental research
Analyse and critically evaluate the validity of experimental design
Apply specialist knowledge of techniques to independently design experiments aimed at answering scientific questions

title: BIO-BUSINESS MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will be required to apply for a job within a virtual biotechnology company and work in groups to produce and market a virtual product. Students will be guided by career development staff and academic staff on a weekly basis, with input from industry professionals. Students will cover aspects of bio-business such as organizational structure, IP, scientific reasoning, market research, and ethics.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and present an argument to support newly generated or existing data
Discuss and explain key elements of finding employment in the biotechnology sector
Effectively collaborate with a group of unfamiliar colleagues to achieve desired outcomes
Present a report/website to disseminate a complex body of work to an expert audience
Demonstrate effective time management while working towards group deadlines
Analyse and evaluate the value of scientific data

title: METABOLIC BIOCHEMISTRY AND CELL BIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Biochemistry is concerned with the function of biological systems at the molecular level. It is central to most studies in biology and life sciences and is directly related to biomedical research and biotechnology. In this subject, you are introduced to cell biology and cell metabolism, building on the concepts developed in BCM201 (Introduction to Biochemistry and Molecular Biology). You will study the generation of energy in cells through the oxidation of carbohydrates and lipids; the formation of ATP, the energy currency of cells; lipids, cellular membranes and compartmentation; and the signalling processes that co-ordinate and regulate cellular activity. The practical exercises illustrate some basic experimental and data analysis skills and reinforce concepts in metabolism and cell biology.
learning_outcomes: Compute basic mathematical calculations and prepare graphical representations of information, to aid in the interpretation of biochemical data consistent with scientific standards

Use the basic vocabulary of biochemistry and molecular biology to describe the generation of cellular energy in the form of ATP from the oxidation of various fuels, and demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the concepts of cellular metabolism, compartmentation, cell signalling pathways and other aspects of cell biology.
Apply biochemical and molecular biology techniques, principles and methodologies in addressing research problems.
Prepare scientific reports that present coherent, concise and evidence-based explanations to communicate to peers, using a variety of presentation modes.
Demonstrate independent learning and research skills by locating, interrogating and evaluating relevant and reliable scientific information.

title: BIOINFORMATICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will be introduced to the ever expanding field of bioinformatics. Students will learn how to locate, use and apply commonly available bioinformatics software programs to address biological problems. Students will also be introduced to molecular modelling software used to solve biological problems. This unit requires no prior experience in bioinformatics
learning_outcomes: Navigate and be familiar with various free web-based bioinformatics programs. Critically analyse and solve scientific problems in the field of Bioinformatics.
Apply biostatistics to solve bioinformatic problems.
Recognise critical issues and limitations in the current bioinformatics field and tools. Apply precise terminology and concepts to describe bioinformatics.

Use advanced bioinformatics techniques, including database searching, alignments, pattern analysis and predictive study to solve scientific problems. Acquire the ability to assess whether the application of advanced tools and scientific approaches are appropriate for a particular scientific problem in the field of Bioinformatics.

title: PROTEOMICS AND GENOMICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will gain theoretical experience with molecular biology, protein expression (in prokaryotes and eukaryotic systems) and protein chemistry techniques most commonly used in the early stages of proteomics and genomics research. The students will also learn a wide variety of advanced topics in proteomics and genomics including (but not limited to) the next generation cloning techniques such as 'Gibson Assembly', 'In-Fusion', 'SLICE', 'LIC' and 'TA' cloning, CRISPR-mediated gene editing, Next Gen Sequencing, RNAseq, epigenetics, post-translational modifications and mass spectrometry (including SILAC). In workshops, which are an integral part of this subject, students will learn about practical problem solving related to various subjects taught in this course. Students will also use online data analysis software to identify DNA and protein molecules and algorithms to identify CRISPR gene targets, RNAseq analysis and methylation analysis. In completing tasks for this subject, students will gain confidence in applying their knowledge to future research problems.
learning_outcomes: Investigate, critically analyse, synthesise and convey complex information in a disciplinary context.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of advanced theoretical concepts in molecular biology and protein chemistry
Apply appropriate bioinformatic software to analyse and critically interpret genetic or proteomic data
Interpret and critically evaluate experimental data

title: PROTEIN CHEMISTRY
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide students with the opportunity to enhance their practical laboratory skills through a variety of protein chemistry applications. A combination of practical classes and workshops will enable students to understand and carry out laboratory techniques to purify and characterise protein preparations. In completing tasks for this subject, students are expected to develop skills in critical thinking, data analysis, teamwork and scientific communication.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate experimental protocols and methodologies.
Collaborate effectively within a laboratory setting, applying strong organisational and teamwork skills.
Communicate experimental findings and data clearly, in formats appropriate for scientific publication.
Demonstrate a strong understanding of protein purification and characterisation techniques.
Demonstrate competency in executing key laboratory techniques in protein chemistry.

title: PRACTICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide you with the opportunity to enhance your practical skills in a variety of contemporary molecular biology applications. Practical classes will require you to carry out laboratory techniques such as PCR, cloning, protein expression, protein purification and immunoblotting. In completing tasks for this subject, you are expected to develop technical competency and skills in critical thinking, data analysis and scientific communication.
learning_outcomes: Present experimental data and methodology in a format appropriate for publication.
Convey an understanding of scientific concepts and specialist methodology, materials and instruments through written communication using appropriate vocabulary.
Acquire, interpret and evaluate experimental data
Critique and accurately execute experimental protocols
Incorporate appropriate organisational, ethical and OH&S practices in a molecular biology laboratory setting.

title: SKILLS IN SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with the opportunity to develop their skills in critical analysis, problem solving and data analysis and presentation. The subject will use published journal articles together with a range of scientific problems to support learning of these skills. The subject does not contain a practical component but complements practical subjects and thesis writing subjects through the analysis of data and experimental design components. These skills form an essential part of any upper level scientific study program. In completing tasks for this subject, students are expected to draw on their prior learning and experiences in scientific problem solving.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and apply appropriate vocabulary to describe experiments
Report data in a relevant, meaningful and clear context
Convey an understanding of current scientific methodology through written communication
Analyse experiments critically

title: RESEARCH PROJECT A
syllabus_overview: This subject is one of two research-based subjects (BIO5RPA and BIO5RPB) completed back-to-back in the Research Project pathway of Master of Biotechnology and Bioinformatics. During the research program students will participate in an individual research project under academic supervision where they will gain practical experience with planning and performing independent research. Students will develop research and communication skills by writing a literature review on the area of the research, presenting research seminars and a research poster. The full program culminates with the submission of a research thesis discussing the year's work.
learning_outcomes: Analyse published scientific information and acquired research data and communicate this to an audience in written form.
Develop advanced knowledge in a specialist topic within the broad field of Biotechnology.
Obtain and refine practical research skills, including responsible planning, conduct, recording and reporting of laboratory based experiments, to contribute to an overarching research project.
Reflect on, synthesise and condense complex information into an accurate and easily understandable format to report research progress effectively.
Extend oral communication skills to present scientific knowledge including experimental data to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.

title: RESEARCH PROJECT B
syllabus_overview: This subject is one of two research-based subjects (BIO5RPA and BIO5RPB) completed back-to-back in the Research Project pathway of Master of Biotechnology and Bioinformatics. During the research program students will participate in an individual research project under academic supervision where they will gain practical experience with planning and performing independent research. Students will develop research and communication skills by writing a literature review on the area of the research, presenting research seminars and a research poster. The full program culminates with the submission of a research thesis discussing the year's work.
