learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of the key concepts of the "Principles of Chemistry" as defined by the Royal Australian Chemical Institute associated with chemical reactions, structure and properties of chemicals, analytical methods for chemical species and physical principles of chemistry.

Integrate knowledge of the key concepts of electronic structure, chemical reactivity, molecular structure and properties of chemicals, instrumental and analytical methods for chemical species to describe and predict the outcomes of chemical reactions.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of chemical topics of relevance to current research activities
Apply advanced concepts of discipline-specific knowledge to the solution of scientific problems, including abstract, routine, and real-world problems of chemical relevance.

title: MOLECULAR STRUCTURE AND SPECTROSCOPY
syllabus_overview: Molecular structure lies at the very heart of chemistry. It accounts for the properties of molecules - how they function, interact with their environment and undergo reactions. Determining molecular structure and understanding its implications enables the chemist to characterize chemical samples and design new molecules. In this multi-faceted subject that builds on your previous study of chemistry, you will learn about powerful and complementary modern approaches to understand molecular structure, combining models of chemical bonding and experimental characterization of structure. You will learn about theories of chemical bonding from Lewis structures, VSEPR and valence bond theory to a focus on molecular orbital theory and its applications. Molecular characterization techniques of mass spectrometry, IR, Raman, UV-Vis, fluorescence, and NMR spectroscopy, and their application to organic, inorganic, biological and gas-phase systems will be explored. In this subject you will also gain experience in conducting and interpreting a variety of spectroscopy techniques.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of principles and concepts of molecular structure, bonding and spectroscopy.
Exhibit professional integrity and safe laboratory practices when designing and performing experiments, collecting data and reporting results.
Analyse and solve problems in chemical sciences by evaluating the qualitative and quantitative chemical information obtained through interpretation of spectroscopic data.
Write coherent descriptions of chemical principles and spectroscopic techniques and report experimental findings with well supported interpretations using correctly referenced professional prose.

title: HONOURS IN CHEMISTRY A
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program in the School of Agriculture, Biomedicine and Environment (SABE) is to provide undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Chemistry consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part-time) individual research project, supervised by a SABE scientist whose research is in the discipline of chemistry. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. The School Honours co-ordinator will provide more information on the application process including a comprehensive list of available research projects. CHE401A is the first subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in SABE. Students must take CHE401A first.
learning_outcomes: Recall knowledge in chemistry when conducting experiments, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.
Extend oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Obtain practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of chemistry.
Show intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice
Understand published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.

CHE401C is the second or third subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in SABE. Students must take CHE401A first.

Compare and contrast published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.

title: CHEMICAL STRUCTURE AND CHARACTERIZATION
syllabus_overview: Chemical Structure and Characterization develops and extends knowledge and skills in understanding molecular structure, and the characterization techniques and tools used to determine molecular structure. Key concepts of bonding and molecular structure will be reinforced, together with structural characterization associated with the instrumental techniques of mass spectrometry, NMR spectroscopy, infrared spectroscopy, ultraviolet/visible spectroscopy, separation science and chromatography. The subject will combine lectures with workshop classes that focus on practical problem solving and real world applications.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant mathematical, graphical and computational methods to acquire, manipulate, interpret and evaluate chemical data and summarise results using appropriate significant figures and units.
Relate molecular structure to models of bonding, intermolecular forces, and chemical characterization techniques.
Analyse Mass Spectrometry, NMR Spectroscopy, infrared and UV-Vis spectra for the identification and characterisation of chemical species.
Describe and apply chemistry techniques and instrumental methods for chemical structural characterisation.
Interpret Infrared and Ultraviolet-Visible spectra in terms of the spectroscopic transitions that occur within vibrational and electronic energy levels.

Build oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Develop practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of chemistry.
Analyse published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Develop intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice

title: MOLECULAR ANALYSIS
syllabus_overview: Chemical analysis is widely used in biomedical, pharmaceutical, and environmental science. In this subject, you will learn about modern analytical chemistry skills including essential methodology for processing and analysing obtained data from analytical techniques. You will also learn cutting-edge analytical technologies, such as biosensors, for the detection of target molecules and compounds. Lectures will present the conceptual background required and then in the weekly workshop classes, this knowledge will be applied to problem-solving tasks.
learning_outcomes: Perform basic numerical calculations and apply statistical methods, including error analysis, to data provided.
Interpret and assess data from chemical analysis of samples accounting for the major strengths and weaknesses of various analytical techniques.
Describe and apply chemistry techniques and instrumental methods for chemical analysis.
Demonstrating a capacity for working effectively in a cooperative environment
Presenting information, articulating arguments and conclusions, in a variety of modes, to diverse audiences, and for a range of purposes

Apply knowledge of the key concepts of the "Principles of Chemistry" as defined by the Royal Australian Chemical Institute associated with chemical reactions, structure and properties of chemicals, analytical methods for chemical species and physical principles of chemistry.

title: SYNTHETIC TOPICS IN CHEMISTRY
syllabus_overview: Applying synthetic strategies from an understanding of reactivity is a critical skill for organic and organometallic chemists. In this subject you will learn about modern approaches to the synthesis of organic molecules, including carbonyl compounds and amines, and be introduced to the key concept of retrosynthetic analysis. You will also examine the structure, reactivity and applications of organometallic compounds, including bonding in transition metal complexes (valence bond theory and MO theory), common organometallic ligands, 'the eighteen electron rule'. Reaction mechanism is a key focus, including ligand substitution, insertion reactions, oxidative addition and reductive elimination, and olefin metathesis. In this subject, you will gain experience conducting and interpreting laboratory experiments related to the synthesis of organic and organometallic molecules.
learning_outcomes: Explain how organometallic reaction mechanisms can be used to account for the catalytic properties of organometallic compounds.
Apply retrosynthetic analysis to design multi-step chemical syntheses of complex organic molecules showing an understanding of reaction mechanisms.
Exhibit professional integrity and safe laboratory practices when designing and performing experiments, collecting data and reporting findings.
Orally communicate chemical knowledge, supported by legitimate evidence and appropriately defended to peers or professionals.
Employ the bonding models of valence bond theory and molecular orbital theory to explain the properties and reactivity of organometallic compounds.

title: CHEMISTRY RESEARCH PROJECT A
syllabus_overview: Masters of Chemical Science students undertake a two-semester long research project (CHE5PRA and CHE5PRB) under the supervision of an academic staff member. Students will meet prospective supervisors and select research projects during the first year of the Masters of Chemical Science course. As part of the research project, students will conduct advanced experimentation, develop independent research skills, and produce a thesis outlining their achievements and results.
learning_outcomes: Apply professional integrity and safe laboratory practices when designing and performing experiments, collecting data and reporting results.
Orally present chemistry matters, supported by legitimate evidence and appropriately defended to peers or professionals
Critically evaluate published scientific work
Apply relevant mathematical, graphical and computational methods to acquire, manipulate, interpret and evaluate chemical data and summarise results using appropriate significant figures and units.
Analyse and report experimental results with well supported interpretations using correctly referenced professional prose.

title: CHINESE 1
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory subject designed for students with no background in Mandarin. In this subject, we aim to provide integrated training in speaking, listening, reading, and writing through interactive classroom activities and home assignments. The topics include an introduction, greetings, family, dates and time, hobbies, and visiting friends. The subject also comprises foundation work on the Romanised phonetics system, pinyin, and the Chinese writing system. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. By the end of the subject, students should attain a basic level of competence in oral and written Chinese and a working knowledge of approximately 160-200 characters. The Chinese Proficiency Test (Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi HSK) Level 1 will be introduced to students. It is recommended that students also take AST1001 with this subject.
learning_outcomes: Write functional sentences and use the appropriate structures with correct grammar in Chinese.
Formulate a brief oral opinion on everyday matters and generally engage in the discussion on China-related topics.
Explore and make sense of the Chinese cultural component through literature and online-based resource in English.
Use bilingual paper-based and online-based dictionaries correctly.
Manage open-ended short communication, listening and speaking, with functional approximations of accurate language and intonation for the context.

title: CHEMISTRY RESEARCH PROJECT B
syllabus_overview: Masters of Chemical Science students undertake a two-semester long research project (CHE5PRA and CHE5PRB) under the supervision of an academic staff member. Students will meet prospective supervisors and select research projects during the first year of the Masters of Chemical Science course. As part of the research project, students will conduct advanced experimentation, develop independent research skills, and produce a thesis outlining their achievements and results.

Analyse and report experimental results with well supported interpretations using correctly referenced professional prose.
Apply relevant mathematical, graphical and computational methods to acquire, manipulate, interpret and evaluate chemical data and summarise results using appropriate significant figures and units.
Critically evaluate published scientific work
Orally present chemistry matters, supported by legitimate evidence and appropriately defended to peers or professionals

title: CHINESE 3
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students develop further skills in oral and written communication in Chinese and are introduced to the more complex grammatical structures of the language. Topics include talking about the weather, dining, asking for directions, organizing a birthday party and seeing a doctor, with an emphasis on expanding vocabulary idiomatic expressions. By the end of the subject, students will have learned a further 200 characters. The Chinese Proficiency Test (Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi HSK) Level 3 will be introduced to students. Students who successfully complete this subject are encouraged to enrol in CHI2004 in the second semester. It is also recommended that students majoring in Chinese enrol in AST3001 in the second semester as a third-year core choice subject.
learning_outcomes: Use bilingual paper-based and online-based dictionaries correctly.
Write functional sentences in Chinese using appropriate structures and correct grammar.
Use the vocabulary introduced in class to communicate effectively on a range of topics.
Demonstrate awareness of cultural differences.
Use Chinese sentence patterns and vocabulary to write short passages on a range of topics

title: CHINESE 4
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will further develop skills in oral and written communication and be introduced to the more complex grammatical structures of the language. You will extend your communicative repertoire to include everyday life in a Chinese context, including dating, renting an apartment, sports, travel and at the airport. By the end of the semester, you will be able to use the most common sentence patterns of colloquial Chinese and will have acquired an additional 250 characters. The Chinese Proficiency Test (Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi HSK) Level 4 will be introduced to students.
learning_outcomes: Write functional sentences in Chinese using appropriate structures and correct grammar.
Use Chinese sentence patterns and vocabulary to write short passages on a range of topics.
Use the vocabulary introduced in class to communicate effectively on a range of topics.
Demonstrate awareness of cultural differences
Use bilingual paper-based and online-based dictionaries correctly.

title: CHINA AND CULTURAL DIVERSITY
syllabus_overview: This professional-level Chinese subject helps you (Chinese and non-Chinese speakers) to acquire an in-depth and comprehensive understanding of China's diverse culture. By studying and analysing both English and Chinese core texts, you will enrich your knowledge of five major aspects of Chinese culture: ethnic and cultural diversity, traditional thought system, food culture, religions and beliefs, and traditional arts. Upon completion of this subject, you will gain a better understanding of Chinese culture (for non-Chinese speakers) and cultural self-awareness (for Chinese speakers). You will also enhance your language skills in both English and Mandarin at a professional level. The subject will lay a solid foundation for students to further their Chinese studies.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this subject, students will be able to to speak culturally appropriate and confidently and use the target language to communicate with native Mandarin speakers

Upon successful completion of this subject, students will be able to enhance both Mandarin Chinese and English proficiency by learning both Chinese and English core texts with 20 new vocabularies each week.

Upon successful completion of this subject, students will be able to compare and contrast Chinese cultural practices and values with those of other cultures, fostering cross-cultural communication skills and promoting an appreciation for cultural differences and similarities.

Upon successful completion of this subject, students will be able to develop an understanding of the rich cultural diversity within China, including its various ethnic groups, traditional thought systems, religions, and arts, and recognize the importance of cultural sensitivity and respect in intercultural interactions.

title: CHINESE 6
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will further develop advanced communicative competence in topics of everyday interest related to the scenarios of university life. Topics include boyfriends and girlfriends, computers and the internet, casual jobs, perceptions of education and China's geography. You will consolidate skills in simple correspondence and expository writing in Chinese. You will also enhance oral and aural skills in Chinese. By the end of the semester, students are expected to acquire an additional 400 characters. The Chinese Proficiency Test (Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi HSK) Level 4 will be introduced to students.
learning_outcomes: Perform a basic analysis, and develop a simple argument in Chinese.
Write a short and fluent paragraph and use appropriate structures with correct grammar in Chinese
Improve and develop communicative competence in topics of everyday interest in Chinese and Australian society, consolidate skills in simple correspondence and expository writing.
Understand cultural differences in Chinese contexts such as family relations and education etc.

Enhance oral and aural skills by reading new texts and viewing Chinese feature films. With the expanded vocabulary range, students can talk about topics including university life, travel, sport, family relations and education.

title: CHINESE 2
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will build on the foundation skills taught in CHI1001 and further extend your communicative repertoire with topics such as making appointments, studying Chinese, school life, shopping, and using transportation. You will learn to write a further 180 characters, bringing the total to around 350, and learn to recognize up to 400 characters. The focus will on the improvement of reading, speaking, listening and writing skills. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. By the end of the subject, the Chinese Proficiency Test (Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi HSK) Level 2 will be introduced to students.
learning_outcomes: Manage open-ended short communication, reading, listening and speaking, with functional approximations of accurate language and intonation for the context
Write functional and short paragraphs using appropriate sentence structures with correct grammar in Chinese
Perform a basic analysis and synthesis, and develop and evaluate simple arguments.
Formulate a short written opinion on familiar matters and generally engage in the discussion on China-related topics.
Explore and analyse the Chinese cultural components through literature and online based resource in English and Chinese.

title: ESSENTIALS OF CHEMISTRY
syllabus_overview: Essentials of Chemistry is an introductory subject for students with minimal background or no previous study in chemistry. The subject introduces chemistry topics with a real-world focus to prepare students for further studies in chemistry and related fields of science. The subject will introduce and reinforce chemistry concepts, knowledge and skills in chemistry to enable students to apply chemical principles and practice during their studies and in future employment. Module 1: General Chemistry covers matter, atoms, the periodic table, chemical bonding, naming compounds, molecular geometry, atomic masses, the mole and chemical reactions. Module 2: Organic Chemistry covers alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes, functional groups and reaction types. Module 3: Physical Chemistry covers gases, energy in chemistry, chemical kinetics, equilibria, acids and bases.
learning_outcomes: Manipulate quantitative relationships to solve chemistry problems.
Employ the scientific method that supports evidence-base practice.
Apply concepts of chemical structure to explain the properties of matter, exploit different types of chemical reactions to create new molecules, and evaluate the extent to which reactions may occur.
Communicate (including read and write) in the language of chemistry; interpreting and using chemical symbols, conventions and nomenclature.

title: CHINESE 5
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will develop advanced communicative competence in topics of everyday interest related to the scenarios of university life. You will consolidate skills in simple correspondence and expository writing in Chinese. You will also enhance oral and aural skills in Chinese. Topics include university orientation, dormitory living, at the restaurant, shopping, and course enrollment. By the end of the semester, you are expected to acquire an additional 320 characters. The Chinese Proficiency Test (Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi HSK) Level 4 will be introduced to students.
learning_outcomes: Speak the Chinese language including in role-play, oral presentations and discussions of daily themes to develop fundamental skills in communication.
Complete assignments and quizzes in and outside the classroom, and show an understanding of and ability to use Chinese written grammar and expression.
Perform a basic analysis and synthesis, and develop and evaluate simple arguments, as well as use bilingual paper-based and online-based dictionaries correctly.
Work as part of a team in class role play activities
Use the vocabulary introduced in class to communicate effectively on given topics.

title: CIVIL ENGINEERING PROJECT MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on a number of essential aspects of construction project management including project scope management and developing an understanding of how planning for buildings and infrastructure projects is undertaken; the requirements for allocation of resources (Materials, Plants and Labour) and processes including construction scheduling principles, cost estimation and budgeting; project risk assessment and decision making; and project execution including relevant management skills such as human resources, communication and quality management. This subject also introduces you to the common corporate structures and project contracts in the Australian context. Emphasis will be placed on the management role of engineers in achieving efficient and effective operations within local and regional government.
learning_outcomes: Work efficiently and effectively as a member of a team to analyse construction projects against relevant quality management frameworks.
Conduct risk assessment for projects to facilitate tendering and change management processes.
Scope out a project and apply project allocation techniques to a project team for a civil construction project.
Analyse and describe stakeholder engagement and identification techniques for large scale civil engineering projects.
Describe and apply project management terms and principles to the engineering industry.

title: GEOTECHNICAL DESIGN
syllabus_overview: This is the second of two geotechnical engineering subjects. The focus of this subject is to extend the student's understanding of earth mechanical properties and enable them to design various types of geotechnical structures. The topics covered include field investigation of soils, an introduction to lateral earth pressure and design of retaining structures, design of shallow and deep foundations for strength and serviceability, analysis of slope stability.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the behaviour of soils and analyse their interaction with the foundation systems and/or the supported structure(to enable their design.
Participate effectively as a member of the team in the design and analysis of geotechnical structures and apply ethical principles and professional standards when working in a team with peers.
Appreciate the role of geotechnical site investigation and field testing and the need to deal with uncertainty, and scope and plan site investigation programs and interpret the field test results.

Interpret the laboratory and field data and estimate the parameters required in the design for strength and serviceability of shallow and deep foundations, assessment of stability of slopes, evaluation of lateral earth pressure and check of stability of retaining structures.
Evaluate design options and provide final design recommendations for varies geotechnical structures based on factors such as sustainability, construction feasibility and cost effectiveness.

title: HYDRAULIC ENGINEERING 1
syllabus_overview: This subject builds upon the knowledge and skills acquired from the introductory subject titled Thermofluids. In this subject, you are provided with an understanding of the elements and behaviour of hydraulic systems. Topics covered include hydrological processes, design rainfall, probabilistic and deterministic flood estimation and open channel flow. Also, hydraulic modelling and design and operation of hydraulic structures including culvert and stormwater drainage systems are delivered in this subject. Moreover, you will learn elements of water sensitive urban design for flood mitigation and environmental protection.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the probabilistic and deterministic approaches to decide the maximum flood for hydraulic structure design.
Adapt the open channel flow theory to model open channels using well-established software.
Articulate the relationship between climate, landscape, catchment, runoff, flow estimation and hydraulic structure.
Exhibit a well-developed understanding of stormwater drainage systems and water sensitive urban design, and apply the theory to size stormwater drainage elements.
Compute the runoff from catchments, determine the time of concentration, and generate and analyse hydrograph.

title: STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS AND DESIGN 2
syllabus_overview: The aim of this subject is to introduce students to the current philosophy for the design of structures against loads required to resist. This is followed by presenting the behavior and detailed design of structural elements constructed from steel and timber materials to resist major actions. The design strategies presented cover action cases including bending, shear, tension and compression in addition to deflection checks for selected structural members and materials. Comprehensive structural design tasks for the covered materials and actions will equip the students with the fundamental understandings of sizing and specifying framing members for structures.
learning_outcomes: Calculate structural load combinations
Apply mechanics of solids principles to design structural members.
Analyse the behavior of structures under load combinations.
Apply the limit state design method in structural design.

Conduct bending test in the laboratory on a scaled steel and timber beams, observe their behavior under load, compare measured data with the predictions of Australian Standards AS4100 and AS1720 and published research, and critically review the findings.

title: SOIL MECHANICS
syllabus_overview: Soil Mechanics is the first of the two geotechnical engineering subjects included in the Civil Engineering course. This subject introduces students to the basic concepts of the mechanics of soils. It covers soil descriptions and classification, the fundamental multi-phase nature of soils and the phase relationships, elementary seepage problems and the effective stress concept, deformation and shear strength of soils. Laboratory techniques to measure these properties will also be studied.
learning_outcomes: Determine the basic physical characteristics of a soil continuum.
Determine the permeability of soils using the results of both laboratory tests and in-situ tests conducted in the field and understand how 2D groundwater flows for a wide range of ground conditions.
Describe and classify soils based on their basic physical characteristics.
Specify soil compaction criteria for field applications and identify suitable equipment for field compaction.
Determine the mechanical properties which characterise the consolidation behaviour from laboratory testing and calculate ground settlements as a function of time due to consolidation.
Apply the method of operation of standard laboratory shear testing apparatus (direct shear, triaxial and derive strength properties of soil from these tests.
Apply the concept of effective stress in soil mechanics and determine stresses in soil from surface loads.

title: STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS AND DESIGN 3
syllabus_overview: Reinforced concrete structures are used extensively in the construction of a wide range of modern structures including bridges, low- and high-rise buildings, dams, reservoirs and wharves. Civil Engineers are expected to understand the behaviour of structural concrete and able to design structures using this composite material. This subject will develop your understanding of the behaviour and design of key elements in reinforced concrete structures. You'll be given numerous practical step-by-step examples to illustrate the design of reinforced concrete members. The design will follow the latest design criteria of the Australian concrete structures standard AS 3600.
learning_outcomes: Apply design concepts applicable to the behaviour, design and construction of reinforced concrete beams, slabs and columns.
Work efficiently and effectively as a member of a team to conduct a bending test on the reinforced concrete slab/beam and compare measured data with the predictions.
Apply the span-to-depth provision for determining the slab thickness and apply the strength limit state philosophy for detailing the steel reinforcement in the slab.
Apply fundamental engineering concepts to calculate the strengths of reinforced concrete members using the latest Australian concrete structures standard AS3600
Calculate amount and distribution of reinforcement required in a reinforced concrete beam to satisfy the strength limit states for flexure, shear, serviceability and to control cracking.
Apply the strength limit state method for the design of short and slender columns and detail the steel reinforcement.

title: DESIGN FOR STRUCTURAL DYNAMICS
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the essential skills for undertaking dynamic analysis for various structural types and systems. Utilizing hand calculations evaluated by commercial computational packages, you will gain the ability to conduct efficient structural dynamics modelling and analysis resulting in more economic and sustainable designs attempted for construction. Upon successful completion of this subject, you will be prepared to undertake professional structural design against earthquake or transient loading types as a graduate engineer under the supervision of a chartered engineer.
learning_outcomes: Apply finite element modelling to perform dynamic analysis
Demonstrate well developed understanding in measuring the dynamic properties of structural systems.
Undertake independent checks of results generated by computer when performing seismic design/checks
Conduct systematic strategies to develop and analyse numerical models for predicting the dynamics response(of investigated structures.

title: ADVANCED WATER TECHNOLOGY AND MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: This subject explores principles and current practices related to hydrology and the management of water resources. You will acquire knowledge on a wide range of topics including hydrological processes, design rainfall, probabilistic and deterministic flood estimation, open channel flow and sustainable catchment management. Additionally, you will gain proficiency in the elements of hydrologic and hydraulic modelling and further refine your understanding through hands-on experience with established models widely employed in water practice and research. Furthermore, you will master advanced statistical assessment techniques for conducting comprehensive analysis of hydrometeorological data.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the approaches for statistical assessment of hydrometeorological data.
Quantify the runoff from catchments and exhibit well-developed understanding and application of advanced computer-based models in hydraulic and hydrologic modelling.
Assess methods to identify appropriate solutions to achieve sustainable catchment water management.
Interpret the relationship between climate, landscape, catchment, flow estimation and hydraulic structure.

title: GROUND IMPROVEMENT & GEOSYNTHETICS ENGINEERING
syllabus_overview: The engineering properties of soil at many sites are not good enough to support infrastructure and buildings load. For these sites, some form of soil improvement methods are usually used to enhance the engineering properties of these problematic soils. It is therefore important for civil engineers to know different types of soil improvement methods; the degree to which soil properties may be improved; and the costs and benefits involved. In this subject, the latest state-of the-art techniques in the field of soil improvement will be studied and the fundamentals of its design approach will be covered.
learning_outcomes: Describe the suitable geotechnical field testing method
Design a geotechnical site investigation project
Demonstrate understanding in the design method of PVD ground improvement technique
Describe the most suitable ground improvement technique based on the geotechnical site investigation results
Understand design method of thermal ground improvement technique
Demonstrate understanding of the advantages and limitations of different ground improvement methods
Demonstrate understanding in the design method of preloading ground improvement technique

title: INFRASTRUCTURE DESIGN
syllabus_overview: This subject provides the essential practical skills required by civil infrastructure engineering professionals in preparing land development conceptual design and detailed infrastructure design. The subject gives an overview of the regulatory context and the administrative processes that govern land parcellation in Victoria. It covers the basic principles and techniques used in site analysis and conceptual site design. The subject also covers the principles and framework for the design of specific infrastructure elements such as roads and pavements. Applications of land surveying and geographic information system (GIS) for civil infrastructure design are included.
learning_outcomes: Work as a team member to design road geometry, including horizontal alignment, vertical alignment and cross sections, and evaluate earthworks and associated costs in a road project.
Apply land surveying and geographic information system (GIS) resources for civil infrastructure.
Produce detailed road pavement design using empirical and mechanistic design approaches
Develop a conceptual site design whilst considering the regulatory context and analysis of the development site.
Appraise different alternatives of a project, considering economic, social and environmental aspects.

title: HYDRAULIC ENGINEERING 2
syllabus_overview: Hydraulic Engineering 2 addresses three of the classical topics of civil engineering practice: water supply, wastewater systems and irrigation practice. The unit content includes understanding and design of water supply, wastewater collection and treatment facilities, manual and computer analysis of pipe networks, disposal of effluent and solid waste products, predictions of water and wastewater demands, and irrigation techniques and applications. Also, climate change effects on hydraulic engineering practice are discussed in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Describe significant concepts applicable to the behaviour, design and construction of water and wastewater supply systems, and treatment facilities
Calculate the size of pipes required to satisfactorily transport present and future quantities of water for residential use, for wastewater disposal and for irrigation purposes

Determine the quantity and quality of water required for residential and industrial water supply, the quantity and quality of wastewater generated by different types of users and the environmental impact of the use of effluent from treatment plants
Apply fundamental engineering concepts to develop specialist models of supply and distribution of water and wastewater transportation
Appraise environmental impacts of the use and disposal of effluent from treatment plants considering professional accountability.

title: TRANSPORTATION ENGINEERING
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the field of transportation engineering through a variety of contemporary topics, including transport systems and transport modes, traffic flow fundamentals, traffic flow theory, analysis of unsignalised intersections, roundabouts, and signalised intersections, capacity and level of service, transport survey, and transport modelling. Public transport and non-motorised transport are discussed along with intelligent transport systems. Road safety issues and countermeasures are also considered.
learning_outcomes: Design and undertake transport surveys, and analyse the survey data.
Evaluate transport system characteristics and issues for different transport modes.
Evaluate capacity of unsignalized intersections and roundabouts, and design traffic signal timings for signalised intersections.
Apply the fundamentals of traffic flow to solve real-world problems.
Identify and implement suitable techniques for various transport modelling tasks.

title: STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS AND DESIGN 1
syllabus_overview: The objective of this subject is to provide the fundamental principles and methods of structural analysis applied to both determinate and indeterminate structures such as trusses, beams, and frames. Commonly used structural analysis methods such as the force method, stiffness method, slope-deflection method, moment distribution method and the principle of virtual work method will be introduced.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principle of virtual work method to calculate the deflections of beams and trusses.
Apply the displacement method to calculate member forces in beams and frames.
Apply the stiffness method to truss members.
Apply the force method to calculate member forces in indeterminate beams, trusses and frames
Apply structural analysis principles to solve for reactions and member forces.
Apply the plastic analysis theory to calculate the shape factor of beams.

title: MECHANICS OF COMPOSITE MATERIALS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn the fundamental principles of the mechanics of composite materials and apply these principles to design of fibre composite laminates. You are provided with a solid grounding of the properties of composite materials, processing and manufacturing methods, micromechanics, macromechanics, lamination theory and the design of composite structures.
learning_outcomes: Explain how lamina/laminate respond to mechanical loads and justify how the fiber angles of individual lamina influence the laminate response
Describe the failure criteria for lamina and then apply for laminate based on failure of individual lamina
Apply equations to find mechanical properties of lamina and develop stress–strain relations for unidirectional and angle lamina
Apply the classical lamination theory to predict the deflection, natural frequency and buckling load of laminate

title: ACTION LEARNING PROJECT
syllabus_overview: In this year long subject, you will complete an action research project in public health, health promotion and health services management directed towards improving health. You will gain practical experience applying analytical and problem-solving strategies to health care issues through a major project, using an action learning framework. This subject integrates skills and knowledge gained in other subjects and deepens skills in reflection, project management and planning and evaluation, enabling you to ultimately make an impact on community health. The concept of reflective practice is applied and you have the opportunity to examine their styles and practice, consider their development needs and how they might ensure ongoing learning throughout your careers. You will be supported in the process to publish an article from the work done in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate mastery of advanced skills in formulation, analysis, documentation and dissemination of ideas.
Plan, deliver and evaluate action learning projects.
Reflect critically on professional practice.

title: COMPARATIVE AND HISTORICAL STUDY OF HEALTH SYSTEMS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn about policy making for public health. The comparative and historical study of health systems underpins the technical languages in which public health policy is analysed and developed. Exploration of key episodes in health development in different countries contributes to deep judgement in public health policy making. This subject explores and compares health systems in different countries including historical and contemporary contexts. It focuses on challenges, options and debates in relation to health care reform (including public health). The study program includes key health policy topics such as: health care financing and health insurance; primary health care and community health; health promotion and pharmaceuticals policy. You will explore themes and issues in health sector reform world wide, including links with economic reform.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced skills in policy analysis and policy development individually and collaboratively
Synthesise complex problems relating to current health system issues from China and draw lessons from comparative and historical policy study individually and collaboratively
Apply key principles of comparative and historical policy analysis individually and collaboratively
Demonstrate theoretical knowledge about health system arrangements, socio-political context and histories of development of selected national health systems
Critically review generic features of health systems

title: HEALTH CARE QUALITY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will acquire practical knowledge of current approaches to the management of safety and quality in health care, and the available evidence of their effectiveness. The major theoretical developments are reviewed, with a focus on their contribution to current methods and tools for quality improvement and quality assurance. Dilemmas in the conceptualisation and measurement of quality are explored, along with the relationship between quality management and clinical outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect and review theories and language for analysing and strategising quality, safety and organisational performance.
Demonstrate mastery and awareness of the applicability of theoretical knowledge for promoting quality, safety and organisational performance individually and collaboratively
Master theoretical knowledge in relation to the models of practice that support risk management, root cause analyses, complaints handling, accreditation and clinical review.
Reflect critically on the dynamics of institutional change individually and collaboratively

title: HEALTH INFORMATION SYSTEMS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, topics you will learn include: information systems; basic concepts of information in health including structure, environment, networking, media, language, data collection, storage, access, analysis and retrieval; characteristics of effective health information systems, IT strategies, requirements specification and system development and evaluation for health system applications; sources of information for health professionals; administrative policies and procedures for health service organisations; types of health information systems.
learning_outcomes: Critically review the use of specific information including diagnosis related groups (DRGs), casemix, classification, clinical indicators and performance audit, quality management and population health indicators.
Master understanding of the requirements for effective information systems including specification and system development processes.
Master theoretical knowledge of health information systems used in health care and how such systems inter-relate.
Reflect critically on new directions in health information systems and their potential impact on health system development.
Identify health information infrastructure needs in terms of policies, standards and procedures.

title: WRITING PAST LIVES
syllabus_overview: In recent years, fictions and popular biographies about people from the past have featured prominently on bestseller lists and in literary awards. Why do writers and readers turn to these representations with such enthusiasm? In this subject we analyse the social and cultural significance of narrative encounters with people from the past. We consider how readers, creators and critics engage with them, and with their historical contexts. We ask: What are the ethical dilemmas of such creative and critical practices? How do understandings of gender, sexuality, race, dis/ability and class intersect in these works? How might they challenge our view of the current moment and its various prejudices? How do they offer new ways to imagine past, present and future identities? Students will engage with these questions through textual analysis, research and the development of creative work. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes daytime live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate creative writing and research skills appropriate for third-year level.
Demonstrate critical writing and research skills appropriate for third-year level
Analyse and articulate the creative and critical contexts of the prescribed texts.
Analyse and evaluate key terms and concepts in the field of biographical and historical fiction studies.

title: READING FOR WRITERS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will undertake a close and scholarly analysis of fiction and creative non fiction. Reading across a range of genres in 20th and 21st century work, you will engage with texts to identify the stylistic and technical choices writers have made and to consider the effects of these both in the prescribed texts and how they can apply these in their own writing. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a literary text, using the tools and vocabulary of the working writer.
Produce a narrative that effectively employs techniques and structures identified in the course of study.
Apply specific authorial techniques in written work.
Identify authorial techniques in texts and articulate how and why they are used.

title: WRITING ADVANCED FICTION
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will extend your understanding of creative writing by developing long-form fiction in a chosen genre. This will be an excerpt of a novel or novella. In your creative and critical practice you will consider how the longer form affects the use of technical elements such as plot and structure, POV, character and setting. You will engage in an intensive revision process, assisted by peer-feedback. The subject will offer further opportunities to develop your professional practice through synopsis writing, reading to peers, integrating workshop comments and editing after a workshop. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Develop the ability to give and receive constructive feedback while managing deadlines.
Write a professional synopsis that conforms to industry standards.
Develop confidence in reading creative work aloud.
Plan, draft and revise an excerpt of long-form fiction that demonstrates control of fiction techniques and genre.
Analyse the relationship between critical theories and creative practice.

title: HEALTH MANAGEMENT STRATEGY AND OPERATIONS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you examine the strategic decisions, actions and leadership that determine the success of health service organisations. To achieve this, you will focus on the health care system and organisations from the strategic planning and management viewpoint, as well as covering marketing fundamentals and key components of operations management and research essential for decision analysis. Major issues and trends with an impact on the strategic and operations management of health services organisations will be discussed. This subject is designed for the student to use much of the material previously covered in other subjects, as well as healthcare management experience, to further develop the skills to deal with real life strategic and operational situations. Practical health services management problems relating to strategic planning and management, marketing and operations management are addressed through group projects and exercises.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically and communicate effectively about strategic planning and operational management using different modes and media.
Synthesise complex problems and concepts used to measure operational performance (without sole reliance on financial measures).
Analyse elements of strategic planning and their transformation in operational management.
Critically review the basic components of marketing pertaining to health systems.

title: PROFESSIONAL WRITING
syllabus_overview: Learning to write well brings benefits within and beyond university. This interdisciplinary unit offers you the opportunity to strengthen your professional, creative and academic writing skills. You will develop a conceptual framework for analysing the writing of others and editing your own work effectively, as well as improving your skills in the generation of ideas, elements of style and identification with the audience. These areas of writing will be explored through modules with theoretical and practical components: -- Academic writing, including essay writing, essay structure, avoiding plagiarism, editing and proof-reading. -- Non-fiction writing across a number of genres, particularly writing for popular media, reviews of the arts and writing for the web. -- Creative writing, which can include fiction, poetry and scriptwriting. This is a level 1 subject.
learning_outcomes: Apply the concepts from the Writer's Toolbox, presented in the subject, to your own and others' work.
Demonstrate independent thinking in your essay materials.
Work co-operatively on various tasks to discuss the strengths and difficulties in your own and others' writing.
Articulate connections between your study of writing and issues of personal or social concern.
Write clear, well-organised and proof-read academic and creative pieces.
Develop a writing portfolio demonstrating different genres and styles.

title: EDITING AND PUBLISHING
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the ongoing evolution of editing and publishing in the twenty-first century, supporting students to develop practical competences that extend into a wide variety of professional settings. It introduces key editorial skills – including proofreading, copyediting and structural editing – and investigates vital ethical, legal and economic considerations in contemporary publishing. Placing both the local and global industries in their wider historical and cultural contexts, we consider how publishing has always been at the cutting edge of both technological and social change, and how external factors continue to shape editing and publishing practices today. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling.
learning_outcomes: Understand structural editing, copyediting and proofreading and put these skills into practice effectively.
Demonstrate knowledge of the history of editing and publishing and the capacity to critically evaluate the significance of the social contexts in which these are practised.
Work cooperatively with peers to communicate with each other clearly in oral and written forms and share knowledges and skills.
Critically engage with the ethical, legal and economic aspects of editing and publishing and sustain this engagement in clearly written prose and oral presentations to the group.

title: HEALTH SERVICE RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will be introduced to financial management in health services, in particular, systems of finance and budgeting. Topics covered include: accounting principles, the analysis and interpretation of financial data and quantitative performance data for management control, and basic techniques of quantitative decision making and operations research for dealing with health service resource utilisation decisions. You will also be introduced to costing and case mix funding.
learning_outcomes: Review and critically analyse the manner in which the Australian Health System is financed, with a view to enhancing understanding of Chinese incremental developments
Analyse accounting and financial statements in both Chinese formats and International Accounting Standards format
Critically reflect on and apply the principles of finance and investment in both Chinese and Western contexts
Demonstrate advanced knowledge in the creation of budgets and their ongoing management
Investigate and reflect critically on the management of costs, and how this differs from pricing

title: PRINCIPLES AND PRACTICE OF PUBLIC HEALTH
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you are provided with an integrated overview of the ways in which different theories and disciplinary perspectives have informed public health principles and practices. You are provided with the foundations for a contextual understanding of the specific methods of public health research, policy development and program planning and implementation. This subject draws linkages between areas that may at first sight appear quite disparate. You are provided with an overview of public health as an organised global and local effort to promote and protect the health of the public. Links are drawn between the past and present to provide the foundations for a contextual understanding of the specific methods of public health practice and policy development. You are encouraged to position yourself within public health debates.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess institutional arrangements and tools for public health and primary health care individually and collaboratively
Reflect critically on public health practices in China, and apply contemporary international health promotion practices individually and collaboratively
Master theoretical knowledge in relation to changing concepts and approaches to public health and community health individually and collaboratively
Master advanced skills in the design of comprehensive community health services based on local health needs collaboratively

title: CREATIVE ARTS HONOURS EXEGESIS A
syllabus_overview: Under supervision, students research and write an extended research essay (exegesis) of 7,300-9,000 words or equivalent. The exegesis will apply appropriate methodologies and critical frameworks in response to a research question and creative body of work developed as part of HUS4THA. The exegesis demonstrates students' capacity to make an original textual contribution to their chosen discipline. The topic must be approved by the discipline honours coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Develop and effectively communicate coherent arguments.
Develop, with supervision, an original research plan, identifying project tasks, timelines and resources that are realistic given the time frame.
Cite evidence appropriately and seek out and deploy relevant data for the solution of analytical problems.
Develop a command of the research literature relating to the project

title: CREATIVE ARTS HONOURS EXEGESIS B
syllabus_overview: Under supervision, students research and write an extended research essay (exegesis) of 7,300-9,000 words or equivalent. The exegesis will apply appropriate methodologies and critical frameworks in response to a research question and creative body of work developed as part of HUS4THB. The exegesis demonstrates students' capacity to make an original textual contribution to their chosen discipline. The topic must be approved by the discipline honours coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Gather and synthesise evidence to formulate a coherent response to an analytical problem.
Under supervision, execute original research and determine results
Understand and critically analyse the research literature relating to the project
Effectively communicate research findings according to the scholarly conventions of the discipline.

title: SERVICENOW APPLICATION DEVELOPMENT
syllabus_overview: As one of the world’s largest and most popular digital workflow management platforms, there is high demand for people with ServiceNow expertise. Designed and offered in partnership with ServiceNow, this subject will prepare you to sit for two valuable industry certifications, the ServiceNow Certified System Administrator and Certified Application Developer. You will learn the fundamentals of creating applications within the ServiceNow platform, including user-access rights, process automation, data integration and pre-deployment application validation. On successful completion of this course, you will receive vouchers which allow you to take the ServiceNow Certified System Administrator and Certified Application Developer exams.
learning_outcomes: Show the database structure of ServiceNow and apply this knowledge to create tables and forms with suitable access controls.
Automate simple ServiceNow tasks by writing scripts and using Flow Designer.
Effectively assess and evaluate the ServiceNow platform and identify the process of automation, data integration and validation.
Develop and employ strategies by collaborating in a team to design and create a ServiceNow application.
Explain the design decisions and usage of the developed application to a general ServiceNow user.

title: INTRODUCTION TO ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
syllabus_overview: This subject gives you an introduction to AI and how AI transforms business and society. You will learn principal AI concepts, explore a variety of AI techniques for solving different types of problems, and examine ethical issues and concerns associated with AI. Upon completion of the subject, you will be equipped to recognise, select, and apply existing AI methods in both computer science and non-computer science fields that engage with AI technologies.
learning_outcomes: Describe the core concepts related to AI and key terminology
Investigate and explain possible AI solutions for business and technology transformations
Examine the issues, limitations, and ethical dilemmas associated with AI
Recognise when and how AI can be used in modern systems, and employ the right AI methods to address a wide range of problems

title: INTRODUCTION TO CYBERSECURITY
syllabus_overview: In the modern Internet era, industries and organisations need to be prepared to defend against cyber threats and attacks. Stakeholders should be familiar with basic principles and best practices of cybersecurity to protect their businesses and personal information. In this subject, these principles and strategies for future cyber security are explored. Key topics include: information security; ethical and legal practices; mitigating cyber vulnerabilities; and the process of incident response and analysis. The subject introduces the broad discipline of cybersecurity and outlines how to ensure the privacy, reliability, confidentiality and integrity of information systems and mitigate against cyber threats and risks.
learning_outcomes: Apply and compare approaches to cyber risk management in addressing real-world digital security challenges.
Demonstrate foundation skills in identifying malware, securing applications, systems, and networks
Analyse emerging cybersecurity practices, regulations, and standards, and evaluate their implications for digital security.
Work efficiently and effectively as a member of a team to investigate possible solutions such as cryptography to enhance data security, and web security, and digital forensics against cyber threats

title: OBJECT-ORIENTED PROGRAMMING FUNDAMENTALS
syllabus_overview: The Object-Oriented (OO) paradigm is a significant influence in software development in the computer industry. It divides a system into objects that exist in the model of the application domain. In this subject, students will be introduced to OO concepts, terminologies, syntax and programming using Java. Topics covered include classes and objects, inheritance, object attributes and methods, overloaded methods, the use of the Unified Modelling Language (UML) for representing these concepts, primitive data types, flow of control, basic input/output, arrays, Java library class, and exception handling. Some software engineering principles are included: program design, algorithm for solving a problem and version control. This subject is designed as inclusive as possible for undergraduate/diploma students.
learning_outcomes: Apply the object-oriented method to designing and implementing a computer program for solving a real-life problem.
Relate the principles behind the use of the abstract data type (ADT) to localise and minimise the effects of modifications through object-oriented approach
Justify the capabilities of the OO model to share and reuse code with OO techniques, reducing the time required to develop an application

Compare the traditional method of analysis/design/implementation and the object-oriented approach, with the OO model’s basic construct being the object, which combines both data structure and behaviour.

title: PROGRAMMING ENVIRONMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you are introduced to the steps involved in designing and creating a software solution to simple real-life problems. To enable students to design a program, the subject introduces the way to break down the problems into smaller parts and analyse them methodically by using simple techniques such as drawing flowcharts. You will be introduced to the Python programming language as a means of creating executable program code to implement working software solutions.
learning_outcomes: Implement executable code in the Python programming language to solve computational problems.
Apply the 3 basic programming constructs of sequence, selection, and iteration to design computational solutions.
Analyse simple data processing problems to correctly identify the data and high-level processing involved.
Use basic data structures such as lists and dictionaries to solve batch data processing problems.

title: PROGRAMMING FOR ENGINEERS AND SCIENTISTS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you are introduced to the steps involved in designing and creating a software solution to simple real-life problems. To enable students to design a program, the subject introduces the way to break down the problems into smaller parts and analyse them methodically by using simple techniques such as drawing flowcharts. You will be introduced to the Python programming language as a means of creating executable program code to implement working software solutions.
learning_outcomes: Implement executable code in the Python programming language to solve computational problems.
Apply the 3 basic programming constructs of sequence, selection, and iteration to design computational solutions.
Analyse a data processing problem to correctly identify both the data and high-level processing involved.
Use basic data structures such as lists and dictionaries to solve batch data processing problems.

title: CYBERSECURITY IN PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: Every organization and business that intends to protect itself from threats of cyber-attacks needs to know current practices in cyber defence. This subject will introduce common technologies used to identify and mitigate threats including firewalls, intrusion detection systems, intrusion protection systems and honeypots. This subject also introduces incident response processes and simple ways to incorporate secure programming practices to make computer programs less vulnerable to attacks.
learning_outcomes: Employ secure software design practices when working in teams
Investigate, evaluate and apply current cybersecurity technologies that protect against cyber threats
Describe the process of threat and vulnerability identification and incident response in cybersecurity environments

title: INSIDE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to the rapidly expanding and influential field of information technology which comprises various types of technologies in computers (both hardware and software) and computer networks. It is therefore relevant to students in a wide range of disciplines: for examples, health sciences, business, engineering and technology. Students will be taught the fundamental principles of computer operations, different types of input/output and storage devices, computer networks including Local and Wide area networks, information systems, Database, the Internet, the World Wide Web and HTML. Students will acquire the knowledge and practical skills in information technology and be able to apply them to their field of study.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate how a computer system processes and delivers data/information to users

Interpret how the role of each of the following components of Information Technology (IT) - computer system, computer network, and World Wide Web - supports the goal of delivering data and information to users from around the world
Practise the IT knowledge such as HTML, computer system/network to address typical real-life issues
Apply the Web Development principles to constructing a Web system

title: SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT, SECURITY AND OPERATIONS
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a modern view on software development, deployment, testing and delivery practices. Covering a range of core principles and practices in DevOps, and utilising a range of modern tools and technologies, this subject will provide in-depth, practical, hands-on experience with implementing continuous integration/continuous deployment/continuous testing (CI/CD/CT) pipelines. This subject includes branching version control strategies, dependency management, containerisation, monitoring and logging, and developing infrastructure as code and pipeline as code solutions.
learning_outcomes: Apply DevOps practices to infrastructure as code and pipeline as code
Apply branching version control strategies, dependency management and containerisation to manage software development projects effectively
Evaluate the principles underlying modern DevOps-based development practices to understand their impact on software delivery and operations.
Design continuous integration/continuous deployment/continuous testing (CI/CD/CT) pipelines to support accelerated delivery of high-quality software

title: AI AND TECH INNOVATION FRONTIER
syllabus_overview: This subject equips students with the mindset, skills, and practical tools needed to identify opportunities, validate ideas, and develop entrepreneurial responses to complex real-world challenges. Positioned at the intersection of innovation, entrepreneurship, and emerging technology, the subject introduces students to the role of AI-enabled tools in accelerating the innovation process, including opportunity discovery, customer insight generation, ideation, prototyping, market validation, and venture communication. While the subject does not teach AI techniques or technical AI development, it enables students to critically and responsibly use contemporary AI tools as part of a broader innovation toolkit. The subject addresses a critical gap in entrepreneurship education by combining the psychological foundations of entrepreneurial thinking with a rigorous, evidence-based approach to market validation, aligning with La Trobe University’s strategic focus on innovation, employability, and industry engagement. Throughout this subject, students will actively ideate and tackle complex challenges, develop robust innovation frameworks and prototypes, and rigorously validate product-market fit. They will use AI-supported tools to accelerate research, explore customer needs and behaviours, generate and refine concepts, test assumptions, and produce actionable evidence to inform product development, marketing strategies, and venture decisions. Students will strategically identify and leverage resources to reduce the risks associated with new ventures, while critically evaluating the quality, limitations, ethical implications, and societal impact of AI-assisted innovation practices. These outcomes empower students to make evidence-based decisions, maximise the likelihood that their product or service will resonate with target audiences, and develop a sustainable pathway to value creation and profitability. Students will also cultivate advanced professional competencies in ethical and moral decision-making and consider their innovations within a broader global context. The subject demands proactive engagement in collaborative group discussions and practical activities, and integrates entrepreneurial theory, applied case studies, AI-enabled innovation workflows, and insights from industry guest speakers addressing start-up challenges, pitfalls, and key success factors. Entry into this subject involves an Expression of Interest (EoI) process, followed by a short interview. Please contact the subject coordinator for further details of this process.
learning_outcomes: Analyse real‑world entrepreneurial challenges to generate and justify evidence‑based solutions.
Develop and iteratively refine prototypes or Minimum Viable Products (MVPs) using design thinking principles.
Apply market‑validation data and lean startup methodologies to make informed decisions about product features, pricing, and marketing strategies while managing project resources effectively.
Work collaboratively to generate and justify entrepreneurial decisions, and communicate resulting solutions clearly to professional and non specialist audiences.
Evaluate qualitative and quantitative market research findings to identify customer needs and reveal market gaps.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FUNDAMENTALS
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the fundamental areas of Artificial Intelligence, focusing on knowledge representation and search. Main topics include historical foundations and application areas; state-space search; game-playing; knowledge representation languages including predicate calculus, semantic networks, conceptual graphs and frames; rule-based expert systems; and an introduction to symbolic and connectionist machine learning.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and design basic machine learning algorithms to model a practical case.
Devise appropriate representations for state space search and game playing to solve practical problems.
Represent knowledge using semantic networks, scripts, frames and logic-based mechanisms and write simple Prolog programs to enable automated reasoning.
Construct simple expert systems to solve a real-world problem.

title: ALGORITHMS AND DATA STRUCTURES
syllabus_overview: This subject covers a range of important algorithms and data structures. Data structures for implementing containers are covered and include linear structures, tree structures and hash tables. Algorithms for insertion and deletion of elements, and algorithms for searching and sorting on these structures are covered where appropriate. Graphs and graph algorithms are also covered. Students will learn the construction and workings of the data structures and algorithms covered. They will learn to analyse the effectiveness of each data structure and algorithm for specific problems and categories of problems. Students will also implement in programs a wide range of the structures and algorithms covered.
learning_outcomes: Design a solution for a problem, implement it in Java, and evaluate its performance using an appropriate measure.
Identify a range of data structures and searching and sorting algorithms in the context of computing.
Compare a range of data structures and searching and sorting algorithms and apply a suitable one to solving a problem.
Explain the overall objectives of the field of Algorithms and Data Structures
Implement a range of data structures and searching and sorting algorithms in Java.

title: DATABASE FUNDAMENTALS
syllabus_overview: This subject starts with an overview of the architecture and management of database systems, and a discussion of different existing database models. The main focus includes relational database analysis, design, and implementation. This subject prepares students for subjects such as the final year industry project which require an understanding of database design and implementation. The students learn: relational algebra as the formal foundation of relational databases; relational conceptual design using an entity-relationship diagram; relational logical database design; foundation of normalization; security and integrity; and SQL implementation of relational database queries. Students are required to design a database application that meets the needs of a system requirement specification, and to implement the system using a commercial standard database system such as ORACLE or POSTGRESQL. In addition, a selection of advanced topics in databases will be introduced and discussed.
learning_outcomes: Identify the appropriate normalization techniques for database design.
Identify the possible risks and ethical and social considerations relevant to a designed system.
Implement a database system using SQL and apply the relevant knowledge in database management and administration.
Define the underlying model of relational database operations using relational algebra.
Apply a database modelling technique using an ER and EER diagram, and use a transformation process to change these to a relational database design.

title: DATA VISUALIZATION
syllabus_overview: The ability to visualise data is one of the most useful forms of data analysis and data presentation. Data visualisation provides an accessible way to see and understand trends, outliers and patterns in data. Nowadays there are many different tools for collecting and querying data. In order to gain full benefit from the collected data we need to visualise the data. In this subject you will learn the following: how to prepare data for visualisation; the design principals for creating effective data visualisations; and how to communicate your data analysis using reports containing data visualisations. You will learn how to use state of the art software tools for generating insightful and interactive data visualisations.
learning_outcomes: Write code to clean and format data in preparation for data visualisation.
Generate informative reports using data visualisations.
Create interactive data visualisations for all users to effectively explore the data.
Design appropriate and effective visualisations that help users gain deep insight into complex the data sets.

title: HUMAN FACTORS IN CYBERSECURITY
syllabus_overview: This subject examines cybersecurity through a human factors lens across societal, industry, and organisational contexts. Students explore how ethical, social, and psychological factors shape human behaviour and cyber risk, and how these vulnerabilities arise and are exploited. They analyse cybercrime business models and global threats, with a focus on how human factors contribute to attack success and organisational risk. Building on this, students apply human factors principles to design organisational cybersecurity solutions, including cultural, communication, and policy strategies aligned to relevant frameworks. Through this progression, students develop professional skills in evaluative judgement, teamwork, and communication to deliver practical, human-centred cybersecurity solutions.
learning_outcomes: Assess the economic impact of and financial implications of investing in human factors in cyber security and propose cost-effective risk management strategies.

Analyse cybercrime business models and threats impacting corporate social and ethical responsibilities, assessing the influence of organisational culture, leadership, and communication on cyber security practices.

Investigate social implications of human factors in cyber security, considering digital divides, socio-cultural norms, and digital empowerment, to inform policies promoting equitable access and participation in secure environments.
Analyse psychological factors influencing cybersecurity behaviours and personality characteristics to develop strategies for secure practices and organisational sustainability goals.

Develop a comprehensive cyber security culture, education and engagement strategy within an organisational context, whilst employing professional skills in evaluative judgement, team building, negotiation, and high-level communication across diverse environments.

title: INTERMEDIATE OBJECT-ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to advanced programming concepts that are increasingly used in modern software development projects. Mastery of these concepts will enable students to choose appropriate programming techniques for real-world software projects, and to take advantage of the latest advances in popular programming languages such as Java and Python. The subject is divided into three modules – advanced topics in object-oriented programming, functional programming, and programming with concurrency. Specific topics include interfaces, abstract classes, programming with exceptions, generic types, collections, recursion, lambda functions, threads, and synchronization.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast procedural, functional, and object-oriented (OO) programming paradigms.
Solve parallel data processing problems using the MapReduce paradigm.
Construct interfaces and abstract classes, and list reasons for their use.
