FTH4001 will broaden and deepen your knowledge through experiential methods, including role play and in-class presentations, and opportunities to apply theory to your specific work context and role. Learning will be assessed through class presentations, reflective practice essays and case reports/reviews that focus on your current practice as well as observation of your skill development in vivo. You will work towards specified levels of skill as set out in defined competencies.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and adapt systemic interventions to ensure respectful and inclusive practice that meets the needs of individuals and families from a range of cultural and diverse socio-cultural contexts.
Identify and synthesise systemic theories, associated frameworks and apply a range of skills and techniques to inform family work practice.
Develop an agenda and focus for family work and demonstrate a collaborative and respectful process in working with families.
Contrast and compare a linear and systemic conceptualisation of families’ presenting issues identifying the implications

title: FIRST STEPS IN FAMILY WORK
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will examine the importance of First Nations' family and community connections in conducting systemic therapy. You will explore foundational family therapy theories and skills, utilising these ideas in the context of cultural safety (working in cross cultural work contexts). You will integrate theory and skills to conduct a first family session. You will also develop a deeper understanding of the ongoing impact of transgenerational trauma on First Nations families and Communities, and apply culturally and trauma-informed practices.
learning_outcomes: Translate and integrate a set of foundational family therapy concepts and skills in conducting a first session of systemic work with First Nations peoples
Develop systemic case conceptualisations for a range of presenting issues and challenges
Working collaboratively and individually, create a safe, respectful and family sensitive context for working with First Nations families with consideration for culture and other diversity issues.

Working collaboratively and individually, using evidence-based knowledge and traditional and digital methods and technologies, develop and present strategies for effective and appropriate responses to the impact of a range of traumagenic factors on First Nations people.

title: CONTEMPORARY APPLICATIONS OF FAMILY AND SYSTEMIC PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, systemic theories and practices are integrated and applied to more challenging family situations such as those involving conflict, trauma, grief and sociocultural diversity. Interwoven through all applications is a reflection on self and the influence of one’s own historical and current context. Alongside this you will engage in experiential exercises including role plays, developing requisite skills for conducting an initial family session.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a systemic understanding of the impact of loss, grief and trauma as experienced by individuals and families.

Integrate key ideas from a range of systemic and associated approaches to develop case conceptualisations and plans as appropriate to the needs and capacities of workers and clients within the mandate and context of the work.

Synthesise and utilise personal learning about the influence of historical factors and current socio-cultural context on the worker's practice with individuals, families and other social and professional groups.
Conduct a culturally sensitive, trauma informed, and effective single session family consultation.

title: TRANSFORMING SYSTEMIC PRACTICES FOR WORK WITH FIRST NATIONS FAMILIES
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will consolidate your theoretical knowledge and develop skills to apply your knowledge across the life cycle as well as in relevant work contexts. You will learn additional family therapy frameworks and how to translate these for use with First Nations families. You will explore your own culture and experiences, identifying constraints in your work with First Nations peoples to increase your effectiveness in your professional practice. You will be supported to safely reflect on your family of origin, current life circumstances, professional history, and other contextual influences. You will deepen your knowledge of relevant theoretical frameworks that are useful for conceptualising and appraising the relationship between the influence of your own self- factors and your interactions with clients. Therapist self- care and ethics are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the influence of family, community and life experiences on personal values, interpersonal style, and capacities as a family therapist/counsellor/advocate with First Nations families.

Develop systemic case conceptualisations and ways of working that creatively integrate First Nations ways of knowing, being and doing with family therapy theories for a range of presenting issues and challenges.
Implement a developmentally appropriate, culturally sensitive and trauma informed approach to working with First Nations peoples across the lifespan in the context of family and community.
Implement strategies to address practice challenges posed by the intersection of identities within the contexts of community and professional life.
Effectively manage challenging family interactions.

title: FOUNDATIONAL FAMILY THERAPY MODELS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you are guided in the integration with your current skill and knowledge level with a more in-depth understanding of family therapy theoretical models relating to the family and other contexts. In lectures/seminars you will explore in greater depth the major family therapy and associated theories and practices with an emphasis on developing a theoretically informed collaborative case conceptualisation. Emphasis in this semester will be on using the theoretical frameworks provided to reflect on your own clinical skill development in the context of your personal and professional history and in formulating, setting and working on goals for improved competence. You will work towards specified levels of skill as set out in defined competencies.
learning_outcomes: Develop an appropriate systemic formulation of presenting difficulties drawing on family therapy and other relevant theoretical frameworks.
Analyse and integrate factors pertaining to values, interpersonal style and capacities that impact on your practice within the therapist-client system, using defined theoretical frameworks.
Execute a respectful, non-blaming, and effective initial family therapy session incorporating a reflecting team process.

title: FAMILY THERAPY - ADVANCED APPLICATION
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will start to expand your use of family therapy theoretical models to develop approaches appropriate to working with complex case presentations as you further refine your knowledge and skills in assessing and analysing family situations and your own capacities to work effectively with them. Approaches explored in the lectures / seminars will be integrated with knowledge and skills from previous subjects to work in small live clinical groups, supervised by experienced family therapy supervisors with families registered with the Bouverie Centre. You will continue to assess, evaluate and intervene with the contribution of influences from your own personal and professional contexts in order to maximise your clinical effectiveness.
learning_outcomes: Conduct interactionally based family interventions with effectiveness and efficiency using a range of appropriate family therapy techniques.
Analyse family situations by using appropriate specialist knowledge pertaining to a range of complex presentations.
Analyse your personal and professional influences and integrate these learnings to facilitate effective clinical practice with families.

title: MOLECULAR GENETICS
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to concepts and methods in molecular and human genetics. Topics covered include: DNA and RNA structure, DNA replication, chromosome structure, transposable elements, transcription, translation, regulation of gene expression, recombination, DNA damage and repair, molecular biology and recombinant technologies, modes of inheritance, single and multigene diseases, epigenetic diseases, diagnosis of genetic diseases, gene therapy, personalised medicine, biotechnology, applications of genetic model organisms, bioinformatics, human evolution and variation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse molecular genetics data
Demonstrate comprehension of genetic concepts, including molecular mechanisms underpinning the inheritance and expression of genetic traits
Understand how to perform and apply molecular genetics techniques

title: FAMILY THERAPY - ADVANCED INTEGRATIVE PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will draw on the range of family therapy theoretical models learned during the course alongside other applicable knowledges and skills to achieve in-depth assessments and analyses of complex family difficulties in general, and also in specialist areas. You will integrate all of this knowledge and skills with awareness of your own capacities and limitations and will synthesise this information to arrive at unique effective courses of intervention with the difficulties experienced by each of your client families. You will continue in your live supervised clinical groups to see families registered with The Bouverie Centre and in this context will refine and deepen your competence as a family therapist.
learning_outcomes: Integrate family therapy and other relevant theoretical frameworks with specialist knowledge and information from the family and other relevant sources to effectively formulate each unique problem presentation.

Conduct effective, collaborative, trauma-informed, inclusive interventions based on accurate assessment, appropriate selection of approaches and skilled implementation of strategies appropriate to the presenting problem/s, and relevant client, therapist and wider contextual factors.
Work together as a team to synthesise and present knowledge about systemic practice to their peers and other professionals
Articulate a comprehensive strategy for ongoing critical reflective practice and development integrating family therapy and other relevant theoretical frameworks.

title: FOOD WATER AND ENVIRONMENT
syllabus_overview: By 2050, the world will be faced with the challenge of providing water, food and a sustainable environment for an estimated 9 billion human inhabitants. Securing our environmental well-being and sustaining global and local food and water supplies are three of the most critical problems current and future generations face. Patterns of food production, land use, consumption and the globalisation of food systems as well as processes of urbanisation and climate change have implications for community health, cultural practices, and economic well-being. This subject examines the role of food production and consumption in securing land and water resources and providing for healthy communities. Case studies, drawn from Latin America, Asia, and Australia, will explore the policy, sociocultural practices, and economies of food production and consumption, emphasising, as well, the role of water security and sustainable development. Students will explore, critique, and develop strategies, policies, techniques and actions for addressing the interconnected challenges of securing food, water and the environment.
learning_outcomes: Understand relationships between food production and consumption in Australia and how food security can be further strengthened
Investigate capacities for local food production and/or water management in a selected case study area
Demonstrate and apply ethical and cultural awareness to the food and water security issues
Contextualise cultural and economic practices of food production and consumption and water management at a local and global level

title: ECOLOGICAL GENETICS AND EVOLUTION
syllabus_overview: In this subject ideas, concepts and methods relevant to the study of population genetics and evolution are presented. Areas covered include theoretical and quantitative methods of population genetic and phylogenetic analysis; macro- and microevolutionary theory; new concepts in evolutionary thinking (such as evolution & development, and epigenetics)
learning_outcomes: Apply basic experimental genetic techniques in research
Conduct an oral presentation of a scientific paper, as a pair with another student, which you have researched to your peers.
Produce grammatically correct scientific reports that present evidence based explanations of laboratory experiments.

Explain genetic concepts, including patterns of inheritance, principles of genetic analysis (e.g., mutations in pedigrees and model organisms, applications of DNA sequences, phylogenetics) and evolution by natural selection
Place theoretical and/or experimental information into the appropriate discipline specific context.

title: GENETIC MODELS OF HUMAN DISEASE AND DEVELOPMENT
syllabus_overview: Genetic models play a crucial role in understanding mechanisms underlying disease and discovering potential treatments. These models involve genetic manipulation of organisms, such as mice, nematodes, fruit fly and zebra fish, to mimic specific human diseases. This subject uses genetic models to illustrate key aspects of reverse genetics approaches in the context of human disease and development processes. You will be able to explore these concepts through laboratory projects and workshop problems.
learning_outcomes: Apply analytical approaches to problems involving genetic models and disease.
Use scientific terminology to describe and explain fundamental molecular genetics concepts associated with genetic models and disease
Synthesise experimental and published data in an authentic scientific communication format.
Demonstrate advanced practical skills in a molecular genetics laboratory setting.

title: FAMILY THERAPY MODELS AND APPLICATIONS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will consolidate knowledge of family therapy theoretical models and integrate these into into your repertoire for analysing and intervening with families and in working on your own resources and constraints as a therapist. You will evaluate the appropriateness of the various models according to your assessment of presenting problems of families from across the life span and formulate interventions that fit with these assessments and your own developing style.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise specialist knowledge relevant to evidence, developmental stages across the lifespan, sensitivity to culture and other diversity factors to develop appropriate case conceptualisations and therapeutic plans.

Further integrate factors pertaining to values, interpersonal style and capacities as they impact on your practice within the therapist client system, using family therapy and other relevant theoretical frameworks to conceptualise and develop strategies to increase your therapeutic flexibility and effectiveness.
Conduct interactionally based family therapy sessions incorporating a reflecting team process.

title: GENOMIC TECHNOLOGIES AND BIOINFORMATICS
syllabus_overview: Genomics is a field of genetics that analyses the genomes and interactions that underlie biological diversity and evolution. This field is essential to studies in genetics and ecology. Genomics is commonly applied in biomedical research, health industries and many other fields. In GEN3003, you are introduced to the principles and bioinformatic methods of genome sequencing, assembly, annotation, and comparison. Techniques commonly used in genomics and bioinformatics; including next-generation sequencing, genome alignment, de novo assembly, SNP identification and transcriptomics, will be introduced through workshop activities.
learning_outcomes: Apply authentic genomic and bioinformatic methods to interrogate biological datasets
Communicate the results and implications of genomic and bioinformatics analyses using appropriate formats and terminology as an individual and as part of a group.
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of various nucleic acid sequencing technologies and bioinformatics tools and resources

title: EVOLUTION IN A CHANGING WORLD
syllabus_overview: Evolution in a Changing World explores how life responds to environmental change, from deep-time climate shifts to today’s human-driven transformations. Students examine the principles of evolution, speciation, and niche theory, and how these shape species’ distributions and biodiversity patterns. We consider the impacts of climate change, including the capacity for adaptation, movement, or extinction, and the limits imposed by biology and the environment. The subject also investigates multiple stressors such as habitat loss, pesticides, and urbanisation, providing a framework for understanding the challenges species face in a rapidly changing world. Using examples from animals, and through critical analysis of scientific literature and hands-on research projects, you will gain a thorough understanding of the mechanisms of evolution and learn how to design and undertake studies to better understand evolutionary processes in a changing world.
learning_outcomes: Report on evolutionary concepts and contemporary issues using scientific language individually and in a group.
Design scientific studies that investigate evolutionary processes.
Critically review factors that impact the distribution of species and biodiversity patterns.
Evaluate scientific literature and scientific data collected via experiments, laboratory procedures, and field observations.
Analyse the impacts of stressors such as climate change, habitat loss, pesticides, and urbanisation on species of animals.

title: CONSERVATION GENETICS AND MOLECULAR ECOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Genetic approaches represent core tool for the understanding and management of biodiversity. This subject investigates the use of genetic tools for conservation management and ecological studies from understanding inbreeding to climate proofing species. Topics covered include core concepts in population genetics, speciation and hybridisation, the impact of human disturbance on genetic processes, as well as applied uses such as managing invasive species, using eDNA and DNA barcoding and even de-extinction. You will learn how constant advances in genetic technology are driving improvements in ecological research and conservation management. Using examples from plants and animals, and through critical analysis of scientific literature and hands-on research projects, you will gain a thorough understanding of applied population genetics, and learn how to design and undertake molecular ecology studies.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise coherent evidence-based explanations and communicate to peers in an authentic communication format as an individual and part of a group.
Analyse and interpret scientific data collected via experiments, laboratory procedures, and/or field observations.
Apply scientific terminology appropriately to describe and explain the fundamental concepts and current issues of the discipline area of conservation genetics and ecology

title: SEX, RACE NATION
syllabus_overview: This interdisciplinary subject enables better understanding of ourselves and of our relations to others in settler colonial Australia. We examine how gender identities are not simply separate from other identities; they are always situated in relation to other differences, such as race, class, sexuality or disability. Beginning with ways sex and race interact in the nation, the subject asks how people develop diverse forms of belonging within systems of social power, governance, fields of knowledge and public debates. We question taken for granted assumptions about identity formation so that differences can be better negotiated in professional and institutional contexts. Materials include readings, film clips, historical texts, personal stories, statistics, and advertisements. The subject entails a deep appreciation of how choices we make affect the natural, economic, social, political and cultural systems in which sex, gender and diversity becomes significant now and in the future. In doing so, we aim to promote social justice.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate diverse positions/arguments surrounding GSDS topic.
Present sustained written argument in GSDS
Apply key concepts to issues and public debates on GSDS topics
Develop cultural awareness and sensitivity
Introduce and develop team work skills

title: GENDER POWER IDENTITY
syllabus_overview: How are gender identities in their diversity formed, represented and lived in our private, professional and public interactions? Exploring debates about how we see, are seen, or not seen, we analyse the places, authorities and knowledges linking sex/gender relations to power and social justice. We observe sex/gender in the context of media, family, relationships, work, violence, sport and the sex industry. We ask how our rights, responsibilities and roles in society are gendered, sexualised, racialised and normalised to the extent that they influence changing patterns of living together more justly and freely. Materials include readings, media images, legal and policy documents, film clips and documentaries. We address the Global Citizenship essential, entailing a deep appreciation of living in an interconnected world; we recognise the global context in which concepts act across cultures and boundaries encountered when working with diverse communities - now and in the future. This is a level 1 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate cultural awareness and distinguish between average trends and individual differences.
Apply key concepts to issues and situations where sex/gender poses problems
Undertake primary and secondary research and summarise scholarship on relevant Gender Sexuality and Diversity topics.
Evaluate and critically discuss conventional ideas as well as diverse positions/arguments about sex/gender relations in written and oral formats.
Identify and quantify demographics of sex/gender identities in their diversity.

title: DIVERSITY AT WORK: ACCESS, EQUITY AND POLICY
syllabus_overview: In this summer subject, you will work to assess and analyse equity and diversity policies in your place of work or study, to identify where policy does not reflect practice, and to develop a set of recommendations for how to achieve and enact equitable and inclusive policy. We explore the contradictory processes through which social policy is developed along the axes and intersections of difference based on class, gender, sexuality, race, disability, and age. We consider the changing context of public policy, work, and new political struggles in both an international and national climate of economic, political, cultural, and environmental instability. This subject gives you the ability to critically and creatively analyse existing structures and systems, including settler colonialism and the cisheteropatriarchy, and to identify where and how institutions can be held to account based on their existing diversity and inclusion policies. It also gives students a practice-based experience of working collaboratively to enact positive change. This subject is delivered over a five-week period, running from Weeks 3 to 7 in Term 1 and Weeks 45 to 49 in Term 6 of 2026. Topics include: power dynamics in institutions, the diversity of social identities, how to make changes in the workplace, and what genuine inclusion means. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate alternative conceptual approaches to social policy and welfare in Australian and comparative contexts.
Develop understanding of the changing relationships between states, markets, families and the community sector.
Demonstrate the capacity to work effectively in groups.
Assess contemporary policy directions and their implications.

title: DIVERSITY DEMOCRACY DISSENT
syllabus_overview: This subject measures the ideal of democracy against its capacity to deal with the diversity of the people. You will lstudy how different identities based on class, gender, sexuality, race (among others) articulate, negotiate and contest their place and (mis)representation in democratic life. You will study the heritage of the concept of democracy in relation to its concrete manifestations in nation states, and compare how the democratic ideal of living together in a political community is debated in various contexts. Topics include: sovereignty and Indigenous politics; free speech, censorship and political correctness; the gendered, sexualised and racialized character of culture wars and social change; religious expression and secularism; political activism, civil disobedience and violence; law and justice; and discourses of human rights. Texts include legal documents, petitions, government papers, propaganda, various media, and academic writings. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively and cooperatively in groups
Summarise research and arguments regarding key debates relating to diversity within democracy
Evaluate diverse positions/arguments regarding topics/ debate
Produce original, well researched response to relevant topic in GSDS
Produce an original piece of sustained complex written argument that can contribute to current public debate regarding diversity and democracy
Present brief and persuasive argument to peers that focuses on GSDS issues within democracy

title: THINKING THROUGH GENDER: BODIES, DEVIANCE, DIFFERENCE
syllabus_overview: Drawing on perspectives of key thinkers in queer and trans theory, critical race theory, and disability/crip studies, we explore the ways we are taught to uphold and upkeep a disciplined (and disciplining) body across different times, places, texts, and histories. We hone skills in research, theory, and critical analysis as we explore how 'marginal bodies' have been and are positioned, represented, and thought in popular culture, social movements, and institutions. Topics include feminist approaches to the body, gender euphoria and queer utopias, writing back to the colony, and posthumanism. The subject's blend of theory, reading, research, and creative writing promotes new ways of thinking about gender, the body, and society. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Produce a sustained, complex written argument about gender and sexuality theories.
Synthesise research and arguments about gender, sexuality and diversity.
Review gender sexuality and diversity studies theories and concepts in different historical and cultural contexts.
Apply interdisciplinary GSDS concepts to understanding issues and debates regarding gender and sexuality.

title: GREEK 1
syllabus_overview: In this subject complete beginners acquire practical skills in understanding and expressing basic information, such as personal details, needs, wishes, likes and dislikes in speech and writing. Relevant aspects of contemporary Greek society and culture are also introduced. The emphasis throughout is on practice at listening, reading, speaking and writing Greek in everyday situations, with various audio-visual aids being used. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Acquire an initial awareness of the Greek world and what shapes it.
Express a simple opinion and express likes and dislikes.
Apply acquired knowledge to new situations; use a bilingual dictionary correctly and apply grammatical rules in the interests of self-expression and meaningful interaction with others.
Write short texts relevant to their daily lives using different tenses, cases, singular and plural, adjective and noun agreement, etc.
Collaborate with a partner or in a group to perform oral dialogues and written tasks.
Read short, simple texts and find specific information in everyday material such as advertisements, menus and timetables.
Communicate and process information in day-to-day situations through spoken Greek.

title: GREEK 2
syllabus_overview: In this subject we continue from 'Greek 1' with students learning to handle common interpersonal transactions in Greek with confidence as well as to understand and produce (in speech and writing) simple descriptions, narrations and expressions of attitudes and opinions. Relevant aspects of contemporary Greek society and culture are also introduced. The emphasis continues to be on practice at listening, reading, speaking and writing Greek in everyday situations, but students are also introduced to the structure of the language. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Read short, simple texts and find specific information in everyday material such as advertisements, menus and timetables.
Write short texts relevant to their daily lives using different tenses, cases, singular and plural, adjective and noun agreement, etc.
Express a simple opinion and express likes and dislikes.
Acquire an initial awareness of the Greek world and what shapes it.
Apply acquired knowledge to new situations; use a bilingual dictionary correctly and apply grammatical rules in the interests of self-expression and meaningful interaction with others.
Communicate and process information in day-to-day situations through spoken Greek.
Collaborate with a partner or in a group to perform oral dialogues and written tasks.

title: GREEK 3
syllabus_overview: In this subject you learn to discuss issues relating to contemporary Greek and Australian society in Greek, extending their vocabulary and knowledge of grammar. Oral and literacy skills are developed through use of news media reports, magazine articles and film.
learning_outcomes: Interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity with native speakers of Greek; present clear, detailed descriptions on a wide range of subjects; present a viewpoint on a topical issue.
Understand the Greek world and what shapes it.
Collaborate with a partner or in a group to perform oral dialogues and written tests.
Understand texts that consist of high-frequency language; understand contemporary factual and literary texts.
Evaluate diverse perspectives in a argument of relevant social and/or cultural nature.
Interact with Greeks with a degree of fluency and spontaneity in accordance with socio-cultural differences.

Write medium texts relevant to one's daily life using different tenses, cases, singular and plural, adjective and noun agreement, etc., as well as write concisely and critically on literary and abstract topics.
Perform critical analysis and synthesis, and develop and evaluate arguments. Use a bilingual and monolingual dictionary correctly.

title: GREEK 4
syllabus_overview: In this subject students learn to talk and write in Greek about a wide range of aspects of modern Greek culture and society in an informed and coherent manner and to interpret short literary texts. Vocabulary and knowledge of grammar are systematically extended in the course of these readings and discussions.
learning_outcomes: Understand texts that consist of high-frequency language; understand contemporary factual and literary texts and write concisely and critically on contemporary factual and literary topics.
Perform critical analysis and synthesis, and develop and evaluate arguments. Use a bilingual and monolingual dictionary correctly.
Evaluate diverse perspectives in an argument of relevant social and/or cultural nature.
Collaborate with a partner or in a group to perform oral dialogues and oral tests.
Interact with Greeks with a degree of fluency and spontaneity in accordance with socio-cultural differences. Understand the Greek world and what shapes it.

title: GREEK 5
syllabus_overview: In this subject your skills in Greek are consolidated and extended through exercises in understanding a variety of authentic spoken and written materials and through practice at speaking and writing. Due attention is given to grammatical accuracy and appropriate usage. The materials used also serve as an introduction to Greek society and culture and aspects of modern Greek history.
learning_outcomes: Express yourself fluently and spontaneously; ability to formulate ideas and opinions with precision and relate these to the contribution of other people.
Understand longer, more complex, factual and literary texts and films to appreciate distinctions of style.
Write argumentative and evaluate texts on studied topics and films using correct language structures.

Apply acquired knowledge to a broad range of situations; extrapolate information from different media sources and use it to formulate an argument. Formulate an opinion on a wide range of topics, including abstract ideas.
Interact with Greeks with a degree of fluency and spontaneity in accordance with socio-cultural differences. Participate in an intercultural dialogue with the Greek world.
Work as part of a team in class discussions and debates.

title: GREEK 6
syllabus_overview: In this subject, your oral and literacy skills in Greek are consolidated and extended through exercises in understanding a variety of authentic spoken and written materials and through practice at speaking and writing. Due attention is given to grammatical accuracy and appropriate usage. The materials used also serve as an introduction to Greek society, culture and aspects of modern Greek history.
learning_outcomes: Formulate an opinion on a wide range of topics, including abstract ideas, and discuss critically longer written texts and films.
Interact with Greeks with a degree of fluency and spontaneity in accordance with socio-cultural differences. Participate in an intercultural dialogue with the Greek world.
Understand longer, more complex, factual and literary texts and films to appreciate distinctions of style. Evaluate texts on studied topics using correct language structures.
Express yourself fluently and spontaneously; formulate ideas and opinions with precision and relate these to the contribution of other people. Work as part of a team in class discussions and debates.
Apply acquired knowledge to a broad range of situations, including extrapolating information from different media sources to formulate an argument.

title: INTRODUCTION TO HUMAN PHYSIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will first be introduced to concepts fundamental to the understanding of Human Physiology such as the organisation of the human body, homeostasis, basic cell structure and function, body fluids and the movement of molecules within body fluid compartments. The basics of nervous system and endocrine system function in the context of physiological regulation and homeostasis will then be explored. This information will provide the foundation for the study of major organ systems of the body including the muscular, digestive, cardiovascular, immune, respiratory, renal, and reproductive systems. This subject will also include content on metabolism of nutrients and acid-base homeostasis.
learning_outcomes: Explain how cellular activity contributes to the function of organs and the body as a whole.
Explain how a given body system contributes to homeostasis under normal conditions.
Interpret scientific information presented as tables, graphs and diagrams and communicate using correct physiological terminology.
Relate the structural organisation of the human body to whole body function.

title: INTRODUCTION TO ANATOMY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will continue with the study of anatomy and physiology and apply the concepts of human structure and function introduced in HBS101, to the musculoskeletal and nervous systems. Anatomical principles and terminology will be applied to relevant body systems and the concept of integrated function of multiple systems in one body region, the trunk, will be introduced.
learning_outcomes: Use appropriate skills to achieve significant outcomes in a human bioscience enquiry.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to integrate structure and function of body systems within an anatomical region.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe the structure and function of selected body systems.

title: HUMAN BIOSCIENCES A
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to human physiology - how the body works. You'll learn how the body is organised and the basics of cell structure and function, and how processes in the body are controlled. This will provide the foundation for the study of the major body systems important for support and movement (muscular system); regulation, integration and control (nervous and endocrine systems); fluids and transport (blood, heart, cardiovascular and immune systems); energy, maintenance and environmental exchange (respiratory, digestive and renal systems, metabolism); and the continuity of life (reproductive systems).
learning_outcomes: Explain the basic physiology of major organ systems of the human body.
Apply knowledge of physiology concepts to clinical and disease states.
Demonstrate oral and written communication skills.
Demonstrate the skills for self-managing, reflection, and successful learning at university.
Describe the structure and function of body cells, tissues, and organs.
Apply specialist terms and language associated with physiology and anatomy to describe the human body.

title: ANATOMY: LOWER LIMB & FOOT
syllabus_overview: In this subject the anatomical principles and terminology introduced in first year anatomy will be applied to the detailed study of the anatomy of the lower limb and the foot. The concept of integrated function of multiple body systems will be developed in each region and relevant medical imaging techniques and clinical assessment skills will be incorporated. Lectures and on-line material will provide an outline of the major content of this subject, but students will be responsible for their own learning through a variety of online and practical learning activities integrated with clinical applications.
learning_outcomes: Apply observational and communication skills, individually and as part of a team, using appropriate medical terminology, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, the living body or medical imaging in a laboratory environment
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the lower limb, and explain its role in support, locomotion and posture.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the foot, and explain its role in support, locomotion and posture.

title: ADVANCED SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY B
syllabus_overview: In this subject you gain knowledge in systems physiology, including the heart, blood,immune, renal, respiratory and acid-base systems. We discuss how the heart is a mechanical pump, followed by how blood vessels control blood flow and pressure. Our focus then shifts to the blood and mechanisms involved in developing immunity. You will gain a detailed understanding of the renal system and how it clears the body of waste while also being an important regulator of blood pressure. The respiratory system then becomes our focus where you will gain understanding of breathing mechanisms and how gasses are transported around the body. We conclude focusing on how the body regulates pH using both renal and respiratory buffers.
learning_outcomes: Effectively and professionally communicate experimental observations and the conclusions drawn from them.
Analyse and integrate experimentally-obtained physiological data with knowledge of basic physiological principles.
Predict how the immune, cardiovascular, renal and respiratory systems of the human body function both during normal physiological conditions and under pathological stress

title: HUMAN BIOSCIENCES B
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you are introduced to the study of anatomy. An overview of anatomical terminology, basic tissue types and a variety of techniques used to visualize the human body will be given followed by a more detailed study of the anatomy of the musculoskeletal and nervous systems. Anatomical principles and terminology will be applied to relevant body systems and the concept of integrated function of multiple systems in one body region will be introduced through the study of the trunk. You will be taught via an online-only OR blended (on-line and face-to-face) approach.
learning_outcomes: Describe the anatomical structure and function of major body systems.
Use appropriate anatomical terminology to describe anatomical structures and events.

Apply observational and communication skills to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using various anatomical resources, the living body or medical imaging.

title: ANATOMY OF LOWER LIMB AND TRUNK
syllabus_overview: In this subject the anatomical principles and terminology introduced in previous learning will be applied to the detailed study of the anatomy of the back, lower limb and thorax. The concept of integrated function of multiple body systems will be developed in each region. Teaching will include both online learning and face-to-face teaching sessions including practical classes involving cadaver materials and surface anatomy. You will be required to work together in small groups to take responsibility for your own learning and understanding of anatomy so that you are able to identify anatomical structure and function on a living body as you would in a clinical context.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems in the thoracic region, including its role in respiration and circulation.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the vertebral column, including its role in support and posture.

Apply observational and communication skills, using appropriate medical terminology, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, the living body or medical imaging in a laboratory environment.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the lower limb, including its role in support, locomotion and posture.

title: ADVANCED SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY A
syllabus_overview: In this subject you gain knowledge in systems physiology, including the nervous system, muscle tissue, endocrinology and the gastrointestinal system. We will discuss how the nervous system controls body systems, focusing on the electrical transmission of information and how this is modulated. Our focus then shifts to muscle tissue and the mechanisms involved in skeletal muscle contraction, force generation and fatigue. You will gain a detailed understanding of the endocrine system and how it is responsible for controlling many of our bodies daily functions and metabolism. The semester concludes focusing on the gastrointestinal systems where you will gain an understanding of the mechanisms surrounding food digestion and nutrient absorption.
learning_outcomes: Predict how the nervous, muscle, endocrine and gastrointestinal systems of the human body function both during normal physiological conditions and under pathological stress
Effectively and professionally communicate physiological principles, experimental observations and the conclusions drawn from them.
Analyse and integrate experimentally-obtained physiological data with knowledge of basic physiological principles

title: ANATOMY: LOWER AND UPPER LIMBS
syllabus_overview: In this subject the anatomical principles and terminology introduced in HBS1HBB will be applied to the detailed study of the anatomy of the lower limb and the upper limb and hand. The concept of integrated function of multiple body systems will be developed in each region and relevant medical imaging techniques and clinical assessment skills will be incorporated. Interactive lectures and on-line activities will provide an outline of the major content of this subject which is reviewed in workshops, but students will be responsible for their own learning using all the learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Apply anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the head and skull and to explain the course and function of neural signalling pathways.
Apply anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems in the upper limb and explain its role in grasp.

Apply observational and communication skills, individually or as part of a team, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, the living body or medical imaging in a laboratory environment.
Apply anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the lower limb and explain its role in support, locomotion and posture.

title: ANATOMY AND NEUROPHYSIOLOGY FOR SPEECH AND SWALLOWING
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will explore the functional anatomy and neurosciences relevant to speech and swallowing and the role of the central and peripheral nervous system in sensory and motor function. The concepts of human structure and function introduced in your first year anatomy and physiology subjects will be applied to the head and neck, respiratory and nervous systems. Emphasis will be placed on developing students' abilities to predict the effects of impaired structure and function. This subject will provide students with foundation knowledge to assist in clinical reasoning, practice and consultation in speech pathology.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively with peers in a small group to understand the anatomical aspects of clinically relevant case studies
Make accurate observations of anatomical structures and events and infer their relationship to function.
Apply anatomical principles to explain normal structure and function of body systems in the nervous system involved in speech, swallowing, vision, hearing and breathing.
Apply anatomical principles to explain normal structure and function of body systems in the head and neck involved in speech, swallowing and hearing.
Apply anatomical principles to explain normal structure and function of body systems in the thoracic region involved in breathing and speech.

title: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject provides you with the fundamental principles of the underlining mechanisms of human disease and how these mechanisms impact on clinical outcomes. Emphasis begins with general disease processes including cell injury, cell adaptations, inflammation, immunopathology, tissue healing, neoplasia and circulatory disturbances and disorders. Specific pathological conditions of body systems e.g. nervous, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal, hepatic and skeletal systems along with diabetes will be addressed. A variety of teaching methods; including interactive lectures, on-line video content, on-line quizzes, clicker workshops and discipline-specific workshops will be delivered in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Explain cellular and biochemical changes that underlie the development of systemic diseases (i.e. Systemic Pathophysiology and relate these changes to the likely clinical course and outcomes of an afflicted individual.
Demonstrate effective communication skills by communicating scientific results, information, or arguments to a range of audiences, for a range of purposes, and using a variety of modes.

Apply the principles of General Pathophysiology to human disorders and reparative states, describing how these general pathophysiologic processes impact on possible clinical courses and outcomes in an afflicted individual.

title: CLINICAL ANATOMY AND NEUROSCIENCES
syllabus_overview: In this subject, anatomical principles will be applied to the detailed study of head, neck and neuroanatomy. Topic materials will be presented face to face and online lectures, videoclips and worksheets, but you will be responsible for your own learning through supported face to face practical activities and online workshops, including examination of appropriate cadaver materials. Emphasis is placed on the application of anatomical principles to correlate structure with function in developing an understanding of the basis of everyday activities and related clinical problems.
learning_outcomes: Independently source, assimilate and appraise basic anatomical principles relating to neuroanatomy. Analyse the neural pathways and develop the basic clinical skills to understand the neurological disorders.
Work collaboratively with peers in a small group to complete an anatomy report

Use available anatomical resources to competently identify a given anatomical structure and assess it in a clinical context. Anatomical structures will be presented either as an image or in situ, and evaluate its orientation and operation within the body.
Independently source, assimilate and appraise basic anatomical principles relating to head and neck anatomy.

title: HUMAN SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY A
syllabus_overview: In this blended subject you will gain knowledge in systems physiology, which includes homeostasis, membrane dynamics, communication and integration, the nervous system, muscle tissue and endocrinology. The detailed online resources will be supported by interactive lectures and a comprehensive program of enquiry-based workshops.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and integrate experimentally obtained physiological data with knowledge of basic physiological principles.
Explore, build and reflect on your experiences that develop your career readiness and employability and actively prepare for life beyond university.
Predict how various systems of the human body function both during normal physiological conditions and under pathological stress.

title: HUMAN SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY B
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will examine the cardiovascular system, the gastrointestinal system, blood, respiratory system and renal system. The detailed online resources will be supported by interactive lectures and a face to face workshop program which will develop critical thinking skills while demonstrating the integrative nature of human physiology.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and integrate experimentally obtained physiological data with knowledge of basic physiological principles.
Explore, build and reflect on your experiences that develop your career readiness and employability and actively prepare for life beyond university.
Predict how various systems of the human body function both during normal physiological conditions and under pathological stress.

title: HUMAN PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will examine disorders which may be experienced by individuals over the life-span, emphasizing the basic pathological processes that underlie diseases and the risk factors and contributing causes of disorders. Specifically, general pathological processes will be discussed with emphasis on disturbed function, adaptation to injury, inflammation, tissue healing, immunological disorders, neoplasia, fluid imbalance, thrombosis, embolism and vascular disorders. In addition to general pathological processes, specific pathological conditions of body systems e.g. cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, gastrointestinal and skeletal systems along with diabetes will be addressed. You will consolidate and apply their knowledge of pathophysiology by communicating a disease state in authentic format to scientific peers and non-expert audiences.
learning_outcomes: Explain cellular and biochemical changes that underlie the development of systemic diseases (i.e. Systemic Pathophysiology and relate these changes to the likely clinical course and outcomes of an afflicted individual.

Apply the principles of General Pathophysiology to selected human disorders and reparative states, describing how these general pathophysiologic processes impact on possible clinical courses and outcomes in an afflicted individual.
Demonstrate effective communication skills by communicating scientific results, information, or arguments to a range of audiences, for a range of purposes, and using a variety of modes.

title: DEVELOPMENTAL AND VISCERAL ANATOMY
syllabus_overview: In this subject the anatomical principles and terminology of visceral cavities and organs introduced in pre-requisite subjects will be applied to the detailed study of the anatomy of the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavity. The subject will also include the study of the microscopic structure, embryological development of the visceral systems and the anatomical basis of common clinical anomalies. The concept of integrated function of multiple body systems will be developed in each region. The teaching sessions will include practical classes including cadaver materials, digital resources and surface anatomy. You will be required to work together in small groups to take responsibility for your own learning and understanding of anatomy so that you are able to identify anatomical structure and function on a living body as you would in a clinical or professional context.
learning_outcomes: Apply an understanding of the normal development of the visceral organs of the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities to be able to explain common developmental anomalies
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems in the abdominopelvic region.

Apply observational and communication skills, individually and in groups, using appropriate medical terminology, to identify anatomical structures and infer their relationship to function using models, the living body or medical imaging.

title: ANATOMY OF UPPER LIMB, HEAD AND NEUROSCIENCES
syllabus_overview: In this subject the anatomical principles and terminology introduced in HBS1HBB and extended in HBS2ALT will be applied to the detailed study of the anatomy of the upper limb, the head and neck, and to the study of neurosciences. The concept of integrated function of multiple body systems will be developed in each region and relevant medical imaging techniques and clinical assessment skills will be incorporated. Lectures will provide an outline of the major content of this subject, but you will be responsible for your own learning through a variety of practical activities and integrated enquiries with clinical applications.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the upper limb, including its role in support, posture and grasp.
Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of the central nervous system, including neural pathways for sensation and movement.

Apply observational and communication skills, including the use of appropriate medical terminology, to make accurate observations of anatomical structures or events and infer their relationship to function using cadaveric material, the living body or medical imaging in a laboratory environment.

Apply relevant anatomical principles to describe normal structure and function of body systems within the head and neck, including its role in housing visceral structures, special sense organs and the central nervous system.

title: FOOD AND NUTRITION PRACTICAL SKILLS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will undertake a series of interactive, application focused practical exercises that apply theory of biochemistry, physiology and human nutrition within a laboratory environment. This subject is delivered as an on-campus intensive program.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate practical skills and laboratory safety for food and nutrition sciences.
Measure and record experimental data relevant to the practical skills required for food and nutrition sciences.
Prepare written scientific reports consistent with industry discipline standards.
Analyse experimental data to draw evidence-based conclusions.

title: WORK AND HEALTH
syllabus_overview: In this subject, work-related determinants of work-related health are reviewed within a broad, macro-ergonomics systems framework. You will have the opportunity to develop an understanding of some of the mechanisms and pathways via which people's jobs and working environments can affect their physical and psychological health, safety and wellbeing, both positively and negatively. Within this framework, the aetiology of a range of the most commonly occurring occupational injuries and diseases will be reviewed. Although both the physical and psychosocial environments impact people at work, this subject focuses on the impact of the psychosocial environment on people's health, safety, wellbeing and performance at work.
learning_outcomes: Contextualise the relevance of positive OHS indicators: 'health', 'wellbeing', and job satisfaction, and understand the relationship with health and wellbeing.
Work collaboratively to analyse the effects of fatigue and stress on health and performance.
Interpret data on common occupational injuries and diseases and identify limitations of different data sources.
Apply key concepts in OHS risk management to various workplace issues.
Apply a macro-ergonomics or socio-technical systems perspective of health and wellbeing in relation to various job and workplace factors.

title: FOUNDATIONS IN PHARMACOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Pharmacology is the study of drugs. Drugs play a key role in the treatment of most human diseases and are used to both cure and prevent disease. In this subject you will learn the general principles of pharmacology including drug classification, formulation, administration and basic pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Drugs affecting the nervous system and major organs will be explored, and the concept of selective toxicity to treat infection will be introduced. You will gain knowledge in commonly prescribed drugs, clinical trials and over the counter and complimentary medications, drugs of abuse and dependence and drugs in sport. Emphasis is placed on human pharmacology including clinical topics, such as, adverse drug reactions and drug interactions.
learning_outcomes: Analyse how pharmacological principles underpin the delivery of safe and effective patient care.
Explain how drug properties and human physiology contribute to contraindications, interactions, and adverse reactions to support safe clinical decisions.
Articulate pharmacological terminology, information, and arguments effectively to diverse audiences across various modes, both individually and as part of a team.
Evaluate how drug classes act on living tissue to modify biological responses and achieve therapeutic effects.
Distinguish between pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, and explain the factors influencing drug processing in the body.

Demonstrate effective communication skills, individually and as part of a team, by communicating scientific results, information, or arguments to a range of audiences, for a range of purposes, and using a variety of modes.

Explain cellular and biochemical changes that underlie the development of systemic diseases (i.e. Systemic Pathophysiology and relate these changes to the likely clinical course and outcomes of an afflicted individual.

title: HONOURS IN HUMAN ANATOMY, PHYSIOLOGY AND PHARMACOLOGY A
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program in the School of Agriculture, Biomedicine and Environment (SABE) is to provide undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Human Anatomy, Physiology and Pharmacology consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part-time) individual research project, supervised by a SABE scientist whose research is in the disciplines of anatomy, physiology and/or pharmacology. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. The School Honours co-ordinator will provide more information on the application process including a comprehensive list of available research projects. HBS401A is the first subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in SABE. Students must take HBS401A first.
learning_outcomes: Extend oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Recall knowledge in anatomy, physiology and/or pharmacology when conducting experiments, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.
Obtain practical experience and advanced knowledge in the fields of anatomy, physiology and/or pharmacology.
Show intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice
Understand published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
