Apply evidence-based database design principles based on contemporary models and frameworks to database construction.
Compare and contrast contemporary principles and theories to develop data visualisation reports and dashboards.

title: ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORDS: IMPLEMENTATION AND MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will apply foundational principles of health informatics to rigorously evaluate and critically appraise the technical requirements, competencies, and methodologies involved in the implementation and management of electronic health records (EHRs). Using an inquiry-driven learning approach, you will develop a comprehensive understanding of the design, structure, and operational dynamics of EHR systems. Topics include EHR architectures, implementation and adoption strategies, interoperability standards, privacy and security protocols, person and provider identification, clinical terminologies, clinical decision-support systems, audit trails, and data linkage methods for integrating disparate health datasets.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critically appraise diverse data linkage and integration methodologies to effectively link disparate healthcare datasets.
Critically evaluate the design and functionality of clinical decision-support systems within electronic health records environments.
Working collaboratively, evaluate and apply electronic health record standards, architectures, and structures in health service implementations.
Evaluate and apply best practices for electronic medical record implementation, (including privacy and security controls) to ensure successful adoption and use.
Critically evaluate the evolution of policies related to electronic health records and supporting technologies.

title: HEALTH INFORMATION PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE C
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will engage in supervised professional practice placements in healthcare and related agencies across the whole-of-health to further develop your health information management knowledge and skills. The purpose of the subject is to enable you to apply theoretical knowledge to practice during your 330 hours of professional practice. You will demonstrate your critical thinking and problem-solving skills through engagement in workplace projects or related activities. Regular contact with University supervisors is maintained during placements via telephone/Zoom, email and/or on-site visits. As this is a final capstone placement subject, it must be completed by all students. No advanced standing is available. To meet professional competency requirements students must pass both the professional placement and academic components of the subject.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise graduate-entry competencies in the practice of health information management through supervised engagement in activities which build upon academic studies and previous placement and experiences.
Integrate skills in project and time management including development and achievement of objectives, ability to work autonomously and to demonstrate initiative in work practice.
Demonstrate high professional ethical standards and maintain awareness of the social and ethical implications of professional and personal activities.
Analyse the processes for the collection and application of health information for clinical and other purposes at agency level.
Interrogate health data through extraction and analysis (including ICD-10-AM coding according to state and national protocols.)
Collaborate effectively in a multidisciplinary team environment and communicate appropriately using a wide range of mediums.
Critically reflect on current theory and practice and evaluate processes across health care agencies translating knowledge into new contexts.

title: EMPIRES, POWER AND THE MODERN WORLD: FOOD AS HISTORY
syllabus_overview: The food you eat is not just a matter of taste. It is the product of histories of imperialism, global trade and commerce, and industrial and scientific revolutions; it tells a story of cultural change and exchange. In this subject, we study global histories of food from the age of empires to the modern world. We will trace commodity chains for products such as chocolate and tea from agricultural production, through industrial manufacture, to retail, marketing and consumption. Along the way we will explore topics including slavery, Indigenous and ethnic food encounters, kitchens and modernity, adulterated food, and wartime food supplies. Through investigating political, legal, economic and cultural histories of food in global and local contexts, you will discover and debate key concepts including gender, class, race and power. You will bring historical understanding to the urgent question of food sustainability. This is a Level 1 subject. This subject includes live sessions in the form of either in-person or Zoom tutorials with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Show how history and historians shape the present and can contribute to envisaging new futures by reflecting on social, environmental and economic change and challenges in relation to food sustainability for future generations.
Practice critical-thinking, creative problem-solving and cultural literacy skills through analysing historical evidence, scholarship and changing representations of the past.

Demonstrate historical understanding of food production and consumption, with reference to processes of imperialism and industrialisation, and applying the concepts of gender, class, race, power and modernity as appropriate.
Develop inquiry/research skills, including the ability to effectively access and interpret a wide variety of primary and secondary materials, both electronic and paper-based.
Develop effective literacy and communication skills through the practice of oral and written communication.

title: MYTH, LEGEND AND HISTORY
syllabus_overview: How and why did people start to compose stories about the past? Why are some of these stories referred to as ‘history,’ when others are classified as ‘myth’ or ‘legend’? How are history and the nation connected? The history we study at school and university is the product of a particular western European tradition, but there are different ways of knowing about the past, and complex reasons why some stories survive over centuries. The discipline of history itself has also changed over time. In this subject you will explore how diverse peoples have constructed stories about their pasts, and how these stories have made an impact over time. You’ll hear from experts in the disciplines of History, Classics, and Archaeology who share an interest in the past but who use different types of evidence and ask different questions of that evidence. Our examination will range from the myths of Classical Greece and Rome; through the ancient texts, oral traditions and archaeology of South Asia, Early Medieval Britain and the Viking world; to uses of the past in the settler colonial worlds of America and Australia from the 19th century, in twentieth-century Nazi Germany, and in contemporary South Asia. You will gain expertise in using a variety of historical sources including written stories, documents, objects, and visual materials such as paintings and film. You will have the opportunity to reflect on what it really means to study 'history’ and why history continues to play both an important and controversial role in politics, culture and in our understandings of ourselves. This is a level 1 subject.
learning_outcomes: Examine how diverse peoples have constructed stories about their pasts by undertaking research according to the methodological and ethical conventions of the History discipline.
Navigate and critically assess historical evidence, scholarship and changing representations of the past.
Demonstrate knowledge and historical understanding of at least one period or culture of the past through an analysis of relevant myths and/or legends.
Construct an evidence-based argument which analyses one or more myths/legends of past societies and communicate this clearly, demonstrating cultural awareness.
Identify and reflect critically upon the knowledge and skills developed in the study of History.

title: A VIOLENT CENTURY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will study the twentieth century, often characterised as the most violent century in history. We will consider world wars, including atrocities committed by the Nazis, attempted genocides of Indigenous and other peoples, and forced labour regimes using a global perspective. How did individuals, states and societies deal with atrocity and violence, both at the time, in its aftermath and in memory? We will evaluate the philosophical underpinnings that justified colonialism, the mass enslavement of human beings, and the thinking that allowed people to be traded as commodities and killed en masse. You will develop a sophisticated and complex understanding of the historical origins of human violence. You will explore why violence recurs and how it has been a driving force in history. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse historical evidence, scholarship and changing representations of violence in the past to construct complex and evidence-based arguments
Examine the historical and ethical issues raised by the study of violent events when undertaking research employing the methodological and ethical conventions of the History discipline.
Construct an evidence-based argument or narrative about histories of violence in the twentieth century.
Apply conceptual understanding of violent global historical events in the twentieth century.
Identify different systems and modes of violence and analyse their historical significance.

title: LOOTING THE PLANET: HISTORIES OF COLONIALISM, CAPITAL, AND CLIMATE
syllabus_overview: The climate crisis and inequality are two of the most urgent problems facing the world today. But how did we get to this point? How are these problems connected? And why are they such difficult problems to solve? In ‘Looting the Planet’ you will examine the deep historical links between the development of capitalism, the building of empires, ecological destruction and the unequal distribution of wealth. You will look beyond European history, to the Global South, Asia, Africa and the Americas, to develop a global understanding of these issues. Beginning in the Mongol Empire, you will study a range of case studies across time and place: the colonisation of the Americas; India and the British Empire; the Scramble for Africa; the Sino-Japanese War (otherwise known as WW2); and the Cold War and the ideology of ‘development’. You will debate key concepts in environmental histories: the relationship between humans and the natural world, the impact empires and nation-states have had on both human and natural history, and the complex interdependent systems that underpin these interactions. This is a Level 2 subject. This subject includes live sessions in the form of either in-person or Zoom tutorials with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply detailed understanding of human/environmental impacts, and the concepts of colonialism, capitalism and power.
Conduct historical research into complex problems relating to environmental histories, considering ethical implications and multiple perspectives
Develop creative, critical and analytical skills to understand and address problems of the relationship between humans and the environment in historical context.
Navigate, critically assess and utilise information from a range of sources, primary and secondary, relevant to the field of environmental history
Demonstrate high-level, ethical, professional and culturally aware communication skills

title: CIVIL RIGHTS HISTORIES: CHASING FREEDOMS
syllabus_overview: U.S. historian William H. Chafe has called the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s “the most significant social movement in all of American history.” The aim of this subject is to explore in detail the central protests and demonstrations of this important movement. Our chronology will largely concentrate on the period from the landmark 1954 Brown v. Board of Education decision through to the 1968 Poor Peoples’ Campaign. The subject, however, will also assess major changes in race relations since 1968, especially in the light of ongoing racial divisions in the United States. These divisions have been highlighted by the recent Black Lives Matter protests, which also illustrate the international reach of U.S. civil rights histories. Students will explore how the American civil rights movement was influenced by global events and how it inspired other protest movements, in the U.S. and beyond. They will also examine how a mass movement mobilizes successfully, identifying the circumstances under which non-violent direct action is successful. In the process, they will assess the key role of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Identify and reflect on the use of primary sources at an intermediate level
Critically compare the arguments employed by various historians and assimilate them with other sources to contextualise particular historical problems.
Identify and critically assess change and its continuity across different protests.
Examine historical events using effective disciplinary skills.

title: GLOBAL MIGRATION: PEOPLE, POWER AND MOBILITY
syllabus_overview: In Global Migrations, you will study the migrations from Europe, Asia, the Pacific, and Africa, which shaped Australia. We examine how migrations since 1800 occurred in response to labour force needs, resource booms, economic depression, and the effects of war and conflict. We explore forced relocation (convict transportation, slavery and indentured labour); aspirational mobility (gold-seekers, assisted immigrants); and post-war resettlement (displaced persons, refugees, asylum seekers). We consider government attempts to control populations, through immigration law, border control, deportation and internment, as well as challenges to such practices by human rights and justice movements. You will address the effects of racial ideology, gender and class and debate concepts of assimilation and multiculturalism. The subject enables you to develop independent research skills by investigating individual/family migration stories. This is a second level subject. This subject includes live sessions and a field trip with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Assimilate historians' lines of arguments and use of visual and textual sources in relation to a particular historical problem, placing all in their contexts.
Frame a line of argument about an aspect of migration history using primary and secondary sources.
Individually, investigate a small historical topic and frame a response in any one of a variety of history genres
In a team and individually, assess continuity and change in the different context of a past.

title: HISTORIES OF INDIGENOUS RESISTANCE
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the history of the resistance to colonisation by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia, with a focus on Melbourne and Victoria, from 1770 to the present day. You will be asked to critically consider the actions of the invaders and reflect on how the lives of First Nations peoples were impacted by invasion. Case studies include frontier wars, missions, the Stolen Generations, exemption policies, war service, sport, interwar activism, land rights and reconciliation. You will explore theoretical frameworks and specific examples to help understand how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have resisted the forces of colonisation. The subject will also ask students to reflect on their own relationship to histories of colonisation, and to think about how the history of the colonisation of Australia has been remembered and forgotten. You will also examine the relationship between the discipline of history and colonialism, including the problems created when knowledge is constructed using the colonial archive. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Develop cultural and ethical sensitivity towards the history of colonisation in a variety of contexts with an awareness that includes best practice terminology and self-reflexivity.
Demonstrate a nuanced understanding of the ways in which Europeans invaded this continent, and of the various ways that Aboriginal Torres Strait Islander people have resisted colonisation.
Create a properly referenced piece of writing using primary, secondary and Indigenous-authored sources to frame an argument about the history of colonisation, activism and resistance.
Locate, analyse and understand the various kinds of sources that can provide information about Indigenous history post 1788.

title: HISTORIES OF SEXUALITY: GENDER, POWER, PLEASURE AND THE BODY
syllabus_overview: In this subject students examine histories of sexualities. We consider changing meanings assigned to sexed and gendered bodies and sexual behaviour and the emergence of sexual and gender categories and identities. We explore how the sexual and gendered body has been subject to social control and regulation. How did the state regulate sexuality and gender diversity? Why were some forms of sexuality and gender behaviour criminalized? What generated moral panics over sexuality? What role did the press play in sex scandals? We consider marriage, birth control, gendered sexual violence, influence of sexology and sexual reformers and nationalism, race and sexuality. We examine the formation of sexual sub-cultures and sexual liberation movements to current LGBTIQA politics and culture. Through analysing sexuality debates we examine shifting notions of transgression and deviance and explore sexuality, gender, power and resistance and the transformation of sexual cultures, ideas and practices. This is a level 3 subject. It includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Understand key issues in the history of sexuality

Examine histories of sexuality by undertaking research according to the methodological and ethical conventions of the discipline and show how history shapes the present and can contribute to envisaging new futures.
Demonstrate an understanding of a variety of conceptual approaches to interpreting the history of sexuality.

Research and interpret historical evidence about human sexual identity, experience and relations from a wide variety of primary and secondary materials to analyse changing representations of the past.
Construct a sophisticated and evidence-based argument about historical sexual cultures.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL HISTORY: GONDWANA TO GLOBAL WARMING
syllabus_overview: Australia was formed, as one of several continents, from Gondwana the ancient super continent, and evolved over forty millennia. Just two centuries after European settlement, the human impact on this land, massive species extinction, and climate change, pose serious threats to the continent's fragile ecology. In this subject, you will explore Australia's geological origins; Indigenous resource management and connection to Country; competing ideas of land use among early settlers; and how various forms of extraction changed the environment. Together, we will investigate how the Australian environment shaped humans in turn. Students will study the Australian continent as part of a global environment, by understanding how settlement was an artefact of colonialism and Empire. We will discover the impact of environmental thinking on Australia and its participation in the global environmental movement. You will assess the methods of environmental history in understanding Australia's changing environment in the context of calls for a sustainable future.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate to construct an evidence-based argument or narrative in audio, digital, oral, visual or written form.

Examine environmental issues in historical contexts by identifying and interpreting primary and secondary sources according to the methodological and ethical conventions of the environmental history discipline.
Develop an understanding of a variety of conceptual approaches to interpreting past environments and their representation.
Demonstrate critical understanding of the environmental legacies of at least one period or culture of the past.

title: ANARCHISTS, TERRORISTS, AND FREEDOM FIGHTERS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore the origins and historical development of terrorism. From the People's Will to Al Qaeda, we will provide a survey of the most significant movements that have engaged in terror. In the subject we will emphasise the importance of ideas and chart the significance of anarchism, revolutionary socialism, national liberation and religious extremism. Particular attention will be paid to primary texts from influential exponents of violence, including Sergei Nechaev, Frantz Fanon and Carlos Marighela. You will debate the problems of developing a meaningful definition of terrorism; investigate the ideas and material conditions that have given rise to various forms of political violence; consider the challenge of formulating an effective and just response to terrorist attacks; and locate modern terrorism in a broad, comparative historical perspective. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Capacity to prepare and complete a substantial historical research project, supported by evidence and an awareness of competing arguments and views.
Evaluate historical questions raised in weekly subject readings and lectures, and formulate arguments and hypotheses based in evidence and specific examples.
Demonstrate a comprehension of the ideas that have led to the adoption of terrorism and related forms of violence in a variety of contexts.
Locate the phenomenon of modern terrorism and insurgency in comparative historical perspective, across a wide range of historical, political, and cultural contexts.
Understand the problems of developing a meaningful definition of terrorism, informed by history, philosophy, and law.

title: MAKING HISTORY: COMMUNICATING THE PAST
syllabus_overview: How is the past made into history? In this subject, you will use digital media to communicate the past. You will make history, researching a topic, event, place or artefact of your choice. Your challenge is to communicate this history via a media form (video, podcast, online essay or museum display) in an engaging way to the public. You will gain practical experience in media communication, independent research, critical thinking and ethics. As you engage with historical debates and media, you will challenge traditional ideas and practices and develop skills in understanding how the past becomes history and in communication. You will go from being the student studying other histories, to being the historian making your own history and communicating it to a public audience. You will gain experience in historical writing, producing a video or recording a podcast. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Communicate historical issues in the public sphere by undertaking advanced research according to the methodological and ethical conventions of the discipline.
Show how history and historians shape the present and can contribute to envisaging new futures.
Analyse historical evidence, scholarship and changing representations of history, with a focus on historians as gatekeepers of the past.
Demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of at least one period or culture of the past via a research project pitched at a general audience.

title: DISRUPTION: HISTORY OF INNOVATION AND TECHNOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will explore the history of societal disruption, focusing on a series of case studies, dating back to antiquity. The subject traces the impact of technological innovations and the seismic social shifts they generated. Through four modules, we examine developments in communications, health, agricultural and food technologies, before concluding with a look at transportation innovations. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate relevant case studies to explore the implications and dynamics of technological disruption.
Use appropriate communication strategies and engage with theoretical knowledge in ways that address practical challenges.
Demonstrate research skills including the ability to effectively identify primary and secondary sources.
Examine significant historical patterns and their influence on the development and reconfiguration of societies.

title: FROM BAD SCIENCE TO GOOD HEALTH
syllabus_overview: We are increasingly faced with controversial debates occurring in our media, with different groups arguing their viewpoints, and the scientific evidence is often swamped by misreporting or distorted evidence. This subject uses a case-based approach to examine the evidence underpinning current topics of debate in healthcare, and the motivations behind research and reporting of research, including the scientific process, peer-review, conflict of interest confirmation bias and cultural identity. This subject introduces skills in research that minimize bias, and are important in understanding and analysing evidence, including systematic approaches to acquiring evidence, critical appraisal of the literature and descriptive and inferential statistics.
learning_outcomes: Identify psychological characteristics and reasoning fallacies that contribute to our susceptibility to believe non-evidence based health claims.
Effectively search for evidence of the effects of a health product or treatment and evaluate the presence of characteristics that are necessary for a fair test of effectiveness.
Examine factors that drive the promotion of health products and treatments, question the plausibility of these claims, and understand the importance of evidence-based healthcare
Communicate effectively and with respect for diversity in opinions to explain complex concepts in understanding evidence-based health.

title: CONTEMPORARY ISSUES IN SEX AND SEXUALITY
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce you to contemporary issues and debates relating to gender and sexuality, particularly with respect to sexual health and wellbeing. The subject will cover core theoretical approaches to understanding gender and sexuality. It will also engage you in discussion and debate about contemporary issues such as: sex and consent, gender roles in contemporary life, the politics of desire and pleasure, global and local approaches to sexual health promotion, the politics of sex education, the medicalisation of sexual and gendered bodies, and the politics of sexuality research. This elective subject is open to, and will be of relevance to, students from a wide range of disciplines including public health, allied health, community development, law and humanities.
learning_outcomes: Identify a range of cultural and historical perspectives, values and discourses through which sexuality is usually understood.
Explain the evidence in relation to sexuality theory, sexual politics, sexual health and wellbeing, and sexual (re)presentation.
Identify the effects of cultural and historical perspectives, values and discourses that underpin recent Australian studies on sexuality.

title: COMMUNICATING IN HEALTH SCIENCES
syllabus_overview: This subject will extend students’ knowledge of the interpersonal and communication concepts and skills required in academic and health science contexts. Students will develop their speaking and listening skills in a range of situations. Oral presentation and academic writing skills will be further developed in workshops around awareness of self and others, and the role of cultural difference in communication. Students will explore professional communication skills required in interactions with clients applicable to a range of health service settings, and further develop their skills in online environments.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to transfer health information to others, utliising appropriate communication techniques.
Demonstrate awareness of self and others while engaging in interpersonal health communication.
Apply knowledge of interpersonal skills relevant to person-centred health communication

title: FOUNDATIONS OF PROFESSIONAL COMMUNICATION
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore the importance of communication as a foundation to your future practice as a health professional. You will examine how personal and cultural factors, values and life experiences may influence professional communication. You will develop a suite of communication skills as a foundation for culturally safe and reflective practice as a health professional. You will study concepts of professionalism, interprofessional collaborative practice and emotional intelligence as it relates to ethical health care practice. You will work in teams to develop an understanding of teamwork that involves individuals cooperating and collaborating towards a shared goal. This subject supports the development of foundation academic skills and information literacy required for university study.
learning_outcomes: Analyse health-related questions concerning professional communication in contemporary health care practice, using search strategies and academic resources.
Reflect on and appraise personal communication practices as a health professional
Identify concepts of professionalism, cultural safety, interprofessional collaborative practice and emotional intelligence as they relate to ethical health care practice.
Demonstrate and use a range of core communication skills that include verbal, interpersonal, reflective and written skills relevant for culturally safe health practice.
Collaborate and cooperate as a member of a team to achieve shared goals

title: HEALTH AND WELLBEING OF PEOPLE WITH DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to people with developmental disabilities and hear directly from them about their lives. Learning about them as individuals, and also about their experiences, will develop your understanding of the roles played by health and human services professionals in supporting their health, wellbeing and social inclusion. You will be introduced to current principles and values that are key to positive interactions between people with developmental disabilities and health and social service providers. You will also develop an understanding of reflective practice and the National Disability Insurance Scheme, and explore the role you will play in your future profession, and the roles of other professions in contributing to the health and social inclusion of people with developmental disabilities. Your learning will be assessed through written tests, and contribution to a group discussion.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and reflect on your own reactions to people with developmental disabilities.
Demonstrate sound writing skills that are appropriate to various media to communicate your critical thinking.
Describe guiding principles, philosophies and values that contribute to respectful and inclusive delivery of health and human services to people with developmental disabilities.
Identify and describe the capabilities of people with varying degrees of physical and/or cognitive disabilities, and identify the supports they require.
Compare the roles of various allied health and human services professionals in supporting the health, wellbeing and social inclusion of people with developmental disabilities.
Explain what it means to have a developmental disability.

title: LEARNING IN HEALTH SCIENCES
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will be provided with an introduction to learning at university with a focus on the academic skills needed to engage successfully in health sciences. You will be introduced to using journal articles, library database searching, improving writing skills, planning for and structuring academic tasks, as well as referencing standards. The subject focuses on extending your engagement with content in other first year subjects by guiding your use of university support systems and independent study strategies.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of university systems and networks to support learning.
Apply skills required for effective use of databases to support research and analysis
Demonstrate proficiency in writing at a university level while adhering to academic writing conventions applicable to higher education.

title: RESEARCH AND EVIDENCE IN PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to the use of research-based evidence in professional health care practice. Working in interprofessional teams and using a range of case scenarios, you will develop research skills in areas relevant to your field of practice. Through online activities and workshops, you will learn about the role of evidence-based practice in health. Areas of study include systematic approaches to acquiring evidence, critical appraisal of the literature, interpretation of research design, descriptive and inferential statistics and assessment of research outcomes. You will learn how an evidence-based approach in health informs clinical practice. You will develop research skills to determine the most appropriate intervention techniques for application in a given clinical population, while understanding the complex interaction between social, economic and environmental influences that contribute to sustainability thinking in health research.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise some components of the validity of health research evidence
Explain the relative merits and uses of the different types of evidence used in practice
Communicate research outcomes appropriate to peers
Develop an effective search strategy to address practice based research questions

title: RURAL COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: The subject provides you with the opportunity to develop your understanding of the diversity and complexity of rural communities. You will work in interdisciplinary teams on defining and developing a project that your team identified through visiting a rural community and community consultation and discussion on needs, priorities and real-world issues. You will have the opportunity to develop skills in communication, teamwork, and self-management and gain insight into the opportunities, complexities of and challenges to health and wellbeing in rural communities.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on professional learning needs to devise a professional plan on self-management and communication.
Collaborate and cooperate as a member of a project team to achieve shared goals.
Apply verbal and written communication skills to engage with rural communities.
Apply key community engagement principles to a rural health and wellness context.
Identify the characteristics of rural communities and opportunities to maximise health and wellbeing.

title: INTEGRATING EVIDENCE INTO PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn to formulate answerable practice-related questions, search for evidence, evaluate the evidence, apply the evidence and reflect on your own performance. During the course of this learning, you also begin to develop an understanding of research processes and, thereby, develop 'research literacy' as an essential tool for health practice and for the utilisation of research evidence in practice. Relevant aspects of research methods are introduced, and you will acquire knowledge relating to the selection and use of measures and/or tests that are used in research and in practice in their discipline.
learning_outcomes: Apply appraised evidence to a practice-related problem or issue or situation
Appraise the strength of evidence generated by a range of methodologies
Assess your own performance in developing capacity to be an evidence-based practitioner.
Ask, develop and refine relevant and answerable practice-related questions using a structured approach
Acquire evidence relevant to practice by developing and implementing complex search strategies applicable to databases

title: CHRONIC SELF MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: There is extensive evidence that the successful management of a person's chronic condition is highly dependent on the self management skills of the client themselves. In this web based subject, students will explore case studies and will gain the knowledge needed to support clients to develop the attitudes, behaviours and skills necessary for successful chronic condition self management. Students will cover the underlying principles, barriers and enablers for effective self management. Through guided activities, students will gain skills in collaborative, interprofessional, self management care planning, and interventions and strategies including health coaching.
learning_outcomes: Develop and implement a self management care plan utilising a range of self management intervention
Work with health professionals from other disciplines to support chronic condition self management
Explain the theory behind and evidence for chronic condition self management
Establish partnerships with clients with chronic conditions, including those with culturally specific needs

title: HONOURS INDUSTRY PROJECT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will apply your knowledge of team project planning and management to plan and execute an industry-relevant team project. In doing so, you will develop experience with team project management, stakeholder engagement, collection and analysis of data, interpretation of the results and dissemination of your findings through preparation of a project report and oral seminar presentation. You will work closely with an academic and/or industry supervisor who'll supervise your progress and provide advice as you work through the team project. You will focus on gaining knowledge and skills required for team project work as relevant to contemporary practice. Upon successful completion of the subject, you will have demonstrated an ability to work relatively independently and collaboratively to undertake a complex industry-relevant project. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of team project management to communicate project processes and outcomes to a range of stakeholders.
Reflect on issues arising in team project management and clearly communicate these to peers.
Apply advanced knowledge and skills to design, plan and execute a substantial team project to solve an industry problem.
Clearly and coherently communicate individual professional capabilities in team project management.
Critically reflect on and apply professional behaviours to successfully lead and influence project management processes.

title: HONOURS RESEARCH PROJECT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will execute your research plan developed in HLT4RPP (Research Project Planning) and in doing so, develop experience with project planning, participant recruitment, obtaining informed consent, the collection and analysis of data, interpretation of the results and dissemination of your findings through preparation of a journal-ready manuscript and oral presentation. You will work closely with an experienced researcher who'll supervise your progress and provide advice as you work through your project. Upon successful completion of the subject, you will have demonstrated an ability to work relatively independently to undertake a research project suitable for publication and presentation.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect and apply initiative and judgement to adapt advanced discipline knowledge in diverse settings.
Critically apply advanced professional behaviours, knowledge and skills to execute substantial research-based projects
Synthesise research findings and effectively communicate theoretical propositions, methodologies and conclusions to professional audiences in both written and oral formats.
Demonstrate effective research skills through integration of academic integrity, ethical conduct and peer review

title: PROJECT PLANNING AND PREPARATION
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore how to initiate, scope and plan health and human services projects effectively to ensure that projects are undertaken to meet objectives within specific resource and time constraints. You will apply and extend your knowledge and skills developed in first- and second-year research and evidence-based practice subjects as well as your disciplines-specific subjects to develop a project proposal informed by a critical literature review. An understanding of a range of topics including the project management life cycle, the functions essential to successful project management, developing a project management plan, verifying and controlling the project scope, defining, scheduling and allocating resources, and monitoring project quality will be examined. Working independently and collaboratively, you will develop the ethical, critical thinking and communication and team work skills required to understand, analyse and conduct health and human services projects. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Integrate team project management theory and processes with discipline specific knowledge and skills to plan substantial industry-relevant projects in collaboration with peers.
Coherently and effectively communicate a project proposal in written and oral formats.
Critically review team project management theory and processes in relation to team project design.
Develop a project proposal integrating principles of academic integrity and ethical conduct
Develop knowledge of team project management theory and processes.
Critically appraise literature to justify a project proposal.

title: RESEARCH PROJECT PLANNING
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn about the epistemology of research and the theoretical constructs in developing an ethical research question. You will apply and extend your knowledge and skills developed in first- and second-year research and evidence-based practice subjects and discipline specific subjects to plan a research project in your discipline. You will develop either a systematic review protocol or a proposal for a research project including: identification of a research question that can meaningfully extend knowledge on a topic, a review of the literature and design of a research method. The subject will enhance your knowledge of the varied philosophical underpinnings and methodological approaches to conceiving and designing research in health and human services. You will subsequently execute the proposal in the final year subject, HLT4HRP # Honours Research Project.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise research literature to identify research gaps and justify research plans.
Demonstrate the ability to work effectively independently and with other members of the research planning team to meet project milestones.
Apply advanced discipline-specific knowledge and skills to design an ethically appropriate research methodology that aligns with a given research question.
Communicate competently and coherently to justify and defend research plans in formats suitable for different audiences.
Apply advanced technical skills, to design and implement database search strategies and solve complex research questions.

title: PROVIDE FIRST AID
syllabus_overview: Students will gain the skills and knowledge required to provide a first aid response to a casualty in range of situations, including community and workplace settings.
learning_outcomes: Communicate details of the incident.
Respond to an emergency situation.
Apply appropriate first aid procedures.
Review the incident.

title: HINDI 2
syllabus_overview: At the end of this subject you should be able to read and write everyday Hindi and understand and participate in conversations on topics such as people's occupations, going on holiday, visiting sacred sites, leisure and entertainment, and Indian food and customs. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. This subject continues from HINDI 1 - completion Hindi 1 or the equivalent of one semester of study is required to enrol, please consider the subject prerequisites before enroling. If you are unsure of your Hindi level, contact the instructor for a langauge assessment. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate awareness of and participation in the target language and cultural aspects of Hindi speaking areas of India
Participate in communicative activities in class, and related creative study in homework and assessment activities
Read and write in Hindi and discuss a broad range of everyday discourse topics
Find, critically evaluate and manage the information they retrieve from dictionaries and grammar summaries and to begin to apply understanding and synthesis.
Speak in Hindi about daily life
Integrate discrete learning to produce a new meaningful whole by participating in class, doing homework and completing assessment

title: HINDI 1
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for students with little or no previous knowledge of Hindi. Primary emphasis will be placed on developing the proficiency necessary to converse with native speakers on a variety of subjects. The Hindi script is introduced and topics covered include: asking questions, forms of greetings, shopping, introducing one's self, train travel, family life, health issues, village life, planning trips, studying in college and popular media. At the end of this subject you should be able to read and write basic Hindi and take part in simple conversations. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Integrate discrete learning to produce a new meaningful whole by participating in class, doing homework and completing assessment
Demonstrate awareness of, and participate in usage of, the target language and cultural aspects of Hindi speaking areas of India
Read and write Devanagari script system and write short texts
Demonstrate communicative skills through pair and group work activities

title: HINDI 3
syllabus_overview: This subject is based around developing the skills you need to read modern Hindi texts. By using texts as exemplars of contemporary Hindi language and perspectives on South Asian society, the subject will enable you to access a wide range of modern Hindi usages. You will read modern texts on topics such as the partition of India and Pakistan, traditional urban and rural lifestyles, and contemporary issues related to the caste system. You will also explore issues related to vocabulary, usage and idiom. In addition the subject will focus on the development of active language skills in both oral and written forms. It is recommended that student take AST2MMA with this subject. This is a level 2 and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Write and read intermediate level texts using a vocabulary of around one and a half thousand words
Engage in enquiry and evaluate complex sources before applying synthesis and understanding at a foundational level
Select appropriate readings, analyse topics and develop relevant language forms
Develop an awareness of the importance of socio-cultural skills
Converse on topics of common occurrence in Hindi speaking areas

title: HINDI 4
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will continue your journey with the development of listening and reading comprehension skills and will focus on the development of active language skills in both oral and written forms. This includes the study of modern Hindi grammar and vocabulary, and training in and reflection on language learning strategies which will be provided every week. You will also study two Hindi stories written by ASHK. You will explore issues related to the parallel Sanskrit and Urdu vocabularies, the structure of complex sentences and the use of idioms and proverbs. You will also reflect on concepts such as perceptions of the partition of India and Pakistan and how they are dealt with in literature and popular culture and will watch Bhag Milkha Bhag film based on this topic. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Converse on topics of common occurrence in Hindi speaking areas
Select appropriate readings, analyse topics and develop relevant language forms
Write and read intermediate level texts using a vocabulary of around one and a half thousand words
Engage in Enquiry and evaluate complex sources before applying synthesis and understanding at a foundational level
Develop an awareness of the importance of socio-cultural skills
Engage in communicative language learning strategies

title: HINDI 5: MEDIA HINDI
syllabus_overview: This subject will focus on the ways in which Hindi is used in Bollywood films and in TV broadcasting across a wide range of contexts typical of contemporary Hindi media. Drawing on film and broadcast sources as well as secondary print literature students will explore the ways in which Hindi media engages with the interaction between traditional Indian cultural values and contemporary international influences. Language areas addressed will include the development of the skills needed for reading, writing and translation of different genres of media Hindi and the development of relevant conversation skills. Teaching will be in a 3 hour workshop format which will include lectures on Hindi in Indian media, discussion of the distinctive features of Hindi use in media, creative activities and group work. Assessment will include activities related to language skills and the preparation of a report, in Hindi, on a selected area in Hindi media. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Apply a language and cultural studies perspective to local and global issues
Produce an original, well-researched response to different areas in the use of Hindi in media
Produce a sustained, complex written report on an area of Hindi usage in Indian media
Apply ethical and cultural awareness to different areas of language usage
Present a brief and persuasive argument on an area of usage in Hindi in Indian media
Summarise research and arguments on an area of Hindi media
Evaluate diverse positions on an area of Hindi media

title: HINDI 6: BOLLYWOOD HINDI
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on a range of materials related to Indian Cinema, both in terms of films, dialogues, songs, magazines and reviews. Teaching will be in a 3 hour workshop format and we will be looking at a number of links to Hindi film related clips on YouTube such as short documentaries, interviews, clips, trailers, and award ceremonies. In addition there will be a weekly passage to read from a Hindi film magazine. There will also be opportunities to watch films and discuss their content. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate diverse positions on an area of Hindi media
Produce a sustained, complex written report on an area of Hindi usage in Indian media
Summarise research and arguments on an area of Hindi media
Apply ethical and cultural awareness to different areas of language usage
Apply a language and cultural studies perspective to local and global issues
Produce an original, well-researched response to different areas in the use of Hindi in media
Present a brief and persuasive argument on an area of usage in Hindi in Indian media

title: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY FOR HEALTH PROFESSIONALS
syllabus_overview: This subject provides you with the fundamental principles of the underlying mechanisms of human disease and how these mechanisms impact on clinical outcomes. Emphasis begins with general disease processes including cell injury, cell adaptations, inflammation, immunopathology, tissue healing, neoplasia and circulatory disturbances and disorders. Specific pathological conditions of body systems e.g. nervous, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal, hepatic and skeletal systems along with diabetes will be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective communication skills, individually and as part of a team, by communicating scientific results, information, or arguments to a range of audiences, for a range of purposes, and using a variety of modes.

Explain cellular and biochemical changes that underlie the development of systemic diseases (i.e. Systemic Pathophysiology and relate these changes to the likely clinical course and outcomes of an afflicted individual.

Apply the principles of General Pathophysiology to selected human disorders and reparative states, describing how these general pathophysiologic processes impact on possible clinical courses and outcomes in an afflicted individual.

title: HUMAN PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will examine disorders which may be experienced by individuals over the life-span, emphasizing the basic pathological processes that underlie diseases and the risk factors and contributing causes of disorders. Specifically, general pathological processes will be discussed with emphasis on disturbed function, adaptation to injury, inflammation, tissue healing, immunological disorders, neoplasia, fluid imbalance, thrombosis, embolism and vascular disorders. In addition to general pathological processes, specific pathological conditions of body systems e.g. cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, gastrointestinal and skeletal systems along with diabetes will be addressed. You will consolidate and apply their knowledge of pathophysiology by communicating a disease state in authentic format to scientific peers and non-expert audiences.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of General Pathophysiology to selected human disorders and reparative states, describing how these general pathophysiologic processes impact on possible clinical courses and outcomes in an afflicted individual.
Demonstrate effective communication of scientific results, information, or arguments to a range of audiences, for a range of purposes, and using a variety of modes.
Explore, build and reflect on your experiences that develop your career readiness, and make judgements on your employability strengths.

Explain cellular and biochemical changes that underlie the development of systemic diseases (i.e. Systemic Pathophysiology and relate these changes to the likely clinical course and outcomes of an afflicted individual.

title: MASTERS RESEARCH THESIS/PROJECT
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students enrolled in all HUSS postgraduate courses an option to complete a research project in an area that they identify as being of interest to them. The project will be designed in close collaboration with the Supervisor nominated by the Coordinator of their Course to fit their interests and the course requirements. Students should contact their Course Coordinator to discuss their options. Students must complete a supervised report/thesis (or equivalent) of approximately 6,500 words. This should be a continuation of a research thesis project (or equivalent) from either HUM5RE1 or HUM5RE2. Supervisor and/or Course Coordinator will assess satisfactory progress against ILOs to determine enrollment into HUM5001.
learning_outcomes: Construct a creative approach to disciplinary problems that is consistent with knowledge creation.
Construct clear arguments supported by a depth and breadth of literature for professional and academic writing.
Review and apply appropriate research methodologies.
Recognise and consider the complexity of problems within a conceptual framework.

The project will be designed in close collaboration with the Supervisor nominated by the Coordinator of their Course to fit their interests and the course requirements. Students should contact their Course Coordinator to discuss their options. Students must complete a supervised report/thesis (or equivalent) of approximately 13,000 words. This should be a continuation of a research thesis project (or equivalent) from either HUM5RE1 or HUM5RE2. Supervisor and/or Course Coordinator will assess satisfactory progress against ILOs to determine enrollment into HUM5002.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and consider the complexity of problems within a conceptual framework.
Review and apply appropriate research methodologies.
Construct a creative approach to disciplinary problems that is consistent with knowledge creation.
Construct clear arguments supported by a depth and breadth of literature for professional and academic writing.

title: MASTERS RESEARCH THESIS/PROJECT
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students enrolled in all HUSS postgraduate courses an option to complete a research project in an area of interest to them. The project will be designed in close collaboration with their Course Coordinator to fit their interests and the course requirements. Topics require approval by the Course Coordinator and are dependent on the availability of appropriate supervisors. Students should contact their Course Coordinator to discuss their options. Students must complete a supervised essay/report/thesis (or equivalent for example a creative practice project with exegesis) of approximately 6,500 words. This may be a stand-alone piece of research or a commencing project proposal/literature review etc. for a larger research thesis/project or equivalent to be completed in HUM5001 or HUM5002.
learning_outcomes: Construct clear arguments supported by a depth and breadth of literature for professional and academic writing.
Review and apply appropriate research methodologies.
Construct a creative approach to disciplinary problems that is consistent with knowledge creation.
Recognise and consider the complexity of problems within a conceptual framework.

title: MASTERS RESEARCH THESIS/REPORT
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students enrolled in all HUSS postgraduate courses an option to complete a research project in an area of interest to them. The project will be designed in close collaboration with their Course Coordinator to fit their interests and the course requirements. Topics require approval by the Course Coordinator and are dependent on the availability of appropriate supervisors. Students should contact their Course Coordinator to discuss their options. Students must complete a supervised essay/report/thesis (or equivalent for example a creative practice project with exegesis) of approximately 13,000 words. This may be a stand-alone piece of research or it can be developed further for a larger project completed in HUM5001 or HUM5002.
learning_outcomes: Construct a creative and insightful approach to disciplinary problems that is consistent with knowledge creation.
Write focused, sustained and clear arguments supported by a depth and breadth of literature appropriate for professional and academic contexts.
Recognise and consider the complexity of problems within an appropriate conceptual framework.
Critically review and apply advanced research methodologies.

title: EXHIBITING CULTURE B
syllabus_overview: Exhibiting Culture HUS3ECB is a gallery-based subject offered in partnership with the nationally and internationally renowned Bendigo Art Gallery. It is designed to deepen learning across a range of arts disciplines and creative practices, such as art history, visual arts, history, archaeology, law, textual studies, education and politics, via the experience of a unique, curated exhibition. It addresses the following broad questions: what type of exhibition is this; what holds this collection of cultural objects together; how does the exhibition direct inquiry and engagement; what types of knowledge does it produce; by what criteria can an exhibition be evaluated; and how successful is this exhibition as a whole? In 2025, the subject will be based on the exhibition Frida Kahlo: In her own image which offers visitors an intimate insight into the life of one of the most influential artists of the twentieth century, featuring Kahlo’s personal belongings, clothing, make-up, accessories, and medical items, on loan from the Museo Frida Kahlo in Mexico for the first time in Australia. The exhibition considers the personal, political, philosophical, and artistic influences which shaped Kahlo’s distinctive world view and informed her groundbreaking creative output. Attendance is required at the exhibition location and the partner gallery for the 4 day face-to-face component held during winter semester (specific dates TBC). All travel and accommodation costs associated with this subject will be at each student’s expense.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate your own creative arts or discipline-based practice in relationship to a critical contextualised position
Critically research a relevant topic using relevant data sources
Communicate visually and in writing your ideas and the relevant ideas of other relating to historical, curatorial and theoretical material explored in the research and the exhibition.
Interpret and evaluate artworks in relation to a in-depth research question
Apply a broad range of analytical, theoretical positions that relate to the exhibition and curatorial intent.

title: MASTERS RESEARCH THESIS/REPORT
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students enrolled in all HUSS postgraduate courses an option to complete a research thesis in areas that they identify as being of interest to them. The project will be designed in close collaboration with their Course Coordinator to fit their interests and the course requirements. Students should contact their Course Coordinator to discuss their options. Students must complete a supervised thesis of approximately 19,500 words. Topics require approval by the Course Director and are dependent on both the student demonstrating the capacity to produce an extended piece of independent work and on the availability of an appropriate supervisor.
learning_outcomes: Write focused, sustained and clear extended arguments supported by advanced conceptual literature appropriate for professional and academic contexts.
Recognise and consider the complexity of nuanced problems within an advanced conceptual framework.
Construct a creative, insightful and nuanced approach to disciplinary problems that demonstrates advanced conceptual knowledge creation.
Critically review, apply and extend advanced research methodologies.

title: INTERNATIONAL STUDY TOURS AND INTERNATIONAL FIELD SCHOOLS
syllabus_overview: This subject is for select international study tours hosted by the School of Humanities and Social Sciences, including international field schools organised by Archaeology faculty. Please note that these programs run at different times throughout the year, and may incur additional fees. Enrolling in the subject requires instance coordinator approval. For details and information on any of the programs listed above, please contact the Subject Coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Development of capabilities to encounter and revise perspectives on a topic or topics by combining research with knowledge of sites, performances, experiences and places.
Development of research capabilities through the presentation of their knowledge about selected topics which relate to the themes of the field trip.

title: HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCE RESEARCH DESIGN
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop your capacity to engage in sophisticated analysis and original research in the Humanities and Social Sciences at Honours level. You will focus on research design, examining the nature of research at Honours level, how to develop a research question, how to locate relevant sources, and how to write a literature review. Throughout the subject, you will be supported to refine your academic writing skills and develop the necessary skills to plan and execute an Honours research project. This subject requires regular participation and engagement with the learning activities and in-class discussions, as well as independent work outside of class time. This subject is delivered in intensive mode: classes are scheduled as 6 whole day sessions, 10am-5pm (one day per week).
learning_outcomes: Enhance critical writing and academic communication skills necessary for completing an Honours thesis, adhering to rules, style, and conventions of academic writing.
Produce written work that reflects a clear understanding of the principles underpinning good research design in the Humanities and Social Science.
Analyse and critically engage with advanced research in the discipline area/s of your thesis research.
Demonstrate an ability to identify a research need and articulate the scholarly significance of a research project in response to this need.
Undertake relevant and in-depth primary and secondary source research into the discipline area/s of your thesis research.

title: TEXTS, CONTEXTS, CRITICISM
syllabus_overview: This subject invites you to think critically and conceptually about a broad variety of textual forms – from literary, cinematic and historical texts to interviews, reports and digital media – and the multiple ways they can be used and understood. You will learn to construct compelling arguments about how texts shape and are shaped by the contexts in which they are created and received. Paying close attention to various social, cultural, historical and political factors that inform the study of texts, you’ll explore how critical, linguistic, conceptual and/or creative practices support a deeper understanding of diverse textual genres and forms. Assessments in this subject will support you to develop and hone your ability to analyse and interpret textual material(s), and will include opportunities for you to explore creative practice itself as a form of critique. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Integrate advanced textual analysis into research
Think critically and/or creatively about a variety of textual forms
Analyse texts at an advanced level

title: CONCEPTS AND THEORY IN HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCE RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: This subject explores how key ideas and concepts frame humanities and social science research. It examines how drawing on particular intellectual traditions, schools of thought, and analytic frameworks shapes the entire research process – from conceptualisation and question development to interpretation and argument. Showcasing research from academics across the School of Humanities and Social Sciences, you will gain first-hand insights into how researchers select and apply conceptual tools. The subject demonstrates the multifaceted ways in which ideas are put to work, how they help engage you with rich scholarly traditions, and allow you to contribute new insights. Assignments are designed to develop your ability to apply key ideas, concepts and/or frameworks in your own research.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced writing skills
Analyse theories and concepts in the Humanities and Social Sciences and apply them in sophisticated ways
Demonstrate advanced critical thinking skills
Demonstrate advanced oral communication skills

title: WRITING BETWEEN AND ACROSS CULTURES
syllabus_overview: How do language and writing inform and describe human experience and difference? In this interdisciplinary subject, we will consider how various forms of representation elucidate deep understandings of the Self in relation to Others, grapple with complex ethical challenges, and have the potential to effect social change. This subject explores the key roles writing plays in communicating meaning, shaping the perception and interpretation of experience, and representing people between and across cultures. Critically deploying the notion of ‘betweenness,’ it also invites reflection on queer theories, temporalities and texts. Through a consideration of translation and adaptation practices over time, you will investigate language(s) as complex modes of travel between culture(s) and sites of experience. You will contemplate your composite roles as producers/interpreters of language/text and have the opportunity to interrogate representation critically and creatively in relation to your own research project.
learning_outcomes: Examine how writing shapes human experience and difference
Engage critically with the role and importance of language in research and writing
Demonstrate sophisticated analysis of writing and representation across a variety of texts

title: HISTORICAL AND ARCHIVAL RESEARCH METHODS
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on the history, practice, politics and ethics of archives as repositories and producers of knowledge. You will learn what constitutes an archive, how to navigate historical and archival research, and expore methods including the queering and decolonising of archival practice and reverence. You will conduct research that considers documents and artefacts and explore research that considers what it feels like to do archival research. While much archival research focuses on the content accessible within the archive, you will also look at the politics that render some things archives and others not.
learning_outcomes: Competently undertake archival research
Effectively employ archival research in research projects
Undertake sophisticated critical analysis of archival research items

title: HUSS HONOURS THESIS A
syllabus_overview: This is the first in a sequence of two subjects in which students complete their Honours thesis. Under supervision, students formulate a question and then research and write an extended research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words or equivalent (for example, creative practice with exegesis). The thesis demonstrates students' capacity to make an original contribution to their chosen discipline. The topic must be approved by the disciplinary honours coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Design, with supervision, an original research plan, identifying project tasks, timelines and resources that are realistic given the time frame.
Demonstrate a practical understanding of the ethical issues associated with conducting research, where relevant
Develop a command of the research literature relating to the project
Commence implementation and reporting of research

title: HUSS HONOURS THESIS B
syllabus_overview: Students undertaking this subject should have completed HUS4THA. In this subject, you will complete your thesis research project. Under supervision, continue to research and write an extended research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words or equivalent (for example, creative practice with exegesis). The thesis demonstrates students' capacity to make an original contribution to their chosen discipline.
learning_outcomes: Plan, conduct and report on research in Honours discipline/s
Understand and critically analyse the research literature relating to the project
Demonstrate a practical understanding of the ethical issues associated with conducting research, where relevant
Effectively communicate research findings according to the scholarly conventions of the Honours discipline/s

title: RESEARCH SKILLS
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a grounding in advanced research skills in the humanities and social sciences for students undertaking original research. You will learn how to locate and critically analyse professional and academic literature in their field. The subject will also consider different ways that the outcomes of social research are used, whether to inform public debate, policy and political decision making, professional practice, or to direct further research on related issues. It will provide you with the skills necessary to design their own study, whether this is for research essays in other subjects, commissioned research in a professional context, or an independent research thesis.
learning_outcomes: Write a substantial review of professional and scientific literature that synthesises and analyses the sources in order to identify major themes, issues and trends in scholarship
Development of the skills for planning and executing a study program to investigate a research topic relevant to the student’s study area
Critically analyse social research literature
Identify and utilise a range of strategies to locate resources, including catalogues and internet search engines

title: CROSS-CULTURAL MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will examine how cultural differences influence management practices and critically assess the challenges commonly encountered in cross-cultural contexts. You will develop the skills to analyse diverse intercultural interactions and be equipped to manage effectively in today’s dynamic international business environment. The subject applies cutting-edge theories and conceptual frameworks to practical, real-world situations.
learning_outcomes: Apply cross-cultural competencies and problem-solving skills to effectively manage organisations in culturally diverse contexts.
Demonstrate informed judgment in complex scenarios of cross-border management.
Analyse how cultural differences and cross-cultural interactions shape international business operations.

title: MANAGING INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS
syllabus_overview: As the international landscape grows increasingly complex and interconnected, effective management of international business has become a vital capability for organisations. This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to managing international business, examining key strategic approaches to cross-border operations, regionalisation, and international competition. You will analyse how organisations engage with external environments, navigate political and social dynamics, and address ethical considerations and social responsibility within international contexts. Through critical study of international business functions, you will explore how organisations adapt structures and strategies to gain competitive advantage in international markets. This subject highlights how cross-national planning, organisational design, and people management interrelate in internationally oriented organisations, equipping you to lead effectively in a rapidly evolving international business arena.
learning_outcomes: Apply contemporary theories to align talent management with the strategic and operational demands of international business.
Examine the role of business ethics and organisational governance in international business management.
Evaluate management challenges by analysing cultural dynamics, regulatory environments, and the complexities of cross-border operations.
Critically analyse how regional and international developments influence managerial approaches and strategic decision-making in international business environments.

title: CORPORATE VENTURING
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an exploration of the unique nature and challenges of Corporate Entrepreneurship (CE), providing you with the knowledge and skills to pursue a career as a professional entrepreneur or innovator in an organisation. Theoretical and practice-based entrepreneurship and innovation principles are introduced for those who wish to manage entrepreneurial ventures in established and/or high growth organisations.
learning_outcomes: Working in a team critically assess a companies venture performance
Critically formulate a strategic position about corporate venturing that takes into account the environmental context.
Present complex corporate venturing ideas in a persuasive, authoritative, entrepreneurial and professional voice
Convey focused and sustained arguments on corporate venturing supported by literature appropriate for both entrepreneurial and academic contexts
Apply theoretical frameworks to interpret corporate venturing performance

title: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS STRATEGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will work on the formulation of a business strategy for firms engaged or looking to engage in international business. With the support of industry leaders, you will apply your knowledge gathered in previous studies in the course to analyse an authentic business scenario. You will then recommend business solutions and devise strategic options to help the business succeed in the global marketplace. Studying this subject will be instrumental in preparing you for a successful career in international business and help you transition effectively into the job market.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively in teams to critically evaluate the merit and application of business theories and practices to recommend business solutions and devise responsible strategic options for the success of firms in international business.
Critically analyse an authentic international business case, and the global forces affecting it, to assess its position or potential position in the global marketplace.
Effectively communicate complex business ideas to a diverse audience, both orally an in written form, in a professional and engaging manner.

title: GLOBAL CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will gain an insight of the emerging field of corporate governance through studying different systems that operate across the world. We will explore the Anglo-American, Asian-Pacific and European governance systems to reflect on how governance affects business structures and operations, with the focus on businesses operating internationally. Numerous corporate failures and environmental disasters in recent times have generated a surge of interest in ensuring that companies reflect not only national and international regulatory and professional standards but also conduct their operations to reflect community and society norms. We will work on further developing your critical thinking, problem solving, and analytical skills through the analysis of real-world organisational problems and scenarios within the broader social and global contexts.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the latest developments in the international corporate governance field and evaluate their application in organisational scenarios.
