Critique corporate governance principles found in different governance systems including legal, professional and ethical regulation and norms.
Evaluate corporate governance policies and practices found in different countries and their role in how businesses navigate the complexities of corporate governance in the global market .

title: GLOBAL AND COMPARATIVE HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: Global and Comparative Human Resource Management provides you with a systematic framework for exploring and comprehending the complexities of managing people in a changing international environment. This subject will expose you to both international and domestic human resource management dimensions and enable you to devise effective solutions for key issues confronting organisations operating within a global context. On completion of the subject, you will have a solid understanding of the role of international human resource management in the success of internationally engaged organisations. This subject will develop your knowledge of Human Resource Management concepts and frameworks in an international context. You will learn to analyse HRM policies and practices from a global perspective. Further, you will learn about actionable solutions to international workforce management issues.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse Human Resource Management policies and practices from a global perspective.
Apply Human Resource Management theoretical frameworks and concepts in an international context.
Develop actionable solutions to issues arising from managing workforces in a changing international environment.

title: INTERNATIONAL TRADE
syllabus_overview: In an increasingly globalised economy, trade and investment decisions made by any country can have significant repercussions for businesses worldwide. Public debates frequently arise concerning this ever-evolving economic landscape, and we must be prepared to engage actively in these changes. Central to these debates is the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 8, which aims to promote decent work and economic growth. By examining the global economy through this lens, we can better understand how international trade may foster economic growth that benefits everyone. In this subject, we will analyse the complex process of globalisation and investigate the economic factors that shape the environment in which businesses operate and nations interact. We will examine the economic foundations behind the trade and investment decisions made by nations and firms. Through the analysis of international trade models and real-world cases, you will explore critical questions such as: What are the gains from free trade and foreign investment? What determines the trade patterns or investment choices of countries? Are there winners and losers in international trade? Which trade policies benefit my business or the country as a whole?
learning_outcomes: Use economic reasoning to critically evaluate the consequences of international trade, investment, migration and policy interventions to countries' welfare, production specialisation and the distribution of income.
Analyse the patterns of international trade and the flow of production factors across countries with the effective use of complex data and the creation of key indicators in international economics.
Apply economic theories to identify and discuss the fundamental features of international trade and the movement of production factors across countries.
Work effectively in groups to examine how countries integrate to the global economy.

title: ITALIAN 1
syllabus_overview: In this subject, aimed at complete beginners in Italian, you develop basic communicative and comprehension skills in spoken and written Italian. Classes are face-to-face and very interactive and assessment takes place in class. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. Teaching and group work are carried out in Italian, and written, audiovisual and online learning materials are used. The subject is equivalent to level A1 in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages.
learning_outcomes: Work with a partner or as part of a team to perform, in Italian, oral tasks related to day-to-day activities, formulating ideas and requests in a culturally appropriate way and relating these to the contributions of other students.
Communicate about everyday topics in basic written Italian, deducing and following appropriate structural patterns and models to achieve clarity and accuracy
Understand simple Italian written and audio texts relating to day-to-day activities and produce appropriate personal responses to these texts

title: ITALIAN 4
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you continue to work towards achieving solid intermediate skills in oral and written Italian, and you learn more about the diverse culture and society of contemporary Italy. Online resources are used to consolidate language skills, and audiovisual material and written texts relating to contemporary Italian life are used to develop your competence in speaking, reading and writing, as well as your knowledge of Italy and its culture. Face-to-face interaction in class is essential, and teaching and group work are carried out in Italian. In this subject, you work towards attaining Level B1 competence in the Common European Framework of References for Languages. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations.
learning_outcomes: Work individually or as part of a team to present, in spoken Italian, reasoned opinions, concise summaries, and viewpoints on topical issues and prescribed texts, interacting with a degree of fluency and spontaneity, and responding to the contributions of others

Understand and comment critically on Italian written and audio-visual texts, using an appropriate linguistic register and displaying an understanding of certain key features of contemporary Italian life
Communicate on a range of topics in clear and logical written Italian, deducing and following appropriate grammatical and structural patterns

title: ITALIAN 3
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you work towards the development of intermediate skills in oral and written Italian. Online resources, audio and audiovisual materials (including films), and short written texts are used to develop your competence in speaking, listening, reading and writing and to broaden your knowledge of contemporary Italian culture and society. Face-to-face interaction in class is central, and teaching and group work are carried out in Italian. In this subject, you consolidate your A2 skills and prepare to transition towards a basic Level B1 competence in the Common European Framework of References for Languages. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations.
learning_outcomes: Communicate on a range of topics in clear and logical written Italian, deducing and following appropriate grammatical and structural patterns

Work individually or as part of a team to present, in spoken Italian, concise summaries, and viewpoints on topical issues and prescribed texts, interacting with a degree of fluency and spontaneity, and responding to the contributions of others
Understand and comment on Italian written and audio-visual texts, using an appropriate linguistic register and displaying an understanding of certain key features of contemporary Italian life

title: ITALIAN 2
syllabus_overview: This subject completes the introduction to the basic grammatical structures of Italian. You build on your work in Italian 1 by extending your oral and written skills through the use of written, audiovisual and online learning materials. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. Classes are face-to-face on campus. Teaching and group work are carried out in Italian. The subject equips you to begin attaining a level equivalent to A2 in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages.
learning_outcomes: Work with a partner or as part of a team to perform, in Italian, oral tasks related to a range of topics and scenarios explored in class, formulating ideas and requests in a culturally appropriate way and relating these to the contributions of other students
Understand simple Italian written and audio texts relating to a range of day-to-day activities and produce appropriate responses to these texts

Communicate about everyday topics and past, present and future events and experiences in basic written Italian, deducing and following appropriate structural patterns and models to achieve clarity and accuracy

title: ITALIAN 5
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students who have already attained working competence in spoken and written Italian. In the subject, you will deepen your knowledge of the structures and vocabulary of the Italian language through class activities and online resources. The study of written, audiovisual and multimodal texts will serve to enhance your analytical, reflective and research skills and your understanding of many of the foremost issues in Italian society today. In particular, you will study texts dealing with experiences of migration, cultural identity and transculturality in contemporary Italy. This subject aims to help you consolidate your level B1 competence and start transitioning towards level B2 competence in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages.
learning_outcomes: Communicate in written Italian with clarity, cohesion, logic, structure and accuracy in a range of contexts and on a range of topics, deducing and following appropriate structural patterns

Write critically about a range of topics including, in particular, those related to migration, identity and global citizenship, using appropriate linguistic registers and vocabulary and displaying an understanding of central issues in contemporary Italian life
Understand and analyse Italian factual and literary texts of some complexity including, in particular, texts on the topic of migration and global citizenship
Work independently and in pairs/groups to perform oral tasks involving critical engagement with issues of migration, identity and global citizenship

title: ITALIAN 6
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will extend your understanding of the structures and usage of the Italian language through class activities, readings and online resources, while also developing your analytical, reflective, and research skills and your understanding of Italian culture and society through the study of Italian literary and audiovisual texts. You will explore, discuss, and analyse matters pertaining to society, politics, and culture in contemporary Italy. In this subject, you will continue working towards attaining level B2 competence in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages.
learning_outcomes: Communicate in written Italian with clarity, cohesion, logic, structure and accuracy in a range of contexts and on a range of topics, deducing and following appropriate structural patterns
Understand, analyse, and reflect on Italian factual and literary texts (fictional and non fictional) of some complexity

Write critically about a range of topics using appropriate linguistic registers and vocabulary, and displaying an understanding of and capacity to analyse central issues in contemporary Italian society and culture.

Work independently to perform oral tasks involving critical engagement with Italian written and visual texts, formulating ideas and opinions with accuracy, and demonstrating a capacity to apply the concepts explored in the subject to our contemporary societies.

title: JAPANESE 1
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students who have no knowledge of Japanese. It is an introductory subject focusing on elementary spoken and written Japanese. You will learn to read hiragana and katakana syllabic scripts as well as approximately 30 kanji characters. You will also be introduced to Japanese culture. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. Those who have prior learning of Japanese should contact the Japanese Program coordinator for a placement test (e.dalton@latrobe.edu.au). You may be asked to move to another level by the subject coordinator prior to the university census date (usually in week 3 or 4). This is a studyflex subject, offered for both face-to-face and online students. The lecture is a pre-recorded video, available to watch each week, uploaded to LMS. Face-to-face students attend tutorials on campus, while online students attend live, online tutorials that are not recorded.
learning_outcomes: Read and write hiragana and katakana as well as 30 kanji. Learn to read and write simple sentences.
Develop basic aural and oral skills in Japanese.
Acquire socio-linguistic and socio-cultural competencies.
Interact in Japanese. Specifically to exchange greetings, introduce oneself, speak about family, professions and one's daily life.
Participate in group language activities.

title: JAPANESE 2
syllabus_overview: In this continuing beginner level language subject, you will focus on the four key elements of Japanese -reading, writing, listening and speaking. Building on the knowledge gained in JPN1001, this unit brings the total number of kanji learnt to approximately 90. You will will deepen your understanding of Japanese language and culture, and Japan's place in the world. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. This is a studyflex subject, offered for both face-to-face and online students. The lecture is a pre-recorded video, available to watch each week, uploaded to LMS. Face-to-face students attend tutorials on campus, while online students attend live, online tutorials that are not recorded.
learning_outcomes: Speak at beginners level about daily life, hobbies, likes and dislikes.
Read and write at beginners level, and recognise a total of approximately 100 kanji.
Develop an appreciation for and acquire socio-cultural knowledge about Japan.
Participate in pair and group work both in and outside of lectures.
Communicate using all four key areas of the target language: speaking, listening, reading and writing.

title: JAPANESE 4
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students who have successfully completed JPN 2003 or hold equivalent proficiency, level N5 of the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT). Those who have not completed JPN2003 but have prior learning should contact the Japanese Studies Program coordinator for a placement test (k.okano@latrobe.edu.au). In this subject you will acquire competence in speaking, reading and writing in contemporary Japanese, and deepen their understanding of Japanese language and culture. Building on the knowledge gained in JPN 2003 this subject brings the total number of kanji characters learnt to approximately 200. You will begin working towards attaining competence level N4 of the JLPT. If you are majoring in Japanese, we recommend you also take 'culture subject', AST3001 (China and Japan: Asian perspectives) in Year 2, as it facilitates reading comprehension in your third year language study. This subject is required for a Japanese major, as well as AT3UJS (Understanding Japanese Society) which you take in Year 3.
learning_outcomes: Interact in Japanese learning grammar that focuses on giving and receiving, the volitional form, favours, apologies, prohibition, transitivity and other relevant items.
Participate in pairs and groups which contributes to a cohesive group dynamic and facilitates learning the target language.
Acquire socio-linguistic and socio-cultural competencies
Integrate of discrete learning - the four components of language learning: speaking, listening, reading, and writing, to produce a new meaningful whole
Learn to write and read up to approximately 200 characters as well as read and write sentences and paragraphs.

title: JAPANESE 3
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students who have successfully completed JPN1002 or hold equivalent proficiency that is midway to N5 of the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT). Those who have not completed JPN1002 but have prior learning should contact the Japanese Studies Program coordinator for a placement test (k.okano@latrobe.edu.au). You may be asked to move to another level by the subject coordinator prior to the university census date (usually in week 3 or 4). In this subject you will acquire competence in speaking, reading and writing in contemporary Japanese, and deepen their understanding of Japanese language and culture. Building on the knowledge gained in JPN1002 this subject brings the total number of kanji characters learnt to approximately 150. You will work towards attaining competence level N5 of the JLPT. If you are majoring in Japanese, we recommend you take 'culture subject', AST3001 (China and Japan: Asian perspectives), in Year 2, as it facilitates reading comprehension in your language study. This subject is required for a Japanese major, as well as AT3UJS (Understanding Japanese Society) which you take in Year 3.
learning_outcomes: Write and read up to 150 kanji characters as well as read and write relevant sentences and short paragraphs.
Interact in Japanese, and become familiar with verb conjugation, comparisons and superlatives, intention, volitional form and prohibitive expressions.
Acquire socio-linguistic competence, including appropriate uses of respectful and humble forms depending on the contexts.
Participate in pairs and groups, contributing to a cohesive group dynamic that facilitates learning the Japanese
Integrate the four components of language learning: speaking, listening, reading, and writing, to produce a new meaningful whole.

title: JAPANESE 6
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students who have completed JPN 3005 or hold equivalent proficiency, approximately Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) N4. You will continue to consolidate their language ability towards an intermediate level. The subject includes the reading, writing and translation of Japanese prose, lectures on Japanese culture and society and a further development of conversation skills. By the end of the of this course, You will learn with approximately 450 kanji. In this subject, students will begin working towards level N3 of the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT). Please note, if you are majoring in Japanese, we recommend you take AST3001 (China and Japan: Asian perspectives) in your second year study of Japanese (i.e., intermediate stream) as it facilitates reading comprehension in your third year language study. This subject is required for a Japanese major, as well as AT3UJS (Understanding Japanese Society) which you should take in your third year.
learning_outcomes: Gain a socio-linguistic and socio-cultural understanding of Japan through critical engagement and development of arguments of issues in contemporary Japanese society
Speak at an intermediate level on general and specific topics in intermediate to advanced Japanese
Communicate using all for key areas of the target language: speaking, listening, reading and writing
Participate in pair and group work both in and outside of lectures.
Read and write at an intermediate level, learn 96 new kanji and recognise a total of approximately 900 kanji.

title: JAPANESE 5
syllabus_overview: This subject is available to students who have completed JPN 2004 or hold equivalent proficiency, somewhere between the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) N5 and N4. Students who have not completed JPN2004 but who have prior knowledge of Japanese should contact the subject or discipline coordinators for a placement test (k.okano@latrobe.edu.au). You will continue to consolidate your language and understanding of Japanese culture to an intermediate level. By the end of the of this course, you will have learnt with approximately 300400 kanji. You will work towards attaining the competence level closer to Level N4 of the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT). If you are majoring in Japanese, we recommend you take AST3001 (China and Japan: Asian perspectives) in Year 2, and/or AST3UJS (Understanding Japanese Society) in Year 3, as it facilitates reading these subjects facilitate a better comprehension in your third year language study. This subject of the culture and society. JPN3005 is required for a Japanese major, as well as AT3UJS (Understanding Japanese Society) which you take in Year 3.major.
learning_outcomes: Communicate using all four key areas of the target language: speaking, listening, reading and writing
Develop an appreciation for and acquire socio-cultural knowledge about Japan.
Speak at an intermediate level on general and specific topics in advanced Japanese.
Participate in pair and group work in Japanese.
Read and write at an intermediate level, recognise a total of approximately 300 kanji.

title: INTRODUCTION TO JOURNALISM
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Journalism introduces you to the shifting roles and responsibilities of journalists and journalism within liberal democratic societies. You will appreciate the contemporary media landscape and the role of journalists and media organisations in relation to social, economic, political and cultural power structures. Topics and issues covered include best practices in news and feature writing, media ethics, and working with sources. Assessment tasks are designed to give you an opportunity to start building a portfolio of journalistic work. This is a level 1 subject.
learning_outcomes: Verbally present research on a newsworthy topic and explain their ideas and questions to groups of other students and staff
Demonstrate awareness of journalistic best practice as it relates to ethical behaviour, media law and relevant codes of conduct.
Identify, analyse and evaluate sources, arguments and evidence in a range of platforms, and reflect critically on their use in their own journalism work.
Demonstrate an understanding of how factors such as power, politics and ethics shape media industries
Utilise archival material, and undertake effective online database and search engine searches to develop and write articles
Identify and write newsworthy stories for print/online publication, using relevant journalistic forms, including the inverted pyramid

title: FEATURE WRITING AND RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: In this subject you’ll learn to research and write compelling feature articles—a staple of contemporary journalism. You’ll develop skills to create engaging and factual stories, while applying journalistic standards of credibility, balance, newsworthiness and ethics. The subject covers key journalism research methods, including how to prepare and undertake interviews with sources who can bring diverse expert and human-interest perspectives to a feature, and locating non-media sources such as academic research findings, relevant statistics, and annual reports. These skills will culminate in the creation of a feature article project.
learning_outcomes: Apply research skills to locate a range of relevant sources and to critically analyse those sources for legitimacy.
Demonstrate an awareness of the ethical and legal responsibilities of journalists related to research, interviewing and factual storytelling.
Demonstrate an understanding of feature storytelling conventions in the creation of a high standard story written to a brief.
Present a story idea in both written and verbal forms, using strong research and news values awareness as justification.
Utilise research skills to create a credible, fact-based feature story that meets industry standards.

title: INTERVIEWING FOR MEDIA
syllabus_overview: As workplaces become more interactive and interconnected, interviewing skills are becoming more important across a range of vocations. In this subject, you will study the processes and skills required for interviewing, focussing on key case studies in literature, print journalism, cinema, broadcasting and online. A key component of the subject will be interviews undertaken you in all or some of the key interview formats, including live discussion, email, pre-recorded audio and written profile pieces. Undertaking this subject will gain a broader appreciation of the art of inquiry and personal interaction and develop greater confidence in everything from one on one communications to public speaking to critical analysis. You will also gain a clear understanding of the use of quotation technique including quote punctuation, in written work and develop an appreciation of key editing issues, both practical and ethical.
learning_outcomes: Writing for an online publishing platform, with particular emphasis on learning how to deploy hyperlinks, and how to best promote one's work.
Practice interviewing skills in different settings such as live interviews, and develop skills to approach subjects to participate in the interview process and researching for an interview.
Critically evaluate interviews and the interview process in different settings
Develop an understanding of the history and formats of interviews in the media, and interview practice in journalism, and non-related fields.
Create written versions of interviews, with specific attention to developing formatting and editing skills and profile writing.

title: PODCASTING
syllabus_overview: This subject teaches the techniques of audio news writing and explores podcasting and the use of sound in storytelling. Through the production of news bulletins and individual podcasts you will develop interviewing, recording, voice presentation and editing skills. The subject also covers how to create, develop and tell stories in the context of a podcast, including how to write to audio, and how to develop and practice presenting skills to enable the production of compelling podcasts. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation in either weekly online or face-to-face tutorials. These classes may fall in business hours.
learning_outcomes: Work with respect to key ethical and legal obligations associated with audio journalism
Identify and research a story, conduct interviews and gather appropriate research and actuality material in the sound medium;
Report in a clear, concise, accurate and engaging way using a variety of audio elements and narrative conventions in an audio environment;
Learn to write, edit and produce audio content.
Maintain a high level of current affairs and general knowledge (of local, national and international events to inform reporting

title: SPORT REPORTING
syllabus_overview: Sports reporting is news reporting. It requires an understanding of sports-specific news values. This subject will introduce you to sports-specific news values through some of the most common forms of reporting in sport, press conference reporting, match reporting, profile pieces and analysis writing. This subject also explores the context in which sports journalists work, focusing on the major changes in the relationship between sports organisations and the media that cover them in the 21st century. In particular, it explores the implications of sports organisations' own media platforms and public relations staff on sports journalists' work.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the current Australian and global context of sport media, and identify opportunities and challenges to sport journalism practice in the digital age.
Apply sports-specific news values to write sport news pieces, such as a match report and press conference report, to an industry standard level, to deadline.
Apply the key fundamentals of professional writing such as correct grammar, punctuation and attribution as they apply to different media styles.
Conduct an interview and create profile style piece using interview quotes and other relevant sources, written to a publishable standard.

title: UPSTART 1
syllabus_overview: In Upstart, you will apply core journalism and media skills in the working newsrooms of La Trobe's student-driven media outlets. Both streams deliver work-ready newsroom skills, as you produce industry standard media content to deadline. In the editorial stream, you will write and edit copy to deadline, manage and edit copy from contributors. You will moderate comments, utilise social media to publicise upstart.net.au's content and activities, and collaborate with other editors, writers and academic staff to ensure content meets industry standards. In the broadcast stream, you will produce and present a series of shows using La Trobe's leading broadcast facilities. You must adhere to industry standard broadcast guidelines, and produce broadcast content that is creative, engaging and aimed at an identified audience.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of news values to develop and promote stories post-production.
Create innovative and interesting media content across multiple platforms, that adheres to industry guidelines.
Demonstrate the ability to work within a team to produce industry standard media content across multiple platforms.
Develop and apply practical knowledge of media audiences, to deliver content that engages its intended audience.

title: ADVANCED JOURNALISM PROJECT
syllabus_overview: In this capstone subject you will learn critical knowledge and practical tools to engage with the evolving landscape of journalism and news industries in Australia and globally. You will investigate the current challenges and opportunities facing journalism and the news media in the digital age. Through the exploration of key journalism frameworks—such as investigative, public interest, solutions-focused, and data journalism—you will develop an understanding of how these approaches can shape storytelling, audience engagement, and public impact. Alongside critical knowledge of industry and practice, students will focus on developing advanced research and critical thinking skills needed to execute these forms of journalism. You will learn to find and evaluate complex information from a wide range of sources, including online sources, media, data, historical and archival research and Freedom of Information, and to identify, approach, and interview credible interviewees in ways that meet professional and ethical standards.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the current Australian and global context of journalism an identify opportunities and challenges to journalism practice and news industries in the digital age.
Design, plan and execute an original major journalism project that demonstrates an understanding of key journalism thinking, and professional-level reporting, editing and storytelling skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of key journalism frameworks and different journalism formats within them.
Develop and utilise research and critical thinking skills to evaluate a diverse range of sources in the course of story production, including finding and conducting ethical interviews..
Demonstrate an understanding of legal and ethical best practice in creating media content.

title: MULTIMEDIA JOURNALISM
syllabus_overview: Journalism graduates are increasingly expected to be jacks and jills of all trades, and masters of combining them. In this subject, you will build skills in multimedia storytelling. You will be creating an online multimedia feature story, incorporating text, video, audio, photography and data visualisation, using a range of platforms. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation in either weekly online or face-to-face tutorials. These classes may fall in business hours.
learning_outcomes: Research a story, including sourcing appropriate interview subjects, archival materials, and conduct interviews
Apply storytelling principles across different media.
Evaluate a story and select the right media to tell it.
Locating and accessing technical documentation and tutorials about publishing platforms, facilitating lifelong learning.
Demonstrate proficiency in using audio, video, text and web-based publishing software and hardware to effectively capture and edit content for storytelling.
Demonstrate an understanding of the legal and ethical challenges of publishing across platforms, especially copyright and defamation, demonstrated in the stories produced in assessment.

title: BROADCAST JOURNALISM
syllabus_overview: You will explore the reporter's role in factual production across broadcast media. In this subject, we aim to provide you with a strong grounding in broadcast writing and production skills, as well as an appreciation of the multiple skills required by the convergence of television and radio in the current media environment. You will undertake practical assessments while developing skills across the broad range of roles in broadcast media. Please note that as some of the assessment is completed in class, this subject is only suitable for students who can attend the weekly face-to-face tutorials and does not have an online option.
learning_outcomes: Identifying and researching original story ideas and interview questions for television news.
Identifying and analysing the appropriate weighting of story angles, writing scripts for television and radio news, identifying appropriate visual and audio materials, and ensuring consistent style.
Filming and editing a television news story including a piece-to-camera and original interviews.
Writing, producing and presenting live radio news as part of a team.

title: INTRODUCTION TO SPORTS COMMENTARY
syllabus_overview: Introduction to Sports Commentary develops and expands your skills in a specialised area of sports journalism, sports broadcasting and sports commentary. At the successful completion of this subject, students will have an understanding of the history and context of sports commentary in Australia and around the world. You will be able to demonstrate an understanding of the different techniques and styles commentators employ, and be able to use this knowledge to prepare and perform live sports commentary. You will also develop skills in other forms of sports broadcasting, such as live crosses. This subject delivers targeted discipline specific skills, such as writing for broadcast, and how to use voice effectively for various broadcast mediums.
learning_outcomes: Identify and understand the key elements of successful match commentary, and apply them to a live match commentary that is of industry standard, in both radio and TV commentary formats.
Identify the key elements of successful live sports broadcasting, and apply them to a live cross that is of industry standard.
Demonstrate an understanding of the craft of sports commentary.
Demonstrate the ability to critically research and apply relevant information in commentary including developing a run sheet and notes that support accurate engaging and informed live commentary.

title: SPORT MEDIA ISSUES
syllabus_overview: Sport Media Issues examines some of the ethical issues that students will come across in the world of sport. As a cultural phenomenon, sport has been both a leader and a lagger in enacting cultural change. This subject asks you to deeply consider coverage of both contemporary and historical issues in the world of sport, and consider how as communicators working within sport these influence our work and practice. You will learn how to apply analysis skills to complex situations within sport, and write clear analysis pieces that incorporate evidence. You should finish this subject with a clearer understanding of some of the inherent problems, but also possibilities, within sport.
learning_outcomes: Analyse complex issues and apply critical thinking skills to a range of complex sources to write an industry-standard analysis piece.
Learn and apply deep research skills, including the ability to find and analyse complex sources for a piece of writing.
Demonstrate an understanding of and ability to consider ethics deeply in sports communication, including the ability to reflect on these through reflective writing.
Apply the key fundamentals of professional writing such as correct grammar, punctuation and attribution as they apply to different media styles.

title: UPSTART 2
syllabus_overview: In Upstart, you will apply core journalism and media skills in the working newsrooms of La Trobe's student-driven media outlets. Both streams deliver work-ready newsroom skills, as you produce industry standard media content to deadline. In the editorial stream, you will write and edit copy to deadline, manage and edit copy from contributors. You will moderate comments, utilise social media to publicise upstart.net.au's content and activities, and collaborate with other editors, writers and academic staff to ensure content meets industry standards. In the broadcast stream, you will produce and present a series of shows using La Trobe's leading broadcast facilities. You must adhere to industry standard broadcast guidelines, and produce broadcast content that is creative, engaging and aimed at an identified audience.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced knowledge gained from previous Upstart and/or La Trobe Live experience, to lead the creation of innovative and interesting media content across multiple platforms, that adheres to industry guidelines.
Apply advanced knowledge of media audiences gained from previous Upstart and/or La Trobe Live experience, to deliver content that engages its intended audience.
Demonstrate the ability to lead a team to produce industry standard media content across multiple platforms.
Apply advanced knowledge of news values gained from previous Upstart and/or La Trobe Live experience, to develop and promote stories post-production.

title: UPSTART 3
syllabus_overview: In Upstart, you will apply core journalism and media skills in the working newsrooms of La Trobe's student-driven media outlets. Both streams deliver work-ready newsroom skills, as you produce industry standard media content to deadline. In the editorial stream, you will write and edit copy to deadline, manage and edit copy from contributors. You will moderate comments, utilise social media to publicise upstart.net.au's content and activities, and collaborate with other editors, writers and academic staff to ensure content meets industry standards. In the broadcast stream, you will produce and present a series of shows using La Trobe's leading broadcast facilities. You must adhere to industry standard broadcast guidelines, and produce broadcast content that is creative, engaging and aimed at an identified audience.
learning_outcomes: Create innovative and interesting media content across multiple platforms, that adheres to industry guidelines.
Apply knowledge of news values to develop and promote stories post-production.
Demonstrate the ability to work within a team to produce industry standard media content across multiple platforms.
Develop and apply practical knowledge of media audiences, to deliver content that engages its intended audience.

title: JUSTICE AND SOCIETY
syllabus_overview: Justice is often referred to as a driver of policy or law reform; however, what ‘justice’ means changes across contexts. In this subject, you will engage with a range of definitions and understandings of justice. You will consider how to apply these conceptualisations to real-world and hypothetical case studies relating to topics such as colonialism, gender, race, class, sexuality, disability, poverty, and the environment. You will develop the capacity to think critically about some of the causes of inequality and injustice, and the institutions and tools needed to address them.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively with other students
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of conceptions of justice
Identify, understand and compare a range of definitions and conceptions of justice
Apply principles of justice to real-world and hypothetical problems

title: DISPUTE RESOLUTION
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces Dispute Resolution as an alternative tool to traditional litigation. It explores the principles of dispute resolution, its use in the legal justice system and the various dispute resolution methods including negotiation, mediation and arbitration. There is a particular emphasis on mediation, where students practise the skills used in mediation and negotiation, through exercises and a mediation assessment. The distinguishing characteristics of various dispute resolution methods will be examined. You will also develop evaluative skills to identify the most appropriate method of dispute resolution to address a given conflict.
learning_outcomes: Apply the facilitative approach to mediation.
Analyse the role of various dispute resolution mechanisms and professionals within the legal system and broader community.
Demonstrate an understanding of dispute resolution principles including key features of various dispute resolution methods.
Apply teamwork and micro-skills in communication, negotiation, and mediation in a small group setting
Practise the skills involved in dispute resolution including active listening, questioning, reflection, summary, re-framing, agenda-setting, and identification of parties' interests and needs.

title: PRINCIPLES OF CRIMINAL LAW
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will examine key aspects of the substantive criminal law. You will analyse the basic concepts and principles in the criminal law such as the onus and standard of proof, evidentiary and persuasive burdens, objective and subjective tests, and principles of offence classification. You will then focus on developing skills in applying the law to factual scenarios so as to provide legal advice. The subject deals with substantive topics including homicide, non-fatal offences against the person, sexual offences, and offences against property. This subject, in conjunction with Evidence and Criminal Procedure, meets the requirements of the Council of Legal Education for admission to practice in Victoria in the area of Criminal Law and Procedure.
learning_outcomes: Work co-operatively in small teams to produce joint work and develop a reflective approach to learning.
Demonstrate well-developed skills in problem analysis, logical argumentation, effective communication, and the interpretation of statutory provisions and case law.
Compose a legal opinion, involving the identification and application of relevant laws, in answer to problems raising a range of criminal law issues
Identify and apply the structure of a range of criminal offences and their underlying general principles.

title: LEGAL INSTITUTIONS AND METHODS
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students with an introduction to the legal system in Australia and its core institutions, with a particular emphasis on courts, including the court hierarchy, the doctrine of precedent and reading and analysing cases. The subject will require students to critically assess the differential impact that the legal system has on particular groups in society, including First Nations peoples.It also introduces students to the role of legal professionals and covers legal methods with particular emphasis on the fundamentals of legal research and problem-solving.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an awareness of the social and ethical impact of the Australian legal system and the role of lawyers in the system
Apply appropriate written communication skills
Demonstrate comprehension of fundamental legal research methods and referencing, including an awareness of the nature of academic integrity and consequences of plagiarism
Demonstrate an understanding of the basic aspects and workings of Australian legal systems such as the main legal institutions and their functions as sources of legal authority
Analyse and apply case law to legal issues using appropriate legal problem-solving methodology

title: PRINCIPLES OF PUBLIC LAW
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore the fundamental principles of public law in Australian and foreign jurisdictions, with a focus on human rights. 'Public law' can be defined as the body of legal rules that govern the relationship between the State and its citizens and the relationship between the institutions of the State (i.e. the legislative, executive, and judicial arms of government). Public law concerns itself with the nature, sources, and extent of State power to ensure that power exercised by the State is authorised and legitimate. Within this subject, there is also a focus on industry-informed career development learning activities to support setting goals for personal and professional development.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique scholarly materials discussing the principles of public law.
Develop career management strategies, including the ability to work collaboratively in a group
Critically discuss contemporary public law issues with a focus on human rights in Australian and foreign jurisdictions.
Compose arguments based on, and accurately cite, scholarly materials in a legal essay.
Locate, by means of legal research, scholarly materials discussing the principles of public law in Australian and foreign jurisdictions.

title: CONTRACT LAW A
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will be introduced to the common law of contract in Australia. After considering the basic theory and history of private law and contractual obligations, you will use case law to analyse and apply the legal principles on contract formation: agreement, consideration, intention, capacity and formalities. We then consider vitiating factors: the doctrines around setting aside a contract that has not been properly formed under common law and statute (eg because of duress, undue influence). You will use case law to analyse and apply the legal principles governing the creation of a contract. This involves the development of techniques to write case analysis, for application of legal rules of contract to fact situations, and for communication of legal opinion to advise a range of audiences. This subject, in combination with Contract Law B, meets the requirements of the Victorian Legal Admissions Board to practice in Victoria in the area of Law of Contracts
learning_outcomes: Identify relevant common law principles governing contracts as they apply to a given fact situation
Identify the outcomes arising from alternative arguments and argue strategically on the basis of the needs of a client in a fictional scenario
Demonstrate an understanding of the language of Contract Law and how to use it in written and oral communications
Demonstrate general legal analysis skills and identify and locate Australian legal information in a range of primary and secondary sources
Write a legal analysis and opinion on a contractual problem

title: CYBER LAW AND POLICY
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to laws and policies regulating Cyberspace. It invites students to critically evaluate the sufficiency and effectiveness of laws, policies and industry self-regulation in addressing challenges to government, business and society in an increasingly online world. The subject specifically examines Australian and International Law and practice in this area paying attention to perspectives from legal, political and technological experts.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness and applicability of laws and policies relating to cyberspace security.
Analyse the application of laws and policies relating to cyberspace.
Describe Security issues associated with the use of the cyberspace.
Identify laws and policies applicable to the use of the cyberspace

title: PRINCIPLES OF CONSTITUTIONAL LAW
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will acquire a general knowledge of federal and state constitutional law in Australia and of the principles of constitutional interpretation. Topics covered in this subject include the sources and limits of Commonwealth and state legislative power, examples of specific Commonwealth powers under the Commonwealth Constitution, and restrictions on Commonwealth power, such as Chapter III judicial power and express and implied constitutional rights and freedoms. You will also learn how constitutional law deals with federal/state relations, including the interpretative approaches that apply where federal and state laws are inconsistent. This subject will develop your constitutional problem-solving skills and your historical and theoretical understanding of Australian constitutionalism.
learning_outcomes: Advise a client on their legal position with respect to a factual situation, where the problem calls for the use of constitutional method and the application of relevant constitutional law.
Explain and assess constitutional methods, including the interpretation and characterisation of a federal or state law.
Demonstrate general knowledge of federal and state constitutional law in Australia.

title: CONTRACT LAW B
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the interpretation, discharge and remedies around contracts. Whereas Contract A examined the formation and setting aside of contracts, this unit starts from there being a valid contract between the parties, and examines how to interpret that contract, the interaction of consumer law and contract terms, and rights around termination. We then consider contractual remedies and end with current issues in the law of contract. This subject reinforces skills in case law and statutory analysis. This subject, in combination with Contract Law A, meets the requirements of the Victorian Legal Admissions Board to practice in Victoria in the area of Law of Contracts.
learning_outcomes: Interpret statutory provisions and associated case law relating to contracts.

Identify the outcomes arising from alternative arguments and argue strategically on the basis of the needs of a client in a fictional scenario, including identification of the opportunities and risks of these alternative arguments.
Analyse the social, economic and ethical context within which the law relating to commercial and consumer contracts operates.
Analyse common law principles at common law and in equity.
Use legal problem-solving skills to compose a legal opinion which applies the appropriate common law and statutory principles to factual scenarios.

title: PUBLIC INTEREST LAW PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you have the opportunity to undertake a placement in the public law sector early in your degree. You are placed in a community legal clinic or an approved public interest law organisation while concurrently undertaking academic study. Besides exploring the scope, practice, and ethical aspects of public interest lawyering, this subject also covers practice skills and industry informed career development learning activities to support your professional development and readiness for placement later in your degree and graduate positions. You will be provided with a placement organised by the Law School or can apply on the basis of a self-organised placement. Self-organised placements must be approved by the Subject or Placement Coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Develop communication skills in a legal environment.
Develop their knowledge of legal practice, through participation, observation, research, and reflection, on their practical experience.
Develop a reflective approach to learning.
Demonstrate critical thinking in relation to the practice of public interest law and its place within legal practice

title: RURAL AND REGIONAL ISSUES IN JUSTICE
syllabus_overview: Students in this subject will be placed in a legal practice or legal organisations based in rural and regional Australia. Students will generally work in organisations assisting disadvantaged clients based in the Loddon Campaspe region for one day a week during semester. Students may be given responsibility for activities such as assisting in casework, community legal education and law reform projects under the supervision of staff lawyers. Students may be involved in taking instructions from clients and assisting volunteer lawyers who provide legal advice to clients. Students also attend a series of seminars on relevant areas of law and practical skills.
learning_outcomes: Develop communication skills in a legal environment.
Demonstrate critical thinking in relation to the practice of law in rural and regional Australia.
Develop legal research skills.
Analyse the professional and ethical responsibilities of a legal practitioner in rural and regional Australia.
Develop a reflective approach to learning

title: PRINCIPLES OF TORT LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the principles of tort law. Tort law provides a private, civil law action in pursuit of reparation (normally in the form of a monetary award of damages) as compensation for harm inflicted by another, with respect to one of a number of recognised interests of a personal and economic nature. In modern society, most of these interests are vindicated by the pivotal action in negligence, hence the majority of attention is devoted to an understanding of that tort. This subject will also introduce you to other torts including nuisance and trespass.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain case-based and statutory tortious principles.
Apply case-based and statutory tortious principles to arrive at a solution to a problem raised in a given fact situation.
Demonstrate an understanding of the language of tort law and its appropriate use.
Demonstrate an ability to write effectively using the principles of plain legal English.

title: FOUNDATIONS OF PROPERTY LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to fundamental concepts of property law in Australia. This subject involves consideration of the notion of property and of proprietary interests. Students will learn about the concept of property, acquisition and regulation of title to property (including possession), the importance of relativity of title and the creation and enforceability of legal and equitable interests. Students will also receive an introduction to statutory schemes of registration of property interests.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to effectively construct written legal advice relating to problems in property law.
Evaluate claims made for property interests using appropriate legal doctrine as it applies to a given fact situation.
Demonstrate strong comprehension of the concept of property as it operates in Australian law.
Critically analyse how to pursue a property law claim or defence for a client as effectively as possible.

title: EVIDENCE AND CRIMINAL PROCEDURE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will learn about the rules of evidence in civil and criminal cases as well as the rules of criminal procedure. These rules have evolved to enable court cases to be conducted in a manner that is deemed to be fair to all parties and, increasingly, to promote the interests of the state in ensuring the 'efficient' disposal of cases by the courts. The law of civil procedure is dealt with in a separate subject. This subject, in conjunction with Criminal Law, meets the requirements of the Council of Legal Education for admission to practice in Victoria in the area of Criminal Law and Procedure. It also meets the requirements in the area of Evidence.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical reasoning and logic skills in order to creatively solve legal problems.
Engage effectively in both written and verbal forms of criminal law advocacy
Interpret and apply the rules of evidence and criminal procedure to an advanced undergraduate level.

title: STATUTORY INTERPRETATION
syllabus_overview: Statutory interpretation is the body of law governing the determination of the legal meaning and effect of legislation. This subject examines the law and practice of statutory interpretation systematically and in depth. The concepts, interpretative criteria, and techniques of the common law are examined, together with federal and state interpretation legislation. In addition to developing students' skills in interpreting legislation, the subject also develops related skills in legal research, in case analysis, in legal drafting, and in writing legal opinions.
learning_outcomes: Research and identify legislation and extrinsic materials that are relevant to a given fact situation.
Analyse and interpret legislation in a fully-informed way.
Write a legal opinion on statutory interpretation in language and form that approximates the standard expected of an entrant to the legal profession.
Demonstrate in-depth knowledge of statute law.

title: CIVIL PROCEDURE
syllabus_overview: Students in this subject examine the procedural laws and rules relating to the resolution of civil disputes in an adversarial system. The following topics are covered: the overarching obligations of parties and practitioners; the civil jurisdiction of Australian courts; initiating proceedings; service; joinder; parties to litigation; defining the questions for trial; obtaining evidence; interlocutory orders; disposition without trial; alternative dispute resolution; settlement; extra judicial determination of issues; trial; appeal; costs; and enforcement of judgements.
learning_outcomes: Apply civil procedure law and rules to find solutions to legal disputes.
Critically analyse ways to pursue a legal claim or defence for a client as effectively as possible.
Apply knowledge of legal procedural rules to analyse particular factual scenarios and to indicate probable outcomes.

title: REAL PROPERTY LAW
syllabus_overview: Real Property Law builds on the concepts and principles of Property Law introduced in Foundations of Property Law. This subject focuses on Land Law. Topics include: the Torrens registration system and indefeasibility of title; acquisition and regulation of real property; concurrent ownership; mortgages, proprietary interests in land owned by another and resolving conflicts between legal and equitable interests in Torrens Land; and the conveyancing process.
learning_outcomes: Effectively construct written legal advice relating to a particular property law situation or problem.
Demonstrate ability to appropriately use the specialised terminology of Australian Property Law.
Critically analyse how to pursue a property law claim or defence for a client.
Apply knowledge of legal doctrine to analyse particular factual disputes and to indicate probable outcomes.

title: SENTENCING LAW AND POLICY
syllabus_overview: Most people charged with a criminal offence are sentenced, which may involve the loss of individual liberty, a fundamental right in our society. This subject examines the law and practice of sentencing in Victoria. The substantive law of sentencing is examined, the theoretical bases of sentencing are critically evaluated and the relationship between political processes, policy and legislation is explored.
learning_outcomes: Develop written and oral communication skills appropriate to law and criminology.
Critically evaluate sentencing law, policy and practice in Victoria and suggest appropriate reform.
Demonstrate an ability to work effectively in a group.
Identify and analyse Victorian sentencing law and policy.

title: FAMILY SOCIETY AND LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject offers an exploration of Family Law in Australia through emphasizing three core components: the substantive legal framework relating to the family, the practical skills necessary for effective legal practice, and a critical examination of how family law interacts with societal changes. Specific topics explored in this subject include the legal regulation of family formation and breakdown, parental responsibility, and children's rights alongside hands-on activities designed to develop essential legal skills such as drafting legal documents, conducting client interviews, and negotiating settlements. These practical skills are complemented by discussions on emerging trends and potential reforms in family law, including the recognition of diverse family structures and the implications of technological advancements.
learning_outcomes: Clearly communicate complex legal concepts and doctrines in a relevant way
Demonstrate knowledge of the legal framework which regulates the responsibilities, rights and duties of family members in Australia and of the factors that have shaped modern family law.
Apply skills in legal analysis and reasoning and improve legal problem solving and communication skills in relation to family law problems.
Consolidate collaborative working skills through group-based tasks.
Develop an awareness of the key issues in contemporary Australian Family Law and an understanding of relevant contextual materials.

title: INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND THE LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the way settler-colonial law impacts upon Indigenous peoples in the territory called Australia and the way struggles for Indigenous justice have engaged the legal system. Providing a historical and socio-legal analysis the subject covers topics including: Indigenous sovereignty; the history of genocide and the Stolen Generations; Indigenous citizenship; police violence, deaths in custody and over-representation in the criminal justice system; land rights and native title; cultural heritage protection; racism and racial discrimination; human rights and self-determination; continuing child removals and gendered paternalistic policies; and constitutional recognition and treaty. The assessment regime also allows you to research relevant topics of particular interest.
learning_outcomes: By means of legal research, locate and analyse primary and secondary materials relevant to Indigenous interactions with law.
Reflect on the way settler-colonial law impacts upon Indigenous peoples and the way struggles for Indigenous justice have engaged the legal system.
Demonstrate an awareness of cultural safety in the context of Indigenous interactions with law.
Analyse contemporary legal issues relating to Indigenous peoples in Australia.

title: LAW AND MEDICINE
syllabus_overview: Medical law is an internationally recognised intellectual discipline and a field of legal practice which is founded on ethical theories, common law doctrines, and human rights principles. It spans other areas of law (torts, criminal, family and administrative law) and must satisfy social policy developments, principles of governance, regulatory mechanisms and dispute resolution processes. In this subject, medico-legal issues are discussed and evaluated in the context of a range of topics which include: ethical duties, consent to medical treatment (adults and children), legal competence and medical treatment (adults), human reproduction law and technologies, professional liability and medical malpractice, regulation of health professionals and end of life decision-making. Informed analysis of law is promoted by examining the case law and legislation together with group discussion. Students are equipped with skills relevant to policy developments and law reform.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the application of legal principles to policy development and law reform in areas related to law and medicine.
Identify, analyse and apply common law principles and legislation relevant to the area of medicine.
Evaluate legal problems related to medical ethics and practice.

title: FOUNDATIONS OF INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the conceptual framework of intellectual property law (IPL) in Australia. You will examine the theories, policies and principles of intellectual property regulation, including the statutory regimes of copyright, patent and trademark protection, the tort of passing off, the action for misleading and deceptive conduct, and the equitable doctrine of breach of confidence. In addition to examining a number of discrete areas of IPL, you will analyse the interrelationships between these laws, the effect of international standards on domestic regimes, and consider topical issues in the field. Contemporary issues might include the effect of artificial intelligence on IPL, legal liability for downloading/streaming media, privacy, and the regulation of social networking, the patenting of living organisms, and, the regulation of character merchandising and celebrity endorsements.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the historical, social, economic and cultural implications of the protection of intellectual property in Australia
Demonstrate comprehension of the conceptual framework and key legal doctrines of Australian intellectual property law
Evaluate problems using appropriate legal doctrine in Australian intellectual property law
Identify, use and appraise research material relevant to the operation and reform of intellectual property law in Australia
Demonstrate enhanced teamwork and collaboration skills

title: INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject offers an introduction to international criminal law and procedure. You will examine the process by which war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and aggression came to be recognised as international core crimes and how each overlaps with and fundamentally differs from the others. The various forms of individual criminal responsibility that are designed to capture the wide range of conduct that typically characterises mass atrocity will also be explored. Using case studies, you will engage in a critical evaluation of the effectiveness of the international community's response to these crimes, with a focus on the operation of international courts and tribunals.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a capacity to effectively apply the legal principles relevant to core international crimes and forms of liability to a factual scenario
Demonstrate an awareness of the practical and legal relevance of international criminal law in past and current world events
Enhance research skills and effectively use them to critically evaluate theoretical and practical issues of relevance to international criminal justice

title: REFUGEE LAW IN CONTEXT
syllabus_overview: This subject explores Australian refugee law and policy in a regional and international context. The subject examines the international and domestic legal frameworks for dealing with refugees. The subject also considers the political and social context in which law and policy is formulated and applied. Throughout the subject the role of law in promoting refugee protection is evaluated; areas requiring reform are identified; and strategies for change considered. Students will also have the opportunity to enhance their research and writing skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate strong comprehension of international law relating to refugees and asylum seekers
Demonstrate well-developed written communication skills appropriate for the dissemination of legal knowledge and ideas to legal and non-legal audiences
Independently locate and appraise material relevant to resolving contemporary refugee protection problems
Critically evaluate Australian refugee law and policy
Demonstrate strong comprehension of Australian refugee law and policy

title: INSOLVENCY LAW
syllabus_overview: Insolvency is a consequence of the availability of credit. Credit has been said to be ‘the lifeblood of the economy’. But credit involves debt, and insolvency law is the legal framework, largely statutory, which facilitates and regulates the consequences of a company or individual defaulting on its debts. After examining the principles and theories behind insolvency law that are common to both individual and corporate debtors, you will focus on corporate insolvency, including the formal options for rescuing companies (both large and small) and/or their business or otherwise dealing with their financial distress, including the role and duties of company directors in circumstances of looming or actual insolvency.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to work and communicate effectively in a team
Apply analytical judgement to identify and explain legal issues, and provide solutions to problems
Identify theories, principles and rules of insolvency law
Critically analyse insolvency law and policy, and conduct independent research

title: COMMERCIAL LAW
syllabus_overview: This unit builds on knowledge acquired in contract law to introduce you to areas of law that regulate and facilitate commercial transactions. These include agency, commercial sale of goods and services, interest over personal property, and insurance. Throughout this unit, you will adopt a skills-based learning approach through problem-solving and promoting an understanding of the dynamic nature of the law in business. These skills will prepare you for your professional career.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the common law and statutory provisions relevant to commercial law.
Apply law to factual situations and develop problem solving skills to determine a likely outcome.
Identify the common law and statutory provisions governing selected topics in the law of commerce.

title: CRIME AND THE ENVIRONMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will critically explore a range of issues concerning the interaction of crime and criminal law with contemporary environmental issues. The need to address environmental harms is more pressing now than ever before. Climate change, environmental degradation, and species extinction are real and present concerns. In this subject we will examine what role the criminal law does, can and should play in addressing such harms. Particular topics to be covered will be drawn from, among others, pollution offences, carbon emission offences, ecocide and large-scale environmental degradation, climate homicide, wildlife and biodiversity offences, animal cruelty and killing, climate criminals, environmental protest and activism, and preventing, prosecuting, punishing and repairing environmental crimes. The subject will look at Australian, foreign, and international criminal laws, and draw upon a range of theories and perspectives in conceptualising and analysing the issues.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate issues and arguments relevant to crime, criminal law and the environment.
Understand a range of issues relating to crime, criminal law and the environment.
Use skills in independent research relevant to crime, criminal law and the environment.

title: ANIMAL WELFARE LAW AND POLICY
syllabus_overview: This subject will consider the relationship between people and animals in ethics, law, and society. Topics to be considered will be chosen from current issues in animal law and may include the legal classification of animals, companion animals, animals in the wild, regulation of the use of animals for food and entertainment, anti-cruelty laws, live export, animals used in scientific experimentation, zoos and circuses, international wildlife trafficking and international developments including public interest litigation in animal law. The subject also considers the political and social context in which law and policy are formulated and applied in animal law matters. You will also have the opportunity to enhance your research and writing skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the capacity to reflect on the interaction between natural, economic, social, political and cultural systems
Analyse the political and social context in which law and policy is formulated and applied in animal law matters
Critique the capacity of current law to improve the welfare of animals
Identify and discuss the common law and legislation impacting on the welfare of animals

title: BANKING AND FINANCE LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to selected fundamental legal issues in relation to corporate banking and finance law. In addition to an examination of key legal issues the subject aims to provide students with an opportunity to develop practical legal skills by drafting and negotiating the terms of a loan agreement. The subject is divided into three themes: 1) regulation of the financial system; 2) the legal nature of different forms of financial accommodation; 3) Guarantees. Topics covered include: regulation of Australia's financial system including the impact of deregulation and the Global Financial Crisis, discussion of the legal nature and structure of different forms of financial accommodation including the nature of the relationship between borrowers, lenders and agents in multi lender financing; the negotiation and drafting of loan agreements; and the law of guarantees.
learning_outcomes: Explain key terms in corporate finance documents.
Characterise the legal nature of the relationship between parties to various types of financial accommodation
Apply negotiating and drafting techniques to a loan agreement at an introductory level.
Identify and apply the relevant banking and finance law applicable to a given fact situation relating to corporate banking and finance.

title: CLIMATE LAW
syllabus_overview: Climate change presents many complex and long-term challenges for society, economy and environment. This subject considers the way in which law and legal regimes can contribute to addressing these challenges and the way legal frameworks might need to be re-conceptualized and changed to respond. This subject examines the international legal framework under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and Paris Agreement, including questions of mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage. It also examines transnational forms of climate change regulation, including through carbon markets and other voluntary measures as well as the ways in which law can promote transitions to a low-carbon society. The course also covers Australian regulatory measures to address climate change, looking at federal, state and local law. The subject concludes by looking at the growth in litigation to respond to climate challenges as well as the interaction between climate change and other legal regimes, such as trade and human rights.
learning_outcomes: Through collaborative processes analyse, generate and transmit legal solutions to complex problems related to climate change governance
Analyse and evaluate the effectiveness, efficiency and equity of different legal responses to climate change
Locate by means of legal research, materials relating to the problem of climate change and its legal regulation, and write well composed, concise and accurately cited legal analysis.
Recognise and describe the different legal regimes and principles applicable to climate change governance

title: COMMISSIONS, INQUESTS AND INQUIRIES
syllabus_overview: Governments have a range of inquiry mechanisms available to them to examine systemic problems, deaths or wrong doing. These include Royal Commissions, coronial inquests, parliamentary committee inquires and law reform commission inquiries. In this subject students will examine how these processes operate and how they differ from each other and differ from court-based proceedings. You will evaluate the role these mechanisms play in Australian legal and policy development and reform, and assess their effectiveness in contributing to such development and reform.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to work effectively in a group
Identify, use and appraise research material relevant to both completed and current inquiry processes
Critically evaluate the role of inquiries in Australian legal and policy development
Develop written and oral communication skills appropriate to law and criminology

title: LEGAL DISRUPTION
syllabus_overview: This subject will explore how and why the legal professional is being disrupted, locally, nationally, and internationally. This subject will explore disruptive innovation within context of regulatory framework, business structures, commoditisation and Old Law versus New Law business models. The subject will consider the application of corporate disruption case studies to disruption of the legal profession but focus on the issues that are driving contemporary practice including the impact of disruptive business models and new practice vistas. Legal and ethical opportunities and challenges arising from legal disruption, the Justice Gap and social media will also be examined.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the social, technological and economic issues having an impact on the role of the professional lawyer
Analyse ethical dilemmas arising from social, technological and economic change
Demonstrate a broad understanding of contemporary issues challenging the legal profession

Interpret and apply the Legal Profession Uniform Law Application Act 2014 (Vic), Legal Profession Uniform General Rules 2015 and Legal Profession Uniform Law Australian Solicitors Conduct Rules 2015 in relation to emerging legal start-ups

title: CRIMINAL JUSTICE
syllabus_overview: The criminal justice system refers to the collection of state institutions and agencies responsible for the processing of persons accused or convicted of a crime. This subject explores the roles of various actors and participants in the criminal justice system. You will evaluate the processes by which decisions are made, reviewed and possibly corrected and the operation of discretionary powers. The factors that contribute to miscarriages of justice are examined, including through case studies, with a view to understanding potential procedural remedies.
learning_outcomes: Consolidate collaborative working skills through group-based tasks
Critically analyse contemporary issues relevant to the administration of criminal justice.
Evaluate areas for reform of the administration of criminal justice and construct a coherent argument for that reform.
Demonstrate comprehension of the law governing the administration of criminal justice in Victoria.
Identify, use and appraise research material relevant to the administration of criminal justice.

title: CRIMINAL LAW POLICY AND REFORM
syllabus_overview: Criminal Law Policy and Reform provides you with the opportunity to explore cutting-edge policy and law reform issues in the area of criminal law. Good lawyers do not merely know what the law is and how to apply it to facts; they also understand how and why the law changes and are able to help shape legal change. This subject is designed to develop your understanding and skills in these respects. You will critically examine a range of topics in criminal law in which policy debates and/or law reform efforts have recently featured, such as hate crimes, cyberbullying, drug law reform, euthanasia, and terrorism, among others. Assessment tasks are modelled on real-world examples of policy development and law reform documents.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical understanding of the debates and processes involved in criminal law policy development and law reform.
Analyse and critique criminal law policy using well-developed legal research skills.
Create academic work that shows an ability to follow instructions and that maintains academic integrity.

title: DISABILITY RIGHTS AND LAW
