In this subject, students will evaluate the effectiveness of the international and Australian legal frameworks aimed to establish, protect and support the exercise of rights for people with disabilities. The organising frame for the subject are the rights embedded in the principles of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) and the legal mechanisms for their enactment in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and transmit information about current anti-discrimination laws that support people with cognitive disabilities and their support network.
Compare and contrast the role of various agencies in safeguarding the rights of people with cognitive disabilities.

Critically examine specific types of legislation in Australia that aim to enact the rights of people with disabilities embedded in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD
Make informed judgements to appeal, through the proper channels, the support provided for a person with cognitive disability.
Critically evaluate evidence for how people with disabilities and their supporters experience the justice system.

title: EDUCATION LAW AND ETHICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject students locate their knowledge of the professional practice of teaching within the context of the legal and ethical environment in which they, as teachers, will operate. Students will develop an understanding of the sources of law and of legal and non-legal obligations, including ethics, with which they must comply as teaching professionals. Students will develop an advanced understanding of the legal and ethical obligation to maintain their skills and knowledge and to maintain professional networks. Students will engage in a series of case studies through which they will critically analyse the application of legal and non-legal principles and practices to the physical and psychological safety of students and others in the school environment, the safe, responsible and ethical use of IT in learning and teaching, responsible and confidential interactions with the school community and the processes, limitations and consequences of risk analysis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of legislative requirements to maintain student safety and develop and evaluate strategies that support students' physical and psychological well-being and safety

Critically analyse legislative and ethical frameworks in which ICT in learning and teaching occurs and advanced understanding of strategies available to support the safe, responsible and ethical use of ICT in learning and teaching.
Develop knowledge and understanding of the legislative, administrative and organisational policies and processes affecting teaching and teachers
Critically understand the necessity for teachers to broaden their professional knowledge and practice through interaction with external professionals and community representatives.

Examine and develop advanced understanding of the legislative, common law and ethical context in which effective, sensitive and confidential engagement of parents and carers in the educative process occurs.

Demonstrate critical understanding of the professional learning needs of teachers to improve practice, including an understanding of the role of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers and the appropriate sources of professional learning.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
syllabus_overview: Australia faces complex and urgent environmental challenges. In this subject, you explore how to respond to environmental problems, individually and collectively, using law as a tool. You consider the economic and social factors that continue to shape the law in this area and the distribution of authority for environmental governance between the Commonwealth, State and local governments. You explore regulatory tools and examine principles of international environmental law and how they have influenced the development of Australian environmental law. You consider environmental management and regulatory challenges in relation to waste and pollution, biodiversity protection, and climate change and energy. You explore processes of environmental planning, development approval and impact assessment, enforcement and compliance, and environmental litigation. The purpose of the content is to understand how law can be deployed to mitigate ecological degradation, advocate for its protection and contribute to its repair.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced collaborative working skills through group-based tasks
Develop specialised understanding of core principles and key contemporary issues in international and domestic environmental law.
Critically analyse, articulate and convey complex ideas regarding international and domestic environment law.
Demonstrate advanced skills at developing legal arguments as applied to novel fact situations

title: PRINCIPLES OF EQUITY AND TRUSTS
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the nature of equity, and includes a discussion of various equitable doctrines and equitable rights and interests, fiduciary obligations, confidential information and contextualises understandings surrounding estoppel in equity and unconscionable transactions. It covers the elements of trust law, including various types of trusts, the rights, duties and powers of trustees, the consequences of breach of trust and provides an overview of equitable remedies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate high level research skills in relation to primary and secondary sources of equity and trusts law and its context
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the conceptual and doctrinal framework of equity and trusts law in Australia
Demonstrate critical analysis of the principles of the law of equity and trusts.
Write a legal opinion on a factual scenario in equity and trusts law in a professional manner

title: EVIDENCE AND CRIMINAL PROCEDURE
syllabus_overview: This subject covers two distinct, yet related, areas of law: criminal procedure and evidence law. We explore the fundamental rules that apply to the conduct of criminal investigations and prosecutions, and consider the extent to which they reflect an inherent tension between state powers and individual rights. We then turn our attention to the principles that govern the admissibility of evidence in legal proceedings, both criminal and civil. We examine the evolution and rationale of these rules, their judicial interpretation and practical application as well as how they shape the forensic determination of legal matters.
learning_outcomes: Construct and effectively communicate persuasive and well-supported legal arguments, both orally and in writing.
Demonstrate advanced understanding of the forensic use of evidence and its relationship to advocacy in legal proceedings.
Critically interpret legal principles of relevance to criminal procedure and evidence law and coherently apply them to practical factual scenarios.

title: PROPERTY LAW
syllabus_overview: Foundations of Property Law introduces students to fundamental concepts of property law in Australia. This subject involves consideration of the notion of property and of proprietary interests and focuses on real and personal property. Topics include: the concept of property; acquisition and regulation of title to property including possession, title and ownership; the importance of relativity of title; creation and disposition of property interests; introduction to statutory schemes of registration of property interests.
learning_outcomes: Ability to solve complex problems and to think rigorously and independently by preparing written legal opinion as it applies to problems in property law.
Strong comprehension and familiarity with the language of property law.
Advanced knowledge and critical evaluation of the key legal doctrines that underpin Australian Property law.
Develop expert skills in evaluating claims made for property interests in a given fact situation, using appropriate legal doctrine.
Advanced knowledge and critical evaluation of the concept of property as it operates in Australian law.

title: HEALTH LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an introduction to core topics and debates in the study of health law and regulation in Australia. It adopts a framework-approach to analysing the relationship between law and health, taking account of ethical, social, cultural, political and rights-based contexts. Topics covered include the regulatory framework of the Australian health system; regulating health professionals; regulating patient safety and redress; consent to, and refusal of, medical treatment; substituted decision-making, medical negligence; and confidentiality, privacy and access to information. Additional topics to be covered may include law and reproduction and law at the end of life.
learning_outcomes: Explain and critique case law and regulation impacting the Australian health system, including the relationship between patients and health professionals in the areas studied in the subject.
Demonstrate a high level understanding of, and capacity to critically evaluate, key frameworks influencing the relationship between law and health
Demonstrate an understanding, and be able to critically evaluate, key debates impacting the relationship between patients and health professionals, in the areas studied in the subject
Demonstrate an understanding of, and be able to critically evaluate, the ethical, social, and political contexts which influence the relationship between law and health

title: HUMAN RIGHTS LAW IN CONTEXT
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the legal principles, institutions and issues at the heart of international and Australian human rights law. It equips you with the legal skills necessary to engage with the international and Australian human rights systems, such as how to draft a Statement of Compatibility under the Victorian Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities or make a complaint to the United Nations Human Rights Committee. It also provides you with the opportunity to critically analyse issues, tensions, and disappointments associated with human rights law, including the purported ‘universality’ of human rights; its treatment of marginalised groups (like Indigenous and gender and sexually diverse people); and the limitations of human rights when addressing some of the most pressing issues of our time, from corporate power to climate change.
learning_outcomes: Assess and critically analyse the practice and theory of human rights law.
Carry out independent research in a specific area of human rights law.
Utilise specific legal principles and domestic and international instruments to create, defend and communicate responses to human rights problems.
Demonstrate an understanding of the main concepts, principles, doctrines and procedures of international, regional and domestic human rights law.

title: INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject is an introduction to the theory and practice of the substance and procedure of international criminal law. You will learn about the major core international crimes including: genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes and the forms of individual criminal liability that arise in relation to these crimes. You will engage with case studies and examine the case law from international courts including: the post WWII International Military Tribunals in Nuremberg and Tokyo; the ad hoc Tribunals relating to atrocities in Yugoslavia and Rwanda; the mixed tribunals dealing with crimes committed in Cambodia and East Timor and the Permanent International Criminal Court.
learning_outcomes: Develop advanced collaborative working skills through group-based tasks
Develop advanced skills in identifying international crimes and determining a legal outcome in a fact based situation
Demonstrate integrated knowledge of the major principles and key cases of international criminal law
Critically examine the theory and practice of the substance and procedure of international criminal law

title: INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION
syllabus_overview: International Commercial Arbitration examines the foundational principles and laws of arbitration both nationally and internationally. Students will explore the main national and international laws, treaties and conventions applicable to arbitration disputes. The procedural framework of the arbitral process will also be examined, along with case studies, where students will draw on their knowledge of arbitration to provide legal advice in factual scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the conceptual and doctrinal framework of arbitration, nationally and internationally.
Demonstrate high level research skills in relation to primary and secondary sources of arbitration law and its context
Critically analyse principles of arbitration with reference to arbitration laws
Evaluate claims made in a factual scenario with appropriate reference to arbitration laws.

title: LAW INTERNSHIP B
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to participate in a placement at an approved organisation to while concurrently undertaking academic study. Placements can be in Australia or overseas in a legal related role. Students are required to complete a research or other type of writing project of their own choosing in addition to reflective elements of assessment. Students may apply for placement opportunities organised by the Law School or apply on the basis of a self-organised placement. Self-organised placements must be approved by the Coordinator.Law School Placement Coordinator or delegate. In this unit there is a focus on practice skills and industry informed career development learning activities to support professional development in readiness for graduate positions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical thinking in relation to the professional and ethical practice of law.
Develop their communication skills in a professional work environment.
Demonstrate an ability to critically reflect on their practical experience.
Develop their knowledge of the application of their law degree in a work environment through participation, observation, research, and reflection, on their practical experience.

title: INQUESTS INQUIRIES AND COMMISSIONS
syllabus_overview: Governments use a variety of standing and ad hoc inquisitorial mechanisms. Examples of standing bodies include Coroner’s Courts, Law Reform Commissions and Anti-Corruption Commissions. Examples of ad hoc mechanisms include Royal Commissions, Truth Telling Commissions and Boards of Inquiry. This subject will equip you to engage with inquisitorial mechanisms whether as Counsel Assisting, as legal advisors to witnesses, as representatives of organisations who prepare submissions, as members of an inquiry secretariat, or as legal policy officers who need to consider how to implement recommendations stemming from Inquests, Inquiries and Commissions.
learning_outcomes: Deploy advanced written and oral communication skills appropriate for the dissemination of legal research to legal and non-legal audiences
Gain an understanding of the workings of inquests' to 'develop a detailed understanding of the workings of inquests
Critically evaluate the role of inquests, inquiries and commissions in the Australian legal system

title: LEGAL INTERNSHIP
syllabus_overview: This subject allows you to participate in an Australian legal practice placement at an approved organisation such as a community legal centre, law firm, government or private organisation, shadowing a barrister while concurrently undertaking academic study. You may apply for placement opportunities organised by the Law School or apply on the basis of a self-organised placement. Self-organised placements must be approved by the Law School Placement Coordinator or delegate. In this unit there is a focus on practice skills and industry informed career development learning activities to support professional development in readiness for graduate positions.
learning_outcomes: Develop their communication skills in a legal environment.
Develop their knowledge of legal practice, through participation, observation, research, and reflection, on their practical experience.
Demonstrate critical thinking in relation to the professional and ethical practice of law.
Demonstrate an ability to critically reflect on their practical experience.

title: INTERNATIONAL TRADE LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to international trade regulations and institutions, with a focus on GATT/WTO (G ATT: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade WTO: World Trade Organisation) its institutional setting, principles and rules. While it has a comprehensive coverage, the subject is intended as a general introduction to international law concerning trade and business. The principal objective is to establish a solid foundation for students who wish to pursue further studies in specialised legal areas of international trade, international investment and international dispute resolution.
learning_outcomes: Identify contentious issues in international trade and business.
Critically understand and describe the law and policy framework governing International Trade.
Critically analyse controversial issues in Trade Law and Practice

title: JUSTICE AFTER ATROCITY
syllabus_overview: How do societies deal with atrocity and its aftermath? In this subject, students are introduced to the manifold ways in which societies have faced atrocities and mass violence, including criminal trials (domestic and international), truth commissions, lustration and art works. By examining a number of case studies from across the globe, students are invited to critically reflect of the difficulties in notions of truth, representation and justice. Focus is on both the theories and the practices of justice mechanisms with the aim of providing students with a well-grounded understanding of the precarious path to justice.
learning_outcomes: Clearly and effectively communicate analyses of issues utilising a range of critical perspectives and disciplines
Demonstrate high level critical understanding of the domestic and international legal landscape in which justice and truth claims are made and tested.
Reconceptualise justice mechanisms using case studies showing a profound understanding of the variety of reactions to atrocity and mass violence
Critically analyse theories of justice in the context of societal breakdown using a range of evaluation tools

title: LEGAL THEORY AND METHODOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will enhance skills in advanced legal research and writing methods. Students will be introduced to a range of socio-legal research methods and techniques, and theoretical approaches to legal scholarship. The subject gives students the opportunity to apply these skills and theoretical frameworks to a number of legal topics.
learning_outcomes: Develop advanced skills in legal research and writing methods
Independently review and critically analyse complex primary and secondary research material
Demonstrate an enhanced understanding of theoretical approaches to legal scholarship

title: PRINCIPLES OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject principally examines the legal limitations on the power of the federal and state executive governments to make decisions, and the legal mechanisms available to aggrieved persons for challenging and reviewing the exercise of such powers. The mechanisms examined at the federal level include judicial review of administrative action under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth), merits review by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, and investigation by the Commonwealth Ombudsman. Related mechanisms which are examined include rights to be given reasons for decisions upon request, freedom of information schemes, and non-legal mechanisms for reviewing government action. The subject also examines administrative law and practice through the lens of administrative law and public law theory.
learning_outcomes: Advance to critically analyse issues of administrative law and public law theory, and learn independently
Employ Critical analysis to interpret complex change.
Formulate submissions of high professional standard to address issues of administrative law before courts and tribunal
Analyse case management situations, and conclude whether clients' aims are likely to be achieved by recourse by the client to administrative law review.
Compose clear legal opinions which address, a range of complex problems for advice based on Administrative Law.

title: PRINCIPLES OF CRIMINAL LAW
syllabus_overview: Principles of Criminal Law introduces you to a range of criminal offences and the legal principles and policies that underlie them. The subject begins with an examination of the aims and sources of criminal law and the nature and elements of criminal offences. You will then examine particular offences under Victorian law, such as murder, assault and related offences, sexual offences, property offences, and strict liability. There will also be selective comparative examination of federal criminal laws. You will develop skills in writing legal advice (involving applying the law to new factual scenarios), analysing current issues in criminal law, and arguing for policy recommendations for law reform.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate cognitive and creative skills in effectively researching, analysing and applying case law and legislation to factual scenarios in order to advise a client as to their legal liabilities.
Formulate and articulate critically reflective arguments regarding issues of principle, policy and/or law reform in the criminal law.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge and analytical skills regarding the conceptual framework and doctrinal principles of criminal law operating in Victoria.

title: PUBLIC INTERNATIONAL LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the history and principles of the public international legal order. It provides students with an understanding of the foundational concepts of international law, its history and contemporary relevance, sources of international law and the role of some key international institutions such as the United Nations. The subject is grounded in both theory and practice in order to better demonstrate how international law works in dealing with a range of issues such as the creation of states, state responsibility, dispute settlement, self-determination, jurisdiction and immunities, and the use of force under international law. Students will be encouraged to critically evaluate the position and relevance of international law by addressing past and current developments in the field.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced skills in applying the principles of public international law to problem-solving within the international system in relation to contemporary international issues including cyber warfare and cyber terrorism
Demonstrate advanced understanding of the history and principles of public international law.

Critically evaluate the operation and application of the principles of public international law in the international system in relation to contemporary international issues including cyber warfare and cyber terrorism.

title: POLICY AND LAW OF COMPETITION
syllabus_overview: Competition law and policy is currently one of the most controversial areas of law and governmental activity. Competition law, in the form Part IV of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, regulates competition by proscribing horizontal and vertical practices which are either per se anti-competitive or substantially affect competition. Competition policy represents the framework for legal change creating and encouraging the developments of markets. This subject addresses both of these topics, dealing both substantially and critically with the economic theory which underpins competition policy and law, the legal techniques involved in creating and encouraging markets, and the laws regulating competition. Students will , inter alia, undertake a case study in competition policy and learn how the law regulating competition applies to various business practices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, describe and critically assess the reasons for and implementation of policies directed at enhancing markets and competition
Ascertain, describe and critically assess general and industry specific pro-competitive regulation

Discriminate between proscriptions, choose those applicable and apply competition law as expressed in Part IV of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and interpreted in case law, and industry-specific pro-competitive regulation to fact situations setting out complex market behaviours.

title: LEGAL PROCESS, METHODS AND INSTITUTIONS
syllabus_overview: Legal Process, Methods and Institutions introduces you to the study of law, the core legal institutions and sources of law in the Australia. The subject places the study of law in the context of legal practice, legal theory and issues of justice. You will develop essential skills for studying law including case analysis, legal problem solving, legal research and written and oral communication. The subject examines what is law and explores the social context in which law operates. Topics include the doctrine of precedent, joining the legal profession (including industry informed career development learning activities to support setting goals for personal and professional development), First Nations peoples and the law and current problems of access to justice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate comprehension of fundamental legal research methods, including an awareness of the principles of academic integrity and the consequences of any failure to comply
Develop industry-specific knowledge relevant to career development, and personal and professional skills relevant to the legal industry including written and oral communication skills
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the framework of the Australian legal system including its core institutions and sources of law and the role of lawyers in the system
Apply astute cognitive and creative skills in working with case law
Critically examine the historical, social and theoretical context of Australia's legal processes, methods and institutions

title: LEGAL PRACTICE AND PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT
syllabus_overview: The subject focuses on what constitutes ethical legal practice and conduct. This includes examining the legal practitioner's duty to the administration of law, the courts, clients and fellow practitioners and issues of personal and professional conduct. The context for this study is the issue of professional responsibility, reforms in the regulation of the legal profession and access to justice concerns. Students are encouraged to reflect on how a legal practitioner's duties and ethics are relevant to daily legal practice, as well as on the efficacy of law, the legal system, the legal profession and the nature of justice.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the regulatory, complaint and disciplinary processes applicable to the Victorian legal profession and problem-solve strategies to handle them in an appropriate and professional manner
Research and reflect on current issues pertaining to legal practice in Victoria
Demonstrate a high level of understanding of the obligations to the holding of money on trust.
Critically examine and reflect on ethical dilemmas facing a legal practitioner and problem solve pathways to handle then in an appropriate and professional manner.
Compare and interpret the professional and ethical responsibilities of a legal practitioner having regard to a variety of lawyering paradigms and conceptual frameworks.

Demonstrate a well developed understanding of the Legal Profession Uniform Law, statutory regulations and rules and the common law governing legal practitioners' conduct in relation to clients, the courts and other practitioners.

title: PRINCIPLES OF TORT LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject provides you with an integrated understanding of Australian tort law - the area of law encompassing private actions arising from harm to legally recognised interests, typically for a monetary award of damages. You gain in-depth knowledge of the most significant modern tort action, namely negligence, as well as nuisance, trespass, defamation and types of strict liability. Analysis of these legal actions is also contextualised by a consideration of legislative compensation schemes in comparative jurisdictions and the interaction between the legislature and judiciary in shaping the recognition and distribution of risk of loss in society.
learning_outcomes: Apply case-based and statutory tortious principles to arrive at a solution to a problem raised in a given fact situation.
Demonstrate an ability to write effectively using the principles of plain legal English
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the key statutes and legal doctrines that underpin Australian tort law
Demonstrate an understanding of the language of tort law and its appropriate use

title: REFUGEE LAW IN CONTEXT
syllabus_overview: This subject explores aspects of Australian refugee law and policy in a regional and international context. The subject examines the international and domestic legal frameworks for dealing with refugees. The subject also considers the political and social context in which law and policy is formulated and applied. Throughout the subject the role of law in promoting refugee protection is evaluated; areas requiring reform are identified; and strategies for change considered. Students will also have the opportunity to enhance their research and writing skills.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate Australian refugee law and policy critically and at an advanced level
Demonstrate advanced comprehension of Australian refugee law and policy
Deploy advanced written communication skills appropriate for the dissemination of legal research to legal and non-legal audiences
Apply advanced skills in identifying, using and appraising research material relevant to resolving contemporary refugee protection problems
Demonstrate advanced comprehension of international law relating to refugees and asylum seekers

title: REAL PROPERTY LAW
syllabus_overview: Real Property Law builds on and expands students' understanding of the concepts and principles of property law introduced in LAW5FPR. In this subject the focus is on property rights in relation to land. Topics include: the Torrens registration system and indefeasibility of title; the acquisition and disposition of property rights in land; leasehold estates; mortgages; easements; the resolution of conflicts between competing equitable interests in Torrens land; and the conveyancing process.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on the key legal doctrines that underpin contemporary Australian land law and the purposes and effects of such doctrines.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the concept of property rights in land as it operates in Australian law and effectively communicate this to specialist and non-specialist audiences
Exercise analytic skill and professional judgment in composing written legal opinions that represent an appropriate response to novel factual scenarios.
Evaluate claims made for competing property interests in land in a given fact situation, using appropriate legal doctrine and reasoning.
Comprehend and use the language of real property law to investigate and analyse complex problems regarding the possession and use of land.

title: STATUTORY INTERPRETATION
syllabus_overview: Statutory interpretation is the body of law governing the determination of the legal meaning and effect of legislation. This subject examines the law and practice of statutory interpretation systematically and in depth. The concepts, interpretative criteria, and techniques of the common law are examined, together with federal and state interpretation legislation. The law and practice is also examined through the lens of statutory interpretation literature. In addition to developing students' skills in interpreting legislation, the subject also develops related skills in legal research, in case analysis, in legal drafting, and in writing legal opinions and legal commentaries.
learning_outcomes: Be able to demonstrate knowledge of the law and practice of statutory interpretation that is informed by statutory interpretation theory
Be able to analyse and discuss the theoretical literature on statutory interpretation
Demonstrate detailed knowledge of statute law.
Be able to write a legal opinion on statutory interpretation in a form that approximates the standard expected of a newly-qualified lawyer.
Be able to interpret legislation in a fully-informed way.

title: SPORT AND THE LAW
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will be introduced to the increasing range of issues that sport managers need to deal with in the context of domestic and international law. After a generic introduction students will deal with sport specific applications of law in relation to contracts, ethics, sporting competitions, sport rights and also overview a number of specific institutions that deal with the upholding of the law in the context of sport.
learning_outcomes: To be able to apply principles of sports law to the facts of problems.
To be able to identify sports law issues in fact scenarios and to explain those issues.
To be able to design appropriate strategies to ensure sports people do not contravene sports law or incur liability.
To be able to analyse and critique, reflect upon and evaluate the effectiveness of various sports law regimes and regulatory practices

title: CRIMINAL PROFILING: MYTH OR REALITY?
syllabus_overview: This subject offers a critical introduction to the various techniques that are broadly referred to as criminal profiling. You will test the theoretical assumptions made by criminal profiling methodologies, particularly questioning whether it is possible to relate criminal actions to offender characteristics and predict criminal behaviour on this basis. The different methodologies that fit under the umbrella of criminal profiling are examined from an evidence-based perspective, with a view to assessing their respective validity and reliability.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to work collaboratively and communicate effectively to share and debate ideas
Understand the evidence to support or undermine the use of criminal profiling methodologies
Explain the various methodologies and processes involved in criminal profiling
Describe the theoretical assumptions of different criminal profiling methodologies

title: TAXATION LAW
syllabus_overview: Taxation is a factor in all commercial and everyday transactions. As such, lawyers are required to be aware of the taxation implications of the advice they provide to clients. As a true multidisciplinary subject, tax law interacts with every legal discipline. In this subject you will learn the fundamentals of Australian tax law including income, capital gains tax, deductions, residency and source, entities and anti-avoidance. The subject will also touch on the tax policy paradigms and philosophies that drive the enactment of tax legislation. The emphasis will be on the practical application of the tax law, allowing technical concepts to be more approachable, with a focus on teaching the skills necessary for practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced skills in identifying relevant Australian taxation legislation and common law, and potentials for their reform
Formulate appropriate business strategies to ensure compliance with the provisions of relevant Australian tax legislation
Develop expert knowledge of Australian taxation law principles and their relevance and application to fact situations

title: MEDIA AND CRIME
syllabus_overview: The media plays a fundamental role in shaping how society understands, and often fears, crime. In Media and Crime you will critically examine the complexities in how traditional and contemporary news and entertainment media reports on crime, harm and justice. In this subject, you will learn a diverse range of concepts related to media representation, including: news values and newsworthiness, performance crime, agenda setting, and the media’s role in shaping public perceptions and discourses about crime and justice. You will also learn about semiotics. The study of signs and symbols is a powerful tool used by the entertainment media to communicate complex ideas and narratives. Entertainment media, including films, TV shows, news broadcasts, and computer and console games often depict crime in ways that reflect and reinforce societal beliefs using semiotics. As consumers of media, it is important to develop critical media literacy skills so you can better analyse and question the messages you consume.
learning_outcomes: Apply criminological concepts to real-world media examples, contrasting media with evidence-based research about crime and justice.
Develop communication and collaboration skills while working in a team
Understand and analyse the processes through which crime news is constructed, disseminated, and consumed.
Analyse and deconstruct media representations of crime, using relevant criminological concepts.
Identify and examine various biases and stereotypes produced by dominant media representations of crime.

title: INTRODUCTION TO THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
syllabus_overview: This subject is a critical introduction to the Australian legal system that addresses the operation, aims, and institutions of criminal justice. It equips students with foundational knowledge of the operation of criminal justice and how the legal system addresses basic questions of criminological and sociological importance. The subject addresses the relationship between crime and law in Australia; the making of laws by the Parliament and Courts; venues and methods of legal adjudication and interpretation; and the complex interactions between actors that comprise the legal system, including lawyers, police, magistrates and the media. The sustainability of the legal system is evaluated in its historical, ethical, economic and social context.
learning_outcomes: Explain the roles and functions of Australian legal institutions and actors.
Demonstrate an awareness of the social and political context and impact of the Australian legal system.
Demonstrate an ability to work collaboratively and communicate effectively to share and debate ideas.
Describe the structure of the Australian legal system.
Understand the process by which law is created, interpreted, and applied.

title: CRIMINOLOGY SKILLS
syllabus_overview: Criminology Skills is designed to develop your academic skills that will be required to achieve success throughout the Criminology degree. Through a series of guided and supported seminars you will participate in applied learning activities to develop your research, academic writing, referencing, and presentation skills. In addition, through group based activities you will also begin to develop employability skills of problem solving, conflict resolution, teamwork, and time management. The subject is also designed for you to begin asking the right questions about crime, harm, and justice. The subject unpacks what crime is, when, where and how it occurs, who is implicated or involved, and why it is understood in particular ways. You will develop important skills in thinking about contemporary criminological debates through understanding varying perspectives surrounding key case studies discussed in lectures and seminars.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply time management and communication strategies to work effectively as a member of a team
Employ effective oral communication practices in informal and formal class contexts
Prepare written academic assessments to an appropriate standard
Develop academic and research skills for university study
Demonstrate an understanding of the purpose and structure of different writing genres, such as essays, reports and literature reviews

title: CRIMINAL LAW FOR CRIMINAL JUSTICE PROFESSIONALS
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed for criminology students to develop a critical understanding of the key aspects of contemporary criminal law. This includes the general structure of criminal offences, as well as some specific and selected offences, including homicide. The course also develops your understanding of criminal process and procedure through the lenses of key institutions such as the courts, police, and juries. Within this unit there is a focus on industry informed career development learning activities to support setting goals for personal and professional development.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the different institutions and actors within the criminal justice system and their interaction.
Analyse the basic structure of a criminal offence
Demonstrate basic skills in interpretation of statutory provisions and case law.
Develop career management strategies.
Evaluate problems within criminal law and criminal justice system.

title: JUSTICE AND COMMUNITY CASE MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: The practice of case management is a common approach used to respond to both offenders and victims in the criminal justice system, as well as people who are accessing services or support from Families and Community service providers. Globally, case management is used in relation to a broad range of people. For example, case managers may work specifically with youth at risk, sexual offenders, victims of family violence, people with addiction, homeless people, released prisoners etc. You will learn about the different risk-assessment, decision-making, referral tools that are used in case management and apply these tools to assessment tasks whilst being guided by the theory, principles, legislation and policies that are employed for case management in Victoria. Additionally, you will gain important skills in relation to communication, client assessment and the creation of case management plans in alignment with best practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the theories, principles and methods associated with case management
Communicate in a clear, accessible and non-judgemental manner when writing and speaking
Consolidate communication and collaboration skills by working as a team
Demonstrate an awareness and appreciation of the ethical dimensions of case management as a practice.
Understand and apply case management legislation, policy and practice, including the use of risk assessment and decision-making matrices.

title: CAN RIGHTS CHANGE OUR WORLD?
syllabus_overview: What happens when an injustice is caused by systemic factors or even by the state itself? Where can we turn when we have reached the limits of the law and rights frameworks in addressing injustice? This subject will invite you to think critically about “justice” and how it is (and should be) achieved. Through a range of case studies, we will consider how systemic injustice might arise and be addressed from the micro (e.g. an individual wrongful conviction, in the context of over-policing) to the meso (e.g. the failure of police to investigate a whole class of crimes) to the macro (e.g. the lack of legal recourse for the harms caused by climate change). The subject will consider the roles of rights, individual agents, legal institutions, media, popular culture, and broader public and policy responses in both contributing to and addressing systemic injustices. The subject will also look at the victim or community impact of these issues.
learning_outcomes: Analyse various methods for redressing systemic injustices, including their limitations, individually or collaboratively in a group setting
Identify a range of factors that may contribute to systemic injustices individually or collaboratively in a group setting
Demonstrate understanding of scholarly and general literature on systemic injustices, their causes and their redress

title: CRIME PREVENTION AND POLICY
syllabus_overview: It is argued that we live in a risk-based society where the focus on crime has moved from capture and punishment to management and prevention. Drawing on key theories from criminology, sociology, psychology, behavioural economics, and public health the individual, community, police, politicians, media, and policymakers’ roles in crime prevention will be explored and critiqued. Specifically, through innovative real-world practical applications of situational crime prevention, developmental crime prevention, individual crime prevention, community crime prevention, and economic disruption, the importance of implementing evidenced-based crime prevention policies will be understood. By reviewing the process of having to carefully design, plan, implement, and evaluate crime prevention strategies, the ethical considerations, and the practical challenges of needing to collaborate with partners from community and government to prevent crime are examined.
learning_outcomes: Understand and explain the role of the individual, community, police, politician, media, and policymakers in designing, implementing, and evaluating crime prevention strategies.
Reinforce collaborative skills by working as a team
Critically analyse evidence-based approaches to crime prevention and know how to use scientific methods to determine the efficacy of these strategies.
Design and analyse crime prevention strategies.
Demonstrate an understanding of the ethical considerations, principles and theories of the crime prevention strategies implemented by the criminal justice system.

title: INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC PSYCHOLOGY AND THE LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to a range of areas where psychological research has shaped criminal law and procedure, such as the rules relating to expert evidence in criminal trials, and how the psychological literature informs criminal justice responses to particular groups of people. This includes exploring factors that may contribute to miscarriages of justice, such as: the psychology of interrogations and false confessions; the psychological dimensions of juror decision-making; and what the psychological research on memory, perception and recall suggests for the limitations of eyewitness identification. The subject also critically examines the laws and procedures relevant to the criminal prosecution of people with mental illness and/or cognitive impairment, including fitness to stand trial and the defence of mental impairment. Drawing on a range of case studies, the subject examines how the criminal justice system has developed to take into account developments in our understanding of human behaviour.
learning_outcomes: Understand and critically analyse key concepts relating to forensic psychology and the law
Evaluate the impact of forensic psychology on criminal law and procedure
Demonstrate an ability to work collaboratively
Understand the policy environment in which psychology and the law interact

title: CRIMINOLOGY INTERNSHIP A
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to participate in a placement at an approved organisation such as a community clinic, court, a government department, or agency, or not for profit organisation, while concurrently undertaking academic study. Students may apply for placement opportunities organised by the Law School or apply on the basis of a self-organised placement. Self-organised placements must be approved by the Law School Placement Coordinator or delegate. In this unit there is a focus on practice skills and industry informed career development learning activities to support professional development in readiness for graduate positions.
learning_outcomes: Develop their knowledge of professional practice, through participation, observation, research, and reflection, on their practical experience.
Develop a reflective approach to learning.
Demonstrate critical thinking in relation to the professional and ethical work practices.
Develop their communication skills in a professional work environment.

title: FAMILY VIOLENCE: POLICY AND PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: Family violence can affect anyone. It is non-discriminatory in that perpetrators and victims of family violence can be found in all social groups and across all stages of the life-course. In developing an understanding of what family violence is, and the types of violence that are recognised as family violence, prominent theoretical explanations will be used to critically examine the role that culture, politics, media, gender, and power play in how society constructs family violence. Specifically, you will study child abuse, intimate partner abuse, and elder abuse. In doing so, the myths and stereotypes reinforcing cultural and societal norms that perpetuate the problem of family violence will be scrutinised, and the role of primary prevention and crisis intervention strategies will be explored. You will also critically examine responses to victims and perpetrators of family violence, including behavioural change programs.
learning_outcomes: Develop appropriate evidence informed responses to educate against family violence myths and stereotypes.
Demonstrate awareness and appreciation of the ethical and moral dilemmas practitioners are faced with working in the family violence sector.
Communicate in a clear, accessible and non-judgemental manner when writing and speaking.
Apply theory, legislation, policy, practice, and evaluation methods to explain best practice responses to family violence.

title: RETHINKING JUSTICE IN A DIGITAL AGE
syllabus_overview: We are living in a digital age, and with new technologies comes new ways of thinking about crime, harm and justice. This subject examines how digital technologies, platforms and spaces intersect with justice and are reshaping how justice itself can occur. The subject provides a theoretical basis for thinking about digital society and justice, as well as key topics including: online vigilantism, image-based sexual abuse, privacy and surveillance, doxxing, and digital activism.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret central concepts in digital criminology
Critically reflect on the impact of digital technologies on both crime and justice.
Work collaboratively in a team to develop innovative responses to digital harms
Interrogate and understand the nature of and societal responses to digital harm and crime.

title: CORONIAL LAW AND FORENSICS
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the theories, practices and procedures of coronial law and forensic medicine in Australia. It will investigate the distinctive roles played by the coroner, forensic pathologist, police officer and medical practitioner during the death investigation process. It will also analyse how coronial institutions can be reformed to produce optimal outcomes for families and the wider society. Students may explore topics such as death prevention and coronial law reform, coronial architecture and mortuary spaces, forensic imaging technologies and artificial intelligence, organ and tissue donation processes, and coronial inquests on deaths in custody.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate legal and policy problems using appropriate doctrine in coronial law, forensic medicine and/or academic scholarship
Consolidate collaborative working skills through group-based tasks
Critically analyse historical, social, ethical, religious and cultural implications of coronial law and forensic medicine
Identify, use and appraise research material relevant to the operation and reform of coronial law and forensic medicine

title: CRIMINAL PROFILING
syllabus_overview: This subject offers a critical examination of the various techniques that are broadly known as criminal profiling. We explore the theoretical foundations of criminal profiling and the fundamental questions of whether we can relate criminal actions to offender characteristics and predict criminal behaviour on this basis. The different methodologies involved in criminal profiling are also examined from an evidence-based perspective, with a view to assessing their respective validity and reliability.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate the evidence available to support or limit the application of criminal profiling in a range of contexts
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the various methodologies and processes involved in criminal profiling
Demonstrate an ability to undertake academic research relevant to the area of criminal profiling

title: CYBERCRIME
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the world of cybercrime. Cybercrimes and digital harms are behaviours that in some way involve computers and information and communications technology, whether as the target, tool or medium of harmful behaviour. You will study a variety of cybercrime and digital harm, from among the following: cyberstalking and harassment, technology-facilitated sexual violence, cybercrimes against children, hacking for profit, cyber extortion, online fraud, "hacktivism", online hate crime, cyberwarfare and cyberterrorism, and the dark web. You will look at the nature and contexts of cybercrime and digital harm, its causes and effects, and how it can be prevented and responded to. You will also examine the social and legal policy issues and current debates about law reform in the rapidly evolving arena of cybercrime and digital harm.
learning_outcomes: Develop written and verbal communication skills to summarise and present course materials
Conduct research and evaluate sources concerning cybercrime and digital harm
Demonstrate effective analytical skills relevant to cybercrime and digital harm
Evaluate key concepts, theories, and case studies in the field of cybercrime and digital criminology

title: HUMAN EXPLOITATION
syllabus_overview: Using an interdisciplinary approach, this subject explores the concept of human exploitation in contemporary criminal justice and criminology. It conceptualises different forms of human exploitation, such as modern-day slavery, human trafficking, forced labour, debt bondage, child exploitation, organ harvesting and other practices similar to slavery (servitude, serfdom and servile marriage), and explores the criminalisation of human exploitation and effective ways of combating those practices. The (global) extent of the problem and the major pull and push factors that render people vulnerable to human exploitation are critically examined, as is the place of victims as bearers of rights with their own agency.
learning_outcomes: Analyse responses to human exploitation and evaluate their effectiveness and areas of potential reform
Demonstrate an understanding of the nature of human exploitation offences
Identify and use credible sources to support arguments about issues of relevance to human exploitation

title: CRIMINAL LAW, ETHICS AND ACCOUNTABILITY
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject is the culmination of your learning in the criminology degree. By expanding and extending skills and knowledge acquired throughout the degree, you will deepen your understanding of criminal law and accountability through a focus on ethics and ethical dilemmas. In the first part of the subject, you will study questions of ethics and accountability as they pertain to criminal law and criminology. In the second part, you will bring your acquired knowledge to bear through an independent research project. After completing this subject, you will be able to critically discuss ethics in the context of criminal law, and have demonstrated independence, critical reflection and a deepened understanding of a relevant topic through your project.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an independent argument that builds on research into a problem of ethics and accountability
Show appropriate cultural and ethical awareness in identifying and discussing ethical issues in criminal justice
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of accountability mechanisms and their limitations
Critically reflect on the relation between ethics and accountability

title: INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL JUSTICE
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the conceptualisation of some of the most heinous atrocities such as genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression as international crimes. You will examine the fundamental features of this form of criminality and how it differs in profound respects from domestic crime. You will consider the role of situational factors, propaganda, and personal agency in the commission of mass atrocity and evaluate the international criminal trial as a retributive response.
learning_outcomes: Consolidate collaborative working skills through group-based tasks
Undertake independent research on topics of relevance to international criminal justice
Critically analyse and evaluate responses of the international criminal justice system to mass atrocity
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the development of and contemporary issues in international criminal law and justice
Demonstrate a capacity to explain the nature of fundamental international crimes.

title: INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL CRIME
syllabus_overview: This subject offers critical perspectives on international financial crime. We will explore the nature and complexity of international financial crime in its various forms, including insider trading and market manipulation, money laundering, terrorist financing, investment fraud and insolvent trading. Specific emphasis will be placed on the legal, policy and regulatory challenges posed by international financial crime and as well as strategies to combat this form of criminality.'
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to work with a systematic body of knowledge in the field of international financial crime
Demonstrate an ability to think critically and creatively about issues relevant to international financial crime
Demonstrate an ability to undertake academic research relevant to the discipline
Apply critical understanding of the professional, social, economic, cultural and ethical dimensions of the discipline
Consolidate collaborative working skills through group-based tasks

title: CRIMINOLOGY INTERNSHIP
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to participate in a placement at an approved organisation such as corrections, court, a government department, or agency, or not for profit organisation, while concurrently undertaking academic study. Students may apply for placement opportunities organised by the Law School or apply on the basis of a self-organised placement. Self-organised placements must be approved by the Law School Placement Coordinator or delegate. In this unit there is a focus on practice skills and industry informed career development learning activities to support professional development in readiness for graduate positions.
learning_outcomes: Develop their communication skills in a professional work environment.
Develop a reflective approach to learning.
Develop their knowledge of professional practice, through participation, observation, research, and reflection, on their practical experience.
Demonstrate critical thinking in relation to the professional and ethical practice.

title: YOUTH JUSTICE
syllabus_overview: This subject identifies and critically examines issues relating to youth offending via an examination of laws, policies and programs shaping this area of practice. The subject explores the historic, ethical and theoretical underpinning of youth justice in Australia. Local and international human rights instruments will also be considered. Explanations of youth offending and the importance of early intervention will be explored, as will the link between child protection, youth justice and the adult criminal justice system. Notions of competence, criminal responsibility and maturity are identified as central considerations in the youth justice system. Risk factors and prevention strategies for child exploitation are examined. Finally, the importance of diversionary practices and the use of alternative forms of justice when responding to young offenders will be explored.
learning_outcomes: Explain and critique case-based and statutory principles relating to youth justice
Demonstrate knowledge of and ability to evaluate key concepts of youth justice
Demonstrate an understanding of the key policy issues arising in the management of young people coming into contact with the criminal justice system
Communicate effectively using the principles of plain legal English

title: SCREENING CRIME AND JUSTICE
syllabus_overview: Images of crime arrest us. Whether at the movies or on screens at home, and whether fictionalised or documentary, crime on the screens entice us. This subject takes seriously screens as a cultural artefact of law and crime and examines the relationship between law, crime and screens through a combination of cinema screenings and face-to-face seminars, guided by readings accessed online. By exploring questions of representation and medium through topics such as consuming foreign crime, the CSI-effect, safe crime series, screens in trials, genocide films, technology facilitated sexual violence, and documentaries, you will develop sophisticated analytical skills necessary to critically assess the role and use of screens in relation to law and crime.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical understanding of criminological theories with regards to tv-shows, film and documentaries
Show profound understand of the role of screens in crime and justice
Critically assess how crime and justice are represented on the screen
Evaluate research and arguments about crime and justice on the screen

title: FOUNDATIONS OF LANGUAGE
syllabus_overview: Language makes us who we are: it is shared by all humans, but each of us is also defined by our own unique use of language. This subject will equip students with concepts, methods, and theories to study language, and give them the foundations they need for lifelong learning about this essential human attribute. We will examine how language is defined, the basic structures and diverse forms of language, language and the brain, how and why languages vary and change, how languages are acquired and learned, and how languages convey social and cultural meaning. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Describe linguistic behaviour in a variety of interactional contexts.
Analyse linguistic resources to find information about a language.
Synthesise linguistic observations in an appropriate academic style.
Identify important linguistic features in everyday language use.

title: IMAGINING LANGUAGE
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to the essential building blocks of language: the sounds and sound systems (phonetics and phonology), how words and sentences are structured (morphology and syntax) and how we understand meaning (semantics). Employing the analytical tools of linguistics, you will begin applying them to the development of a new language of their own imagining. The inspiration will come from a range of human languages, including major world languages, minoritized and endangered languages, and constructed languages.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic structural features of language Phonetics (sounds), Phonology (sound systems), Morphology (meaningful elements), Syntax (the arrangement of meaningful elements), Semantics (meaning and context)
Compare the structural features of a range of spoken and signed human languages
Create your own linguistic variety, employing your knowledge of the structural features of language
Analyse these structural features of language in real world linguistic data using linguistic techniques

title: LANGUAGE, SOCIETY AND CULTURE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will reflect on how society and culture shapes language use and communication between individuals and between groups. Drawing on a range of ideas from the fields of intercultural communication, sociolinguistics and linguistic anthropology, students develop tools, knowledge and awareness to assist them in understanding and positively engaging with the linguistic and cultural diversity around them.
learning_outcomes: Research and examine an intercultural or sociolinguistic issue in depth and present your findings in writing
Demonstrate an understanding of a range of ideas related to language, society and culture presented within the subject
Apply tools and concepts from intercultural communication, sociolinguistics and linguistic anthropology to novel situations
Critically reflect on your own and others’ societies cultures and how they influence interactions

title: MAKING MEANING
syllabus_overview: Language serves as a system for encoding the full spectrum of human thought and experience. While a perfect one-to-one mapping between concepts and words is infeasible, every language finds its own way of grouping and distinguishing meanings, often shaped by the communicative, cultural, and cognitive needs of its users. This subject examines how meaning is structured and conveyed in language, covering both semantics (the study of meaning in words, sentences, and texts) and pragmatics (the study of meaning shaped by context and interaction). It also considers the relationship between meaning and cognition, the role of culture in interpreting meaning, and how meaning changes over time.
learning_outcomes: Develop an ability to present and analyse data in written form and increased sophistication in articulating and defending linguistic analyses
Appropriately employ a range of tools for the analysis of meaning
Collect and present natural linguistic data and use the tools learned in this subject to analyse and explain that data

title: CHILD LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the features of child language and how children acquire language. From before birth, to infancy, early schooling years and beyond, this subject examines the development of language and also the cognitive processes behind language acquisition. This subject includes the study of children who learn more than one language, and children with both typical and atypical language development. This subject is a useful introduction to the topic for anyone who has children in their lives and/or is planning to work with children.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role of social context in language acquisition processes
Describe key stages of linguistic development
Analyse linguistic productions from a range of children in relation to developmental stages
Support observations of child language with different theories and models of language acquisition

title: THE SOUNDS OF THE WORLD'S LANGUAGES
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on Phonetics, the study of the link between language and the physical world. In it, you will learn how humans use their bodies to create linguistic signals, how to measure those signals as they travel through the world, and how those signals are interpreted by receivers to convey linguistic and social information. You will learn to use specialized linguistic tools and software to accurately transcribe and analyse spoken language. Finally, you will apply what you’ve learned to real language data to create an original research report.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the relationship between phonetic and social factors.
Analyse the patterns of sounds within and across spoken languages using specialized linguistic software and methodologies.
Use the International Phonetic Alphabet to transcribe and produce the sounds of the world’s spoken languages.
Describe the phonetic processes involved in producing, transmitting, and perceiving language.

title: SYNTACTIC DIVERSITY IN A CONNECTED WORLD
syllabus_overview: The world is home to over 7,000 languages. These languages have a wide range of ways that users create grammatical structures. In this subject you will learn to analyse the syntactic patterns found in human languages. Alongside this, you will learn about the diversity of the world’s languages, and the challenges facing the sustainability of our existing linguistic diversity.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the structure of unfamiliar languages and identify elements and their functions in language
Identify and describe in writing the diversity of languages from different families
Apply the terminology of morphology and syntax in the analysis of data

title: LANGUAGE IN ABORIGINAL AUSTRALIA
syllabus_overview: Language is crucial to Indigenous people right across Australia. This subject will explore the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, and the profound changes that have shaped them since colonization, providing students with insights into the history and future of Indigenous languages in Australia. It will benefit everyone who wants a better understanding of Australian society today, and will be particularly useful for anyone who will engage with Indigenous people in professional settings.
learning_outcomes: Apply and extend ideas presented in the subject in an original piece of writing and research, demonstrating an understanding of connection between postcolonialism/postcolonial studies, linguistics and Aboriginalities.
Critically engage with the use of contemporary revival language present in a diverse set of artefacts and uses and meanings of new varieties, Kriols and Aboriginal Englishes.
Demonstrate understanding of different perspectives on Aboriginal languages, including Aboriginal perspectives, in both discussion and writing

title: INTRODUCTION TO BUSINESS AND COMPANY LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the core principles of contract law, consumer protection and the law of negligence, and examines business structures including the law relating to the incorporation of companies. This subject also introduces students to ethical standards that apply to business activities, such as contractual relationships and special legal protections against unethical business practices, and examines the practical operation of the law in the business environment. This subject adopts a skills-based learning approach through teaching the basic techniques of problem solving and promoting an understanding of the dynamic nature of the law in business and corporations. These skills prepare students for more advanced law subjects as well as their professional careers.
learning_outcomes: Explain the key features of the Australian legal system and their relevance to business and company law
Apply principles of contract law, consumer protection, and negligence to basic commercial scenarios
Analyse ethical frameworks of the laws relating to data protection and privacy regulation in corporate contexts
Evaluate common law and statutory principles and apply them to business and company legal problem-solving scenarios

title: LANGUAGE AND GENDER
syllabus_overview: Language and gender examines the many ways in which language both produces and reflects cultural understandings of gender, sex, and sexuality. In this subject, you will be introduced to different theoretical and methodological approaches of linguistics regarding gender, applying and critiquing these in context. The subject includes an examination of the relationship between language and sexualities. The focus is on both gendered language use and language about gender and sexualities. While the majority of existing literature focusses on English and countries such as the US and UK, we explore the application of current ideas beyond these societies, incorporating an intersectional perspective. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the relationship between culture and language for our understanding of gender, sex and sexuality
Identify the ways in which gender is constructed and performed through language
Critically reflect on personal experience of language and gender

title: LAW AND (DIS)ORDER
syllabus_overview: This is a level one subject, which examines law and legal issues as sites of contest where conflicting interests, understandings and agendas come into play. The insights and methods of the social sciences are used to explore law's interconnection with cultural, economic and political contexts as well as its role in constituting social relations within and across communities. Attention is focused upon three key overarching areas: law, legal consciousness and social order; crime, criminalisation and justice; and global experiences of 'the rule of law.' Included within each of these is consideration of key concepts and contemporary issues of local and global significance. This subject considers how citizens, states and the law advance and sometimes impede cross cultural understanding, equality and human rights.
learning_outcomes: Communicate about law and justice issues in a manner that is clear and concise and reflects an interdisciplinary perspective.
Demonstrate an understanding of the complex relationship that exists between law, social and legal change, and political, economic and cultural contexts.
Identify ways in which the law reflects and constitutes varying forms of social relations.
Critically reflect upon key issues and debates relating to law and justice.
Demonstrate an awareness of the ethical and cultural considerations related to law and justice issues.

title: FROM PRISONS TO DETENTION CENTRES
syllabus_overview: Where did the modern prison and detention centre come from? In this subject you will explore how present day imprisonment practices are part of a long tradition that includes workhouses, asylums, missions and reserves, juvenile reformatories and internment camps. We investigate how, in varying domestic and international contexts, imprisonment and other forms of confinement have been justified and used as a response to social problems and political conflicts. We reflect upon the implications of this for the individuals and communities most affected, and how prisons and detention centres shape society more broadly. The relationship between borders, colonisation and imprisonment is also considered, raising questions about power, human rights and the role of states in a globalised world. This is a level 1 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Communicate in a clear, coherent and knowledgeable manner about contemporary forms and practices of imprisonment and detention in Australia and selected countries.
Critically assess different forms of imprisonment in the past and present taking into account their distinctive development, functions and impacts.
Recognise and appreciate the ethical issues that arise in relation to detention, imprisonment and other forms of confinement.
Critically analyse the nature and role of representations in creating understandings about different forms of confinement and the people and problems associated with them.

title: UNDERSTANDING CRIME
syllabus_overview: This is a level one subject, which explores how different understandings of crime have emerged as a response to changing social, political and economic contexts. It explores the usefulness of understandings developed since the eighteenth century to date, for explaining and responding to different types of crime today. The nature and impact of key criminological approaches ranging from classicism and positivism through to current day critical perspectives will be illustrated and analysed through consideration of contemporary case studies. The way in which criminological theories inform practical responses to crime within and beyond the criminal justice system will also be highlighted. In this subject we also consider social inequalities, intersectionality and how theory can help us understand these in the context of criminal justice system.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the relationship between criminological theory and practical responses to crime within and beyond the criminal justice system.
Critically engage with key theoretical ideas and ideological concepts about crime and criminal justice system.
Demonstrate applicability of the criminological approaches in explaining crime and criminality.
Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamental differences between different criminological approaches by being able to clearly distinguish between them.
Present your understanding of criminological perspectives on crime and criminality in a concise, relevant, and well-informed manner.

title: DRUGS, GOVERNANCE AND MODERN SOCIETY
syllabus_overview: In this online subject, students will acquire an understanding of the complexities surrounding drugs and drug use in contemporary Australia. The subject addresses: the classification and effects of licit and illicit substances; the development and nature of contemporary drug distribution networks; major approaches to regulating drugs and drug use; and the key debates and challenges involved in formulating policy and practice in this area. Specific topics we will explore include: alcohol and other drug consumption patterns among young people; pill testing debates; the rise of online illicit drug markets; drug court models; drug education in schools; decriminalization and legalization efforts; ongoing tensions and debates on how to regulate vaping and similar practices; performance and image-enhancing drugs, and contemporary debates around harm reduction strategies (e.g. medically supervised injecting facilities). No pre-existing knowledge is required, but students will be urged to examine any prior assumptions or moral judgements they hold about the 'right' way to approach the 'drug problem'. A key theme in this subject is exploring how the framing of such problems - through various social, political, cultural, and economic lenses - shapes how we then respond to them, and that even well-intentioned policies can have unintended adverse outcomes. Please note this Term 6 subject - commencing in early November and concluding in mid-December - is entirely asynchronous (meaning no live lectures or tutorials).
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the social, political, economic and ethical challenges involved in formulating effective approaches to drugs and drug use.
Identify and assess key approaches to the regulation of drugs and drug use.
Distinguish between different drugs according to their composition and effects, and consider the socio-political factors that shape their legal classifications
Recognise and communicate how social, economic and political factors have shaped drug distribution practices, locally and globally.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an overview of the legal and regulatory frameworks to protect and manage the Australian environment at the federal, state and local level. It introduces students to the scope and sources of Australian environmental law, the regulatory tools utilised and overarching environmental law principles. The environmental management and regulatory challenges in relation to waste and pollution management, biodiversity protection and climate change and energy are examined. Environmental planning, impact assessment and development approval, dispute resolution, enforcement and compliance are considered through readings, asynchronous activities and synchronous seminars.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to read and engage with legal materials and to produce legal writing with appropriate referencing, vocabulary and structure
