Critically evaluate the adequacy of legal and policy frameworks to address key environmental challenges facing Australia

Demonstrate skill in identifying legal issues and applying relevant Federal, state and local government planning, management and/or environmental assessment rules to problem situations involving the environment
Understand the scope, structure, regulatory tools and basic principles of Australian environmental law
Ability to research, analyse, discuss and evaluate specific areas of Australian environmental law
Consolidate collaborative working skills through group-based tasks

title: LAW, JUSTICE AND POWER
syllabus_overview: Law, Justice and Power is the core subject for second year students undertaking a major in Crime, Justice and Legal Studies. This subject investigates how power works and the ways justice is experienced within and beyond the law. While you will be provided with a general understanding of a range of legal institutions and processes, you will also consider the limitations and possibilities of law as a practice. Case studies include trials and court buildings, restorative justice, sexual offence law, therapeutic jurisprudence, kaleidoscopic jurisprudence, riots, human rights and royal commissions. You are invited to explore how law, as a range of social, political and cultural systems, exercises and regulates power while it administers and inhibits justice. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling.
learning_outcomes: Facilitate and participate in group discussions of the principles, processes, values and functions of Australian criminal justice system, and organisations in an international context.

Assess knowledge and practices relevant to law, justice and power in light of ethical and cultural considerations. From a critical and interdisciplinary perspective, discuss the centrality and complexity of power and the elusiveness of justice.
Discuss concepts and perspectives relevant to law, justice and power and the principles, processes, values and functions of the Australian legal system.
Identify and write about current trends, issues and debates relevant to the gap between the theory and practice of law, as well as problems in knowledge or practices relevant.

title: POLICE, SOCIETY AND DEMOCRACY
syllabus_overview: This subject discusses the history, institutional configuration, role and performance of police in Australia's democratic political context, and offers points of comparisons to other countries (democratic or else) around the world. To these ends, we explore a variety of questions concerning the police and its role in our criminal justice system; the relevance of policing for a democratic society; police culture; the links between police and community; contemporary challenges of policing (including transnational policing),among other relevant aspects of police and policing. After completing this course, students should be able to understand fundamental facts about police and policing, and critically evaluate the police's role in Australia and beyond. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Critique police reform efforts in Victoria, Australia and internationally
Develop familiarity with the key theoretical underpinnings of police and policing, plus a survey of the current institutional framework in Victoria
Understand and analyse the importance of police culture in police-society relations
Discuss the contemporary challenges of policing in Australia and beyond
Demonstrate knowledge of the history of the police, with an emphasis on Victoria and other law enforcement agencies in Australia

title: SENTENCING, IMPRISONMENT AND SOCIAL INEQUALITY
syllabus_overview: This subject explores the processes, practices and complexities involved in sentencing and imprisoning people in contemporary Australia and how these reflect and reproduce forms of social inequality. The aims of sentencing, the technical processes involved, and public perceptions of them are considered and assessed, as well as technological innovations and human experiences in the courtroom. Varying types of sanctions are examined with particular attention paid to current issues in imprisonment, including high rates of remand, prison architecture, and private interests in prison operations and expansion. The subject places Australian penal cultures in international context, and assesses the extent to which imprisonment can reduce cycles of crime and social disadvantage, and enhance community safety. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling.This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Identify key aims and processes involved in sentencing in contemporary Australia.
Communicate in a clear, well informed and critically engaged manner about sentencing, imprisonment and social inequality.
Assess the impact of legal, social, economic and political factors upon sentencing and imprisonment.
Assess the extent to which imprisonment and community supervision achieve sentencing aims, reduce crime and enhance community safety.

title: VICTIMOLOGY: VICTIMS, JUSTICE AND THE LAW
syllabus_overview: Students will analyse the concept of 'victim' within domestic and international contexts, utilising practical and theoretical understandings of victimisation. Four key variables (gender, age, race and class) are investigated to expand student understandings of who and what constitutes an "ideal victim" within the media and the courtroom. The subject also examines the impact of victim's rights discourses in shaping traditional and alternative responses to crime and punishment. The concept of 'victim' will be further explored to consider the ways in which some groups might be victimised by the law, including Indigenous Australians, injured workers, and asylum seekers. Students will also deconstruct the concept of 'victimhood' and determine the extent to which it is useful in legal and social settings. This is a level 2 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Identify and examine key trends and issues in victimology.
Identify and explain the key elements of different theoretical approaches within victimology
Synthesise interdisciplinary theories and methods to critically analyse patterns of victimisation and institutional responses in contemporary society.

title: FROM VIOLENCE TO SOCIAL JUSTICE
syllabus_overview: This subject examines competing accounts of violence in the academic research, media, and everyday conversation, and how these impact on personal safety and social justice. It explores why media focuses on extreme cases of violence, and how this produces social panics around some problems while concealing other more serious issues. It shows how patterns of social media and everyday talk about violence cause people to worry about specific risks to their safety and not others, and why anxieties about violence often lead to demands for certain kinds of law enforcement or attempts to weaken human rights. The subject explores how accounts of violence in everyday life are based on underlying theories about people and society, revealing unrecognised assumptions that shape how we understand the world. It covers a range of themes including violence against children, sexual and intimate violence, masculinities and violence, police and violence, state violence, wars and genocide, and broad issues of social inequality and structural violence. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Apply theories to contemporary social problems.
Formal presentation of academic analysis.
Demonstrate knowledge of key theories and findings in the field of violence studies

title: LAW, RIGHTS AND SOCIAL JUSTICE
syllabus_overview: This subject considers various approaches to understanding the relationship between law, rights, and social justice. It focuses on how domestic and international laws can promote, hinder, or violate rights and asks critical questions about the nature and source of those rights. The subject begins by examining the philosophy and practice of rights, including within domestic and international law, and then considers the relationship between rights and various social justice issues. These include Indigenous self-determination; women's political movements; ableism; children's rights; discrimination against LGBTIQ people; poverty and homelessness; asylum seeking; counter-terrorism and torture; armed conflict, genocide and transitional justice; and environmental and animal justice. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Write about the role of law in protecting human rights and preventing future human rights abuses, as well as the efficacy of law as a defender of human rights
Write coherently on the gap between law in theory versus law in practice in relation to human rights and social justice, reflecting on both ideals and ideology

Critically reflect on the definition, efficacy and scope of human rights law and practice, including discussing the concept of human rights, reflecting on the problems of both "conflicting rights" and human rights as "ideology", and using complex theories on rights from the literature
Locate relevant Internet material on human rights and social justice matters, summarise this material and then identify problems and/or issues raised
Illustrate an understanding of domestic and international human rights law and how they relate to each other
Apply complex theories to examine "case studies", demonstrating an understanding of the problem of universalism, cultural relativism and human rights

title: CRIME AND SOCIO-LEGAL RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: Designed for third-year students, this subject introduces the essential principles and practical tools used to design and conduct research in Criminology and Socio-Legal Studies. You will explore what makes research in these fields unique; how it blends legal theory, social context, and real-world impact. Through hands-on learning, you will gain the skills to craft compelling research proposals, build insightful literature reviews, and critically evaluate academic work. You will also learn how to develop your own original argument and choose the most effective research methods to support it, whether qualitative (like interviews and case studies) or quantitative (like surveys and statistical analysis) or mixed-method (like surveys and focus groups). This subject is well suited for students who want to deepen their understanding of justice systems and prepare for advanced study, policy work, or careers in law, criminology, or social research. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with recommended attendance.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically evaluate distinctive features of socio-legal and criminological research
Demonstrate an understanding of different research methods, assess their relative merit when planning and conducting research
Develop and contexualise a basic research proposal by formulating an original research question, define a research topic, and identify basic literature
Critique sophisticated scholarly work to contexualise your research proposal
Apply autonomy and judgement recognising and assessing ethical issues associated with conducting research

title: FOUNDATIONS OF COMPANY AND COMMERCIAL LAW
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore some of the core principles of contract law, corporations law and the law of negligence. You will discuss various business structures including the law relating to the incorporation of companies and a strong emphasis will be placed on important company law topics such as directors' duties, member rights and remedies, financing of companies and company insolvency. You will examine the purposes of these legal frameworks and analyse the practical operation of these legal principles in the business environment. This subject adopts a skills-based learning approach through teaching the basic techniques of problem-solving and promoting an understanding of the dynamic nature of the law in business and corporations. This is a core subject accredited by CA/CPA.
learning_outcomes: Identify legal principles, including case law and statute, relevant to company law and commercial law, applying them appropriately to problem-solving scenarios.

Identify the key purposes and principles of contract law, the law of negligence and corporations law, including the legal status of corporations, and explain how these purposes and principles apply to commercial transactions.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the key features of the Australian legal system.
Critically analyse the ethical frameworks for the laws relating to data protection and privacy regulation in business and corporations.

title: INTRODUCTION TO COMMERCIAL LAW
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to give you an understanding of the core areas of commercial law and how they relate to each other. You will examine the core principles of contract law, commercial sale of goods and services, corporations law and the law of negligence. It is suitable for those of you who want an overview of commercial law as well as if you want to bring yourself up to date with recent developments in this field. This subject provides you with practical experience in applying commercial law to solve contemporary commercial issues. This skill-based learning approach helps you to demonstrate your ability to apply commercial law concepts and legal advice to authentic legal problem scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Identify and demonstrate detailed knowledge and understanding of the theoretical principles and law relating to contract law, the law of negligence, consumer protection and introductory company law and explain how these principles apply to commercial transactions.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the Australian legal system and principles relevant to commercial law.
Analyse cases and interpret statutory provisions relevant to company and commercial law and apply them appropriately to resolve real-world commercial scenarios.

title: MANAGING RISK AND LAW IN SPORT
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the identification and mitigation of corporate risk, the legal rights of sport stakeholders, and threats to sport integrity. Specific topics include regulation of sport, doping, match-fixing, corruption, conflicts of interest, athlete misbehaviour, athlete selection, defamation, discrimination and human rights (including freedom of speech and freedom religion), occupational health and safety (including player welfare and safety), member protection, intellectual property and ambush marketing, domestic tribunals and natural justice, negligence, and restraint of trade.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the role of the law in maintaining the integrity of sport
Identify legal rights of sport stakeholders
Analyse risks and design effective mitigation strategies in sport management

title: ACADEMIC WRITING
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the purposes and conventions of academic essay writing. Students develop transferrable skills in academic research, essay planning and forming a coherent argument, and processes of writing including editing and proofreading. Assessments are nested, and students are supported with feedback at each step of the essay process
learning_outcomes: Recognise and apply essay-writing practices including drafting, editing and proofreading
Identify and apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Demonstrate principles of academic integrity in relation to the attribution of work
Assess research materials to support an academic position
Analyse an essay question and develop an academic argument

title: ACADEMIC CULTURE
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to academic culture and different forms of academic communication. Students examine the conventions of academic culture and identify strategies to support learning success. They compare the purposes of different genres of academic communication in the context of discipline differences and are introduced to the concept of academic integrity. Students develop transferable skills in time-management, note-taking, academic writing, critical reading, case study analysis and online learning. Assessments are low stakes and include text summary and written comprehension as well as text analysis.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and apply the specific characteristics of academic communication and culture
Compare different academic genres and styles and identify their requirements required for specific purposes
Identify principles of academic integrity and relate them to the attribution of work
Identify and apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment

title: BIG ISSUES: POLICY AND SOCIAL CHANGE
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the critical criminological and socio-legal concepts and challenges shaping public policy today . In particular, it asks you to consider how criminology and socio-legal research informs better government policy. You will examine various case studies throughout the semester concerning crime, health, welfare, sexuality, and migration to understand how law and policy making processes frame and respond to emerging social problems. Investigating tensions between policy aims and their political, legal and social effects, you will learn how to critically analyse public policy. Applying skills and knowledge developed within the subject and throughout your undergraduate degree you will have the opportunity to formulate a strong, evidence-based, ethically and culturally aware policy proposal concerning a critical issue of your choosing. By the end of the semester, you will have a critical appreciation of the contextual dynamics and outcomes of law and policy, and have acquired methodological proficiency in policy analysis and creation. This is a level 3 subject. It is the capstone for the CJLS major. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate contemporary criminological research, focusing on its social and political relevance, methodological and ethical quality, theoretical grounding, and practical implications.
Work effectively with a group as a group member and/or a group leader to deliver a critique of policy development and delivery.
Produce an original, well researched and theorised response to a problem concerning public policy. Recognise the benefit of lifelong learning to the production and delivery of policy.
Critically analyse existing policies and propose evidence-based recommendations based on an evaluation of criminological research.
Demonstrate the capacity to synthesise diverse sources of information, form coherent arguments, conduct independent research and summarise research and arguments about relevant policy areas.

title: ACADEMIC PRESENTATIONS
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the purposes and conventions of public speaking and presentations in a university context. Students examine the unique characteristics of public speaking, and develop skills in academic research, drafting and rehearsing a script, as well as creating digital presentations. Assessments are nested, and students are supported with feedback at each step of the presentation journey.
learning_outcomes: Deliver a presentation for academic purposes using selected technology
Analyse all factors of an academic presentation and compose a well-developed argument
Demonstrate principles of academic integrity in relation to the attribution of work
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Assess research materials to support an academic position

title: THINKING MATHEMATICALLY
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to a spectrum of mathematical thinking and mathematics skills required for future learning in general university programs. Students will develop conceptual knowledge and procedural skills in a range of topics including arithmetical rules and operations, percentages and decimals, rates and ratios and measurement and data. Students will be enabled to solve a variety of mathematical problems using appropriate strategies, methods and techniques and to apply mathematical concepts and knowledge to different real-world situations. Assessments tasks are based on cumulative development of skills and include online quizzes and two project tasks.
learning_outcomes: Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Apply appropriate methods to solve mathematical problems
Formulate problems from everyday and scientific contexts into mathematical concepts
Articulate foundational operations and notation in mathematics, including whole numbers, fractions, percentages, decimals and ratios
Explain mathematical solutions for different audiences and purposes

title: FOUNDATION ALGEBRA
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to algebra within mathematical reasoning. Students use algebraic concepts and knowledge to solve a variety of everyday and scientific problems and make mathematical inferences. Students develop transferrable skills in mathematical problem-solving, data collection and interpretation, mathematical representation and translation. Assessments include data collection and report writing, and are designed to support future learning in general university programs.
learning_outcomes: Explain mathematical solutions for different audiences and purposes
Articulate algebraic operations and notation in mathematics
Apply algebraic methods including substitution and simplification to solve mathematical problems
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Formulate problems from everyday and scientific contexts into mathematical concepts

title: FOUNDATION STATISTICS
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to statistical reasoning and skills. Students use statistical concepts and knowledge to solve a variety of everyday and scientific problems, make statistical inferences, and identify errors in statistical thinking and representation. Students develop transferrable skills in mathematical problem-solving, data collection and interpretation, mathematical representation and translation. Assessments include data collection and reporting, and are designed to support future learning in general university programs.
learning_outcomes: Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Formulate problems from everyday and scientific contexts into mathematical concepts
Explain statistical solutions in different formats, including through graphs, for different audiences and purposes
Articulate foundational concepts and operations in statistics
Apply basic data collection and statistical analysis to solve statistical problems

title: THINKING CRITICALLY
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to critical thinking as concept and as practice. Students are encouraged to engage with differing viewpoints, question received knowledge and to recognise the difference between lower- and higher-order thinking. Opportunities are provided for the development, transference and application of metacognitive thinking, critical analysis and creative problem-solving. Using the concept of "world view", students interrogate their own opinions and analyse how social, cultural, environmental and biological factors impact their perspectives. Through a range of learning tasks, students develop capacity for reasoning, analysis and reflection. Assessments include reflective journal entries and a short essay.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate principles of academic integrity in relation to the attribution of work
Explain and apply critical thinking concepts related to metacognition and higher-order thinking skills
Demonstrate skills in reflective and critical writing for academic purposes
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Evaluate different perspectives as the result of diverse biological, social, cultural, ideological and environmental factors

title: CRITICAL REASONING
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to formal logic and logical reasoning. Students use a variety of textual and visual representations to recognise and apply different structures of formal and informal argument. Students develop transferrable skills in textual analysis and critical thinking, as well as higher-order evaluation of argumentation and evidence. Assessments are nested, and are designed to help students use critical thinking skills in a variety of different contexts.
learning_outcomes: Articulate academic arguments related to contemporary issues
Assess different forms of faulty reasoning, including logical fallacies
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Interpret the structural forms and principles of logical argument
Evaluate different texts using formal logic

title: THINKING SCIENTIFICALLY
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to scientific reasoning. Students use experimental design and hypothesis construction to understand the scientific method, constituted by different processes rather than specific outcomes. Students develop transferrable skills in critical thinking, data collection and interpretation, experimental design and communication in everyday and scientific contexts. Assessments are multi-modal and designed to support future learning in general university programs.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate familiarity with language and concepts in science including scientific methods and the creation and validation of a hypothesis
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Propose a simple scientific experiment
Locate scientific processes in everyday contexts
Elaborate the scientific method as a multi-stage scientific process

title: CRITICAL ENQUIRY
syllabus_overview: Students develop and enhance their critical thinking skills and critical literacy through the analysis of a diverse range of media and popular cultural texts. In the context of contemporary issues and arguments, students learn to identify a range of persuasive techniques and representational strategies and to recognise that all media is socially constructed. Students are encouraged to engage with differing view points, challenge received knowledge and to question issues of voice, identity, access and power. Through a range of learning tasks, students develop capacity for textual analysis, creative reasoning and critical reflection.
learning_outcomes: Identify and give examples of specific representational strategies and persuasive techniques
Analyse the direct and indirect impacts of media on structures of power and received knowledge
Deliver a presentation using digital technology
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Explain why media representations should be subject to critical analysis

title: WORLD CHANGING SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to a range of world changing ideas in science, from initial concept to gradual adoption to mainstream understanding. Key scientific advances in agriculture, medicine, technology, energy and conservation are overviewed in the context of their global impact. The ethical considerations of scientific advancement are analysed and applied to real-world situations, as well as how scientific information is reported and communicated. Students will write a report on a selected field of scientific research and development.
learning_outcomes: Explain the relationships between science, technology, human society and the environment
Synthesise information to form a well-supported academic argument
Interpret ethical considerations and their applications in science
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Apply the styles and principles of academic communication, including academic integrity

title: MATHEMATICAL COMMUNICATION
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to concepts and conventions relating to mathematical expression and communication. Students will develop conceptual knowledge and procedural skills in a range of topics, including the application and interpretation of significant figures and scientific notation. Students will be enabled to solve and express a variety of mathematical problems using appropriate language, strategies, methods and techniques and to apply mathematical concepts and knowledge to different real-world situations. Assessment tasks include online quizzes and a project task.
learning_outcomes: Apply significant figures to data and measurement
Recognise and apply index and logarithmic laws at an introductory level
Apply study and learning strategies in an online academic environment
Interpret and use scientific notation to express and solve problems at a foundational level
Articulate the language of mathematics when applied through measurement

title: INDUSTRY PLACEMENT
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to extend their formal academic learning beyond the classroom. Students complete a minimum of 80 hours of work placement combined with academic activities that require reflection on self-efficacy, skill application and skill development. Subject to approval from the University, placements can be undertaken within an organisation, remotely, or as a virtual experience. This subject provides students with opportunities to apply and adapt their skills from a STEM discipline to a real-world environment and network with employers. It brings together the expertise of industry partners and La Trobe University staff for the benefit of students' professional development. There are deadlines associated with this subject. Refer to the University WIL Subjects webpage for more information.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the work placement experience, your skill development and strengths, and develop strategies for achieving career goals.
Apply discipline knowledge and skills from a STEM discipline in relevant professional contexts.
Understand the roles of giving and receiving feedback to improve work-related performance and capability.
Communicate effectively in professional contexts with people from diverse groups and backgrounds.
Evaluate transferable employability skills, knowledge and personal attributes and formulate a learning development plan.

title: ACADEMIC INTEGRITY MODULE
syllabus_overview: The academic integrity module introduces academic integrity standards to inform and support students in avoiding plagiarism and academic misconduct. Students complete four parts that encompass academic misconduct and academic integrity decisions, including cheating, plagiarism, and collusion. Students learn about Turnitin (the text-matching tool) used at La Trobe University, and how to get help and support their development of referencing skills.
learning_outcomes: Understand the importance of the acknowledgment and the referencing of sources
Locate, select, and utilise information about La Trobe's approach to academic integrity to support appropriate acknowledgement of references used.
Recognise and understand academic integrity responsibilities.

title: INDUSTRY PROJECT
syllabus_overview: This subject provides you with an opportunity to develop a real-world solution to a real-world project devised and developed in consultation with industry partners. You will work in a multidisciplinary team to critically engage with an industry project and develop, design and test a creative solution. By participating in the industry project, you will have the chance to collaborate with students from diverse educational and professional backgrounds, while also establishing connections with industry experts. There are deadlines associated with this subject. Refer to the University WIL Subjects webpage for more information.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the industry experience, your skill development and strengths as member of a professional team and develop strategies for achieving career goals.
Work effectively in a team to creatively and collaboratively solve real world problems.

title: GLOBAL EXPERIENCE 1 - STUDENT EXCHANGE
syllabus_overview: This subject facilitates the opportunity for you to undertake the equivalent of 15 La Trobe University credit points of your choosing at a La Trobe University approved exchange partner https://www.latrobe.edu.au/students/opportunities/exchange/partners
learning_outcomes: Collaborate and communicate, in a professional and ethical fashion, with people from varying cultural groups, nationalities and belief systems.
Work and learn both independently and collaboratively, and demonstrate effective teamwork to complete tasks in new and challenging environments.

Apply broad knowledge of cross cultural competency across a range of fields, with in-depth understanding of the major discipline of study, to analyse and evaluate investigations into real world problems.

title: PROFESSIONAL PLACEMENT 1
syllabus_overview: Immerse yourself in industry and build your pathway to the working world. The primary focus of Professional Placement 1 is to gain 100 hours of work experience via completion of a work based learning placement as part of your degree. You will complete assessments that support your learning through placement, with a focus on building your understanding of employability including self-assessment and reflection on your individual skills, knowledge and attributes. The University approved placement should be with an organisation in Australia and can be completed on-site, remotely or a combination. All students are expected to source a placement themselves or through placement opportunities advertised by the University, on Career Hub and other job websites. Support and resources are available to assist you to find a placement that aligns with your course or career aspirations. LTU2PP1 can be taken as an elective or as a suite of Professional Placement subjects leading to an Industry Placement Minor.
learning_outcomes: Construct and articulate goals that support your career and professional development.
Proactively seek feedback to achieve a realistic insight into work-related performance and capability.
Identify your transferable skills, knowledge and personal attributes that can fulfil the requirements of a variety of work roles and work environments.
Examine and articulate how your career decisions have been, or are influenced by, personal characteristics (skills, knowledge, attitudes, interests, values and beliefs).

title: PROFESSIONAL PLACEMENT 2
syllabus_overview: In Professional Placement 2, you will continue with or commence a new placement of 100 hours and continue to build a network through connecting with colleagues as part of a team in the workplace. You will learn techniques to identify information for career decision making and reflect on your professional practice and employability as part of a team. The University approved placement should be with an organisation in Australia and can be completed on-site, remotely or a combination of both. All students are expected to source a placement themselves or through placement opportunities advertised by the University, on Career Hub and other job websites. Support and resources are available to assist you to find a placement that aligns with your course or career aspirations. LTU2PP2 can be taken as an elective or as the second subject in a suite of Professional Placement subjects leading to an Industry Placement Minor.
learning_outcomes: Work with people from diverse groups including different cultural and language backgrounds, age groups and genders.
Connect with people in the workplace to build a professional network.
Use career information resources to identify work opportunities that are available to someone with your set of work skills, knowledge and attitudes.
Reflect on how you have applied your knowledge and skills in the work placement.

title: PROFESSIONAL PLACEMENT 3
syllabus_overview: In Professional Placement 3, you will continue with or undertake another 100 hours of work based learning. In this placement, you will continue to extend your employability and career management, articulating evidence of your skills and experiences. You will also explore trends and issues of organisations aligning to your career aspirations as well as how your individual capabilities contribute to organisational success. The University approved placement should be with an organisation in Australia and can be completed on-site, remotely or a combination of both. All students are expected to source a placement themselves or through placement opportunities advertised by the University, on Career Hub and other job websites. Support and resources are available to assist you to find a placement that aligns with your course or career aspirations. LTU3PP3 can be taken as an elective or as the third subject in a suite of Professional Placement subjects leading to an Industry Placement Minor.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively online and in-person to a wide range of stakeholders.
Reflect on the macro trends affecting business, industry, and professions.
Evaluate the impact of social, demographic, technological, occupational, and industrial trends on your future work and learning opportunities.
Plan your independent learning and demonstrate self-awareness through active reflection.

title: PROFESSIONAL PLACEMENT 4
syllabus_overview: In Professional Placement 4, you will complete a final 100 hours of a work based learning culminating in the development of an ePortfolio articulating your learning and employability development, professional development and career narrative throughout the Industry Placement Minor and beyond to potential employers. The University approved placement should be with an organisation in Australia and can be completed on-site, remotely or a combination of both. All students are expected to source a placement themselves or through placement opportunities advertised by the University, on Career Hub and other job websites. Support and resources are available to assist you to find a placement that aligns with your course or career aspirations. LTU3PP4 is the fourth subject in a suite of Professional Placement subjects leading to an Industry Placement Minor.
learning_outcomes: Use a variety of written communication skills that support job search and career self-management.
Critically appraise the outcome of self and employer evaluation to identify your professional development achievements, employability outcomes and further professional development needs.
Reflect on how your work placements have confirmed or changed your career plans.
Reflect, articulate and collate evidence of your experiences and development of skills over work based learning placements through creation of a portfolio of work.

title: PEOPLE, CULTURE AND COMMUNICATION
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students for postgraduate study in the Australian context. Students will build their competence in effective communication, participation and interaction in Australia and at university. Through an exploration of the people (structures of universities), culture (student body, staff and communities), students will improve their agency to navigate higher education systems and respond appropriately in varied multicultural and social environments.
learning_outcomes: Develop familiarity with the cultural context of Australian higher education.
Reflect on personal worldview, skills and attributes.
Demonstrate skills in reflective and critical writing for academic purposes.
Understand the responsibilities and expectations of students and staff in Australian universities.

title: PREPARING FOR POSTGRADUATE CRITICAL THINKING
syllabus_overview: This subject supports students to extend their critical and analytical thinking skills ahead of postgraduate studies. Students will be introduced to critical thinking methods that are applied to scholarship by critically engaging with, and evaluating, the arguments of others. Students are encouraged to not only challenge the views of others, but also communicate their own position based on reasoning and effectively formulating an argument.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and formulate questions for academic inquiry.
Identify, source, critically analyse, organise and reference research materials to support an opinion.
Analyse a question, form an opinion and develop an academic argument in response.
Critically compare different viewpoints by using critical reading and note-taking strategies.

title: LITERACY FOR POSTGRADUATE STUDY
syllabus_overview: This subject provides students from a range of educational, linguistic and cultural backgrounds with tools to develop the academic voice and language skills necessary for postgraduate studies. Students will explore academic conventions and practices to complete tasks in a range of academic genres and text types such as writing essays, reports and case studies, formal presentation and delivery of academic material as well as participating actively in university lectures, seminars and tutorials.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in argumentative and report writing for academic purposes.
Apply knowledge of a range of information types and genres to the analysis and construction of academic texts.
Compare different academic genres and styles and identify their requirements required for specific purposes.
Critically review written work using proofreading skills and selecting and applying feedback.

title: THEORETICAL UNDERSTANDING IN CLINICAL TEACHING AND LEARNING
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore educational theories underpinning human learning, and their application to clinical teaching and learning. You will consider processes by which theoretical learning is applied in practical situations along with the impact of diversity on clinical learning. In addition, you will analyse factors that can influence learning in practice-based settings. You will learn how to use established principles of cognitive science and contemporary behavioural psychology to design clinical learning experiences for maximum impact.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate scientifically-aligned educational theories and practices related to clinical education
Utilise evidence-based approaches to enhance clinical education practices
Recognise impacts of diversity on clinical learning
Apply educational theories to enhance clinical learning and teaching

title: EFFECTIVE CLINICAL TEACHING AND EDUCATION SKILLS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will delve deeper into the nuances of clinical learning and teaching and develop your skills as a clinical educator. You will examine theories and practices aimed at provision of effective clinical teaching and learning, including feedback and assessment, and consider strategies to support learning in practice for diverse learners.
learning_outcomes: Deliver constructive and effective feedback on clinical learning
Facilitate the delivery of high-quality clinical learning outcomes
Develop strategies for managing complex situations in clinical education
Apply evidence-based approaches to analysing, designing and evaluating clinical learning experiences

title: INTRODUCTION TO MEDIA PRODUCTION
syllabus_overview: This subject will introduce you to the basics of video production including camera work, editing, sound and audio. You will learn to analyse video news and feature stories to understand how story, structure and style make meaning and appeal to audiences. You will learn to write, produce and edit your own stories on timely, newsworthy topics. You will also become familiar with the workings of a TV studio by undertaking studio roles in a live simulation of a television current affairs program, where you will present your video packages as part of the show. This is a level 1 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Develop and demonstrate an appreciation of the social production of newsgathering, production and distribution through the process of a news production simulation.
Evaluate the ethical, legal, commercial and industrial context of news production and distribution and reception
Demonstrate rudimentary skills and knowledge in the operation of cameras, editing software, sound recording equipment and lighting in a location and studio environment.
Demonstrate an understanding of working in a team by undertaking a specific craft role and successfully participating in, and completing a studio group Assessment
Demonstrate an understanding of the various genres, formats and technical styles and processes associated with field to studio workflows.

title: INDUSTRY PLACEMENT
syllabus_overview: This subject allows students to extend their formal academic learning beyond the classroom. Students complete a minimum of 100 hours of work placement combined with academic activities that require reflection on self-efficacy, skill application and skill development. Placements are expected to be self-sourced by students and be related to their studies. Subject to approval from the University, placements can be undertaken within an organisation, remotely, or as a virtual experience. This subject provides students with opportunities to apply and adapt their skills to a real-world environment and network with employers. It brings together the expertise of industry partners and La Trobe University staff for the benefit of students' professional development.
learning_outcomes: Perform at a professional level, work tasks and projects by applying discipline knowledge and employability skills in professional contexts.
Communicate effectively with team members from different backgrounds, using in-person and technology-based communication channels.
Collaborate with team members in professional contexts to achieve negotiated project and organisational outcomes.
Critically appraise your professional development achievements, employability and career development needs.
Work with an organisation to design and plan the scope and aims of a project to complete in a 100-hour work placement.

title: MEDIA, LAW AND ETHICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will investigate the ethical and legal questions that confront journalists and content providers on an everyday basis, and the new dilemmas forged by rapidly evolving media technologies. To what extent have the ground rules changed with the explosion of new kinds of media content and platforms? You will explore how privacy, professional liability, conflict of interest, copyright and fair dealing, defamation, and confidentiality are dealt with by the law, through journalist codes of practice, and by media institutions. You will also examine the court system, the notion of contempt of court and the process of sentencing. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation in weekly tutorials. These classes may fall in business hours.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of Australian copyright law and how to apply it effectively in journalism and media practice.
Develop the capacity to evaluate and synthesise arguments about competing dilemmas involving ethical and legal issues in journalism and media practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of relevant codes of practice and codes of ethics that journalists and media professionals are required to know to practice in Australia.
Demonstrate an understanding of the legal framework that journalists and content providers are required to know in Australia in order to function as media professionals and self-publishers.
Develop an understanding of the impact of new and emerging media platforms on existing laws and codes of ethics.

title: WRITING FOR MEDIA
syllabus_overview: Writing for Media introduces you to the practice of writing for various media platforms and audiences. The focus of the subject will be to teach you how to write a range of media texts and to develop skills in editing and honing your work. The key learning outcomes of writing concisely, effective revision, distilling information and sound knowledge of grammar and style are transferable across a range of vocations. You will develop a folio of written work.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the codes and conventions of different media writing forms and audiences.
Discern and explain information in order of importance and then write media texts for a range of platforms.
Apply key fundamentals of professional writing such as correct grammar, punctuation, style and attribution.
Demonstrate a comprehension of the pre-tutorial stimuli such as readings and videos related to industry practice, grammar and style.
Create a coherent folio of media writing.

title: USING SOCIAL MEDIA
syllabus_overview: Social media platforms are an integral part of news and media. In Using Social Media, you will learn how to use different social media platforms to both create and share media content. The subject explores how to use social media to create original media content for professional purposes. You will learn how to identify and verify credible sources. You will also learn how to analyse social media strategy and develop a strategy for social media content dissemination, including how to determine an audience, and create engaging content specifically for social media, such as text, graphics and images. As well as key skills, this subject delivers key knowledge on misinformation and disinformation in social media, and legal and ethical implications, including defamation, privacy and copyright. This is a level 2 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Find, evaluate and verify social media sources for use in media content.
Understand the legal and ethical framework in which social media platforms operate in Australia.
Understand, evaluate and compare social media platforms with respect to their suitability for media content.
Critically evaluate social media strategies and content.
Develop a social media dissemination strategy for an original piece of media content.

title: PROFESSIONAL INTERNSHIP
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will complete internships in the media, journalism and communications and related industries with a specific organisation. Students develop skills in accessing these industries from the perspective of an industry-ready future employee and undertake an in-depth experience of work as an emerging professional in the media and related fields. You will develop an understanding of issues internal to the organisation such as its goals, structure, management style and work practices. In addition, they acquire an understanding of the organisation's relationships to clients, audiences and other elements of media and communications professions. Internship opportunities will be advertised through this subject or you can self-source internships, but self-sourced internships must be approved by the subject coordinator before the student starts placement.
learning_outcomes: Develop practical employability skills through securing a professional internship placement.
Apply professional communication skills developed across their La Trobe course to a professional workplace.
Demonstrate the ability to customise and professionally format documents to effectively apply for roles in specific jobs and industries.
Demonstrate knowledge of and sensitivity to issues associated with workplace culture including, professional expectations, ethics, social and cultural diversity and personal responsibility.

Demonstrate an understanding of the legal and ethical framework in which they are expected to work as a professional in the media industry and as representatives of La Trobe University on student placement.

title: TOOLS FOR MODELLING THE WORLD
syllabus_overview: By modelling natural and engineered phenomena we can understand how the world works. In this subject you will build your problem-solving skills while gaining familiarity with mathematics as the natural language to describe the patterns that make up the world around us. You will explore a coherent treatment of vectors and vector geometry that includes matrices and solutions of systems of linear equations as well as eigenvalues and eigenvectors. We will study fundamental ideas then reinforce them and give them life by showing their connection to applications like population growth and disease spread, the motion of waves, facial recognition, inferring the recipe for a dish from the nutritional label, and the techniques used to create virtual 3D worlds. Emphasis is placed on a deeper understanding of fundamental mathematical concepts and the way they connect to each other and describe the world. You will learn to use technology to extend your understanding, combining the core ideas with the power of a computer. Using a computer package allows you to investigate larger problems than are otherwise possible by hand, such as connecting millions of points in a 3D maps of a landscape. You will learn to structure your thoughts and reasoning skills to enable you to transform problems into a form you can solve, while also clearly communicating your solution.
learning_outcomes: Present mathematical thinking meaningfully and succinctly using words and mathematical notation.
Solve algebraic problems involving complex numbers.
Apply vector techniques and matrix operations to find and describe objects in three-dimensional space.
Communicate mathematical processes and outcomes effectively.
Use modelling techniques and computer packages to solve applied problems.
Use key mathematic properties to solve algebraic and numerical problems and sketch solutions without a graphing calculator.

title: MODELLING CHANGE IN SCIENCE, SOCIETY AND ENGINEERING
syllabus_overview: One constant in the world is change. The mathematical language of change is calculus, so using calculus allows us to model phenomena to better understand the world. You will learn the fundamental principles of calculus and how to combine its powerful mathematical properties so you can apply this knowledge across areas as diverse as the evaporation of water from a wetland, the snap of a mousetrap, to calculating how much cloth you need to make a parachute that could keep a falling elephant safe. You will develop this understanding of the concepts and techniques of calculus and move on to the ideas of differential equations whose mathematics describes the sustainable level of fishing in an area, the spread of disease, the dangerous shaking frequencies of an earthquake, the cooling of a cup of coffee and the warming of the planet. An active learning approach is used, so you will solve mathematical problems and explore the detail of mathematical concepts in a hands-on way, solving simpler problems by hand to build the understanding that you will use to engage with complex problems using computer packages. Reasoning skills and the ability to clearly present written arguments will be developed. Verbal communication skills are practiced through group-work and interaction with staff. Students enrolled into the online instance of this subject must complete in person examinations at one of the following La Trobe University campuses: Bendigo, Albury/Wodonga, Shepparton, Mildura or Bundoora.
learning_outcomes: Use modelling techniques and computer packages to model change in applied areas.
Apply basic techniques of differentiation and integration in calculations.
Present mathematical thinking meaningfully and succinctly using words and mathematical notation.
Use derivative functions to solve common problems associated with tangents and rates of change in science and engineering contexts.
Draw conclusions from mathematical models representing real-world phenomena based on hand and computer calculations.

title: CRYPTOGRAPHY AND SECURITY
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a strong foundation for cryptography and coding, which are fundamental for mastering cybersecurity. Technical skills in mathematics will be developed, enabling the introduction of a range of common cryptographic techniques, including public and private key encryption, hashing, and cryptanalysis.
learning_outcomes: Identify and summarise a range of cryptographic techniques, including private key systems such as AES (Advanced Encryption System), and public key systems such as RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman).
Explain basic mathematical principles and constructions underlying cryptographic methods and employ these to solve simple problems.
Identify and describe different contexts of application of cryptographic techniques in communication and cybersecurity, such as authentication and secure transmission.

title: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS
syllabus_overview: The subject is an introduction to discrete mathematics, which is a fundamental part of modern mathematics. The subject contains a range of important mathematical topics not taught in secondary school or in other undergraduate subjects. Students interested in going on with mathematics are strongly encouraged to enrol in this subject. Among the topics covered are: combinatorics, numbers in bases other than 10, recurrence relations, complexity of algorithms, graph theory, Boolean logic, and finite state machines. All these topics are central to the application of mathematics in electronics and computer science. Examples within each topic are chosen with a view to helping students develop their problem-solving skills.
learning_outcomes: Perform arithmetic in number bases arising in the study of computing processes.
Analyse network graphs and related objects in order to identify various inherent properties.
Present mathematical thinking in succinct written form using both words and mathematical notation.
Implement algebraic and graphical methods in logic and circuits.
Obtain formulas describing iterative and recursive processes in enumeration.
Analyse mathematical processes and use algorithms arising in computer science.

title: MATHEMATICAL APPLICATIONS IN BIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Students will be introduced to how mathematical models are used in biological, biophysical sciences and we will emphasise insight into how models may be derived from biophysical assumptions. A small but representative range of biophysical applications is investigated. The strengths and limitations of models to make predictions about ecological sustainability are explored. The subject is organised in modules, each focusing on a specific application. Learning resources including all lecture materials will be available on-line. Students participate in two 1-hour problem solving classes per week to work through problem sets designed to strengthen basic mathematical skills. Considerable use will be made of spreadsheets as a tool for understanding mathematical models and performing calculations.
learning_outcomes: Apply simulation techniques to investigate the behaviour of mathematical models.
Express mathematical arguments in a clear and concise way.
Apply algebraic techniques to transform equations used to specify mathematical models.
Explain how mathematical models are derived from biophysical assumptions and what conclusions can be drawn from the models.
Use spreadsheets to investigate the behaviour of mathematical models.

title: MODELLING OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the use of mathematical models to describe the transmission and control of infectious diseases and to guide policy decisions. You will be introduced to the theory of infectious disease modelling, including numerical and analytical methods for analysing models. These models have advantages and disadvantages, including how they account for the inherent random events underlying epidemics. You will learn how to model different mechanisms of disease transmission such as respiratory transmission (e.g. COVID-19); sexual contact (e.g. HIV); or vector-borne (e.g. malaria). By considering real world use of models to support practice, you will gain the skills to choose the best model framework for a given policy decision.
learning_outcomes: Construct simple models to incorporate host and pathogen factors determining variation in infectious disease dynamics.

Both individually, and working efficiently and effectively as a member of a team, differentiate between alternative modelling frameworks and approaches to select the most relevant framework for specific infectious disease policy decisions.
Identify appropriate model structures and key epidemiological parameters to describe the dynamics of infectious diseases.
Analyse and interpret the results of simple mathematical models.

title: LINEAR ALGEBRA
syllabus_overview: Linear algebra is a cornerstone of modern mathematics. In this subject you will begin with familiar geometric ideas such as lines, planes and vectors in Euclidean space and develop a rich theory of spaces of 'vectors' which can take a wide variety of forms. You will then apply this theory to a surprising array of problems in mathematics and beyond, including signal processing, numerical approximation of differential equations, computer graphics and more. You will hone your understanding of the deeper mathematical concepts that connect these various applications. You will use software to explore larger and more realistic problems than could be done by hand.
learning_outcomes: Perform calculations using vectors and matrices, including solving systems of linear equations.
Demonstrate understanding of basic definitions and utilise them to prove elementary results in linear algebra.
Describe vector spaces, vector subspaces, and the linear maps between them in terms of bases.
Demonstrate understanding of linear algebra using both words and formal mathematical notation.
Apply the methods of linear algebra in applications including: Fourier approximations, differential equations, quadratic forms, and approximation.

title: GRAPH THEORY
syllabus_overview: Graph theory is a part of discrete mathematics which deals with the interrelationships between a group of objects - in this context a graph is simply a set of nodes together with lines connecting some of them. In addition to their intrinsic interest, graphs are used to model structures as diverse as molecules, sentences, communications networks, and social networks. We will explore these models as well as the underlying mathematical structures. Algorithms are fundamental to the subject, for example, communications networks rely heavily on algorithms which minimise costs or maximise efficiency. Particular applications will depend on the interests of the class. This subject is especially suitable for computing, mathematics, and engineering students. It is offered at 2nd and 3rd year levels: the 3rd year level is a core subject in the Mathematics and Statistics major in Bendigo.
learning_outcomes: Analyse different types of graphs, such as trees, bipartite graphs, and planar graphs, and describe their properties.
Communicate graph theory concepts and solutions effectively through written assignments, oral examination, and in class discussions.
Explain the fundamental concepts and terminology of graph theory, including vertices, edges, paths, cycles, and connectedness
Identify the principles of graph algorithms, such as Euler tours, shortest paths, and minimum spanning trees

title: VECTOR CALCULUS
syllabus_overview: In Calculus, we learned about functions of a single variable and how to do things like calculating how much of something there is or what an optimal value might be. However, in our lives, things usually depend on more than one variable: our income depends on our experience, the hours we work, and our education; we may choose our commuting method based on cost, time, and ease. Water flowing in the oceans or Carbon Dioxide mixing into the atmosphere exist and move in a three dimensional space. Multivariable Calculus deals with the study of functions of multiple variables (dimensions). In this subject, students will learn methods to study two- and three-dimensional scalar and vector functions using Cartesian, Spherical, and Cylindrical coordinate systems. Students will learn how to identify different stationary points and develop tools to calculate the work done moving objects through force fields, particularly conservative fields. The subject addresses higher dimensional generalizations of derivatives: the gradient vector, curl, and divergence as well integration in higher dimensions. The concepts of integration and differentiation are related through the Divergence Theorem and Stokes' Theorem. The Laplace Transform is used to solving linear differential equations. Applications from physics, biology, and engineering are emphasised. (For engineering students: stage one competencies 1.2, 3.2 and 3.4 are developed.)
learning_outcomes: Use Stokes' Theorem and the Divergence Theorem to simplify calculations in different geometries.
Use the Laplace Transform to solve linear differential equations and interpret the results.
Describe and classify features of a function of several variables, analysing them using graphical and computational techniques.
Apply the processes of calculus (differentiation and integration meaningfully to functions of several variables in rectangular and curvilinear coordinates.
Clearly and precicely communicate an understanding of vector calculus using both words and mathematical notation in a clear and precise manner.

title: ADVANCED CALCULUS AND CURVATURE
syllabus_overview: This subject unifies linear algebra and vector calculus from second year into the sort of calculus used in differential geometry and analysis. The central objects of study are curves and surfaces in the space and differentiable maps. Topics include: the implicit and inverse function theorems, tangent space and tangent map, curvature and torsion for curves, intrinsic and extrinsic curvature for surfaces, and the Theorema Egregium of Gauss.
learning_outcomes: Construct curves and surfaces explicitly and implicitly, as well as their tangent and normal spaces
Calculate the curvature of curves and surfaces
Apply the apparatus of calculus and differential equations to calculate geometric invariants and to derive equations of geodesics.
Communicate your understanding using both words and mathematical notation in a precise and succinct manner
Correctly invoke the inverse and implicit function theorems in mathematical arguments

title: COMPLEX ANALYSIS
syllabus_overview: The subject extends calculus to the complex domain, where many beautiful new features appear. This gives a new perspective to many topics studied in previous years. The new tools covered are also very useful in applications to a wide variety of areas within mathematics, as well as in other mathematically-oriented sciences. Students will apply theoretical content knowledge and graduate capabilities in their practical classes. This subject addresses La Trobe's Innovation and Entrepreneurship Essential. Innovation and Entrepreneurship entails developing the ability to tackle problems creatively, generating new ideas, taking calculated risks and creating change to achieve ambitions - now and in the future.
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of techniques for the calculation and inversion of Fourier transforms and apply the theory of Fourier transforms in the solving of differential equations
Calculate Taylor and Laurent series for complex analytic functions and classify singularities.
Differentiate and integrate functions defined on the complex plane.
Construct complex extensions of the familiar rational, logarithm, exponential and trigonometric functions.
Solve problems by exploring the distinctive features of complex functions, such as the possible existence of branches.

title: GRAPH THEORY
syllabus_overview: Graph theory is a part of discrete mathematics which deals with the interrelationships between a group of objects - in this context a graph is simply a set of nodes together with lines connecting some of them. In addition to their intrinsic interest, graphs are used to model structures as diverse as molecules, sentences, communications networks, and social networks. We will explore these models as well as the underlying mathematical structures. Algorithms are fundamental to the subject, for example, communications networks rely heavily on algorithms which minimise costs or maximise efficiency. Particular applications will depend on the interests of the class. This subject is especially suitable for computing, mathematics, and engineering students. It is offered at 2nd and 3rd year levels: the 3rd year level is a core subject in the Mathematics and Statistics major in Bendigo.
learning_outcomes: Communicate complex graph theory concepts and solutions effectively through written assignments, oral examination, and in class discussions.
Critically analyse advanced graph theory concepts, including graph colourings, matchings, and graph isomorphisms
Investigate advanced graph algorithms, such as network flows and graph connectivity algorithms.
Solve proof-based graph theory problems, demonstrating creativity and critical thinking.
Evaluate the properties of various graph classes, such as Eulerian graphs and Hamiltonian graphs.

title: MATHEMATICS THESIS A
syllabus_overview: Students commence a project that takes the equivalent of six months of continuous work under the supervision of a member of staff. MAT4001 will include elements of research training as directed by the supervisor. The project is completed and written up as a thesis when the student completes the subject MAT4002. All students are required to present a 10-minute talk outlining the proposed project at a time to be determined by the Department of Mathematical and Physical Sciences Honours Coordinator. A list of prospective topics and supervisors is available from the Department of Mathematical and Physical Sciences.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate autonomy, well-developed judgement, adaptability and responsibility as a researcher.
Use advanced communication skills to transmit knowledge and ideas of the research to others.
Select and apply research methods to critically analyse, evaluate and interpret literature relevant to the topic.
Demonstrate advanced theoretical and technical knowledge of the topic of the thesis.
Analyse, generate and transmit solutions to, or an exposition of, complex problems relevant to the topic.

title: MATHEMATICS THESIS B
syllabus_overview: Students complete the project commenced in MAT4001, writing up the results as a thesis. MAT4002 will include elements of research training as directed by the supervisor. All students are required to present a 20-minute talk on their project after the thesis has been submitted. A list of prospective topics and supervisors is available from the Department of Mathematical and Physical Sciences.
learning_outcomes: Use advanced communication skills to transmit knowledge and ideas of the research to others.
Demonstrate advanced theoretical and technical knowledge of the topic of the thesis.
Demonstrate autonomy, well-developed judgement, adaptability and responsibility as a researcher.
Select and apply research methods to critically analyse, evaluate and interpret literature relevant to the topic.
Analyse, generate and transmit solutions to, or an exposition of, complex problems relevant to the topic.

title: ADVANCED TOPICS IN MATHEMATICS A
syllabus_overview: This subject enables 4th year mathematics and statistics students to enroll in externally offered subjects (including AMSI subjects). Enrolment into this subject must be approved by the Department of Mathematical and Physical Sciences Honours Coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced theoretical and technical knowledge in a specified mathematical topic.
Use advanced cognitive and technical skills to select and apply methods to critically analyse, evaluate and interpret tasks relevant to the topic.
Demonstrate autonomy, well-developed judgement, adaptability and responsibility as a mathematician
Use advanced communication skills to transmit mathematical knowledge and ideas to others.
Use advanced cognitive and technical skills to analyse, generate and transmit solutions to complex problems relevant to the topic.

title: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS
syllabus_overview: This subject is a foundation introduction to discrete mathematics, which is a fundamental part of modern mathematics and essential background knowledge for computer scientists. This subject is designed for students enrolled in coursework masters programs to achieve proficiency in the mathematical underpinnings of concepts in computing and information science. There are a range of topics not typically taught in a standard undergraduate mathematics curriculum, including: combinatorics, numbers in bases other than 10, recurrence relations, complexity of algorithms, graph theory, Boolean logic, and finite state machines. Examples within each topic are chosen with a view to their relevance to computer science. Some independent learning tasks will be given to help you develop their mathematical problem-solving and research skills.
learning_outcomes: Implement algebraic and graphical methods in logic and circuits.
Independently investigate and implement outcomes to perform basic mathematical and computer operations
Analyse and classify network graphs and related objects according to various significant properties.
Perform arithmetic in number bases arising in the study of computing processes.
Analyse mathematical processes and use algorithms arising in computer science.
Present mathematical thinking and interpretations of computing processes in succinct written form using both words and mathematical notation.
Analyse computing processes and algorithms to devise mathematical formulas to describe iterative and recursive behaviour.

title: ADVANCED TOPICS IN MATHEMATICS B
syllabus_overview: This subject enables 4th year mathematics and statistics students to enroll in externally offered subjects (including AMSI subjects). Enrolment into this subject must be approved by the Department of Mathematical and Physical Sciences Honours Coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate autonomy, well-developed judgement, adaptability and responsibility as a mathematician.
Demonstrate advanced theoretical and technical knowledge in a specified mathematical topic.
Use advanced cognitive and technical skills to select and apply methods to critically analyse, evaluate and interpret tasks relevant to the topic.
Use advanced cognitive and technical skills to analyse, generate and transmit solutions to complex problems relevant to the topic.
Use advanced communication skills to transmit mathematical knowledge and ideas to others.

title: MATHEMATICS FOR DATA SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: Important mathematical ideas which underpin the theory and techniques of data science are introduced and consolidated in this subject. Matrices are used to store and work with quantitative information, and the methods of calculus are used to find extreme values and accumulation. The Gamma and Beta functions are introduced, as are eigenvalues, eigenvectors and the rank of a matrix. Emphasis is placed on the relevance of the mathematics to data science applications (such as least squares estimators and calculation of variance in data), and on the development of clear communication in explaining technical ideas. This is a foundational subject for the Master of Data Science.
learning_outcomes: Apply mathematical skills to analysis of data science literature.
Perform mathematical calculations relevant to data science fluently and accurately.
Creatively apply mathematical techniques to unfamiliar problems.
Present mathematical thinking in written form in a meaningful and succinct way using both words and mathematical notation.

title: COMPLEXITY, CRYPTOGRAPHY AND COMPRESSION
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will develop the mathematical basis for cryptography and compression. A variety of specific methods of encryption and data compression will be learnt, including examples of historical relevance and examples of current usage in information transfer and storage. A number of underlying mathematical concepts will be encountered, including an introduction to computational complexity and randomness.
learning_outcomes: Appraise compression algorithms and processes and apply to digital information
Compare a range of cryptographic techniques and apply to encode and decode information.
Assess computational problems in terms of basic complexity classes, and analyse comparative complexity by way of basic reductions.
Write clear, well-structured written arguments to justify and prove the validity of problem reductions.
Implement low-level encryption and compression techniques within computer algebra package.
Discriminate between compression and/or encryption techniques and implement appropriately for context.

title: OPTIMISATION
syllabus_overview: Optimisation is the process of maximizing or minimizing some objective of interest, while satisfying constraints. Optimisation problems are fundamental and ubiquitous in the study of machine learning, signal processing, and statistics. This subject will develop the mathematical theory, introduce useful tools, and explain the algorithms and their implementation. A variety of distinct optimisation problem types will be encountered including linear programming, nonlinear problems, as well as various unconstrained problems. Real world instances of such problems will be considered, and solution methods for such problems will be studied. A basic knowledge of calculus and real analysis is assumed.
learning_outcomes: Translate real-world problems into mathematical form, using the language of optimisation theory.
Employ tools and implement solution methods and algorithms for unconstrained optimisation, linear programming and nonlinear problems.
Apply optimisation techniques to a range of practical problems.
Synthesise information, concepts and theories of unconstrained optimisation, linear programming and nonlinear problems.

title: MECHANICAL COMPONENT DESIGN
syllabus_overview: Mechanical components are all around us facilitating transportation and robotics through to defence and even in DVD players. In this subject you will be introduced to the core concepts in the analysis and design of mechanical components of machines. This includes principles of materials engineering, solid mechanics, materials selection, stress, deformation, wear, failure mechanisms and safety. Standard methodologies for conducting machine component design including gears, camshafts and screws will be presented and used to solve mechatronics problems of mechanical power transfer and conversion. Relevant engineering standards and codes will be included to provide the framework for the solutions to the above problems.
