Analyse rehabilitation interactions to identify barriers to change to support self-critique of your own performance and facilitate engagement in undertaking reflective practice to address your learning needs.
Analyse and synthesise evidence-based knowledge to inform high level independent judgements to identify core presenting themes or relational issues in a counselling session.

title: SERVICE COORDINATION AND CASE MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will develop: (i) an understanding of basic concepts that underpin care coordination in community settings; and (ii) the opportunity to examine current models of service coordination and case management as these have been applied to meet service needs of individuals with chronic conditions or disabilities in these settings.
learning_outcomes: Identify, review, analyse, and synthesise the background, rationale, objectives and key influences on the development of service coordination and case management approaches to the provision of care.
Reflect and describe about how case management should be explained to a target audience within a group of peers.

Analyse models of case management application to clients with disability or chronic conditions, and evaluate concepts of complex assessment and implications for management and referral to other services.
Critically interpret and analyse common procedures and tools used for the assessment of individuals with disability and/or chronic conditions.
Initiate, plan and implement evidence-based strategies to manage services for optimal outcomes and client-focused goals.
Analyse, consolidate and synthesise knowledge of case management models within the disability, rehabilitation and aged care sectors.
Critically evaluate research into case management effectiveness
Identify, review and critique models of case management used by health and human health service organisations.

title: SOCIAL AND CULTURAL PERSPECTIVES IN PUBLIC HEALTH
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore the multi-disciplinary partnerships between public health and social science disciplines, especially sociology and anthropology. Particular attention will be paid to the ways in which cultural beliefs and practices shape population risks for both infectious and non-infectious diseases, and how social factors such as social status, ethnicity and gender impact on health inequalities. This subject will provide you with a solid grounding in understanding different ways in which the social sciences contribute to public health theory and practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse how cultural and social factors shape population health and public health interventions
Critically reflect on social science influences on public health theory, method and practice
Critique ways in which key social science disciplines inform understandings of health
Critically appraise health literature in terms of social and cultural content

title: SYSTEMS THINKING AND LEADERSHIP
syllabus_overview: Whether dealing with public health issues or trying to improve the performance of a hospital, many of the issues are complex, seemingly embedded within a web of interconnected and often contested causes. Push on one part of the system and something changes to counter the good work. Complexity is often used as shorthand for intractability. In this subject we consider if systems thinking provides the insights needed to grapple with complexity. Systems thinking is interested in the parts of a system and the connections among those parts, the structures established as a result of those connections and the behaviours those structures allow or discourage. You will examine the notion of systems, as an object of study and a way of thinking that changes the way we might look at health problems and work towards their solution, the language of systems, and its concepts, and some of the methods used to define issues, build consensus for action, and evaluate strategies to address problems.
learning_outcomes: Recommend the best systems methods for analysing, understanding and addressing different problems
Critically assess selected systems methods and their uses in practice to improve decision-making.
Employ systems concepts to solve contemporary public health or health management problems.

title: COMMUNITY BASED HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY SYSTEMS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you are introduced to a range of community-based service delivery systems for those living with permanent impairments or chronic conditions. Populations studied include those suffering traumatic injury, post-traumatic stress disorder/injury, lifelong physical impairments, and those with mental health conditions living in the community.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique the philosophy, structure and effectiveness of community-based aged care services
Initiate, plan and implement evaluations of rehabilitation services, programs and policy.

Analyse and critique the philosophy, scope and effectiveness of the community-based Australian based service delivery sector for traumatic injury including rehabilitation for veterans and those in the military
Analyse and critique the philosophy, scope and effectiveness of Australian based service delivery models for mental health conditions

title: VOCATIONAL REHABILITATION
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide you with the knowledge and skills to (i) assist rehabilitation clients achieve optimal vocational outcomes and (b) advise employing organisations about the best way to achieve optimal rehabilitation outcomes for their employees. You will examine topics including: (i) the psychology of work and unemployment; (ii) occupational rehabilitation: systems and practice; (iii) workplace disability management; and (iv) vocational assessment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply an evidence-based assessment process in order to prepare a client for securing and retaining work.
Identify, evaluate and apply client centred vocational assessment to select suitable vocational options and make appropriate modifications where required.
Identify, critique and systhesise resources and supports within relevant return to work schemes and workplace disability management research.
Identify, analyse and critique core theories of vocational assessment and disability.
Initiate, justify, plan and implement the vocational assessment process to cater to the client needs in relevant legislative context.
Identify, critique and apply general labour market information relating to client vocational needs using evidence based models.
Critique and synthesise theoretical knowledge and evidence-based professional judgment to assess the suitability of vocational assessment and practice of occupational rehabilitation

title: THE SERVICE USER PERSPECTIVE IN HEALTH CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you focus on the development and implementation of client-centred services for people with disability or chronic illness. You are given the opportunity to explore disability and chronic illness from the perspective of the person with the disability or chronic illness and how this perspective can be reflected in effective support services. Content is organised into three modules: (i) client related psychological and social dimensions of disability and chronic illness, and their relationship to effective service provision, (ii) self-management models of service delivery: theoretical approaches, strategies and interventions which facilitate involvement of the person in the management of their own condition, and (iii) the service user as a consumer: models and strategies regarding service user participation in health service planning and delivery.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, generate and implement solutions to sSolve complex problems related to how social support can impact on behaviour in rehabilitation settings and implementation of social support needs assessments
Identify and evaluate concepts of personal control impacts on behaviour in rehabilitation settings and apply to provision of effective client-centred services in these settings.

Identify, analyse and critically assess the concept of adjustment to chronic conditions and a client's coping style and attitudes can impact on behaviour in rehabilitation settings and demonstrate evidence-based practice to provide more effective practice, i.e. client-centred services, in these settings
Critique and apply an advanced and specialised body of conceptual, theoretical and practical evidence base to the rehabilitation counselling environment within a changing health care environment
Identify, analyse and synthesise application of contemporary evidence-based theories, concepts and practices for service user involvement.

title: STRATEGY AND OPERATION MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will examine the strategic decisions, actions and leadership that determine the success of health service organisations. To achieve this, you will focus on the health care system and organisations from the strategic planning and management viewpoint, as well as covering marketing fundamentals and key components of operations management and research essential for decision analysis. Major issues and trends with an impact on the strategic and operations management of health services organisations will be discussed. This subject is designed for you to use much of the material previously covered in other subjects, as well as healthcare management experience to further develop the skills to deal with real life strategic and operational situations. Practical health services management problems relating to strategic planning and management, marketing and operations management are addressed through group projects and exercises.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise and recommend operations management tools and techniques to optimise service delivery and align operational systems with strategic objectives.
Analyse and evaluate evidence-based operational reporting tools to support performance monitoring and strategic decision-making.

Critically analyse the legislative, regulatory, and policy frameworks governing (influencing) health service delivery across public and private sectors, and assess their implications for strategic and operational decision-making.
Design, implement, and critically evaluate strategic plans for health services, departments or organisations, integrating stakeholder needs, organisational goals, and contextual complexities.
Evaluate and apply project management tools and evidence-based approaches to facilitate and sustain organisational change in healthcare settings.

title: QUESTIONS THAT MATTER
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to topics in a range of the major philosophical areas, including epistemology (what can we know?), metaphysics (what is the nature of reality?), ethics, and political philosophy. We will examine some of the central questions that have captivated philosophers throughout millennia, as well as those that scientific advances and cultural changes have only recently brought to our attention. These might include: What is it to be a person, or a citizen? What makes your actions right or wrong? Could a machine think or be conscious? Is it morally acceptable to eat meat, or to design children genetically? Are we defined by our sexuality? What are the proper limits and functions of government or the state? Is there a rational basis for belief in the existence of God? Questions That Matter will focus on exploring the various answers to such questions, and the merits of arguments for views about them. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Identify the cultural context of production of a philosophical text.
Identify a philosophical problem and raise critical questions about its assumptions, merits or weaknesses.
Outline a philosophical claim and write a brief defence based on your critical assessment of a philosophical text.
Locate and review an unfamiliar idea or line of argument in the light of your experience or previous knowledge.
Identify and formulate a text-based and standard form argument.

title: CRITICAL THINKING
syllabus_overview: Psychological studies have repeatedly shown that our thinking can be biased, distorted, and misinformed. This subject introduces you to some of the most common mistakes that people make in reasoning and equips you with essential tools to recognise and sidestep these errors. Among other things, you'll master the use of argument diagrams and basic logical principles to dissect and assess arguments as they occur in everyday life. Throughout this subject, you will improve your ability to think with clarity and autonomy, and to participate constructively in discussions and debates. Though critical to the practise of philosophy, these competencies are also vital across all disciplines in academia and are highly sought after in numerous professional fields. Consequently, students often report that the skills they acquire in this course prove to be of extraordinary benefit, regardless of their future career paths. This is a level 1 subject and includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate arguments pertaining to a wide variety of topics and drawn from a wide range of sources (e.g., books, newspapers, podcasts, videos)
Represent complex arguments in visual form, using argument diagramming technicques
Demonstrate an understanding of elementary technical concepts pertaining to argumentation, including deductive soundness and inductive strength
Produce clear, precise and well-informed writings that analyse, critique, and develop arguments on a wide variety of topics

title: ETHICS
syllabus_overview: Ethics concerns questions of how we should live, what is good in life, how we can tell right from wrong, or what we owe to each other. This subject will examine traditional and emerging ethical theories, and a range of applied ethical questions. Ethical theories to be examined will include consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics and care ethics. Students will gain an understanding of these theoretical approaches and their main critiques, as well as links to moral concepts such as moral status, human rights, dignity, and autonomy. We will also apply the theories and concepts in different contexts by examining issues in applied ethics, drawing a selection of controversial topics from a number of areas. These may concern questions of life and death, such as abortion and euthanasia; ethical issues raised by new technologies, such as those relating to social media use, robotics, or artificial intelligence; and global issues, such as the international trade in organs and body parts, global poverty, and the ethics of climate change policy. This is a level 2 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Apply theoretical approaches to a range of issues to develop skills of ethical analysis that are adaptable and transferrable to emerging problems.
Locate, review and analyse unfamiliar ideas and arguments using methods that take into account relevant cultural and other background assumptions.
Identify and analyse the underlying issues and problems in contemporary debates about controversial social issues and assess strategies to resolve the problems.
Critically evaluate normative ethical theories in relation to complex local and global issues.
Develop a coherent and well-structured argument in relation to a complex philosophical claim concerning a contemporary social issue.

title: KNOWLEDGE, INDIVIDUALS AND SOCIETY
syllabus_overview: Think of all the different beliefs you hold about various matters. How many of these, if any, constitute genuine knowledge rather than mere opinion? What does this distinction amount to and why is it important? To what extent do the standards for what counts as knowledge depend on context? Can you know something without knowing that you know it? What makes a belief justified or reasonable? Is it ever reasonable to hold a belief if you have no evidence to support it? What is the value of knowledge in our individual lives and in society? These are some of the central questions in epistemology-- the philosophical study of the nature, extent, and value, of knowledge and justified belief. In this course we will explore these and related questions using both historical and contemporary sources. Epistemological questions crop up absolutely everywhere--i n science, the humanities, politics, religion, and everyday life--and this course will give you the tools to tackle such questions wherever you find them. This is a level 2 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Research, critically analyse and synthesise unfamiliar ideas and lines of argument, whilst locating them in their historical and cultural context of production
Work collaboratively towards the formulation of a shared position in relation to the defensibility of a philosophical idea, claim or argument
Employ rigorous and systematic methods in the resolution of complex philosophical problems
Write articulate, focused and well-structured essays in support of a philosophical claim

title: MAKING OF THE MODERN WESTERN WORLD VIEW
syllabus_overview: Focusing on major themes in the intellectual development of the Western world, from Greek metaphysics and ethics, through Christian theology to Modern (17-19 century) scientific, political, ecological or aesthetic understandings of our place and responsibilities in the wider world, we will investigate ideas that continue to inform and guide much contemporary thinking on the social, economic, or environmental challenges of our times, such as, living well, happiness, justice, freedom, knowledge and the power to produce change in the world. We will consider differences in approach, including competing empiricist, rationalist or idealist assumptions that underpin our knowledge claims, as well as the choices that these differences enable and their consequent impact on the public good now and in the future. We will ask: how might an appreciation of the historical emergence of such ideas assist us in reflecting on our responsibilities in relation to the demands of our times? This is a level 2 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Identify the underlying issues in a complex problem or controversial debate and analyse its structure.
Write a sustained defence of a philosophical claim based on your critical assessment of a philosophical problem raised in a text from the history of philosophy.
Identify the cultural context of production of a text from the history of philosophy, compare the former to current times and ideas.

Locate and review an unfamiliar idea or line of argument in the light of your understanding of the intellectual context in which it was formulated and analyse it in relationship to other relevant ideas.

title: BIOSCIENCES TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on ethical and philosophical issues that arise in the biological sciences, including the medical and health sciences, and the technologies they employ. Scientific disciplines, the biosciences are committed to objectivity and neutrality, but also interact with categories that are socially coded such as race, gender, and disability. Concepts such as health and disease can be understood as natural, biomedical concepts, but also as evaluative concepts that play social roles; and biological conceptions of intelligence, mental illness or disability can be even more contentious. Further, technological advances give us new ways to change human beings, some of which are seen as improvements or enhancements. In examining a series of topics, including race science, eugenics, intelligence, disease, disability, and bioenhancement, you will learn how to critically examine the role of social processes and values in the biosciences, and of the biosciences in society. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Implement active learning strategies to act as self directed learners.
Investigate the ways in which biological sciences embody social values and inform individual and societal decisions.
Analyse the social dimensions of biological theories, practices and technologies.
Critique the ways that science both reflects and impacts the societies we live in.
Critically reflect on readings in the area to grapple with issues concerning concerning biology, society, and values.

title: INTRODUCTION TO LOGIC
syllabus_overview: Logic aims to uncover the most general patterns of good reasoning, so as to improve the way we draw inferences and even allow us to automate parts of that process. It is fundamental to the study of philosophy, mathematics, and computer science, and it has strong connections with many disciplines including law, psychology, and linguistics. Reasoning also occurs everywhere, from the privacy of one's own mind to political and scientific debates in the public domain, and all good reasoning is implicitly governed by logical principles. Developing an explicit grasp of those principles then is an important transferrable skill, as that understanding can help one to spot when arguments have gone awry and how to get them back on track. This subject will provide a gentle introduction to some of the basic elements of deductive logic, including the formalisation of arguments, propositional and predicate logic, and an accessible method of proof known as "semantic tableaux". It will also touch on a number of more discipline-specific topics. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Investigate a number of discipline specific issues involving logic.
Manage some essential meta-logical concepts such as soundness, completeness, and decidability.
Represent the structure of natural language statements and arguments in propositional and predicate logic.
Implement active learning strategies to act as self directed learners who have the capability to use symbolic logic in assessment conditions.
Analyse and evaluate the properties of formal arguments using truth tables and truth trees, and develop critical thinking skills by using these techniques to evaluate real-world arguments.

title: POLITICAL THEORY
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an advanced introduction to some of the most important values, concepts, and theories that have defined political philosophy since the second world war. You will begin by considering how influential political philosophers have historically understood their tasks and methods. You will then analyse how political philosophers responded to several key social problems of the postwar period, including the rise of the civil rights and social movements, conscientious objection during the Vietnam War, the justification of civil disobedience, and the existence of unjust institutions derived from slavery. We will then turn to more recent political philosophy, which has tackled social problems in the last two centuries, including the distribution of punishment by police and the courts, the problem of uncivil disobedience and envious rioting, demands for justice across gender diversity, changing structures of family life, and ecological collapse. By engaging with the work of political philosophers who have tackled various social problems in their own times, you will be encouraged to consider how new social problems might also demand new thinking. This subject will help you further your understanding of the relationship between politics, philosophy, and economics (PPE), clarify your own thinking on contemporary political issues, and sharpen your capacity to advance and evaluate arguments. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Develop and refine close reading and critical thinking skills.
Understand some of the major methodologies and approaches employed by contemporary political philosophers.
Understand how contemporary political philosophers formulated their theories as responses to important social problems in their own societies.
Consider how political philosophy might help us tackle new social problems in our contemporary world.

title: VIRTUAL REALITY AS PHILOSOPHY
syllabus_overview: This subject discusses the philosophical significance of Virtual Reality (VR) and other related technologies (like Augmented Reality and Video Games). These developing technologies raise many interesting ethical, social, metaphysical, and existential questions. This subject will introduce you to these issues and give you the conceptual tools to evaluate and analyse them, not only now but into the future as these technologies continue to change and evolve. Some of the questions we may look at include: Is a virtual life always less valuable than a real life? Is VR an empathy machine that can help us to better understand the inner lives of other people? Are the objects and events in VR real or fictional? What ethical constraints are there on our actions in virtual environments? In this subject you will also be encouraged to explore some of the virtual worlds we will be discussing (a cheap pair of cardboard VR goggles and a smartphone will suffice), and to let those experiences influence your thoughts and philosophical arguments. This is a level 3 subject. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Resolve problems and complex debates by identifying the underlying issues, analysing their structure, and employing appropriate reasoning strategies and creative solutions (in the form of new objections, arguments, and ideas).
Analyse and write carefully constructed arguments in support of philosophical conclusions.
Articulate, analyse, and evaluate, standard form and text-based arguments, using appropriate methods of analysis and critical reasoning.
Examine how philosophical concepts and theories can interact in innovative ways with issues raised by Virtual Reality and other new and emerging technologies.

title: MINDS, BRAINS, AND MACHINES: CONTEMPORARY PHILOSOPHY OF MIND
syllabus_overview: What is the mind and what is it made of? Can we say that mind and brain are the same thing? Are mental states, like thoughts and feelings, nothing more than brain states? Can machines be conscious? Do they have a mind? Do they think? Is language necessary for thinking? These and other questions will be the focus of this subject, which introduces you to contemporary philosophy of mind and to the philosophical underpinnings of contemporary cognitive science, psychology and linguistics. This is a level 3 subject. Please consider the subject pre-requisites before enrolling. This subject includes live sessions with the expectation of student attendance and participation.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on key philosophical texts in the philosophy of mind, including classic 20th Century texts and cutting edge contemporary works.

Learn how to analyse and evaluate central arguments, issues, and positions in the philosophy of mind including: the hard problem of consciousness, artificial minds, extended cognition, animal minds, dualism, and functionalism.
Work collaboratively to assess the merits of philosophical ideas and arguments taking into account the different views and starting points of group members.
Write a carefully constructed research essay in support of a substantive position in the philosophy of mind.

title: PRINCIPLES OF PHYSICS B
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on PHY1SCA and extends the knowledge into areas of electromagnetic fields and early 20th century physics of space and the atom. Specifically, you will study the topics of optics, electrostatics, magnetostatics, magnetic induction, special relativity, nuclear and atomic structure. Through the laboratory program, you will explore these key concepts by making detailed measurements and analysing data. Together with PHY1SCA, this subject forms a foundational background in Physics for further study in the physical sciences.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of optics, electromagnetism and modern physics to solve conceptual and numerical problems.
Present findings of laboratory experiments in written form.
Safely execute experiments related to electromagnetism, optics, radiation and relativity using standard physics laboratory techniques and equipment.
Use accurate terminology and appropriate SI units to describe physical phenomena related to optics, electromagnetism and modern physics..
Analyse and interpret laboratory results in the context of the topics covered in the subject.

title: PRINCIPLES OF PHYSICS A
syllabus_overview: In this foundation subject, you will be introduced to the concepts of classical physics that underpin the physical sciences, engineering and other sciences, and which provides the basis for further study in these fields. You will learn about mechanics, linear and rotational kinematics and dynamics, thermodynamics, waves, and simple harmonic motion. On completion of this subject, you will be able apply the concepts and terminology of classical physics to solve problems. Through a tailored laboratory program, you will gain hands-on experience of the essential apparatus of classical physics to make and analyse measurements. The subject is paired with the second semester subject PHY1SCB, and together constitute a mainstream University course in first-year Physics.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of mechanics, thermodynamics and waves to solve conceptual and numerical problems.
Use accurate terminology and appropriate SI units to describe physical phenomena related to mechanics, thermodynamics and waves.
Safely execute experiments using standard physics laboratory techniques and equipment.
Present findings of laboratory experiments in written form.
Analyse and interpret laboratory results in the context of the topics covered in the subject.

title: APPLICATIONS OF QUANTUM COMPUTING
syllabus_overview: Quantum computing is a modern alternative to traditional computer technologies. It uses quantum physics to enable computing in a way which can solve some problems significantly faster, as well as being able to solve some problems which classical computing cannot practically handle. This makes quantum computing an important step forward in a range of modern computing applications, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), quantum chemistry and weather modelling. In this subject, students will explore the principles and practice of quantum computing in an accessible way, without relying on any previous knowledge of physics or advanced mathematics. Students will develop a conceptual understanding of why quantum computing is transformative and how it works, both in principle and in practice. Students will learn how to use the Microsoft Quantum Development Kit (QDK) to program quantum computers, developing key skills relevant to the emerging quantum computing job market and advanced computation. These applications form cutting-edge technologies to improve job productivity in numerous engineering industries.
learning_outcomes: Conceptualise the quantum physics underpinning quantum computing
Analyse a variety of experimentally realised quantum computing technologies
Recognise and appropriately combine the key elements of a variety of quantum logic gates
Analyse the key differences between classical and quantum computing leading to specific advantages of quantum computing
Implement application-relevant programming for quantum computers using the Q# language, within the Microsoft QDK environment

title: CLASSICAL PHYSICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will come to appreciate the elegance and simplicity of classical optics and thermodynamics, two key fields of classical physics. This subject will provide an important bridge between the first year introduction to thermodynamics and optics and the study of quantum mechanics and electrodynamics covered in third year. A knowledge of optics is essential for understanding light, X-rays and the wave formulation of quantum mechanics. Thermodynamics adopts a macroscopic view of the world to explore properties of heat and matter and their measurement as functions of energy flows. Together with PHY2MOD, the subjects constitute a mainstream University course in physics at the second-year level. Knowledge and competence in the material presented in PHY1SCA, PHY1SCB, MAT1NLA and MAT1CDE is assumed.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate the outcomes of experimental investigations quantitatively using appropriate statistical error analysis.
Communicate key findings from experimental investigations in the form of a detailed written report.
Describe and mathematically derive key thermodynamic relationships from first principles and apply them to solve given real world problems.
Use mathematical techniques such as the matrix method and Fourier transforms to analyse complex optical systems and the images they produce.
Verify the optical and thermodynamic relationships described in the theoretical section of the subject through performing detailed experiments.

title: MODERN PHYSICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore two of the most important concepts in modern physics; special relativity and quantum mechanics. Special relativity considers the consequences of Einstein's postulates of the finite speed of light and its constancy in different frames of reference including simultaneity, mass-energy equivalence (E = mc^2), causality and the possibility of inter-stellar space travel. In quantum mechanics, you will consider the consequences of the wave nature of matter such as particles which appear in two places at once. You will learn the essential mathematics of quantum mechanics used to describe expectation values and operators, stationary and time-dependent states, quantisation of angular momentum, and spin. On completion of this subject you will be able to apply the concepts of modern physics to solve problems in special relativity and quantum mechanics. By undertaking three experimental investigations related to these topics you will develop your conceptual understanding and laboratory skills. Knowledge and competence in the material presented in pre-requisite PHY1SCB or MAT1NLA and MAT1CDE is assumed.
learning_outcomes: Predict the outcomes of observations of systems moving at speeds approaching the speed of light using the framework of special relativity.

Describe and explain, in appropriate written and verbal style, the findings from laboratory experiments performed by the student. Answer verbal queries about the findings as presented in the context of modern physics.

Analyse quantum mechanical systems, whose length scales approach that of the hydrogen atom to determine their mechanical properties and consider how they differ from those described by classical theory.
Verify the relationships described in the theoretical section of the subject through performing detailed experiments.
Communicate key findings from experimental investigations in the form of a detailed written report.

title: NANOTECHNOLOGY AND BEYOND STUDY TOUR
syllabus_overview: Through a 1-2 week overseas tour, you will gain an understanding of the scope and scale of international activity in the field of nanotechnology. A tailored program will be developed based around available opportunities for visits to international exhibitions, scientific agencies, government agencies and educational institutions. You will learn about professional business conduct and etiquette in an international setting, and develop skills collaborating as a group during the study tour. You will develop an advanced understanding of cultural issues and cultural diversity within a scientific and business context through the creation of a daily reflective journal and post-tour group sharing. The study tour will be offered outside of normal teaching weeks with a pre-departure session on the Melbourne campus followed by a visit to the international country, and a follow-up debriefing on return.
learning_outcomes: Exemplify professional business conduct and etiquette on the international stage
Work effeciently and effectively as a member of a group to Interpret cultural issues, values and diversity in the context of international relationships
Investigate the scale of international endeavour in the field of nanotechnology and the current state of the art in the discipline

title: ELECTRODYNAMICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore classical electro dynamics theory and applications, which expands on the concepts and theories related to electromagnetism that were encountered in first year physics. You will also be introduced to the emerging field of plasma physics which describes the rich behaviour of an electrically conducting fluid. Using this theory you will explore electro magnetic fields in matter, Maxwell's equation, electro magnetic waves and also the physics of the earth's upper atmosphere and magnetic fields, the Aurora, and magnetic confinement of high energy particles in fusion reactors. This subject is one of four physics subjects at 3rd year level that together constitute the physics major in the Bachelor of Science.
learning_outcomes: Structure and write solutions to problems, which draw on the theories of electrodynamics and plasma physics to concisely and professionally communicate important results.
Visualise and analyse conceptual and mathematical problems related to electrostatics, magnetostatics and behaviour of dielectric materials, electrodynamics and plasma physics.
Critique and assess advanced concepts in electrodynamics and plasma physics with a view to applying them real world scenarios and problems.

title: SENIOR PHYSICS LABORATORY
syllabus_overview: In this capstone laboratory experience in physics and nanotechnology, you will develop advanced laboratory and research skills by undertaking three extended experiments where by you aim to reproduce classic results from fields relevant to the research strengths of the discipline. You will acquire the appropriate skills to design an experiment, acquire and analyse data, and present your results at a professional research level through writing a report. You will provide an oral defence for each report. This subject is one of four physics subjects at 3rd year level that together constitute the physics major.
learning_outcomes: Design experiments related to essential concepts in contemporary physics using standard physics laboratory techniques, equipment and software.
Compare and interpret research data with reference to the scientific literature.
Analyse and critically review research data.
Describe and explain, in appropriate written and verbal style, the findings from laboratory experiments designed by the student.

title: PHYSICS OF QUANTUM MATTER
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore fundamental quantum physics and apply it to solve problems involving the electronic and thermal properties of matter. You will further develop concepts in classical and modern physics previously considered in PHY2CLP and PHY2MOD. This subject is one of four such subjects at third year level that together constitute the physics major in the Bachelor of Science.
learning_outcomes: Appropriately apply the tools of quantum mechanics to predict the fundamental electronic properties of crystalline systems through the application of the tools of quantum mechanics to systems of condensed matter.
Correctly use the mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics in the context of atomic systems including the use of operators and the Hamiltonian to derive the Schrodinger equation.
Design solutions to complex problems in solid state physics integrating diverse aspects of quantum mechanics.
Use standard technical software to implement computational solutions to problems too complex for analytical mathematical solutions.

title: ATOMS AND QUANTUM OPTICS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will study the quantum description of atomic systems and the electro magnetic wave and apply this to 'real-world' problems. At the completion of this subject you will understand the fundamental physics of the LASER from the perspective of quantum optics, you will also gain an understanding of quantum cryptography, quantum teleportation, and quantum computing. This subject is one of four such subjects at third year level that together constitute the Physics major stream. It provides a solid foundation for honours and a post-graduate research studies in Physics.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, visualise and solve conceptual and mathematical problems in the area of atomic physics and quantum optics.
Implement computational solutions to problems too complex for analytical mathematical solutions.
Generate and communicate solutions to complex problems in the field of atomic physics and quantum optics relating to the quantum nature of the atom-light interactions.

title: SENIOR PHYSICS RESEARCH PROJECT
syllabus_overview: In this subject students are provided with the opportunity to undertake a physics / nanotechnology research project under the supervision of La Trobe University staff or jointly with La Trobe University staff and appropriate outside organisations. Students are encouraged to develop their own interests and may gain experience in areas such as functional materials, quantum materials and X-ray science. The project outcomes will be presented at a seminar at the end of the teaching period.
learning_outcomes: Assess, interpret and explain the scientific findings of the project in some depth, in appropriate academic style, relating the findings to any relevant findings published in appropriate scientific literature, and determining which, if any, of the findings are novel.
Communicate effectively the key concepts and techniques used in completing the research project and the scientific findings in an appropriate scientific manner.
Plan and complete a short research project which involves acquiring, interpreting and explaining scientific findings in an academic or industrial setting.

title: HONOURS IN PHYSICS A
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program is to provide undergraduate students with the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Physics consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part- time) individual research project, supervised by an academic whose research is in the discipline of Physics. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. PHY401A is the first subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in Physics. Students must take PHY401A first.
learning_outcomes: Obtain practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of physics.
Show intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice.
Understand published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Recall knowledge in physics when conducting experiments/simulations, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.
Extend oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.

title: HONOURS IN PHYSICS B
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program is to provide undergraduate students with the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Physics consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part- time) individual research project, supervised by an academic whose research is in the discipline of Physics. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. PHY401B is the second or third subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in Physics. Students must take PHY401A first.
learning_outcomes: Develop intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice.
Develop knowledge in physics when devising experiments/simulations, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.
Analyse published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Build oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Develop practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of physics.

title: MESOSCOPIC NANOSCIENCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore advanced concepts beyond those traditionally taught in condensed matter physics, including modern electronic systems that have arisen primarily through an ability to construct devices on nanometre length-scales and in reduced dimensions. You will examine semi conductor materials and doping, band structure engineering, quantum confinement and electronic transport in wells, wires and dots, quantized conductance and the quantum Hall effect. These will be used to analyse the electronic properties of emerging carbon materials, such as carbon nanotubes, diamond and graphene, and of metallic systems engineered on the atomic scale.
learning_outcomes: Communicate knowledge, skills and ideas to others in the area of mesoscopic condensed matter.
Generate and transmit mathematical solutions to complex problems related to mesoscopic condensed matter.
Critically analyse, evaluate and transform information required to solve problems using quantitative techniques.

title: ADVANCED QUANTUM MECHANICS
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide you with a solid theoretical background in quantum mechanics coupled with practical examples. You will explore the matrix mechanics formalism, perturbation theory, the variational method and virial theorem, and relativistic quantum mechanics. You will develop advanced problem solving techniques, which will be applied to solve complex problems in quantum mechanics.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply problem solving approaches specific to the field of quantum mechanics.
Devise and explain solutions to problems in quantum mechanics in seminar format.
Generate and transmit solutions to complex problems related to quantum mechanics

title: SURFACE AND NANOMATERIAL CHARACTERISATION
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore solid material surfaces and inter faces, which are key to modern manufactured materials and devices. You will investigate the elemental, chemical and molecular properties of materials relevant to adhesion, biocompatibility and environmental protection, sensing and devices . You will investigate industrially important characterisation and data analysis techniques including surface analytical techniques, X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy, Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry, and Auger Electron Spectroscopy, and related synchrotron techniques.
learning_outcomes: Critically review the published scientific literature regarding a given current topic in surface science.
Interpret and analyse data acquired during demonstrations of surface science laboratory experiments in order to demonstrate competence in data analysis
Describe and explain the operation and function of key surface science instrumentation and software.
Demonstrate a professional competence in communicating key findings from experimental investigations and research of the current literature.

title: PHYSICS HONOURS THESIS A
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program is to provide undergraduate students with the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Physics consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part- time) individual research project, supervised by an academic whose research is in the discipline of physics. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. PHY4THA is the second or third subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in Physics. Students must take PHY401A first.
learning_outcomes: Develop advanced oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Demonstrate knowledge in physics when devising experiments/simulations, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.
Compare and contrast published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Develop intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice.
Refine practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of physics.

title: PHYSICS HONOURS THESIS B
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program is to provide undergraduate students with the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Physics consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part- time) individual research project, supervised by an academic whose research is in the discipline of physics. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. PHY4THB is the final subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in Physics. Students must take PHY4THB last
learning_outcomes: Utilise intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice.
Formulate an original research question based on the comprehensive review of published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Apply advanced oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Apply knowledge in physics when devising experiments/simulations, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.
Apply practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of physics.

title: ESSENTIALS OF QUANTUM INFORMATION SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces quantum information science and technology, with a focus on quantum computing, for those who need to understand how it will transform science and industry. Students will learn about underlying physical principles that make quantum computers possible and exponentially faster than digital supercomputers for certain calculations. This knowledge will be applied to consider the implications of this new frontier of computing for cybersecurity and secure communication, information processing, and numerical simulation. No prior knowledge of quantum physics is required. Abstract quantum effects, including superposition and entanglement, will be explored through practical activities that help students understand tangible applications, including encoding quantum information, quantum logic operations and quantum cryptography. Students will then learn to code simple algorithms and execute them on real quantum computers and in simulation environments. The application of key quantum algorithms to real-world problems will be investigated, along with their potential performance advantage over classical algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate key technology requirements for quantum computers to be able to function properly.
Assess quantum algorithms and quantum protocols for application to information processing and communication.
Describe the differences between quantum and classical computation and differentiate their computational capabilities.
Critique the potential for quantum computing to disrupt modern computation, communication and cryptography.

title: X-RAY SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will be introduced to the optics and applications of X-rays, with an emphasis on imaging and synchrotron-source related applications. The major topics that you will encounter include propagation of X-rays in free space, partially coherent fields, interactions of X-rays with matter, X-ray sources, X-ray optics, and synchrotron based applications of X-rays. You will develop advanced problem-solving skills within the weekly problem-solving classes, whereby sophisticated techniques will be modelled in solving practical and computational problems in X-ray physics.
learning_outcomes: Generate and transmit solutions to complex problems related to X-ray physics.
Communicate knowledge, skills and ideas to others in the area of X-ray physics.
Critically analyse, evaluate and transform information to complete a range of practical and analytical activities related to the area of X-ray physics.
Critically evaluate the current relevant peer reviewed literature

title: QUANTUM TECHNOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be introduced to the practical implementations of quantum information technologies. Students will develop an understanding of how to implement quantum computers and other related devices. Students will explore existing and future quantum devices through workshops presented with quantum technology industry partners.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the opportunities and risks of quantum technology for society.
Critique physical realisations of qubits, including methods of initialisation, control and measurement, and sources of decoherence.
Articulate key concepts in quantum technologies
Examine the physical principles and applications of key types of quantum information technology, such as computing, communications and sensing.

title: QUANTUM INFORMATION THEORY FOR COMPUTER SCIENTISTS AND ENGINEERS
syllabus_overview: Recent advances in quantum technology have not only opened up a whole new world of applications, but also changed the way that we understand quantum theory. In this subject, students will learn about quantum theory as a framework for information processing, instead of the traditional approach to learning quantum theory as a theory of microscopic matter. Emphasis will be given to relevant concepts of measurement, probability, correlation and transformations, rather than waves and particles.
learning_outcomes: Investigate how features of quantum systems are related to concepts of information theory.
Critically review differences between classical and quantum information
Critically analyse different aspects of quantum computation, communication and cryptography using the framework of quantum theory.
Elucidate basic problems of quantum information theory.

title: DIRECTED LEARNING IN QUANTUM TECHNOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject provides an opportunity for students to focus on their future career in quantum information technology. Individual students will explore a particular quantum technology platform, with either a technology or business development focus. Students will reflect on the emerging nature of commercialisation in quantum technology. Examples include a detailed study of a particular quantum technology platform; an analysis of the market opportunity for a quantum technology; and the development of a quantum technology start-up concept and pitch.
learning_outcomes: Articulate key concepts in quantum technologies.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the business and social opportunities and risks of quantum technology.
Effectively communicate key concepts, methods, applications or commercial context associated with the selected topic using appropriate scientific or commercial language.
Critically assess current literature relevant to a particular quantum information technology from a scientific or commercial perspective.

title: QUANTUM SOFTWARE
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine quantum programming and quantum algorithm design. Students will be introduced to quantum logic gates, programming platforms and languages. Students will use these to write quantum programs that can be executed using emulators and cloud-based quantum computers. Fundamental quantum algorithms will be studied and implemented. Application of these algorithms for quantum error correction, quantum cryptography and quantum machining learning will be investigated.
learning_outcomes: Implement quantum programs by using quantum hardware emulators and cloud -based quantum computers.
Analyse quantum algorithms.
Design quantum algorithms that are relevant to real-world applications.
Compare performance across classical and quantum approaches to equivalent problems.

title: PHYSICS MASTERS THESIS B
syllabus_overview: Students complete a project that takes the equivalent of six months of continuous work under the supervision of a member of staff. The project is completed and written up as a thesis when the student completes the unit PHY5THB. All students are required to present a seminar outlining the proposed project at a time to be determined by the physics postgraduate coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Assess and interpret the scientific literature relevant to a chosen topic in some depth and plan and execute a scientific investigation in a research environment supported by a member of staff.
Communicate effectively the key concepts, techniques, and research outcomes associated with the research project in an appropriate scientific manner.

title: PODIATRIC PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND ASSESSMENT
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists require high-level understanding of common pathophysiology affecting the foot and ankle, and advanced knowledge and skills in assessment. This subject will firstly extend your understandings of foot and lower limb anatomy, and continue to build your knowledge of the pathogenesis, causal pathways, and clinical presentation and management principles of common medical pathologies of relevance to podiatric practice. Secondly, you will work with the context of podiatric clinical cases, to develop foundation knowledge and skills in the assessment of the podiatric client. This subject will support you to develop your ability to evaluate lower limb neurological and vascular competence, laboratory tests and key diagnostic imaging techniques used in podiatry (i.e. plain film radiographs, musculoskeletal ultrasound, computed tomography, bone scan and magnetic resonance imaging).
learning_outcomes: Select and justify assessments to evaluate lower limb and foot vascular and neurological status.
Discuss pathophysiological changes and causal pathways for common conditions of the foot and ankle.
Select and justify laboratory tests and diagnostic imaging techniques for foot and ankle conditions.
Apply principles of best available evidence and team collaboration skills to explain the pathology and assessment of common foot and ankle conditions in different clinical contexts.
Identify and describe normal and abnormal vascular, neurological, laboratory and diagnostic imaging assessment findings for patients.

title: CUTANEOUS SCIENCE OF THE FOOT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will develop your understanding of the pathology, assessment and management of dermatological conditions of the foot. Podiatrists frequently assess and manage clients with pathology of their skin and nails. You will develop an understanding of the normal anatomy and function of the integumentary system. You will then develop an understanding of the pathophysiological processes involved in development of common dermatological conditions affecting the foot and design intervention programs to effectively manage these conditions. You will engage with online resources, published journal articles, and case studies.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and describe skin anatomy, function and flora.
Explain treatment plans for dermatological conditions of the legs and feet in a culturally capable manner.
Describe the pathological processes that are involved in a range of common skin disorders of the lower limb.

title: PODIATRIC PRACTICE A
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists are required to use clinical skills to manage a variety of foot and ankle conditions. In this foundation clinical practice subject, essential knowledge and skills for safe and effective clinical practice are taught. Specifically, you will learn about basic instrument handling, infection control and safe work principles. This subject will prepare you for the clinical subjects that are delivered later in the course. The concepts will be introduced in workshops and consolidated through virtual clinical experiences. Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure. Your attendance at professional placements will contribute to meeting this requirement for professional recognition as a podiatrist. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Apply safe work principles to ensure safe clinical practice and engage in team collaboration to develop interpersonal skills and working strategies.
Perform manual clinical tasks in the management of simulated patients requiring basic foot and ankle care.
Describe the purpose and use of podiatry equipment used in clinical environments.

title: PODIATRIC POPULATIONS A
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists require knowledge and understanding of the complex issues and specific needs related to the management of paediatric, geriatric and indigenous patients relevant to podiatry practice. In this subject, students will learn about the specific needs of these population groups and issues that may affect their care management, including the potential role of other health professionals. Students will discuss factors relating to effective translation of health care information to paediatric, geriatric and Indigenous patients and their carers. Students will engage with online resources, published journal articles, case studies and face-to-face workshops, to acquire skills and knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Discuss factors relating to effective translation of health care information to paediatric, geriatric and Indigenous patients and their carers.
Outline the specific needs of paediatric, geriatric and Indigenous populations that may affect their management.
Collaborate as a member of a team, including the potential referral to other health professionals or services, to achieve shared goals in the care of a paediatric, geriatric and Indigenous patient.
Summarise complex social and physical issues relevant to podiatric practice for paediatric, geriatric and Indigenous populations.

title: PODIATRIC PRACTICE B
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists are required to use clinical skills to manage a variety of foot and ankle conditions. In this subject, you will extend your clinical knowledge and skills to the management of patients with foot and ankle conditions requiring introductory podiatric care. This subject will prepare you for the clinical subjects that are delivered later in the course. In addition, you will describe knowledge related to the prescription of foot orthoses. Specifically, you will be introduced to the use of foot orthoses to manage foot and ankle conditions and consolidate knowledge regarding the management of common dermatological conditions. The concepts will be introduced in tutorials and consolidated by managing patients in the Health Sciences Clinic. Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure. Your attendance at professional placements will contribute to meeting this requirement for professional recognition as a podiatrist. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Explain the aim and mechanism of foot orthoses as part of treatment plans.
Select and explain assessment techniques and differential diagnoses for patients requiring basic foot and ankle care.
Explain the management of basic foot and ankle conditions.
Discuss and summarise the patients presenting complaints and medical history
Perform manual clinic tasks in the management of patients requiring basic foot and ankle care.

title: PODIATRIC PRACTICE C
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists are required to assess, diagnose and manage patients with a variety of foot and ankle conditions. In this subject students will continue to develop manual clinical skills, while learning to select and justify assessment techniques to diagnose foot and ankle conditions. Students will be guided to apply frameworks to enable them to implement management plans for patients with introductory podiatric foot and ankle conditions. Specifically, students will build on their knowledge of foot orthoses to manage foot and ankle conditions and common musculoskeletal conditions. This subject will prepare students for the clinical subjects that are delivered later in the course. The concepts will be introduced in workshops and consolidated by managing patients in the Health Sciences Clinic. Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure. Students' attendance at professional placements will contribute to meeting this requirement for professional recognition as a podiatrist. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate safe work principles during clinical practice and when manufacturing foot orthoses.
Implement strategies to communicate in a safe and effective manner with patients, family/carers, and other health professionals.
Perform manual clinical skills, in a safe and effective manner, to manage patients requiring basic foot and ankle care.
Demonstrate critical thinking and reflective clinical practice.
Outline and demonstrate assessment techniques to inform management plans for patients requiring basic foot and ankle care
Apply knowledge to prescribe and manufacture foot orthoses to inform management plans for patients requiring basic foot and ankle care

title: PODIATRIC BIOMECHANICS
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists require knowledge and understanding of foot and ankle biomechanics related to the clinical management of patients. In this subject students will be supported to develop an understanding of podiatric biomechanics. Authentic clinical cases and enquiry-based activities will be used to develop their understanding of the role of podiatric biomechanics in commonly encountered conditions in the context of evidence-based practice. Students will engage with online resources, published journal articles, case studies and face-to-face workshops, to acquire skills and knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Perform biomechanical assessments of the lower limb and foot and explain the rationale for the procedures.
Analyse the findings of biomechanical assessments and interpret the implications for podiatric care.
Justify the selection of biomechanical assessments of the lower limb and foot.
Apply best available evidence in the collaborative management of patients that takes account of their individual biomechanics.

title: THE HIGH-RISK FOOT
syllabus_overview: This subject prepares students for initial supervised clinical practice with patients who present with medical conditions, such as diabetes mellitus, which result in a significantly higher risk of serious lower leg and foot complications developing. Through exploration of the pathophysiological processes involved in development of the clinical complications, including chronic ulceration, serious infection and lower limb amputation caused by altered vascular, neurological and/or mechanical status, students will gain skills in applying knowledge and evidence to clinical cases. Management of wounds that occur in high-risk feet is emphasised. Students will engage with online resources, published journal articles, case studies and face-to-face workshops, to acquire skills and knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse assessments required for diagnosis and classification of patients with, or at risk of, complications from the high-risk foot.
Devise and evaluate wound management plans for chronic ulceration arising from complications of the high-risk foot.
Reflect on professional practice and best available evidence to ensure contemporary care in high-risk foot practice.
Generate management plans for patients with, or at risk of, complications from the high-risk foot.
Explain the physical, psychological and social effects for patients, their families and community, of the high-risk foot.

title: MUSCULOSKELETAL PATHOLOGY FOR PODIATRISTS
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists frequently assess and manage clients with lower limb musculoskeletal pathology. In this subject you will extend your understanding of anatomy, pathophysiology and biomechanics of the musculoskeletal system by describing the pathophysiology and explaining the risk factors for common lower limb musculoskeletal injuries. You will then apply concepts of physical assessment to accurately diagnose lower limb musculoskeletal pathology and design intervention programs to effectively manage common lower limb musculoskeletal pathologies. You will engage with online resources, published journal articles, case studies and face-to-face workshops, to acquire skills and knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Create intervention programs to manage common lower limb musculoskeletal pathologies seen in podiatric practice using best available evidence and critical thinking.
Diagnose common lower limb musculoskeletal conditions seen in podiatric practice using an evidence based, culturally responsive, and person-centred approach
Describe the aetiology and pathophysiology of common lower limb musculoskeletal conditions seen in podiatric practice.

title: PODIATRIC PRACTICE D
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists are required to assess, diagnose and manage a variety of foot and ankle conditions. In this subject, you will extend your clinical knowledge and consolidate your clinical skills to manage patients with foot and ankle conditions requiring intermediate podiatric care (patients with diabetes and musculoskeletal complaints, deemed at higher risk). You will apply previous clinical skills and knowledge through managing patients in the Health Sciences Clinic and observe patients requiring podiatric care while attending an external placement. This subject will prepare you for the clinical subjects that are delivered later in the course. In this subject, you will be seeing a variety of patients and conditions, consolidating your clinical reasoning and patient management skills. Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure. Your attendance at professional placements will contribute to meeting this requirement for professional recognition as a podiatrist. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Apply effective, culturally responsive and person-centred podiatry assessments and demonstrate results to develop a diagnosis and differential diagnoses.
Critically reflect on clinical performance to improve ongoing practice. Demonstrate critical thinking and reflective clinical practice.

Identify risks and demonstrate safe work principles to ensure safety (including cultural safety) and quality of practice that complies with legal, regulatory and professional requirements, responsibilities and guidelines.

Interpret information from patients presenting complaints and medical history, choose a management plan, demonstrate appropriate treatment and demonstrate safe and effective communication to both patients and other health professionals.

title: PODIATRIC POPULATIONS B
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists require knowledge and understanding of complex issues and specific needs related to the management of paediatric, physically-active and surgical patients relevant to podiatry practice. In this subject, students will be taught to further develop their skills in podiatric treatments, therapy, intervention techniques and patient management in paediatric patients, physically-active individuals and those requiring advanced foot and ankle surgery. Clinical reasoning and management skills when working with these patient groups will be explored, as will an understanding of evidence-based practice and enquiry-based learning as a number of complex clinical scenarios presenting to the podiatry clinic are investigated. Students will engage with online resources, published journal articles, case studies and face-to-face workshops, to acquire skills and knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Clearly and coherently communicate health care information to diverse populations
Analyse and synthesise complex issues related to paediatric, physically-active and surgical patients.
Collaborate as a member of a team, including the potential referral to other health professionals, to achieve shared goals in the care of a paediatric, physically­ active and surgical patients.
Formulate, recommend and evaluate clear evidence-based management plans to meet the specific needs of paediatric, physically-active and surgical patients.

title: PODIATRIC PHARMACOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists require knowledge and understanding of pharmacological management, to provide safe clinical practice and improve patient outcomes. In this subject, you will extend your understanding of therapeutics and pharmacology by comparing and contrasting authentic clinical cases and reflecting on teaching and learning activities Relevant to evidence-based pharmacological management. You will apply pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacological guidelines to prescribe schedule 2, 3 & 4 medicines available to podiatrists. This will occur under the guidance of podiatrists who are endorsed to prescribe scheduled medicines. In addition, you will use a person-centred approach to evaluate adverse effects and potential complications of medicines, understand the importance of reviewing the outcome of medicines prescribed, and communicating with patients and members of the patient's healthcare team. You will learn how to administer foot injections safely and effectively. This will prepare you for clinical experiences delivered later in the course.
learning_outcomes: Outline effective strategies to communicate the agreed treatment decisions and outcomes of treatment with patients, carers, and health professionals.
Outline legal, regulatory frameworks, and guidelines for prescribing as an endorsed podiatrist, including standards from the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care.
Apply a person-centred approach to collaboratively agree on treatment plans, prescribe medicines, and review the outcome of treatment for patients from specific populations.
Administer injections safely and effectively for the surgical and therapeutic management of conditions of the foot and ankle.
Critically examine the classification, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, indications and contraindications, and adverse effects of different medicines available to endorsed podiatrists.
Compare evidence-based sources to identify, review, and tailor the prescription of medicines based on person-specific factors.

title: EVIDENCE-BASED PRACTICE IN HEALTH
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists use the best available evidence to manage patients in practice. In this subject you will build on the skills developed in previous subjects related to evidence-based practice to produce a critical appraisal of a topic at a level that is suitable for publication. This resource will also be peer reviewed, with you applying evidence-based practice skills by critically appraising the work of other students. Doing so will further develop skills to perform evidence-based practice, whilst gaining a greater understanding of the peer review process and contributing to a valuable evidence-based resource. You will engage with key databases, scholarly information, and evidence appraisal tools to critically appraise a topic.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate clinical knowledge and identify gaps to adapt for best available evidence.
Critically reflect on and apply professional behaviours to productively participate in group situations.
Critically appraise the methodology of study designs to determine the relative weight of evidence of effectiveness.
Critically review the strengths and weaknesses in evidence based practice steps to develop more efficient processes
Integrate findings from research to formulate answers to clinically focused research questions

title: PODIATRIC PRACTICE E
syllabus_overview: Podiatrists are required to assess, diagnose and manage a variety of foot and ankle conditions. In this subject, you will further extend your clinical knowledge and consolidate your clinical skills to manage patients with foot and ankle conditions requiring intermediate podiatric care (e.g. patients with higher risk status of developing lower limb amputations, musculoskeletal and biomechanical issues) through consulting with patients in the Health Sciences Clinic and observe patients requiring podiatric care while attending an external placement. This subject will prepare you for the clinical subjects that are delivered later in the course. In this subject, you will further develop your clinical reasoning and patient management skills. Professional accreditation requires a minimum level of clinical exposure.
