learning_outcomes: Critically assess and communicate current knowledge regarding the epidemiology, clinical assessment, diagnosis, management, and rehabilitation of different sporting injuries.
Critically reflect on knowledge and clinical expertise to provide leadership to peers and/or the community related to sport and exercise physiotherapy.
Provide expert guidance to peers on how to apply current research evidence on the causes, treatment, and prevention of sports injuries across the lifecycle.
Develop engaging written, visual and presentation content to facilitate knowledge translation of evidence in sport and exercise physiotherapy practice to peers and/or the community.

title: ADVANCED ISSUES IN HEALTH AND WELLBEING RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: You will study and analyse content presented in three main modules - Past, Present and Futures - and relate these to your Master or Doctoral research proposal through individual and class activities and assessment tasks. You will contextualise your research topic historically and in relation to contemporary and emerging trends and issues and future scenarios. You will advance your understanding of population health and wellbeing paradigms, eras, grand challenges, key events, concepts, values, frameworks, systems, practices and tools. You will critically explore the roles of government and other institutions, healthcare and other sectors, various disciplines and professions and communities and citizens in public health analysis, advocacy and action. This subject is designed to complement research training subjects by providing continuous opportunities for you to further develop aspects of your research proposal, including its significance, key questions, methodology and ethical dimensions. You will explore ways to optimise the relevance of your research project and its potential impact on people, environments and systems. To support your development as leaders in your profession, sector, organisation and/or field of practice, you will gain basic skills in futures literacy and professionalise your oral, written and audio-visual presentation skills in order to effectively communicate research to interdisciplinary audiences.
learning_outcomes: Create a strategy for how you will use your research project, experience and skills to develop leadership in your profession, sector, organisation and/or field of practice.
Apply skills for developing and delivering professional-quality presentations.

Generate an approach to strengthening the significance, focus, methodology and ethical dimensions of your research project to optimize its potential contribution to socio-ecological health and wellbeing.

Critically analyse public health paradigms, eras and key events; historical developments in public health concepts, values, frameworks, systems, practices and tools; contemporary challenges for socio-ecological health and wellbeing and approaches to change; and health futures.

title: SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND EVALUATION OF HEALTH RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: In this subject, graduate researchers develop a detailed protocol for a systematic review of research literature on a health-related topic relevant to their field. The subject is particularly beneficial for students commencing graduate research degrees. You will undertake background work to justify your systematic review, construct and refine a review question, design a comprehensive search for relevant research literature, designed unbiased methods to select and evaluate the research literature, and select appropriate methods for the extraction and synthesis of data from the included studies. You will work closely with your thesis supervisor and the subject coordinator as required.
learning_outcomes: Write a systematic review protocol in an academic writing style.
Identify relevant literature, develop a search strategy and formulate and refine a review question.
Justify the need for systematic / literature reviews and demonstrate an understanding of various types of literature reviews.
Extract data from a published study and critically appraise potential biases.

title: METHODS FOR GRADUATE RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn how to develop and refine research questions select appropriate research designs and develop analyses for quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods studies. This subject is designed specifically for Graduate Researchers, therefore emphasis will be placed on evaluating the appropriateness of research questions, and associated methods and analysis for their research thesis.
learning_outcomes: Formulate research questions and plan and justify research methods that answer them. and research plans
Select, plan and justify data exploration and analysis techniques suitable for research questions
Critique and evaluate different research methods related to quantitative, qualitative and mixed methodologies

title: FOUNDATIONS OF GRADUATE RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will learn about the epistemology of research and the theoretical constructs in developing an ethical research question. This subject is designed for students commencing a graduate research degree, and will provide you with an opportunity to develop literature searching skills necessary to undertake graduate research. The subject will enhance your knowledge of the varied philosophical underpinnings and methodological approaches to conceiving and designing research.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the ethical conduct of research including plagiarism and the importance of the appropriateness of the research question.
Assess the major philosophical and methodological debates that frame contemporary research practice.
Efficiently source manage, critique and reference authoritative literature using relevant library tools, to identify important theoretical and empirical contributions to your area of research.
Apply your own research question/context in the exploration of coursework theory

title: INDUSTRY PLACEMENT
syllabus_overview: The industry placement provides students opportunities to consolidate knowledge and enhance skills developed throughout the course in addition to gaining perspectives and skills essential for employment in the industry. Practical experiences and application of scientific and business theory in a commercial agricultural environment will assist students to critically evaluate technical and generic aspects of the agricultural sector as required by employers and the broader industry. These include not only an understanding of seasonal and other agricultural processes necessary for human food production but also management, operational and administrative requirements of an enterprise. Students will be required to understand and demonstrate safe work practices, initiative and the capacity to work independently in a team environment. The placement will provide opportunities for students to create a portfolio that is relevant to a career in a rapidly changing industry.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the organisational structure, management practices and operations in the context of the broader industry
Demonstrate safe work practices and an awareness of environmental and ethical issues
Prepare and arrange evidence of experiences and skills to create a career portfolio
Apply and critically evaluate technical and generic skills in relation to those required by the employer and the broader industry
Work independently and collaboratively as a member of a team

title: ECOLOGICAL SYSTEMS
syllabus_overview: This subject will develop and expand student knowledge and skills in ecological systems that are considered essential to an understanding of agricultural science, including its practical application and its relationship to the surrounding environment. A healthy ecological system is a key indicator of a sustainable environment. Students will explore biotic and abiotic components of ecosystems and the interactive processes between them. Topics include: the physicochemical characteristics of water and their biological applications and implications; the principles and concepts of aquatic science; aquatic ecosystems such as lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams and coastal habitats; energy flows in food chains and nutrient cycles in natural and agro ecosystems; soil origin and formation; soil physical description; , soil chemistry; and soil carbon and organic matter.
learning_outcomes: Identify different ecosystems and develop techniques used for sampling and monitoring their health
Identify ecological concepts, including ecosystem components, interactive processes, nutrient cycling and energy flow
Evaluate and interpret physical, chemical and biological parameters of soil and water, for purposes of sound management of agro-ecological systems.
Describe the relationship between physicochemical parameters of soil and water and environmental health

title: BAD SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: We are increasingly faced with controversial debates occurring in our media, with different groups arguing their viewpoints, and the scientific evidence is often swamped by misreporting or distorted evidence. This subject uses a case-based approach to examine the evidence underpinning current topics of debate, and to investigate what is meant by evidence looking at the scientific process, peer-review, and the possible motivations behind research (and reporting of research), including examples of where the process has failed. You will gain experience in analysing different sides of an argument and explaining your findings in different formats for different audiences.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the key factors which influence the reproducibility of scientific arguments research.
Analyse the ethical and social implications of 'bad science'.
Analyse case studies to distinguish between good and poor scientific practice and evidence.
Identify our inherent limitations in reasoning and psychology which make us susceptible to pathological science.

title: BIG IDEAS IN SCIENCE: LIFE, THE UNIVERSE AND EVERYTHING
syllabus_overview: What happened during the first microseconds of the universe? Why is the cosmos filled with galaxies, stars and planets? How did that lead to life on earth? How do we know what happened and when? Why is all life built from cells using information in DNA? Why does it matter? How does this tie into cutting-edge research at La Trobe and internationally? The big ideas of science are a set of cross-cutting concepts that are fundamental to our understanding of the world around us - and how science works. In this subject, you will be introduced to these concepts, which link seemingly different phenomena via fundamental principles and laws of nature and form the basis of the major scientific disciplines. Using cutting-edge research as examples, you will see how scientific evidence is produced, and how that can lead to controversy, conflict - and scientific progress.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the social nature of science, ethics in science, and scientific progress.
Work independently and collaboratively in teams
Communicate basic scientific ideas clearly in written and oral formats
Illustrate how scientific knowledge is generated and used
Demonstrate academic integrity by appropriately acknowledging sources of information
Apply basic understanding of big ideas in science across a range of disciplines

title: PLANT PHYSIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will consolidate and extend your knowledge of plants and plant physiology, and examine the impact of, and interactions between, components of crop production. You will study the biological processes occurring in plants at a cellular level from seedling emergence to maturity. Through theory and experimentation you will develop an understanding of the impacts on plant physiology and growth of natural and artificial influences. You will use the knowledge gained through lectures and experiments to develop a management plan for a crop, vine or pasture production system.
learning_outcomes: Describe how plants function and identify the ways in which environmental factors can influence plant physiology and growth
Describe the basic terminology of plant morphology, taxonomy and physiology
Apply physiological processes of plant growth to a plant production system for a selected crop, pasture or vineyard
Produce and present plans to manage plant nutrition using language suitable for a professional audience

title: STATISTICS AND EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
syllabus_overview: This subject will provide an introduction to statistical concepts and techniques and the application of statistics in management and decision making in a variety of primary industries contexts. You will develop a practical knowledge of selected statistical concepts, theories and methodologies including an understanding of experimental design and sampling techniques within a management context for a range of primary industries. You will develop practical skills in basic statistical analysis techniques to interpret, transform, manipulate and present data. This includes the use of statistical software to analyse and interpret sample data summaries and draw inferences that inform enterprise and industry decision-makers. An understanding of and the ability to use appropriate terminology will assist students to develop confidence in presenting findings and in-turn enhance future career opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Interpret results of statistical analyses and report the conclusions in a clear and comprehensible manner
Select and perform appropriate basic statistical methods, such as confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, regression and ANOVA
Apply fundamental concepts of data, population and samples, measures of central tendency, variability and dispersion, probabilities and normal distribution
Describe concepts of experimental design and identify the effect of design on interpretation of results
Summarise data and present statistical findings appropriately using correct terminology

title: SCIENCE PROJECT
syllabus_overview: In this subject, the student undertakes a semester-long research or development project related to his or her major studies under the guidance of an academic supervisor. The student will solve a given problem with creativity and imagination and will develop new ideas about an aspect of their chosen field and how to manage and communicate these. They will achieve this by applying theory, locating or creating new knowledge and synthesising it along with their results into a project report. Many problems in science are multi-disciplinary, thus students will experience the needs and benefits of collaboration and net-working across discipline boundaries to gain insight into the process of working as a scientist. Developing the ability to tackle problems creatively, generate new ideas, and take calculated risks supports students to create change to achieve ambitions - now and in the future.
learning_outcomes: Formally present research findings to peers and academics clearly and coherently.
Critically evaluate scientific literature relating to a specialist area of science research, identify existing gaps and justify the need to address these.
Investigate research questions independently and collaboratively in creative and innovative ways that are based on sound scientific principles.

Analyse, evaluate and synthesise information obtained through independent and collaborative research to prepare reports that reflect broad theoretical and technical knowledge and skills in a specialist science area.

title: ADVANCED INDUSTRY PLACEMENT
syllabus_overview: This extended industry placement subject provides you with opportunities to develop their technical/applied, discipline specific and professional skills with the aim to enhance you career prospects. You will be responsible for identifying a suitable work placement prior to the semester with support of the Subject Coordinator and online materials. Industry experience can be gained in Australia or overseas for most disciplines. You will conduct a course-related original project, in an appropriate format that demonstrates analytical, research and problem-solving skills relevant to the sector. You will identify and articulate your knowledge and skills and apply them to relevant contexts and work-settings. You will be encouraged via self-awareness to evaluate the strengths required to facilitate a future role in your chosen career, develop curriculum vitae and resumes, creates professional digital profile via platforms such as LinkedIn, gain an understanding of industry and professional networks and develop interview skills. These skills will allow you to devlop a detailed career plan.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively in written format to a wide range of stakeholders.
Demonstrate self-awareness through active reflection evaluation and comparison.
Demonstrate and apply safe work practices and an awareness of environmental and ethical issues in a workplace
Apply problem-solving skills and knowledge to common workplace issues through a process of justification and critique, and show initiative in finding potential solutions

title: INTRODUCTION TO RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: In the first module of this subject, you will be introduced to the scientific process and the ethical and regulatory requirements underpinning research. You will critically analyse case-studies where misreporting or fraudulent science has occurred. In the second module, you will learn about the scientific publishing process and develop critical thinking skills that are required for a variety of research activities. Finally, you will explore some foundations of scientific communication practice communicating in different media. You will learn necessary practical skills and techniques to bring complex ideas to life for expert and generalist audiences.
learning_outcomes: Analyse different scientific approaches to answering research questions, considering their theory, use and limits.
Apply science communication principles to communicate scientific ideas orally and in writing to general scientific audiences.
Interpret and compare scientific information from multiple sources within a scientific discipline, with guidance.
Critique approaches to investigating problems and testing solutions with understanding of ethical principles and constraints.

title: HONOURS IN HEALTH AND EDUCATION A
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program in the School of Agriculture, Biomedicine and Environment (SABE) is to provide undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Science Education consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part-time) individual research project, supervised by a SABE academic whose research is in the discipline of science education. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. The School Honours coordinator will provide more information on the application process including a comprehensive list of available research projects. SCI401A is the first subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in SABE. Students must take SCI401A first.
learning_outcomes: Extend oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Understand published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Show intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice.
Recall knowledge in science education when conducting experiments, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.
Obtain practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of science education.

title: HONOURS IN HEALTH AND EDUCATION B
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The aim of the Honours program in the School of Agriculture, Biomedicine and Environment (SABE) is to provide undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program intends to impart undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Honours in Science Education consists of a one year (full-time) or two years (part-time) individual research project, supervised by a SABE academic whose research is in the discipline of science education. Students can commence either in February or July. Students should consult with potential supervisors during their final undergraduate year and will only be accepted into the subject with the written support from a willing supervisor. The School Honours coordinator will provide more information on the application process including a comprehensive list of available research projects. SCI401B is the second or third subject of a 90CP research component for Honours in SABE. Students must take SCI401A first.
learning_outcomes: Build oral communication skills to present knowledge and ideas to audiences including individuals with and without detailed specialist expertise.
Analyse published scientific information and acquired data and communicate this to a scientific audience in written form.
Develop intellectual independence through responsibility and accountability for own learning and practice
Develop practical experience and advanced knowledge in the field of science education.
Develop knowledge in science education when devising experiments, analysing results, and drawing conclusions.

title: HONOURS IN SCIENCE EDUCATION C
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and have fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree, with a major in a relevant discipline. The Bachelor of Science (Honours) program provides undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program imparts undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Under supervision of a La Trobe University academic, you will formulate a research question, conduct a research study, and write a research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words in which you demonstrate the capacity to make an original contribution to your discipline. SCI401C is the first subject of a sequence of two subjects in which students undertake a research project in science education and write a thesis. You must complete SCI401C before SCI401D.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and integrate scientific information from diverse sources to support reasoned arguments in the science education discipline.
Communicate scientific ideas clearly and effectively to scientific audiences, demonstrating sound use of disciplinary conventions.
Apply advanced knowledge and technical skills in science education to address research questions, with guidance.
Demonstrate intellectual initiative and sound judgement in planning and executing scholarly activities with guidance.

title: CAREER OPTIONS AND PROFESSIONAL IDENTITY
syllabus_overview: This subject supports you to be “career ready” for your professional journey. This subject is designed to help you navigate your career paths and develop a strong professional identity. Through guided activities and reflective practice, you will assess your personal competencies and identify areas for improvement. You will explore various career options, set personal career objectives, and conduct thorough career research to understand the opportunities and challenges in your fields of interest. Additionally, you will learn to articulate your professional capabilities using industry-standard language, preparing you to present yourself effectively to prospective employers.
learning_outcomes: Undertake career research and analyse opportunities and challenges in pursuing careers in areas of interest
Assess personal competencies and identify competency gaps through reflective practice.
Articulate personal professional capabilities to prospective employers using professional language
Reflect on career path options and articulate personal career objectives

title: HONOURS IN SCIENCE EDUCATION D
syllabus_overview: Honours is a fourth year of undergraduate study offered to students who demonstrate academic success and have fulfilled the requirements of a Bachelors degree with a major in a relevant discipline. The Bachelor of Science (Honours) program provides undergraduate students the opportunity to gain first-class practical, field, and/or theoretical expertise in a major area of scientific study. Moreover, the program imparts undergraduate students with professional skills that extend their career opportunities. Under supervision of a La Trobe University academic, you will formulate a research question, conduct a research study, and write a research thesis of 12,000 to 15,000 words in which you demonstrate the capacity to make an original contribution to your discipline. SCI401D is the final subject of a sequence of two subjects in which students undertake a research project in science education and write a thesis. You must complete SCI401D last.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate independent and reflective learning and scholarly practice with ethical and academic integrity.
Apply advanced knowledge and technical skills in science education to address research questions.
Justify approaches used to investigate problems by drawing on advanced knowledge and evidence in the science education discipline.
Communicate complex scientific ideas orally and in writing to scientific audiences, demonstrating knowledge of scholarly conventions in the science education discipline.
Critically evaluate, interpret and synthesise scientific information in the science education discipline.

title: SOCIETY AND CULTURE: AN INTRODUCTION TO SOCIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: Every society has its own dominant norms, expectations, and assumptions about the ‘good life’ and the ‘right’ ways to behave in our everyday lives. In this engaging and accessible introductory subject, open to all students, we challenge these views by demonstrating how ‘common sense’ claims are always open to debate. For example, is the ‘Australian Dream’ a reality? Is Australia really ‘the Lucky Country’ and an egalitarian society, where everybody gets ‘a fair go’? Can anybody succeed in Australia, and who is left behind? This subject examines these fundamental questions about inequality, power, and our different ‘life chances’, as well as the question of how we sustain social cohesion and meaningful lives amid ongoing cultural, political, economic, and technological change. We explore this through exciting and relevant case studies on consumption, technology, health, gender, sexuality, race, ethnicity, class, status, age, migration, education, religion, popular culture and more. By questioning taken for granted assumptions about Australian society, we can exercise our ‘sociological imagination’ to see our social worlds in new ways. These analytical capabilities in seeing possibilities for change are crucial in practically all vocations. This subject thus not only enables you to see your daily life in new ways, but will equip you with valuable research, problem-solving, and critical thinking skills vital for future employment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sociological understanding of social relationships and institutions, patterns of social diversity and inequality, and the processes that underpin social change and stability
Adapt sociological theories, concepts and evidence to analysis of local and global issues
Evaluate diverse sociological evidence, positions and arguments
Critically review, analyse, summarise and synthesise sociological scholarship including quantitative and qualitative data

title: YOUNG PEOPLE IN A CHANGING WORLD: SOCIOLOGY IN ACTION
syllabus_overview: In this online or in-person introductory subject, open to all students, we explore how rapid social change in recent years has transformed the lives of young people. This subject traces and illuminates the social forces that are reshaping how we live, work, consume, and relate, and how we might meaningfully respond to these changes in pursuit of social justice, inclusion, and imagining alternative worlds. Specifically, we will explore how sociologists apply their insights to a range of everyday settings. How do sociologists work to create solutions to some of the most pressing challenges facing young people today, such as: homelessness and poverty; persistent gendered and racialized inequalities; the mental health crisis among young people; algorithmic bias and misinformation on social media; insecure work and exploitation in the workplace; and fostering sustainable, liveable worlds? Each week we will explore how sociologists tackle these fundamental real-world problems of identity, belonging, security, and care. A key skill for sociologists is to communicate their research in accessible and engaging ways. Therefore, students will be tasked with creatively responding to contemporary social issues of their choosing. This subject addresses topical issues of urgent relevance and is suitable as an elective for all students (no pre-requisites must be met).
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate diverse sociological evidence, positions, and arguments
Present complex and sustained arguments exploring contemporary social issues from a sociological perspective
Apply sociological theories, concepts, and empirical evidence to the analysis of social change

title: SOCIOLOGY OF EMOTIONS
syllabus_overview: Emotions are embedded in an individual's personal, biological and psychological experience of self, and in relationships with others. Emotionality, or the experience and expression of emotions, is fundamental to an individual's identity and more generally to the practices and tone of everyday social life. In this subject, we consider emotions as phenomena that are intimately experienced, socially contextualised, and culturally learned. Our inquiry leads us to explore particular realms of emotional experience from small-scale interactions to broader relationships between individuals, groups and society. The subject is organised around three modules: the emotional self; love; and suffering and sympathy.
learning_outcomes: Summarise research and arguments on a specific topic in the sociology of emotions.
Explain key concepts and theories in the sociology of emotions.
Apply sociological concepts to examine the experience and expression of emotions.

title: FAMILIES, INTIMACY AND SOCIAL CHANGE: THE SOCIOLOGY OF RELATIONSHIPS
syllabus_overview: Families and relationships continue to be a central part of our everyday lives, yet how we relate and how we 'do' family is changing as a result of rapid social, cultural, technological and other changes. In this subject, you will explore how and why relationships are changing, from our most intimate bonds to our casual acquaintances, from families and friends to pets and treasured possessions. You will consider the role of media representations, government policies and emotions in shaping the relationships we value and seek to protect. From recent shifts in online dating and same-sex marriage, through to expectations of parenting and grandparenting, and norms of pet ownership and friendship, we examine a wide range of current issues related to love and care, distance and loss, loneliness and connection. Examples from Australia and around the world are used to help think critically and analytically about the role of cultural diversity and social change in relationships, both within and beyond the family, and in relation to new technologies.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness of individualisation as a social theory for understanding contemporary relationships
Analyse contemporary social issues relevant to families and relationships
Analyse the key changes in contemporary families and/or relationships

title: REVOLUTIONARY IDEAS IN SOCIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: In this subject we meet some of the most provocative and revolutionary thinkers who have changed the way we understand things like power, gender, class, race and capitalism. Beginning with Marx’s Communist Manifesto we work our way from the 19th century to the present day, exploring groundbreaking explanations of the modern social world such as de Beauvoir’s Second Sex and Foucault’s Discipline and Punish. Each week you’ll be introduced to some of the big debates in Sociology: Can we escape the influence of gender norms, or is sex destiny? Are we slaves to our mobile devices or has the online revolution led to more freedom? Is equality possible in a capitalist society? You are invited to join these critical conversations. This subject will make you see yourself and your place in the world differently, whilst providing insight into some of the most pressing social problems in today’s neoliberal societies, including loneliness and social isolation, lack of meaningful work, and surveillance technologies.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical and cultural awareness to issues in sociology
Apply a sociological perspective to local and global issues, considering the implications for economic, social, political and cultural systems
Articulate and evaluate key sociological concepts and debates
Produce a well-researched and complex written argument relevant to a topic in Sociology
Evaluate diverse arguments regarding a relevant topic in Sociology

title: MIND, "MADNESS" AND SOCIETY: AN INTRODUCTION TO THE SOCIOLOGY OF MENTAL ILLNESS
syllabus_overview: Do you ever wonder why mental health has become such a big issue in today’s society? And why we seem to have an epidemic of anxiety and depression, and ADHD? Or why there are such high rates of suicide among males in rural areas and psychological distress experienced by Indigenous people, refugees, and young people? In this subject, we will explore the history of different social responses to mental illness; the expansion in diagnosable mental disorders; inequalities in mental health related to class, gender, Indigeneity, age, and other markers of difference; subjective experiences of mental illness; family caregiving practices; and the rise of the “happiness industry”. Our examination of these topics is organised around several key questions: Can we claim that people are more distressed today than in previous generations? If so, is this linked to particular changes in our social and material conditions, or to how we define and respond to mental illness and emotional suffering? Are we getting better at supporting neurodiverse persons? Or do assumptions around ‘normality’ still constrain forms of recognition and belonging? We will use a broad range of sociological studies to build an understanding of the social causes and consequences of mental illness, and an awareness of lived experience perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate awareness of lived experience of mental ill-health and family care-giving.
Summarise and evaluate research and arguments on a specific topic in the sociology of mental health and illness at the appropriate level
Apply sociological concepts to understanding and analysing mental health and illness.
Critically analyse key concepts and theories in the sociology of mental health and illness.

title: MIGRATION, MULTICULTURALISM AND RACIALISATION: IDENTITIES IN CONTEXT
syllabus_overview: What do we mean when we talk about our identities, about who we are as individuals, and as members of ethnic, racialized, Indigenous, religious, national or transnational communities? Sociology can help us to understand how our identities are shaped by economic, social and political relations in specific places and historical settings. This subject explores different perspectives on identities as ‘fixed’ or ‘given’, as ‘in flux’ or freely chosen. Migration can disrupt and transform identities, but in what ways do we change, or stay the same, when we move between different countries and contexts? What are the impacts of living in a settler-colonial society such as Australia? What does multiculturalism mean? Is it a myth or an everyday reality? How can we think about ‘race’ in contemporary societies, and how does it relate to racism and ‘whiteness’? What role can anti-racist activism play in bringing about meaningful change? Drawing upon your own lived experiences, these are just some of the questions that you will explore in this subject.
learning_outcomes: Contribute critically to current public debates on contested social issues, drawing on social scientific evidence
Critically apply sociological theory to social issues and changes related to migration and multiculturalism in Australia and other contexts.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of key sociological concepts such as ethnicity, identity, race, racism, multiculturalism, nation.
Identify, understand and analyse key issues, theories and debates related to racial, ethnic and national identities in Australian and other contexts.

title: THE POLITICS OF PLAY: CONTEMPORARY ISSUES IN SPORTS, GAMES, AND LEISURE
syllabus_overview: Sport, games, and play are a part of everyday life. Formal or informal, solitary or shared, physical or virtual, organised or spontaneous, high stakes or 'just for fun', games are a means of escaping the ‘real’ world or exploring it in new ways. Our shared values can be demonstrated through play, either by celebrating those we deem to be ‘good sports’ or shaming those who don’t play ‘in the spirit of the game’. But how are these norms of ‘fair play’ shaped, by whom, and how can they change over time? How can urban sports such as skateboarding and parkour be seen as ‘subversive’ and framed as a public menace, and yet offer opportunities for personal expression and communal belonging? How are video games shaping new understandings of both fun and competitive interactions, and how are e-sports influencing the future of play? Meanwhile, more ‘traditional’ forms of sport are undoubtedly among the most influential in Australian society. No less than three Australian Test cricket captains and tennis players have been recognised as Australian of the Year. Prime Ministers and other political leaders desperately promote their support of popular teams to make themselves relatable, and Victoria has not one, but two public holidays dedicated solely to sporting events. But why is this the case? Why does sport seem to possess such an enormous influence in Australian society? Sport can unite us and foster community-building, but it can also divide us through forms of exclusion based on race, gender, sexuality, faith, age, and class. In short, sport may claim to be ‘fair’ while in reality proving ‘foul’. In this subject, we address debates around sports and games and explore how forms of play can create welcoming social spaces. This is an online, entirely asynchronous subject, meaning there are no live lectures or tutorials. Instead students can work through the varied, engaging, and highly topical content on their own schedules (while, of course, keeping in mind the assessment deadlines). In 2026 this subject will commence on January 5 and end around February 20. However, it is possible to submit the final assessment prior to the deadline and complete the subject earlier.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise empirical research and demonstrate reflective thinking on the forms and role of sport, games, and play in everyday life
Understand classic and contemporary theories and arguments in the sociological study of sports, games, and leisure
Critically evaluate current public debates on contested social issues relating to value of sport and games in wider society
Apply sociological concepts to the analysis and evaluation of the influence of sports, games, and play in society

title: CULTURE, MEANING AND SOCIAL LIFE
syllabus_overview: What is culture? How do individuals and societies make meaning? Does culture shape social life, or does social life shape culture? In this subject, you will be introduced to sociological perspectives on culture, with a particular focus on how meaning is constructed individually and socially. We begin by exploring popular cultural forms – art, literature, music, film and television – before examining the influence of traditional and new media. You will learn about cultural production and consumption in the digital age, and how technology shapes our social worlds. We then consider how culture and meaning are embedded in every aspect of our lives. By exploring a range of topics, from happiness and love to memory, therapy talk and collective trauma, you will discover how meaning functions as a central driving force for individuals, communities, and societies.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate theories and arguments in cultural sociology
Present a complex sustained written argument in cultural sociology
Understand theories and arguments in cultural sociology
Demonstrate reflective thinking on the nature and role of culture and demonstrate a capacity to apply sociological concepts to everyday life

title: WORLDS OF EXCLUSION: GLOBAL SOCIAL INEQUALITIES
syllabus_overview: Individuals may perceive social inequality differently based on their observations, knowledge, and life experiences. What does “social inequality” really mean, and how does it appear and evolve in different societies? Do you wonder why gaps between the rich and poor, along with other social disparities, persist despite technological and societal progress? Are you interested in comparing your views on social inequality with global perspectives or academic insights? This subject provides an opportunity to explore social inequalities and their impacts, and to address equity challenges through sociological and interdisciplinary approaches. You will critically examine diverse inequalities in Australia and globally, addressing issues such as the economic divide, gender inequality, racial biases, social class tensions, unequal access to education, employment, and healthcare, barriers to civic engagement and social mobility, and international divisions and imbalances. You will also investigate how social inequality can be made visible or hidden, using analytical lenses on resource distribution and power dynamics to identify the structural factors influencing these issues. Through real-world examples, case studies, and empirical evidence, this subject will help you navigate the complexities of social inequality and assess whether strategies and policies can effectively reduce disparities and foster inclusion. In addition, it will contribute to advancing academic inquiry and establishing a strong foundation to prepare you for diverse career opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine sociological theories of social stratification and inequalities
Coherently apply a sociological perspective to social inequalities within Australia and in global contexts
Produce a coherent written argument addressing social issues
Effectively conduct research projects on social stratification and inequalities

title: CULTURE, MEANING AND SOCIAL LIFE
syllabus_overview: What is culture? How do individuals and societies make meaning? Does culture shape social life or does social life shape culture? In this subject you will explore sociological engagements with culture. Our central concern is with culture as meaning-making. We begin by considering sociological analyses of cultural forms, such as art, literature, music and television, and we examine cultural production and consumption in the digital age. We then turn to cultural perspectives on meaning-making as embedded in every aspect of social life. Through close up study of a range of topics, such as happiness, trauma, memory and love, we look at meaning as a central driving force for individuals and for societies more broadly. This is a level 4 subject. Please check the subject rules before enrolling. This subject includes live tutorial sessions.
learning_outcomes: Advanced understandings of theories and arguments in cultural sociology
Present an advanced and theoretically-driven sustained written argument in cultural sociology
Demonstrate a sophisticated capacity for reflective thinking on the nature and role of culture and a capacity to apply complex sociological concepts to everyday life
Critically evaluate high-level and complex theories and arguments in cultural sociology

title: QUANTITATIVE SKILLS FOR SOCIAL RESEARCH
syllabus_overview: When you hear the term “quantitative”, what comes to mind – just numbers and data, or something with broader potential and impact? Have you considered that learning quantitative analysis can be both enjoyable and adaptable to your learning needs? Could developing quantitative skills enhance your analytical abilities and offer new perspectives on social phenomena or contemporary issues? This subject introduces quantitative research in an approachable and engaging way, seeking to benefit students from a wide range of academic backgrounds. In this subject, you will explore the foundations of designing and conducting quantitative research in the social sciences, learning how to formulate research questions and utilise data analysis techniques to identify evidence-based solutions. You will gain hands-on experience in designing surveys and questionnaires, working with various data sources or relevant information, and using SPSS, known for its user-friendly interface, to generate valuable insights. Numerous real-life case studies and examples will illustrate how these quantitative skills can be applied across diverse disciplines and fields. This subject intends to help you discover your potential and build confidence in quantitative work, equipping you with practical skills that are in demand both academically and professionally. It will also support your career development and create diverse opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Engage in discussion with peers in class about quantitative research
Understand and apply quantitative methods to addressing social issues
Use relevant software to conduct quantitative research
Implement and report on research practice
Evaluate strengths and weaknesses of different quantitative methods

title: SPANISH 1
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you receive a practical introduction to the Spanish language. You acquire the language largely in simulated real-life situations, through an authentic and communicative approach to language learning. Throughout the semester, cultural aspects of the Hispanic world are introduced in language classes. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. Students are expected to attend and participate in practicals/live sessions at set times and days during the week, whether in person or online. Please note that this subject can be taken at any year depending on course enrolment and language skills.
learning_outcomes: Accurately utilise the vocabulary seen in class throughout the semester.
Correctly apply the grammar structures seen in class throughout the semester.
Hold a 10 minute conversation about the topics seen in class throughout the semester
Write texts of up to 125 words using the range of vocabulary and grammar structures seen in class throughout the semester.
Understand and answer questions about simple audio texts that deal with the topics seen in class throughout the semester.

title: SPANISH 2
syllabus_overview: You will continue to acquire Spanish through an authentic and communicative approach to language learning but at a more advanced level than Spanish 1. Throughout the semester, cultural aspects of the Hispanic world continue to be incorporated into language classes. Culture is embedded throughout language, so learning another language develops your intercultural communication skills, preparing you to be responsive and agile in varied situations. There is an expectation that you will attend and participate. Please note that this subject can be taken at any year depending on course enrolment and language skills.
learning_outcomes: Hold a 10-minute conversation in Spanish about the topics seen in class throughout the semester.
Understand and answer questions in Spanish about simple audio texts that deal with the topics seen in class throughout the semester.
Use accurately and in context the vocabulary seen in class throughout the semester.
Write texts of up to 150 words using a range of Spanish vocabulary and grammar structures appropriate for this level.
Use accurately and in context the Spanish grammar structures seen in class throughout the semester.

title: SPANISH 3
syllabus_overview: This subject is a continuation of Spanish 2. While emphasising the skills of speaking and listening in Spanish, you further develop your reading and writing skills. You are involved in a wide range of language acquisition activities and exposed to the Spanish language and Hispanic culture more broadly. There is an expectation of attendance and participation. Please note that this subject can be taken at any year depending on course enrolment and language skills.
learning_outcomes: Use accurately and in context the grammar structures seen in class throughout the semester.
Hold a 10 minute conversation in Spanish about the topics seen in class throughout the semester.
Write texts of up to 250 words using a range of Spanish vocabulary and grammar structures appropriate for the level.
Use accurately and in context the vocabulary seen in class throughout the semester.
Understand and answer questions in Spanish about intermediate-level audio texts that deal with the topics seen in class throughout the semester.

title: SPANISH 5
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will combine the further development of language skills through a variety of activities, with the study of aspects of Spanish and Latin American cultural texts (News, Films, and TV Series). Grammatical study is complemented by advanced practical oral work. Please note that this subject can be taken at any year level depending on course enrolment and language skills.
learning_outcomes: Make notes on predictable matters. Ability to write about subjects of limited complexity in a letter, short essay or report. Ability to select a style appropriate to the reader in mind.

Communicate and process information in day-to-day situations through the spoken and written word in Spanish. Ability to understand everyday speech even when not clearly structured, and public announcements or instructions.

Apply the linguistic and cultural knowledge you obtain in this subject to see meaningful connections with puzzling questions arising in an exam or in real life situations (for example, when travelling in Spanish-speaking countries or interacting with Spanish speakers in Melbourne).
Analyse and synthesise ideas on a subject which you had previously not paid much attention to, to formulate an argument and your own thoughts about it.
Negotiate day-to-day situations in terms of the social culture and appropriate language registers specific to Spanish-speaking countries.

title: SPANISH 4
syllabus_overview: In this subject we continue to emphasise performance in the skills of speaking, listening, reading and writing, but on a more advanced level than Spanish 3. There is an expectation of attendance and participation. Please note that this subject can be taken at any year depending on course enrolment and language skills.
learning_outcomes: Understand and answer questions in Spanish about intermediate-level audio texts that deal with the topics seen in class throughout the semester.
Hold a 10 minute conversation in Spanish about the topics seen in class throughout the semester
Write texts of up to 700 words using a range of Spanish vocabulary and grammar structures appropriate for the level
Use accurately and in context the grammar structures seen in class throughout the semester
Use accurately and in context the vocabulary seen in class throughout the semester

title: SPANISH 6
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will combine the further development of language skills through a variety of activities, with the study of aspects of Spanish and Latin American cultural, social and political aspects, as well as Hispanic cinema and literary texts. Grammatical study is complemented by advanced practical oral work. Please note that this subject can be taken at any year depending on course enrolment and language skills.
learning_outcomes: Produce a clear, detailed text on a reasonable range of subjects. Ability to synthesise in writing various ideas on a cultural subject and to formulate an argument of your own about them in Spanish.
Discuss topics with a more advanced degree of fluency and spontaneity in Spanish with classmates and with native speakers of Spanish.

Explain a view point on a topical issue giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. Ability to undertake research in Spanish for a project and to understand and analyse a variety of scholarly sources.
Understand the main ideas of a complex text on a variety of topics in Spanish.

title: INTRODUCTION TO SPORT AND EXERCISE SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will be introduced to the key sub-disciplines of sport, exercise, and allied health and begin to develop the foundation knowledge and skills that underpins practice in these fields. Students will explore the real-world application of these sub-disciplines to illustrate the multidisciplinary nature of sport, exercise, and allied health. Finally, students will investigate the associations between exercise, sedentary behaviour, and health.
learning_outcomes: Interpret fundamental health screening and exercise testing results from a health perspective.
Explain basic sport and exercise science concepts related to exercise physiology, biomechanics, motor learning, sport psychology, and performance analysis.
Demonstrate fundamental academic, digital literacy, and numeracy skills required to succeed in the Bachelor of Sport and Exercise Science course.
Describe the roles of exercise and health professionals within sport, exercise, and allied health settings.
Discuss the risks and benefits of exercise and the relationships between sedentary behaviours and lifestyle-related disease.

title: GROWTH, DEVELOPMENT AND NUTRITION
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will be introduced to foundational concepts of nutrition, growth, and development in sport and exercise science. The subject will provide you with an understanding of growth and development from prenatal life through to older adulthood, factors that influence these processes, and key considerations relevant to each life stage. Additionally, you will be taught the core concepts of human nutrition, including basic nutritional assessment, the components of human nutrition and diet, and their relationship to health and exercise. The subject aims to develop your knowledge and application of how physical activity influences (and is influenced by) growth and development across the lifespan and the role of nutrition in sport and exercise science.
learning_outcomes: Describe the strengths and limitations of commonly used methods for measuring and analysing dietary intake including implications for general health and wellbeing.
Describe the stages of growth and development throughout the lifespan, and the factors that affect these.
Identify and describe the basic function and common sources of macronutrients and micronutrients including their role in energy balance and health.
Explain the relationship between physical activity and the structural, physiological, motor and cognitive changes occurring throughout the lifespan.
Use peer-reviewed literature and evidence-based physical activity and exercise principles to interpret lifespan case studies.
Understand the scope of practice for exercise scientists and use current Australian guidelines to provide general advice on nutrition as appropriate or refer onwards as appropriate.

title: RESEARCH AND STATISTICS IN SPORT AND EXERCISE SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore research methods, statistical analysis and data science techniques specific to sport and exercise science. You will be taught various research designs and statistical approaches that will allow you to interpret data to apply results in a practical environment. The subject will teach you how to perform various data handling techniques, develop statistical models and data visualisation techniques to interpret data in sport and exercise context.
learning_outcomes: Appraise research methods and reports, including statistical results to understand methodological and ethical aspects of research, and integrate this knowledge into all areas of exercise science practice.
Describe the primary types, applications and limitations of qualitative and quantitative research study designs.
Select and apply basic data analysis techniques appropriate to exercise science subdisciplines.
Use research databases to access peer-reviewed scientific literature and conduct searches to identify relevant information.

title: FOUNDATIONS OF RECREATION
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to the recreation industry and the unique features of recreation and leisure while developing skills of analysis, appraisal, and reflection. You will examine the value and history of society’s engagement in recreation, patterns of consumption of recreation, the role of all tiers of government in facilitating recreation for communities, the structure of the recreation industry, and the challenges and issues involved in providing sustainable, safe and meaningful recreation experiences for consumers and participants. You will reflect on the role of policy makers and recreation managers in shaping the recreation experiences for communities.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role of policy makers and recreation managers in shaping the recreation experiences for communities.

Analyse the role of all tiers of government in facilitating recreation for communities, and the challenges and issues involved in providing sustainable, safe and meaningful recreation experiences for consumers and participants.
Examine the unique features of recreation management and the structure of the Australian recreation industry.
Examine the value and history of society’s engagement in recreation, the role of recreation in society, and patterns of consumption of recreation.

title: FOUNDATIONS OF SPORT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to the sport industry and its unique features while developing skills of analysis, appraisal, and reflection. You will examine the value and role of sport in society, trends in the consumption of professional and elite sport, participation trends in organized sport, the role of government in facilitating access to sport for communities, the structure and governance of the sport industry, and the challenges and issues involved in providing sustainable, safe and meaningful sport experiences. You will reflect on the role of policy makers and sport managers in influencing the sport experiences for communities.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the role of government in facilitating sport opportunities for communities, and the challenges and issues involved in providing sustainable, safe and meaningful sport experiences.
Evaluate the role of policy makers and sport governing bodies in shaping the sport experiences for individuals and communities.
Examine the value and history of sport’s role in society, and the unique features of sport and patterns of consumption of professional and elite sport, as well as trends in sport participation.
Examine the unique features of sport management and the structure of the Australian and international sport industry.

title: CONTEMPORARY ISSUES IN SPORT COACHING
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will be introduced to contemporary social and cultural factors that have a bearing on coaching and exercise science practice, with a particular emphasis on sport coaching. These may include issues around; barriers to participation; violence and off-field conduct; gender, culture, race, and religion; social media usage; data and information storage, usage and privacy; and winning and ethics. You will be asked to reflect on contemporary issues and problem-solve specific scenarios from a number of perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Working collaboratively in a group to explore, analyse and review a contemporary issue in sport, and present a collective, evidence-based, and supported view on the issue.
Explain ways in which social issues are addressed in sport coaching.
Discuss the key current social issues relevant to participation and competition in sport.
Discuss the most relevant approaches used to understand social issues and ethical practice in applied sport coaching.
Analyse contemporary case studies of relevant social issues in sport coaching practice.

title: CLINICAL BIOMECHANICS OF MOVEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to the mechanical principles used to describe and quantify human movement. You will explore the mechanics of human movement with an emphasis on gait in health and disease.
learning_outcomes: Analyse normal gait patterns using appropriate terminology with understanding of the changes associated with pathology.
Perform basic clinical measurements to quantify and analyse human movement.
Identify and describe factors that contribute to efficient human movement.
Apply biomechanical principles that demonstrate understanding of the internal and external forces associated with human movement.

title: FOUNDATIONS OF SPORT AND EXERCISE SCIENCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore a foundation knowledge of concepts related to sports and exercise science practice. Such concepts include: pre-exercise screening, exercise testing and assessment, body composition, and kinathropometry. Additionally, you will be taught the core concepts of human nutrition, including the components of human nutrition and diet and their relationship to health and exercise, including basic nutritional assessment.
learning_outcomes: Apply theoretical knowledge of the nutritional components of diet to health, exercise and chronic lifestyle-related diseases.
Apply knowledge of the sub-disciplines of sport and exercise science to solve real world problems both independently and in a group.
Interpret and clearly communicate the outcomes of basic nutritional assessments and physiological tests.
Apply knowledge of scientific principles, medical contraindications and other limitations, and inter-professional referral to select and perform relevant pre-exercise assessment procedures.
Select and explain common equipment and test protocols used to perform accurate and safe health, exercise sport, and kinathropometric assessments.

title: GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF SPORT COACHING
syllabus_overview: You will be introduced to the profession of sports coaching and will be provided with a contextual model that will include the history and evolution of sports coaching, styles of coaching and lesson planning. Practical sessions will involve observation and evaluation techniques to self-evaluate coaching styles and effectiveness in coaching athletes at different levels. At the completion of this subject, you will be expected to hold a Community Coaching General Principles accreditation (or have proof of accreditation) from the Australian Sports Commission. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Use a range of communication, risk mitigation and behaviour management strategies to facilitate participants' performance development.
Demonstrate a range of communication skills relevant to the delivery of sports coaching sessions in training and competition.
Apply foundational principles of coaching that inform coaching session plans to meet the needs of participants and achieve performance goals in sport.
Collaborate in small groups to design and deliver a coaching session
Review planned coaching sessions to identify strategies to assist in improving session designs and coaching practices.

title: FOUNDATIONS OF EXERCISE PROGRAMMING
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be provided with the fundamental knowledge to design exercise training plans for apparently healthy and athlete populations. In addition, the use of field test results to direct exercise programming will also be discussed. In the practical component, you will be taught how to instruct common resistance training exercises and conduct basic field tests of fitness qualities.
learning_outcomes: Select and employ methods to monitor training intensity and load throughout exercise programmes.
Apply knowledge of functional anatomy to evaluate and conduct a simple movement analysis for exercise prescription.
Identify the best-practice principles of prescribing exercise and apply this knowledge to determine safe and progressive exercise programs aimed at improving general health and fitness.
Explain the risks and benefits associated with exercise to healthy individuals and how assessment data can be used to prescribe exercise
Deliver exercise programs - Safely progress or modify exercise programs for healthy individuals or groups.

title: HUMAN GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to the physiological, motor, cognitive, and social characteristics of lifespan growth and development in sport and exercise science. The unit will provide you with an understanding of growth and development from prenatal life through to older adulthood, factors that influence these processes, and key considerations relevant to each life stage. The subject aims to develop your knowledge and application of how physical activity influences (and is influenced by) growth and development across the lifespan.
learning_outcomes: Discuss relevant health outcomes associated with each stage of life, including factors that affect these.
Select and assess peer-reviewed literature individually and in groups, on exercise, growth, and development across the lifespan.
Explain how structural, physiological, motor and cognitive changes throughout the lifespan affect physical activity and exercise behaviours.
Describe the stages of growth, development and ageing throughout the lifespan, including pregnancy.

title: PHYSICAL ACTIVITY AND HEALTH
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to the role that increasing physical activity and reducing sedentary behaviour plays in the prevention and development of lifestyle-related chronic disease. At the individual level, you will learn how to apply models of behaviour change to encourage people to overcome barriers to physical activity and to reduce sedentary behaviours. At the community and population level, you will examine the importance of public policy and settings-based strategies to promote physical activity across the lifespan.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe core behaviour change principles, motivational interviewing techniques and core communication principles that facilitate physical activity behaviour change for individuals.
Describe and interpret the role and impact of physical activity in disease prevention across the lifespan.
Explain approaches that promote physical activity and reduce sedentary behaviour at the individual, community and population level.
Use scientific evidence and models of behaviour change to promote physical activity and reduce sedentary behaviour, including addressing barriers and facilitators to physical activity.

title: SPORT DEVELOPMENT IN PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore sport through a development and coaching lens. Its foci are on critiquing athlete and coaching pathways and how pathway policy filters through from National and State Sporting Organisations to community sport, the role of stakeholder management in sport, knowledge and skills in operational planning for change, and personal competencies in marketing and presenting an idea. It is an applied subject that requires you to critique, create, and plan change within the sport ecosystem.
learning_outcomes: Develop, individually and collectively an operational plan for a grassroots sporting organisation to introduce a new program.
Develop and present an evidence-based proposal for change at a community sport club.
Evaluate and critique athlete and coach pathways across the sport ecosystem.
Collaborate in small groups to design a program with guidelines for a sport organisation.
Appraise the role of stakeholder engagement in community sport.

title: SPORTS SCIENCE FOR COACHING
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore the key disciplines of sports science (physiology, biomechanics, and nutrition) and the role they play within the field of sport coaching. The application of these concepts to sport will also be outlined to illustrate the interdisciplinary nature of the sports coaching process. This will provide you with the opportunity to understand how these key disciplines can be applied within a real-world context for the purposes of sports science related activities such as talent identification and athlete development.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of physiology, biomechanics, and nutrition to the coaching process
Perform accurate and safe sports-related assessments using common equipment and processes
Identify and explain basic physiological, biomechanical, and nutritional concepts, structures, and functions
Analyse theories, concepts and athletic data to enhance performance

title: MOTOR LEARNING AND PERFORMANCE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you are introduced to the processes and techniques used in the acquisition of motor skills. The common theoretical approaches to understanding how people learn and perform motor skills will be examined. You will learn about key concepts in motor learning and techniques such as the use of feedback, verbal instruction, implicit learning, and constraints-based design as well as how to measure and track the results of learning. You will apply knowledge of practice design to create and test learning programmes to influence the development of sport and exercise skills. The subject will also provide you with an understanding of how to adjust tasks to suit the needs of individual learners and selecting appropriate approaches to learning.
learning_outcomes: Explain the common theoretical models in skill acquisition.
Examine the changes in motor skill performance that occur with learning .
Analyse the major factors that influence the learning and performance of motor skills.
Apply principles of learning design to change performance outcomes.
Assess motor learning programs that include performance testing to measure rate of learning, for individual needs

title: SPORT AND RECREATION PROGRAM DESIGN
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be introduced to the principles of designing sport and recreation programs for a range of participants and client groups. Sport and recreation programs are one of the key mechanisms for consumers to experience a variety of recreation services and this subject provides students with the knowledge and information to develop, plan, and document sport and recreation programs to different client groups.
learning_outcomes: Develop a program plan for a sport and recreation program, event or activity.
Undertake a needs analysis and feasibility assessment to inform the design of a sport and recreation program
Employ the Rossman and Schlatter Program Development Cycle to designing sport and recreation programs.

title: PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE IN SPORT AND EXERCISE SCIENCE 1
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will apply theoretical principles to conduct exercise assessments and prescribe and deliver safe and effective exercise programs in an exercise science placement setting. In doing so, students will demonstrate the professional and non-technical skills required to contribute within a team environment and when engaging clients one-on-one on placement and in a simulated learning environment. Students will complete a range of activities to improve their employability, which includes development of a career portfolio and cover letter and resume development to create a job application. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Silver Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Critically review the skills and attributes required for employment in sport and exercise science and prepare a job application for relevant employment and placement opportunities.
Apply discipline-specific knowledge and skills to conduct safe and effective exercise assessments, and prescribe and deliver exercise, in collaboration with clients and supervisors.
Demonstrate professional behaviour in accordance with Exercise and Sports Science Australia's Code of Professional Practice and Ethical Conduct as an entry level practitioner
Demonstrate an ability to prepare job applications for relevant employment advertisements.

title: SPORT AND RECREATION PLANNING
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the concepts of sport and recreation planning as applied to sport and recreation infrastructure and services. It explores the social and spatial aspects of recreation planning in an urban setting, the methods in use, and the political framework of planning and resource allocation, including the concepts of mapping recreation behaviour and activity, and demand and supply of recreation infrastructure and space. It will use case studies at the local, state and national level.
learning_outcomes: Examine the political framework of planning and resource allocation for sport and recreation services and infrastructure in the context of local, state and national government providers.
Examine the process, outcomes and impacts of contemporary sport and recreation planning case studies.
Examine the concepts of sport and recreation planning as applied to sport and recreation infrastructure and services.
Explain the social and spatial aspects of sport and recreation planning in an urban setting, and the methods available to support this activity.

title: GOVERNMENT POLICY AND FUNDING IN RECREATION AND SPORT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will explore the role of government in shaping recreation and sport through policy development and funding mechanisms. You will explore the unique grant system that underpins community sport and recreation. You will examine how public policies influence the growth and sustainability of sport and recreation sectors at local, state and national levels. You will gain a deep understanding of the relationship between public policy, funding and the development of recreation and sport programs. This subject includes professional learning, practical experiences or portfolio activities which contribute to the completion of the Career Ready AdvantageTM award.
learning_outcomes: Research and evaluate policy documents, funding reports, and case studies, to make informed policy recommendations in the field of recreation and sport management.
Apply effective leadership and teamwork to develop funding applications in the sport and recreation sector.
Communicate ideas and analyses of recreation and sport policy frameworks, funding structures, and their impacts on community recreation programs and professional sport to a variety of audiences.

Appraise the ethical and social responsibilities of government policy and funding decisions in the sector including the broader social impacts of these policies around inclusivity, equity, and fairness in access to sport and recreation opportunities for diverse populations.

title: SPORT AND RECREATION PROGRAM DELIVERY AND EVALUATION
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will demonstrate the application of the principles of designing sport and recreation programs for a range of participants and client groups. This subject provides students with the knowledge to develop, plan, document and deliver sport and recreation programs to different client groups.
learning_outcomes: Employ the Rossman and Schlatter Program Development Cycle to design and deliver a sport and recreation program.
Prepare a self-evaluation of a sport or recreation program
Demonstrate the ability to effectively work in a team to deliver a sport and recreation program, event or activity

title: ADVANCED SPORT COACHING A
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will be taught to further advance the theoretical knowledge, competencies and skills at the advanced coaching level. Specifically, you will be provided with an understanding of the high performance environment for athlete preparation and competition. The content and practical skills provided will include topics wider than traditional coaching and include short and long-term athlete planning, management of the high performance program, organisational culture and values, and leadership and communication styles for different stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Review best practice in coaching principles and to improve individual coaching practice.
Transmit knowledge effectively with a range of stakeholders in the context of high performance sports programs.
Apply knowledge of sport coaching theory and practice to manage and support elite athletes with different personality types.
Working collaboratively in a group, design and justify appropriate pedagogy, practice and communication methods to deliver a coaching session that facilitates the learning needs of athletes
Practice responsibly in accordance with accepted national and international sports coaching professional standards.

title: BIOMECHANICS AND MOVEMENT ANALYSIS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will be introduced to the biomechanical principles of human movement. You will explore how biomechanical principles relate to the analysis of movement in a range of contexts, with an emphasis on sporting technique and performance enhancement. The application of these principles to sport, exercise, and health will also be covered. Practical classes will reinforce knowledge and assist you in developing practical skills in movement analysis, with an appreciation for the requirements for, and justification of, movement-based analysis. You will need to demonstrate skill in conducting and interpreting biomechanical measurements. At the end of this subject and through the integration of applied knowledge and practical skills, you will be expected to describe, measure, analyse and evaluate the mechanical principles underlying human movement.
