Apply and appraise professional knowledge and skills in the context of the Australian Association of Social Workers Practice Standards with autonomy and expert judgement as a social work practitioner.

title: PATHWAYS INTO C21 SOCIAL WORK
syllabus_overview: This subject provides graduate entry students into the Master of Social Work with opportunities to utilise their prior learning and experience to: (i) identify and define the key social problems confronting today's social workers and the consequent social purpose and distinguishing functions of twenty-first century social work; (ii) develop an understanding and awareness of culturally competent practice through recognition of the experiences of 'difference' with particular reference to Indigenous Australians; (iii) understand diversity, particularly as this relates to the critical tradition's emphasis on marginalisation/exclusion; and (iv) analyse the history and development of social work as a key profession in the pursuit of social justice.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an emerging social work identity
Critically reflect on Western and First Nations’ worldviews recognising the ongoing impacts of colonisation and the complexities of inclusive practice.
Identify and explain the key areas of foundational knowledge for social work practice.
Critique and define the key social problems confronting social workers in the twenty-first century and discuss theories and concepts relevant to sound professional social work practice.

title: REFLECTION, INTEGRATION & APPLICATION A
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will draw on their experiences in their first placement to critically reflect upon the purpose of social work, its knowledge values and skills and how they integrate these into practice competencies. They will apply critical reflection to explore and develop knowledge about the issues they are facing in placement and the knowledge and skills they need to apply to address these issues. Students will also explore their professional boundaries and self-care plans and how they approach learning in the field placement.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on and integrate professional knowledge, values, skills and assumptions to inform professional practice.
Interpret the role of critical self-reflection to effectively practice in the social work profession
Critically analyse and coherently communicate the assumptions, values and theoretical principles that underpin critical reflection.

title: SOCIAL WORK RESEARCH B
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will explore the role and application of research in social work practice. By building on previous research education, this subject aims primarily to provide research skills and knowledge for direct application in social work practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically analyse the important steps in planning, designing and implementing a social work practice research study
Investigate and synthesise previous research in order to link a social work practice research question/hypotheses with appropriate designs and methods
Demonstrate knowledge of key qualitative and quantitative research methods for use in social work practice
Demonstrate a capacity to plan quantitative and qualitative research.

title: REFLECTION, INTEGRATION & APPLICATION B
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will integrate the knowledge, values and skills gained in previous years and apply these to the types of social issues which are the concerns addressed in social work. You are expected to be able to demonstrate their understanding of the purpose of social work through the application of the concepts, theories, values and skills. You are expected to demonstrate their ability to critically reflect on their practice as part of this process.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse human service organisations with particular focus on their responses to the identified social issues
Critically analyse complex social issues by integrating theory and practice to determine the implications for practice as social workers across all social work domains
Integrate and implement social work theory and practice to diverse (or new professional practice settings

title: INTRODUCTION TO TOURISM, HOSPITALITY AND EVENTS
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to the fields of tourism, hospitality, and event management, combining theoretical knowledge with practical skills that are highly valued in today’s dynamic global landscape. It explores key concepts, theories, and terminology across these interrelated industries, with a particular focus on the Australian context. Students will gain an understanding of the structure, scope, and activities that define tourism, hospitality, and events, while also examining the data and information these sectors generate. Students are encouraged to critically engage with current trends and issues shaping the industry and to consider their future impact in designing, planning, and delivering meaningful experiences. This subject also serves as a foundation for making informed decisions about future study and career pathways in these vibrant and interconnected industries.
learning_outcomes: Describe and compare the diversity, characteristics, and organisational structures of the tourism, hospitality, and events sectors.
Explain and apply managerial approaches in tourism, hospitality, and events to demonstrate how they create value and meaningful experiences for stakeholders.
Analyse the environmental, economic, and social impacts of tourism, hospitality, and events on host communities.

title: SOCIAL POLICY ANALYSIS AND ADVOCACY
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will critically reflect on your experience of policy in social work practice and build your capacity for policy analysis and advocacy. You will appraise social policy theory, in particular, key social welfare ideologies and theories of justice, rights, needs and capabilities. You will apply this policy knowledge to analyse and evaluate contemporary social policy. You will demonstrate critical understanding of institutional and other diverse factors that shape social policies and the rational and political processes by which policy is developed and implemented. You will develop the skills necessary to become beginning policy practitioners who can use experience and research to identify issues, interpret policy, and contribute to processes of policy development and change.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate rational and political policy process theories and models.
Apply communication and technical skills to interpret and implement policy
Critically analyse and evaluate contemporary social policies against social work values.
Appraise and justify different policy advocacy theories and strategies to selected policy areas.
Critically reflect on current social policy with reference to the Australian history of social welfare .

title: INTRODUCTION TO EVENT MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces the study of event management to develop the theoretical knowledge and highly sought-after practical skills to add value to the events industry. The subject promotes inquiry into the trends and issues affecting the events sector in today’s everchanging global landscape. We take a deep dive into the event experience to identify how to construct a narrative that engages and immerses event attendees. Areas of focus include an overview of the event field, the event context, conceptualising events, strategic planning, project management, event marketing, risk management, sustainability, event design and production and event evaluation. You will be guided to consider the future impact they will play in the designing, planning, and delivery of meaningful event experiences.
learning_outcomes: Identify how events can impact host communities through both strategic planning and sustainability.
Compare and contrast the different types of events, their characteristics, and structure of the event industry.

Demonstrate how managerial approaches to project management, human resource management, event marketing, risk management, event design and production and event evaluation impact the way people gather to celebrate and connect through events.

title: HOSPITALITY MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: The hospitality sector complements the tourism and event sectors and differentiates itself by highlighting food and beverage and accommodation options. In this subject you will examine the management of the hospitality sector including food and beverage outlets, types of accommodations and trends in service delivery. You will analyse issues of sustainability and ethical concerns in tourism and hospitality management. You will explore other management concerns in a constantly changing environment as business models, innovations and technological advancements require constant adaptation.
learning_outcomes: Develop innovative hospitality facilities, services and online marketing campaigns for competitive advantage in a sustainable and ethical manner
Analyse and report on the sustainable development goals in the hospitality sector
Identify and analyse major issues in hospitality and tourism management

title: BUSINESS EVENTS
syllabus_overview: Business events are staged to achieve commercial objectives, including increasing sales, opening up new markets, facilitating innovation and knowledge transfer, and developing networks. They include conferences, exhibitions, trade fairs, business meetings and product launches. Even in a world of virtual and hybrid events the opportunity to have face-to-face business meetings between colleagues and between company employees and their potential or actual clients remains strong. The business events sector is closely associated with hotels, resorts, convention and exhibition centres which are important elements in the tourism and hospitality industries. This subject explores the business events sector and considers the key success factors in developing, planning and operating successful business events while considering the main trends shaping the ways in which such events are designed and operated.
learning_outcomes: Identify the key stakeholders in the business events sector and understand the key components in the organisation of successful business events, including ethical and social responsibilities
Explain differences between the different types and characteristics of business events (namely meetings, conferences, networking events; exhibition and trade shows)
Critique how different types of business events help companies reach their business goals via brand awareness, image enhancement, staff development, motivation and profile-raising

title: HALLMARK EVENTS
syllabus_overview: This subject provides a comprehensive examination of hallmark and mega events to equip you with specialist event knowledge for industry practice. You will learn about the relationship between hallmark and mega events and tourism. You will explore the planning, people and place elements of hallmark and mega events to create meaningful event experiences for attendees and stakeholders. The economic, social, environmental, and digital dimensions of staging hallmark and mega events will be analysed. Using case studies and progressive views of hallmark and mega events, you will further develop their understanding of event legacies. This subject will position you to make sustainable contributions to the role of hallmark and mega events in contemporary society.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the economic, social, environmental, and digital dimensions of staging hallmark (and mega) events to potentially support the broad sectors
Explore the planning, people, and place elements of hallmark (and mega) events to strive to achieve meaningful event experiences
Examine hallmark (and mega) events, their stakeholders with the ability to articulate their connections to tourism and their role in contemporary society

title: DESTINATION MARKETING AND MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: In this subject you will examine the management and marketing of tourism destinations at supra-national, national, state, regional and local/city levels. You will cover a variety of topics such as the tourism demand; destination choice behaviour; destination competitiveness; the role of Destination Marketing Organisations (DMOs); and the role of partnerships and alliances to promote the destination; destination image, branding and marketing. You will learn about the important link between destination marketing and strategic planning for development.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate, propose, and communicate approaches to destination marketing and management
Analyse the strategic challenges, complexities, and special issues involved in destination marketing and management
Analyse the role of Destination Management Organisations (DMOs) and other relevant stakeholders in destination marketing and management

title: BUSINESS EVENTS
syllabus_overview: Business events are staged to achieve commercial objectives, including increasing sales, opening up new markets, facilitating innovation and knowledge transfer, and developing networks. They include conferences, exhibitions, trade fairs, business meetings and product launches. Even in a world of virtual and hybrid events the opportunity to have face-to-face business meetings between colleagues and between company employees and their potential or actual clients remains strong. The business events sector is closely associated with hotels, resorts, convention and exhibition centres which are important elements in the tourism and hospitality industries. This subject explores the business events sector and considers the keys success factors in developing, planning and operating successful business events while considering the main trends shaping the ways in which such events are designed and operated.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate between the different types and characteristics of business events (namely meetings, conferences, networking events; exhibition and trade shows)
Critique how different types of business events help companies reach their business goals via brand awareness, image enhancement, staff development, motivation and profile-raising
Recognise the key stakeholders in the business events sector and understand the key components in the organisation of successful business events, including ethical and social responsibilities

title: TOURISM, HOSPITALITY AND EVENT FUTURES
syllabus_overview: This cutting edge subject challenges you by anticipating the future of the tourism, hospitality and events sector. By the end of this subject you will be expected to understand the range of factors likely to be influential in the future of this industry. Such factors include the demographic, political, economic and technological changes which will influence the nature, trends and participation in tourism, hospitality and events. These factors are important to be recognised to ensure the long-term sustainability of tourism in different countries and destinations.
learning_outcomes: Analyse current and future trends in tourism, hospitality and events to inform decision-making
Evaluate tourism, hospitality, and event strategies with respect to current and future trends
Create innovative, plausible ideas for tourism, hospitality and events that align with current and future trends

title: SUSTAINABLE COMMUNITY EVENTS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will build upon the knowledge gained from your previous degree studies. You will develop an event bid proposal for a small-scale, sustainable community event of your choice, applying your event management skills to create the essential documents needed for planning and operating the event. Emphasising a triple bottom line approach, you will examine the importance of integrating relevant and current frameworks, theories, and issues throughout the planning and event design process. Your deliverables will include an Event Bid Proposal, a Strategic Plan, and a Logistics Pack of logistical planning documents.
learning_outcomes: Apply current event management knowledge and skills to design a cohesive, sustainable, and responsible event proposal, strategic plan and logistics pack that meets stakeholder and community needs.
Solve complex event-related challenges by sourcing, evaluating, and integrating up-to-date information relevant to sustainable community event design and delivery
Identify and justify the need for a specific community event experience within broad and complex parameters, in consideration of socio-cultural, economic, and environmental dimensions.

title: TOURISM AND HOSPITALITY SIMULATION
syllabus_overview: This capstone subject explores the real-time working of a hotel through the use of a computer-based simulation called HOTS . Based in teams, you will be able to use the HOTS software to simulate all business decisions of a hotel over a five year period. You are required to apply your knowledge of service operations, finance and marketing principles through SWOT analysis, cash flow statements and other appropriate methods of interpreting data. The HOTS program simulates real decision-making and will prepare you for working in teams and making managerial decisions for hotels.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret financial data and make decisions based on authentic data operating a simulated hotel from a senior management perspective
Develop a S.W.O.T. and P.E.S.T. analysis based on the current hotel position prior to the simulation
The opportunity to develop professional judgements to adapt to market forces and competition via hotel objectives set by the senior management team

title: ANIMAL CARE AND MANAGEMENT
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces you to the care and management of a range of common animal species. Subject content includes animal husbandry in companion animals and a range of other common species. The areas of nutrition, behaviour, and preventative health care of dogs and cats are covered consistent with the requirements of veterinary nursing practice. You will consider the importance and application of professional codes, animal welfare legislation, animal ethics, the human-animal bond, cultural context and genetics within the veterinary nursing context. You are also introduced to the important role of the veterinary nurse in educating and guiding clients in the care of their animals. During the work integrated learning placement, you will assist with the care and management of animal patients.
learning_outcomes: Design and communicate animal care and management plans
Advise clients on common companion animal training and behaviour problems
Explain the husbandry requirements of a range of healthy animal species
Explain the role of professional codes, animal welfare legislation, ethics, cultural context and the human-animal bond in animal care and management decisions

title: VETERINARY CLINICAL PERSPECTIVES: ANIMAL FORM, FUNCTION AND HEALTH A
syllabus_overview: This subject integrates functional animal anatomy and physiology with its intimate relationship with an animal' state of health. Students undertake and/or observe some dissections, and practice safe tissue and instrument handling. A range of common health related case studies are examined for each body system. Knowledge of common breed anatomical abnormalities and their physiological, health and welfare implications are embedded into the case study learning approach. Safe animal handling is included in this subject, ensuring students learn and practice how to safely handle and restrain a range of common animal species before they undertake placement. Work integrated learning (WIL) is included in this subject, allowing students to apply their class based learning to real life contexts with veterinary teams. Students will participate in assessing, running diagnostic tests and nursing patients during placement. This subject is a pre-requisite for Animal Form, Function and Health B.
learning_outcomes: Identify a range of common animal breeds in Australia and evaluate how the anatomical extremes of some breeds can influence the effective functioning of organ systems
Demonstrate strategies and skills required to safely handle, restrain, and interact with, a range of common animal species
Explain, from an anatomical and physiological perspective, the signs displayed by animals in a range of common health conditions.
Apply effective team work with peers by working constructively and collaboratively on group tasks
Develop a nursing care plan in order to advise peers/owners of the appropriate basic care and management of a common animal health condition

Identify and assess, using anatomical, directional and physiological terminology, the key anatomical features, locations, positions, and physiological functions of key organ systems in different species

title: EQUINE HEALTH SYSTEMS
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop the knowledge and skills required for successful and economically-rational equine health management. The ability to recognise and evaluate problems early and determine the need for veterinary attention versus treatment by non-veterinary personnel is fundamental to such management. This subject is not designed to develop expert diagnostic skills and does not equip students to prescribe treatments. Upon successful completion of this subject, students will be able to recognise the clinical signs of an ill horse, triage the significance of the presenting clinical problem, seek veterinary assistance when required, and appropriately manage the recovery of the horse. This subject develops the knowledge required for graduates to form a productive working partnership with an attending veterinarian in the health management of the horses under their care.
learning_outcomes: Discuss legal and ethical responsibilities associated with equine health care
Explain the differences between passive and active immunity, and how this knowledge is applied when managing a horse's health
Identify common equine diseases and explain their normal prevention and management procedures.
Perform clinical skills appropriate for commencing equine nurses including evaluating the health of a horse recognising normal equine parameters
Reflect upon one's own performance of procedures undertaken when simulating the management of common equine health problems

title: VETERINARY CLINICAL PERSPECTIVES ON ANIMAL FORM, FUNCTION AND HEALTH B
syllabus_overview: This subject builds on learning in Animal Form, Function and Health A with a continued examination of the functional anatomy and physiology of body systems. Topic areas, including fluid regulation and thermoregulation, will also be introduced where students will integrate the body systems into a whole animal perspective. Case studies will be used to explain an animal's overall physiological response to a number of diseases, and to assist students to further develop their collaborative problem solving skills. Through their Work Integrated Learning (WIL) placement, students will continue to assist with the care and management of animal patients, including assisting within veterinary teams to assess, undertake diagnostic tests and nurse patients. The WIL placement will enable students to see the relevance of the subject to real-world veterinary practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain, using anatomical, directional and physiological terminology, the key anatomical features, locations, positions, and physiological functions of key organ systems in different species
Explain from an anatomical and physiological perspective, the signs displayed by animals in a range of common animal health conditions
Integrate knowledge of the functional anatomy and physiology of individual body systems into a whole animal perspective
Demonstrate effective team work with peers by working constructively and collaboratively on group tasks
Advise owners of the appropriate basic care and management of common animal health conditions

title: COMMUNICATION FOR THE VETERINARY TEAM
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to effective human communication techniques, strategies and their application in a veterinary and global context. Students will learn personal cognitive and coping skills to help them appropriately respond to a range of authentic professional workplace situations in a professional, ethical, caring and empathetic manner. The role of communication in supporting the wellness of all stakeholders in veterinary care is considered. Students will practice and critically review communication methods through the extensive use of role play scenarios, including the development of skills to interact sensitively and effectively with a range of people and in diverse cultural contexts. During placement, students will observe and, under supervision, begin to assist with a broad range of veterinary team communication requirements including, for example, client consultations, patient handover rounds, and patient record keeping. Students will also learn personal cognitive and coping skills to help them appropriately respond to a range of authentic professional workplace situations in a professional, ethical, caring and empathetic manner so that students play an active role in their own professional responsibility and employment satisfaction.
learning_outcomes: Reflect upon one's own internal self-communication and plan strategies to enhance self-care, resiliency and wellness in response to challenging experiences whilst on placement.

Communicate in an ethical, professional, empathic and effective manner in a range of veterinary nursing practice contexts including colleagues, management, and other animal and veterinary industry members.
Apply principles of clinical governance and legislation, laws and codes relevant to a veterinary nurse in practice
Identify, analyse and implement appropriate non-technical professional skills and competencies in a range of veterinary nursing practice contexts

Utilise appropriate communication styles and educational approaches according to the circumstances and needs of clients and colleagues, paying special consideration to cultural context, diversity, community focused veterinary care, and recognition of the human-animal bond (HAB).
Recognise and respond appropriately to people in distress including recognition of one’s own distress and explore mechanisms of self-help

title: FOUNDATION STUDIES FOR VETERINARY NURSING
syllabus_overview: This subject is designed to enhance a range of foundation academic skills for tertiary study, including academic literacy, referencing techniques, information literacy, scientific literacy and numeracy, so that key threshold concepts are achieved by subject completion. Students will develop and apply a range of academic skills designed to ensure they have the skills required to succeed in an academic environment. Students are introduced to the concept of an evidence based scientific approach, and its application from the perspective of a student and veterinary nurse. Through a work integrated learning (WIL) context, students will be exposed to veterinary nursing applied concepts in mathematics, chemistry and biology. Students will discuss, reflect upon and evaluate the use of evidence-based practice during their placement in the veterinary hospital under the guidance of the academic supervisory staff.
learning_outcomes: Write clearly and concisely in an appropriate academic style with correct referencing
Work as a team to explain how to use an evidence based approach to enhance developing veterinary nursing protocols and procedures
Demonstrate knowledge of key underpinning science concepts relevant to applied animal sciences and veterinary nursing.
Communicate effectively, professionally and sensitively through oral presentation
Identify a range of relevant peer reviewed literature sources using data base searches
Apply key mathematical concepts to successfully complete routine calculations required by practicing veterinary nurses

title: INTRODUCTION TO VETERINARY NURSING PRACTICE
syllabus_overview: This subject introduces students to the various roles of a veterinary nurse, other veterinary team members, and their roles and interactions in a veterinary context. Students are also introduced to the different areas of a veterinary hospital/clinic and their layout. The veterinary nurse's role in working with animals, owners, team members, facilities, equipment and supplies within a business environment will be examined. The subject is designed to allow students to begin to develop and practice a wide range of veterinary nursing technical skills required by practicing veterinary nurses. The students are introduced to the important role of reflective practice and develop this approach through the use of a weekly reflective journal. Students participate in regular laboratory workshops which introduce a number of clinical skills required in veterinary nursing practice, which are practiced further during work integrated learning placements. Students further develop their understanding of a veterinary nurse's role, including legal, ethical and work, health and safety (WHS) responsibilities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate introductory level skills in routine veterinary nursing practice to prepare for supervised tasks in clinical practice
Apply the relevant regulations and WHS considerations to dispensing and supplying a selection of common veterinary pharmaceuticals
Reflect upon one's own knowledge and skill gaps in clinical settings and be able to give peer feedback on developing clinical skills.
From a legal, ethical, animal welfare and clinical perspective, reflect upon the appropriate role of a veterinary nurse as part of a collaborative veterinary team.
Explain how to recognise and mitigate Work Health & Safety (WHS) risks, and apply a one-health perspective within a veterinary practice

title: APPLIED VETERINARY NURSING PRACTICE A
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will develop and practice a wide range of nursing and technical skills required by practicing veterinary nurses. Students' applied learning will be undertaken in a controlled laboratory environment. Nursing approaches taught include: an examination of the nursing process, models, plans, and protocols, and their application in practical veterinary nursing. Students will begin to learn skills required within emergency nursing and ICU areas. Students will consider ways in which a sustainable veterinary practice can be achieved and maintained. The concepts of peer education and peer review will be taught, and students will be guided through their approach to these. Through their work integrated learning (WIL) placement, students will work in a veterinary hospital with an experienced veterinary nurse to further practice and develop a range of level appropriate veterinary clinical skills. During their weekly workshop, students will be guided in how to prepare themselves to gain employment in veterinary nursing, and will be encouraged develop their resume and apply for trainee positions.
learning_outcomes: Apply "One Health" principles to veterinary nursing procedures in the areas of emergency nursing, barrier nursing, and shelter medicine
Constructively reflect upon clinical placement learning experiences in the areas of knowledge, skill and emotional perspectives
Collaboratively develop nursing care plans which provide holistic evidence based veterinary nursing care for animal patients
Actively participate in peer education and review in a constructive manner
Apply scientific knowledge to the nursing of a range of animal species
Perform clinical skills appropriate for commencing student veterinary nurses

title: DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING AND ANAESTHESIA
syllabus_overview: This subject examines the applied science of imaging, anaesthesia and pain control and it teaches students how to integrate theory with practice. This subject also examines the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of a range of common veterinary pharmaceuticals. Students refine these clinical skills through simulated settings and work integrated learning placements. During placement, students will participate in a surgical operating theatre, so that anaesthetic induction, maintenance and recovery of animals can be observed and skills applied. Under supervision of the veterinary team, students will assess the pain levels of medical and surgical patients, as well as assist with imaging procedures, such as radiology and ultrasonography, on a range of veterinary cases.
learning_outcomes: Design pain management approaches by integrating accurate pain scoring with knowledge of pain control, to help maximize veterinary patients' welfare outcomes
Perform a range of routine veterinary nursing radiological imaging procedures
Perform a range of anaesthetic management procedures
Work collaboratively as part of a team to develop radiology practice procedures and documentation for a veterinary practice to ensure compliance with relevant regulatory and safety requirements.
Compare and contrast the physiological changes that a range of common anaesthetic agents will induce in a veterinary patient
Explain the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of common veterinary pharmaceuticals
Explain, using scientific principles, how a range of modern imaging modalities operate, and why they may present as an occupational health hazard to personnel

title: SMALL ANIMAL BEHAVIOUR AND TRAINING
syllabus_overview: This subject offers a thorough and practical introduction to the basics of small animal behaviour and training at a level appropriate for student veterinary nurses. Students will develop the underlying knowledge and basic skills required to conduct puppy classes, and advise owners on common behavioural and training problems. Students will learn to take a thorough history and to perform a careful behavioural "triage" to enable a sound decision as to when veterinary intervention is required. Students will also develop the skills required to assist with behaviour modification as directed by veterinarians in the treatment of behavioural problems. Through a work integrated learning (WIL) placement, students will have the opportunity to observe and assist with the care of a wide number of hospitalised and visiting dogs and cats. An integral part of these interactions will involve applying behaviour and training theory, and critically reviewing how they have seen veterinary team members do the same.
learning_outcomes: Recognise when referral to a veterinarian is required for the diagnosis and treatment of behavioural problems
Perform safe and appropriate animal handing and restraint techniques which promote positive animal welfare outcomes for a range of small animal behaviours
Educate others in an accurate, appropriate, clear, empathetic and professional manner
Critically self-reflect on one's own role and effectiveness within a team
Using an evidence based approach, design and assist owners to implement training programs and behaviour modification plans for their animals

title: EVIDENCE BASED PRACTICE FOR VETERINARY NURSES
syllabus_overview: In this subject students will further develop their knowledge and application of research and scholarship in a veterinary nursing context. Students are introduced to basic quantitative and qualitative research methods and the concept of validity assessment via basic statistics. This subject teaches students how to search veterinary nursing databases to find relevant published peer reviewed literature, which they then critically assess. Students are supported to further develop their writing skills either through the task of writing a critical literature review, or preparing a case study at a level suitable for publication in a veterinary nursing journal.
learning_outcomes: Outline the background, rationale and processes of evidence-based practice and integrate principles of evidence-based medicine in practice
Distinguish statistical procedures and evaluate the statistical analyses of published research studies
Critique the design and methodology of research studies and provide constructive feedback on written articles both individually and with your peers
Conduct evidence-based research constructing recommendations or solutions to moderately complex veterinary nursing problems
Develop and deliver an oral presentation appropriate for delivery to an audience of veterinary nurses and other veterinary professionals

title: INTRODUCTION TO ADVANCED VETERINARY NURSING
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will consolidate the skills they have learnt in previous Veterinary Nursing Practice subjects, as well as being introduced to advanced veterinary nursing knowledge and skills. This introduction will help students to prepare for the advanced veterinary nursing skills which they will learn during third year. Students will become proficient in a range of progressively more complex and demanding veterinary nursing skill requirements. Veterinary nursing skills to be learnt and applied at an introductory advanced level include: emergency and critical care, surgical nursing and care for complex medical cases such as caring for the neurological patient and adopting a holistic animal nursing approach. Students will use an evidence-based and reflective approach to solve problems and to plan for best practice with all aspects of patient care. Through their work integrated learning placement, students will integrate their theoretical knowledge with practice, ensure their proficiency in basic veterinary nursing competencies, and gain introductory exposure to advanced veterinary nursing skills.
learning_outcomes: Communicate accurately, professionally and with empathy with colleagues and clients
Perform competently a range of day one veterinary nursing skills
Design nursing care plans for complex cases, both individually and as a team
Critically evaluate and reflect on all aspects of patient care
Integrate applied science knowledge with veterinary nursing practice to resolve complex veterinary nursing situations.
Demonstrate the ability to problem solve using an evidence-based approach and critical reflection

title: VETERINARY PROFESSIONAL SUSTAINABILITY AND LEADERSHIP
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will explore essential leadership principles and sustainable practices within the veterinary nursing profession. Emphasis will be placed on developing leadership skills, understanding how relevant legislation influences managerial and clinical decision-making, and implementing sustainable practices in veterinary settings. During on campus workshops, you will apply theoretical concepts in simulated classroom scenarios. You will learn how to assist with stock management, care and maintenance of physical resources, and will understand the financial and practice management aspects associated with the provision of veterinary care and running a sustainable veterinary business. You will also learn advanced professional communication techniques, including conflict resolution methods, to enhance your leadership capabilities and contribute to the overall sustainability of the veterinary nursing profession.
learning_outcomes: Identify relevant legislation and protocols that apply to the management of veterinary practices and personnel
Manage and lead others in the workplace to create a physically and psychologically safe working environment
Develop plans for the sustainable and compliant management of the physical, human and financial resources elements of a veterinary practice
Create plans and resources to support professional sustainability initiatives within a veterinary team, both individually and as part of a team

title: THE PRACTICING VETERINARY NURSE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will undertake an extensive work integrated learning placement, in the form of internships in a number of workplaces. This subject is designed to ensure that students will be ready for practice at the Associate Degree level for a Veterinary Nurse. Topics covered include: reflective practice, employment seeking, preparing for an interview, and registration. Students will continue to apply their theoretical nursing knowledge throughout their placement to refine their clinical skills in veterinary nursing practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain the value of registration for a para-professional
Communicate competently and effectively with colleagues, clients and the public, including key industry stakeholders, in a variety of professional and social contexts.
Perform at a level of work ready competency, the day one skills listed within the Bachelor of Veterinary Nursing Skills List
Demonstrate critical self-reflection and ongoing self-directed learning
Demonstrate successful development of key clinical and professional competencies appropriate for a Veterinary Nurse at Associate Degree level

title: VETERINARY NURSING AND ANIMAL DISEASE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will gain an understanding of disease processes, including common infectious and non-infectious animal disease categories, from a veterinary nursing perspective. You will be taken through the process of animal disease management, including aetiology, investigation, treatment, management and prevention. Students will also acquire skills in performing a range of common clinical pathology tests. You will apply the theory learnt in this subject via their work integrated learning placement.
learning_outcomes: Perform, read and record a range of common veterinary clinical pathology tests, recognizing if any results are abnormal.
Work collaboratively as part of a team to design and develop evidence-based educational materials for clients and colleagues using appropriate language
Recognise potential zoonotic and notifiable diseases, know the requirements for reporting them and implement appropriate actions to limit the spread of infection.
Explain the disease processes and devise nursing management plans, including the infection control of common veterinary infectious and non-infectious diseases

title: VETERINARY NURSING RESEARCH PROJECT 1
syllabus_overview: This subject aims to develop students’ theoretical knowledge of the methods and relevant project management skills required to plan and undertake an applied research project in the veterinary field. Elements covered include: searching for, analysing and synthesising relevant academic literature, selecting appropriate research methodologies, incorporating research design and methods of data collection, considering ethical factors, and participating in the peer review process.
learning_outcomes: Provide and critically reflect on peer feedback to research
Compare and critique a variety of literature related to the inquiry
Develop a project plan utilising appropriate research techniques
Form industry relevant research questions

title: APPLIED VETERINARY NURSING PRACTICE B
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will deepen their skills, knowledge and application in a range of key areas associated with independent paraprofessional practice in veterinary nursing. Key areas taught include: nursing care plans, the nutrition of unwell patients, professional client communication, client service and career preparation. During their work integrated learning placement, students will be supported by an experienced veterinary team as they develop a range of core veterinary nursing skills with a view to practicing autonomously. Students will develop deeper professional judgement and the ability to manage more complex professional situations.
learning_outcomes: Integrate the science, specialized knowledge and practical skills to undertake a range of veterinary nursing roles
Manage surgical cases in the hospital from admission to discharge
Train a peer in appropriate veterinary hospital protocol.
Evaluate the nutritional requirements of a range of animals with a variety of clinical conditions
Critically self-evaluate and reflect upon both challenging incidents and current knowledge gaps.
Create and implement, under veterinary team supervision, animal nursing care plans to maximise potential animal welfare outcomes

title: ADVANCED EQUINE HEALTH CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students deepen and apply clinically their underpinning equine health knowledge, by learning how to plan and provide for the nursing care needs of equine patients, and to work as an effective team with equine professionals. Students will examine legal and ethical impacts on the equine sector to help prepare them for ethically and legally challenging decisions and for ensuring that the advice they give to owners is appropriate. Students will integrate the husbandry requirements of horses with health and nursing knowledge to plan holistic individually tailored patient care. Students will also plan how to create and implement evidence based infection control protocols, including for serious zoonotic diseases. Finally, students will learn about equine reproduction and the knowledge and skills required for veterinary nurses to play an active role in assisting with equine reproductive care and management.
learning_outcomes: Examine the nursing care requirements of the pre, peri and post-operative surgical period of equine species
Critique the legal and ethical influences impacting current controversial areas within the equine sector
Research the role of equine industry professionals who care for horses, including those who care for mares and neonates
As a collaborative team, develop protocols to manage infectious and zoonotic diseases of equine patients
Plan and manage care plans for a range of equine life stages, health conditions and procedures

title: VETERINARY NURSING RESEARCH PROJECT 2
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will complete the second part of an applied research project initiated in the subject VET3001. You will apply knowledge and skills to undertake a small research project including the collection, analysis and interpretation of data, adherence to ethics considerations, the development of recommendations and/or materials for industry, and the presentation of the research in a variety of formats suited to a professional audience. You will develop time management skills and an ability to organise, liaise and work closely with external collaborators. You will be required to demonstrate the processes you used to manage the project.
learning_outcomes: Collect, statistically analyse and evaluate research data
Write a scientific report on the research and its conclusions
Communicate research findings in a variety of suitable formats to a professional audience
Critically reflect on the achievement of milestones and individual research goals

title: EXOTICS, AVIAN AND WILDLIFE CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students learn how to plan and provide evidence based nursing care for a range of exotic, avian and wildlife species. To deepen their knowledge, students will examine the anatomy, physiology, behaviour, handling, husbandry requirements and common conditions of a range of animal species, including pocket pets (rabbits, rats, guinea pigs, mice and ferrets), birds (covering a range of common species), reptiles, amphibians, fish, and native Australian wildlife (kangaroos, possums, wombats and echidnas). Through a work integrated learning placement, students will plan the specific surgical, clinical and nursing care needs of these patients. Students will examine the relevant legislation, and evaluate its impact on the nursing care approaches required for different species. Students will holistically examine the importance of habitat for wildlife, and work together to plan a response to the needs of vulnerable animal populations following natural disasters, such as fire, flood and drought.
learning_outcomes: As a team, plan the emergency care response required for wildlife in a natural disaster situation
Research a range of common conditions of exotic, avian and wildlife species
Compare and contrast the legal, behavioural and husbandry requirements of a range of injured legally owned exotic pets versus injured native wildlife
Compare and contrast the anatomy and physiology of a range of exotic, avian and wildlife species
Plan the management of the nursing, surgical and clinical care of exotic, avian and wildlife species undergoing diagnostic, surgical or medical procedures
Examine the importance of habitat on the health and welfare of wildlife

title: ADVANCED VETERINARY SURGICAL PATIENT CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn how to move beyond routine surgical nursing, to work as a senior surgical nurse and manager. Students will learn how to manage surgical theatres and wards within a veterinary hospital, to ensure that patient care at the pre-, peri- and post-operative stages is prioritised appropriately and maintained to a high standard. Students will learn how to plan, monitor and manage the anaesthesia and analgesia of a range of complex veterinary surgical patients. Students will also learn how to critically examine theatre space design and workflow. The management of theatre personnel, equipment and patients involved in a surgical theatre's daily operations will be taught. Finally, students will plan the specific pre-, peri-, and post-operative care requirements of a range of complex surgical patients. Students will undertake a work integrated learning (WIL) placement which allow them to further develop their depth of knowledge and practical experience in surgical theatre and ward management, including the nursing, anaesthesia and analgesia management of complex surgical cases.
learning_outcomes: Develop anaesthetic and analgesic protocols for a range of life stages, health conditions, procedures, emergencies and complications
Work individually or as a team to appraise the design, management and purpose of theatre spaces, equipment and personnel
Generate plans for the pre, peri and post-operative care of a range of surgical patients
Select, set up, assist with, clean and maintain appropriate equipment, instrumentation and miscellaneous consumables for a variety of surgical procedures
Recommend care interventions based on the evaluation of data related to the physiological effects of anaesthesia and analgesia from a variety of monitoring techniques

title: EMERGENCY AND CRITICAL CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, you will undertake a work integrated learning (WIL) placement to learn and apply the knowledge and skills required to manage the veterinary nursing emergency and critical care (ECC) area of a veterinary clinic or emergency referral centre. Using an evidence-based approach, you will learn how to triage, prioritise and manage the nursing care of emergency and critical care veterinary patients. In doing so, you will learn how to integrate knowledge of the pathophysiology of a range of critical care and emergency veterinary conditions, with each animal's specific history and nursing care needs. You will learn how to monitor complex and seriously ill emergency and critical care patients, interpret the data obtained and take appropriate actions based on the results. Finally students will learn how to work as an effective member of a veterinary ECC team, including how to lead such a team when required.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and prioritise veterinary patients for treatment based on their presenting clinical signs and symptoms.
Select appropriate diagnostic and monitoring techniques and interpret data produced for emergency and critical care veterinary patients
Plan, implement and review the nursing care of a range of small animal emergency and critical care conditions
Manage and direct a veterinary team using clear, concise and accurate communication at a level appropriate for each team member
Appraise the pathophysiology and treatment of a range of emergency and critical care veterinary patients

title: LARGE ANIMAL HEALTH CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will extend their knowledge and practical skills with production animals, beyond the introductory husbandry, handling and preventative health care of sheep and cattle covered earlier in the course. Via a work integrated learning (WIL) placement, students will learn how to safely work with large domesticated animals such as cattle, sheep, goats and alpacas whilst undertaking a range of farm animal management procedures and assisting a veterinarian with the management of animal health conditions. Students will learn how to perform a number of reproductive assistance techniques in cattle, including: artificial insemination and assisting cows through parturition (calving), as well as learning how to assist veterinarians with the diagnosis, treatment and surgical management of large animal health conditions including conditions like: bloat, caesareans and foot abscesses. Students will evaluate animal production systems from an animal health and welfare, and biosecurity perspective, examine preventative health care programs, including preventing zoonoses, and compare and contrast small and large animal veterinary practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the differences in ruminant animal anatomy and physiology, compared with other domesticated species, in order to identify specific and different nutritional and nursing care requirements of ruminants and other production animals.
Educate others regarding preventative health care programs for production animals, including zoonotic diseases and biosecurity
Perform and explain procedures on large animals, including animal handling and restraint techniques and large animal nursing care requirements.
Critically analyse the animal health and welfare aspects of large animal husbandry in production systems

title: ADVANCED VETERINARY MEDICAL PATIENT CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn how to plan and deliver gold standard veterinary nursing care to medical ward patients with a broad range of serious complex medical conditions. Students will deepen their understanding of the complex disease processes involved, and will apply this knowledge to plan appropriate personalised holistic veterinary nursing care. Students will also be expected to research current best practice in the veterinary literature, and to integrate this evidence into their plans. Supported via a work integrated learning (WIL) placement, students will critically evaluate nursing care delivered to complex medical cases, including methods of communication with clients, colleagues and the general public alike. Students will learn how to plan the delivery of multiple pharmacological agents and how to recognise potential side-effects with complex medication plans. Finally, this subject will enable students to learn how to best educate clients about the management of complex medical conditions, so that pet owners are able to properly manage the in home care of their pets.
learning_outcomes: Integrate an evidence based approach into veterinary nursing care strategies.
Plan and evaluate the nursing care of complex medical veterinary cases
Work in a team to create educational materials for clients that are ethical and culturally sensitive.
Plan and evaluate the administration of the pharmacological component of a veterinary patient's care
Evaluate the use of a range of diagnostic and therapeutic modalities in the management of veterinary medical patients

title: PHYSICAL THERAPY FOR VETERINARY NURSING PATIENTS
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will examine the anatomy and physiology of the body systems involved with conformation, locomotion and biomechanics in a range of animal species, and will consider how damage to, or altered structure and/or function, can result in changes to animal gait and ease of movement. Aided by a work integrated learning (WIL) placement, students will learn about the types, indications and methods of physical therapy available for animals, that trained veterinary nurses are capable of competently and safely undertaking, under the direction of a trained animal physical therapist. Students will also appreciate the importance of early intervention and referral of patients to trained animal physical therapists. Upon completion of this subject, students will be able to competently and safely perform a range of basic physical therapy techniques included within prescribed plans and scope of practice as well as provide ongoing support for the provision of family centred patient care and develop an understanding of the limitations of both themselves and the client.
learning_outcomes: Perform a range of physical therapy techniques in veterinary care
Examine the anatomy and physiology involved in locomotion and biomechanics in a range of animal species.
Support family centred patient care through the implementation of prescribed physical therapy care plans for a range of species, life stages and conditions
Analyse the physical therapy requirements of veterinary patients

title: VETERINARY SHELTER MEDICINE AND PATIENT CARE
syllabus_overview: In this subject, students will learn how to plan and manage the behavioural, husbandry and health care needs of animals living within an animal welfare shelter or other animal housing facility. . To achieve positive animal welfare outcomes and compliance with the Codes of Practice and legislation around the Management of animals in shelters, pounds and other facilities. Topics covered include: animal welfare and ethics, relevant legislation, animal behaviour and husbandry, quarantine and biosecurity and shelter medicine. Using an evidence-based approach, students will review the design and management practices of a shelter or other animal housing facility they have visited or undertaken placement at, in order to recommend changes and/or improvements. Students will also learn how to present an evidence-based argument regarding a contentious area in animal welfare and ethics. Through their shelter and facility visits and placements, students will be exposed to the emotional and physical challenges faced by staff that work within animal welfare shelters, and will come to learn how to maximise staff well-being within these environments. They will also learn to recognize zoonotic, infectious, notifiable and reportable diseases and how to respond appropriately to limit the spread of infection.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the health, husbandry and behavioural requirements of animals in a shelter or facility environment and those in general veterinary practice
Argue the complexities of the animal shelter world in order to maximise welfare and ethical outcomes for at-risk animals
Appraise relevant legislation to make recommendations about its appropriate application to animal shelters and other facilities that house animals outside the home environment
Critically evaluate shelters and other companion animal facilities’ design and management
Develop plans to maximize clinical staff wellbeing in an animal shelter environment

Recognize and implement an appropriate infection control strategy for a number of important infectious, zoonotic and notifiable diseases including understanding the reporting requirements and government response to exotic diseases.

title: INVESTIGATE VICTORIAN ABORIGINAL CULTURAL HERITAGE LANDSCAPES
syllabus_overview: Students will learn to apply basic principles of geology and geomorphology to archaeological site formation and to the identification of sites and assessment of threats in cultural landscapes.
learning_outcomes: Assess aspects of disturbance and degradation
Identify cultural sites, places and landscapes
Investigate basic principles of geology, geomorphology and site formation

title: WORK EFFECTIVELY IN THE VICTORIAN CULTURAL HERITAGE INDUSTRY
syllabus_overview: Students will learn the skills and knowledge required to work at an entry level position in the cultural heritage industry, including history, structure, legislation and protocols.
learning_outcomes: Obtain information about the industry and its historical context
Observe workplace requirements and make a productive contribution to a cultural heritage workplace

title: IDENTIFY AND DESCRIBE TANGIBLE ABORIGINAL CULTURAL HERITAGE
syllabus_overview: Students will learn to identify and record a range of Aboriginal cultural heritage place types and artefacts, including stone artefacts, shell middens and culturally modified trees.
learning_outcomes: Identify and record Aboriginal cultural heritage to industry standards
Analyse and interpret artefact assemblages

title: MANAGE THE DISCOVERY OF ABORIGINAL ANCESTRAL REMAINS
syllabus_overview: Students will learn to manage the discovery of human skeletal remains, particularly Aboriginal ancestral remains, in accordance with relevant legislative processes.
learning_outcomes: Access resources used to distinguish human and animal bones
Explore the prehistoric and historical context of Aboriginal burial practices in their environmental context
Follow reporting and recording procedures
Manage burial sites and repatriation of remains

title: CONTRIBUTE TO THE CONSERVATION OF ABORIGINAL PLACES
syllabus_overview: Students will gain the skills and knowledge required to contribute to conservation planning for a cultural heritage place or area by applying knowledge of cultural heritage significance assessment criteria, threats to cultural heritage significance and mitigation strategies
learning_outcomes: Confirm the cultural heritage significance of a cultural heritage place
Identify and mitigate threats to cultural heritage places
Document the results

title: ISSUES IN CONSERVATION
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the major issues in conservation biology. Topics covered may change yearly, dependent on current issues in conservation biology but will generally include biodiversity and its assessment, extinction, the interaction between biology and management, threatening processes, conservation on and off reserves, and the global context of conservation. Critical to the subject is a 5 day compulsory field camp at Wilsons Promontory National Park, where you will be exposed to the interaction between conservation and management and learn to "read landscapes" and observe natural history and introduced to ecological research techniques. During this camp you will conduct research addressing important conservation questions which you will analyse, present and write up during the semester.
learning_outcomes: Apply scientific method to biological questions through practical investigation and written report.
Define and explain biodiversity, threats to biodiversity, issues in the conservation and management of biodiversity.
Analyse and interpret the results of a group investigation and communicate the findings to peers and supervisor
Describe, record and reflect on field observations and conservation issues at local and global scales.

title: ANIMAL PHYSIOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject will examine the physiology and anatomy of vertebrates. This subject will cover muscle and nerve physiology, signallaing, selected sensory systems, sleep, digestive, reproductive, cardiovascular and respiratory systems. You will gain an understanding of the physiology and anatomy of these systems through a mixture of F2F and online practicals, group work and recorded lectures supported by Q&A sessions. You will learn how the various physiological systems work in an integrated way to allow animals to function and respond to environmental factors such as oxygen supply, food and energy, temperature and water supply.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate analytical and dissection skills.
Distinguish the structure and function of different vertebrate organ systems.
Distinguish, describe and explain the physiological mechanisms underlying vertebrate organ system function both individually and as part of a team.
Interpret physiological data in correctly formatted scientific reports.

title: AUSTRALIAN FAUNA AND ECOLOGY
syllabus_overview: This subject covers the evolution, biology and ecology of Australian terrestrial fauna. It will introduce different phyla, with a particular emphasis on Arthropoda and Chordata, how they differ in form and function, and in the use of keys for identifying them. The taxa considered include: insects, spiders, reptiles, amphibians, birds and mammals. The unit places a strong emphasis on examining evolutionary processes and how this has contributed to diversity. In so doing, students will be introduced to important biogeographical and ecological concepts and processes that are relevant to Australian fauna. Practical classes involve identification of major invertebrate and vertebrate groups and make use of reserves managed by the University or Parks Victoria. They will introduce students to field survey techniques used in terrestrial and aquatic habitats and the appropriate presentation of invertebrate collections.
learning_outcomes: Define and explain key concepts in Animal Ecology.
Apply fauna survey techniques to create reference collections of insects and other fauna.
Communicate the outcomes of fauna surveys in writing.
Classify Australian animals into taxa using physical characteristics and/or dichotomous keys.
Apply key morphological features to distinguish the major animal groups in Australia and related evolutionary processes.

title: HERON ISLAND MARINE PHYSIOLOGY FIELD COURSE
syllabus_overview: This subject covers an array of topics with a focus of the physiology of various marine organisms. Topics focus on osmotic and ionic regulation, influence of temperature and climate change on physiological processes, respiratory adaptations, and sensory capacities in various marine organisms. Other topics including deep sea vent communities, physiology of bivalve molluscs, whole-body transparency, buoyancy, diving and adaptations to deep oceans might also be discussed. The subject is run completely (lectures and practical classes) at the Heron Island Research Station, Great Barrier Reef. Note: enrolments for the 2026 delivery close on the 1st May 2026.
learning_outcomes: Use scientific terminology to describe and explain the fundamental biological concepts and current issues of the discipline area of Marine physiology.
Collect, summarise, analyse, evaluate and interpret scientific data collected via experiments, laboratory procedures, field surveys and literature review.

Produce clear, concise, grammatically correct written and spoken work that presents coherent evidence-based explanations and communicates the results of scientific experiments, current scientific/discipline issues, or theoretical concepts to peers
